Agronomi sa kojima smo razgovarali pominju Schöfield-ovu metodu i SMP pufer test, ali mi nemamo kapacitet da sami razvijemo model koji bi to primenio na konkretne serije zemljišta u Vojvodini. Naš tim su agrohemičari koji dobro razumeju analitiku, ali modelovanje puferske sposobnosti po tipovima tla zahteva agronomsku i pedološku dubinu koju trenutno nemamo. Imali bismo interes da izgradimo kalkulator koji uzima pH, teksturu i humus kao ulaz i vraća preporučenu dozu CaCO3 prilagođenu tipu tla. Raspolažemo podacima o parcelama za koje imamo i višegodišnja merenja, što bi moglo da posluži za validaciju modela. Rok koji nam odgovara je do sledeće prolećne sezone.

challenges.text: We manually generate around 3,200 AUTOSAR software component configuration files per project and it takes two engineers three weeks; one of our competitors apparently automated this and turned around the same job in four days — at current rates we are losing bids on price.
challenges.detail: Every new project hands us a System Extract from the customer and we then have to produce AUTOSAR SWC configuration files — port definitions, inter-runnable variables, timing constraints, the lot — by hand inside DaVinci Configurator. On the last two projects we counted roughly 3,200 files each time. Two senior engineers spend three weeks doing nothing else. We have tried building Excel-based templates to speed up the repetitive parts, and that helped a little, but the real problem is that the mapping logic between the System Extract and the final ARXML is still done by a person reading a document and typing. We heard from a contact at a Romanian company that they built something — probably a script or a generator layer on top of the tool API — that brings the same volume of work down to four days. We do not know the details. We have the DaVinci API documentation and we have two engineers who write Python, but nobody has had time to build the tooling properly. We are losing price-sensitive bids. A good outcome is a generation process that gets us from a clean System Extract to a reviewable first-draft configuration set in under one working day, with engineers only doing review and exception handling.

challenges.text: Our test coverage reports show 87% branch coverage but we keep finding integration bugs in the CAN communication stack after delivery; we suspect the problem is at the boundary between components from different suppliers but we have no systematic way to find those interaction faults before shipping.
challenges.detail: Our LDRA reports consistently show 87–89% branch coverage before we ship, which satisfies the contract threshold. But in the last four delivered projects, three of them came back with CAN communication faults found during customer integration testing. In each case the fault was at a boundary: one SWC from us, one SWC or COM configuration from a different supplier, both conforming to spec individually but producing unexpected behaviour when connected. We have tried adding integration test cases that exercise the COM layer explicitly, but we write those tests based on our own reading of the interface specification, so we tend to test what we already think is correct. We do not have a systematic way to generate tests that specifically target the assumptions each component makes about what the other will send. We have full access to the ARXML descriptions of all components in the project, the COM configuration, and the CANoe environment. What we need is a method — or tooling — that reads those descriptions and generates test scenarios aimed specifically at the interface contracts between components from different sources. Budget is not fixed but we would not start something that cost more than €40,000 in the first phase.

challenges.text: Three of our five engineers who do ECU flashing and diagnostic tooling learned on the job and have no formal training in UDS or OBD-II protocol internals; last year two of them left for a bigger company in Novi Sad within 18 months of joining and we had to restart their replacements from scratch — the training cost alone was over €25,000 each time.
challenges.detail: Five engineers handle ECU flashing and diagnostic work. Three of them learned by sitting next to a more experienced colleague and reading our internal cheat sheets. They can operate the tools but when something unusual comes up — a NRC they have not seen, a timing issue during a diagnostic session, a service routine behaving differently on a different ECU variant — they escalate to Andrej or to our one engineer who has formal protocol training, and that creates a bottleneck. The deeper problem is retention. In the last two years we lost two of those five engineers to a larger company in Novi Sad that offered higher salaries. Each time we had to hire a replacement and start from scratch. We calculated the internal training cost each time at just over €25,000, and that does not count the three to four months of reduced output while the new person gets up to speed. We have tried writing better internal documentation and we ran one informal workshop, but it was not systematic. We want something that a new hire can work through at their own pace and that tests their understanding before they touch a real vehicle. A structured, self-contained training path for UDS and OBD-II internals, ideally with practical exercises on simulated ECUs, would let us onboard faster and reduce how much senior engineer time gets burned on repeated explanations.

challenges.text: Our hub processes around 4,200 parcels a day and we sort them manually into route bins; mis-sorts run at roughly 3%, which means 120 wrong deliveries daily and a re-delivery cost we estimate at €18,000 a month. We need an automated vision system that reads label barcodes and diverts parcels to the right chute, but our conveyor belts move fast and labels sometimes wrap around curved surfaces.
challenges.detail: Every parcel that comes through our hub needs to end up in one of 34 route bins — one per van. Right now, four workers stand along the conveyor and manually read the barcode or sender label and physically throw the parcel into the correct bin. We move about 4,200 parcels on a peak day and we get it wrong roughly 3% of the time, which is around 120 mis-sorts. Each one means a driver has to backtrack or we send a second van, and when we add it all up we are spending about €18,000 a month fixing these mistakes, plus the client complaints. We looked at one commercial vision system from a German supplier but the quote was €280,000 installed and it required us to replace our entire conveyor line. We cannot do that. What we actually need is a camera-and-software layer that sits above our existing belt, reads the barcode even when the label is curved or partly folded, and triggers a diverter arm we can have a local metalworker fabricate. Our conveyor runs at about 0.4 metres per second. We have the physical space above the belt. Budget for a pilot is roughly €25,000–€35,000 including hardware.

challenges.text: We are expanding into same-day grocery delivery for three Novi Sad supermarket chains starting Q3, and our current route-planning software (off-the-shelf, bought in 2017) recalculates a full day's routes in about 22 minutes — that is fine at 6 a.m. but useless when 40 new orders drop at noon and drivers are already on the road. We need re-optimisation in under 90 seconds on our existing server.
challenges.detail: From Q3 this year we are taking on same-day grocery delivery for three supermarket chains — Merkur Namirnice, Frišmarket and Zeleni Košić — all based in Novi Sad. Grocery is completely different from parcels: orders arrive throughout the day in unpredictable batches and a driver already on the road needs to be re-routed in real time. Our current RouteMax Pro software was fine when we built one big route at 6 a.m. and sent everyone out. It takes 22 minutes to recalculate a full day's plan, which is acceptable at start-of-day but completely unworkable at noon when 40 new grocery orders land and six drivers are already moving. We need something that can take the current driver positions via GPS, the unassigned orders, and the remaining stops, and give back an updated assignment in under 90 seconds. We do not want a cloud subscription — our IT policy keeps operational data on our own servers. The existing server is a dual-socket machine with 256 GB RAM that is currently underused outside the 6 a.m. window. We are open to a purpose-built optimiser or a wrapper around an open-source solver, as long as it fits inside that hardware and meets the time constraint.

challenges.text: Driver turnover hit 38% last year — we trained 31 new drivers and lost 29 — mostly because younger people don't want fixed shifts and the pay band is capped by what our retail clients will tolerate. We've tried signing bonuses and a referral scheme, but nothing is sticking, and HR costs for constant onboarding are eating our margin.
challenges.detail: Last year we hired 31 new drivers and 29 left before the year was out. The people who quit are mostly under 32. When we do exit interviews the themes are consistent: fixed early-morning start times, no flexibility on days off, and a feeling that the pay ceiling will not move. We are squeezed on pay because our retail clients negotiate hard on per-parcel rates and we cannot pass cost increases upstream easily. We have tried a €200 signing bonus, a referral scheme that paid €150 per successful hire, and one experiment with a four-day working week for a small group — none of it produced measurable retention improvement after six months. The real cost is not just the bonuses; it is the 12–15 hours of onboarding and in-cab supervision every new driver needs before they run a solo route, and that time comes out of experienced drivers and dispatchers. We do not have an HR department — onboarding is managed by our two senior dispatchers, Nikola Prćić and Jelena Oros, on top of their regular work. We are open to structural ideas, scheduling tools, or anything evidence-based that other logistics operators have used.

challenges.text: About 11% of our parcels are returned by recipients and have to travel back through the hub; we have no reliable forecast of how many returns will arrive on a given day, so we either overstaff the returns desk or create a backlog that delays re-dispatch by 48 hours. We want a model that predicts daily return volumes at the SKU-sender level using our two years of transaction history.
challenges.detail: On any given day we might receive 200 returned parcels or we might receive 600, and right now we have no way to know in advance. That uncertainty forces us to guess how many people to put on the returns desk. If we understaff, parcels sit for up to 48 hours before they get scanned, logged, and either re-dispatched or returned to the sender, and that delay triggers penalty clauses with two of our larger clients. If we overstaff, we are paying people to stand around. We have two full calendar years of transaction data in our PostgreSQL database — every parcel, every delivery attempt, every return event, tagged with sender ID, product category code, recipient postal code, and the reason code the driver entered. We also know from sender manifests what SKUs are going out each day. What we want is a model that looks at what is going out today and the last few days and gives us a forecast for returns arriving in the next 24–72 hours, broken down by sender so we can also alert senders proactively. We have one person on the operations team, Bojan Latinović, who has basic Python skills and could run and maintain a model if someone helps him build it.

challenges.text: Writing ISO 26262 test cases by hand takes most of our verification budget.
challenges.detail: Every time we start a new body control module project, our verification team has to sit down and write test cases from scratch against the ISO 26262 requirements. This is almost entirely manual work. An engineer reads the requirement, interprets it, decides what boundary conditions to cover, writes the test case in our template, and then a second engineer reviews it. For a typical BCM project we produce somewhere between 800 and 1,400 test cases. At our current pace that work consumes roughly 60 percent of the total verification budget before we have run a single test. We have tried using requirement coverage matrices and reusing test cases from previous projects, but carry-over rate is rarely above 20 percent because customer requirement documents differ enough that direct reuse creates traceability gaps that auditors flag. We have a full set of historical requirement documents and test case archives from six completed projects, all structured in DOORS. We have the engineering time to support a trial, but we cannot afford a long integration project — anything we adopt has to fit into our existing DOORS and Jenkins workflow. A good outcome would be cutting manual test-case authoring time by half on a real project within one product cycle.

challenges.text: We need a cheaper hardware-in-the-loop bench for smaller projects.
challenges.detail: Our current hardware-in-the-loop setup is built around a full dSPACE SCALEXIO rack. It works well for large series-production programmes where the customer is paying for the full programme lifecycle, but the capital cost and the setup time mean we cannot justify using it for feasibility studies, small change requests, or prototype work that might run for only six to eight weeks. We have turned down two smaller projects in the past year because the HIL cost alone would have made them unprofitable. What we need is a leaner bench — something that can simulate the basic electrical environment of a body control module, inject CAN and LIN traffic, and log responses — that a single engineer can configure and run without a specialist. We have looked at using a PC-based approach with open-source CAN tools and a simple load box, but we have not been able to get the signal fidelity and fault-injection capability we need for anything we could stand behind commercially. Budget for hardware is in the range of ten to fifteen thousand euros per bench. A working prototype bench that passes a defined set of our standard BCM smoke tests would be a concrete proof of concept.

challenges.text: Reconciliation jobs that match transactions across Stripe, Adyen, Klarna and local acquirers take up to 90 minutes to run for clients with 50,000 daily orders — merchants need the numbers closed before their morning finance meeting.
challenges.detail: Naši rekoncijacioni poslovi trenutno rade kao Spark batch zadaci koji se pokreću svakih sat vremena. Za klijenta koji ima 50.000 porudžbina dnevno — a to nam je sada troje od desetoro aktivnih klijenata — ceo ciklus od prijema podataka do finalnog izveštaja traje između 70 i 90 minuta. Finansijski timovi tih klijenata imaju interni rok od 08:30 ujutru da zatvore prethodni dan. Mi to trenutno ne možemo da ispoštujemo. Pokušali smo da optimizujemo Spark konfiguraciju i particioning strategiju, ali dobitak je bio oko 12 minuta, što nije dovoljno. Svesni smo da negde između batch i streaming pristupa postoji rešenje, ali nemamo u timu nekoga ko je prošao kroz tu vrstu migracije na produkcijskom sistemu sa strogim zahtevima za konzistentnost podataka. Imamo Kafku postavljenu za prijem podataka od providera, ali je ne koristimo za samu rekoncijaciju. Cilj je da celokupan proces završimo za manje od 20 minuta bez gubitka tačnosti.

challenges.text: We want to add a cash-flow forecasting widget to the dashboard — merchants keep asking for it — but we only have 60 to 90 days of transaction history per client and seasonal patterns are hard to capture with that little data.
challenges.detail: Više od polovine naših klijenata nas pita kada će u dashboard-u moći da vide prognozu novčanih tokova — makar za narednih sedam do četrnaest dana. Problem je što imamo između 60 i 90 dana istorije transakcija po klijentu, jer su većina njih prešli na FinPuls tek nedavno. Sa toliko malo podataka, standardni sezonski modeli ne funkcionišu dobro — Q4 špic, praznici, regionalne kampanje, sve to ostaje van vidokruga modela. Probali smo jednostavne linearne projekcije i pokretne proseke, ali klijenti odmah vide da prognoze nisu pouzdane i prestanu da ih koriste. Razmišljamo o pristupu koji bi kombinovao naše kratke serije sa nekim oblikom eksternog ili sintetičkog signala, ali nismo sigurni koji pravac je izvodljiv u kratkom roku. Nemamo data science kapacitet interno — naš backend tim može da implementira rešenje, ali ne može da ga osmisli od nule. Prihvatljiv ishod bi bio widget koji klijentu daje relativno pouzdan signal za narednih sedam dana uz jasno prikazanu marginu greške.

challenges.text: We are trying to close our seed round — we've spoken to seven regional VCs and two said our data-processing terms in the standard merchant contract create GDPR liability that could block a German institutional lead investor.
challenges.detail: Nalazimo se u procesu zatvaranja seed runde. Razgovarali smo sa sedam regionalnih investitora, od kojih su dva nezavisno ukazala da naš standardni ugovor sa merchantima — konkretno odredbe o obradi i zadržavanju transakccionih podataka — može da stvori GDPR problem za nemačkog institucionalnog ko-investitora sa kojim jedan od VC fondova već razgovara. Problem je što naš ugovor nije pisao ekspert za GDPR u fintech kontekstu, već generalni pravnik, i verovatno nismo dovoljno precizno definisali pravnu osnovu za obradu, rokove brisanja i odnos controller-processor između nas i klijenata. Razgovarali smo sa jednim pravnim konsultantom koji radi opštu GDPR usklađenost, ali on nije imao specifično iskustvo sa payment podacima i PSD2 okruženjem. Rok nam je de facto kraj sledećeg kvartala — ako ne rešimo ovo pre nego što potencijalni lead investor pošalje zahtev za due diligence, izgubićemo momentum. Tražimo nekoga ko razume presek GDPR-a, payment regulative i ugovornih struktura u B2B SaaS kontekstu.

challenges.text: When we import parcel boundaries from the state cadaster they frequently have 2–4 metre positional errors, which means our variable-rate application layers do not line up with the physical field edges and clients get under- or over-application strips along headlands; we lose about half a day per farm correcting this manually.
challenges.detail: When we pull parcel boundaries from the state cadaster through their web service, the coordinates we receive are often shifted by two to four metres relative to where the field edges actually sit on a satellite image or on the ground. That gap might sound small, but when we build a variable-rate application layer for, say, nitrogen or herbicide, the prescription zones stop matching the real headland. The tractor's section control opens or closes two to four metres late, and the farmer ends up with a strip of over-application or a strip of missed crop along every field boundary. We have measured this on dozens of parcels in Bač and Kula municipalities and the problem is consistent. Right now our surveyors manually shift and snap each imported boundary against our own RTK reference points, which takes roughly four hours per farm on a first setup. We have about 320 active farm accounts and we bring on thirty to fifty new ones each season, so the backlog is real. We have tried writing a simple affine-correction script in Python but the error is not uniform across the region, so a single offset does not fix everything. We need an automated or semi-automated method that uses our RTK ground-truth points to estimate and apply a local correction for each incoming parcel. A good result would be getting boundary error below half a metre without manual intervention on at least eighty percent of incoming parcels.

challenges.text: Our farm management software is used on cheap Android tablets in tractor cabs and it crashes on older firmware versions (Android 8 and 9) which still account for about 40% of our installed base; we have tried three times to fix it but each patch introduces new problems on a different device.
challenges.detail: NjivaManager runs on Android tablets that farmers buy themselves, mostly budget Lenovo and Samsung models purchased two or three years ago. About forty percent of our installed base is still running Android 8 or Android 9 because the tablet manufacturers stopped pushing firmware updates. Our app uses a local SQLite database, a background sync service, and a map tile renderer, and the combination behaves differently across older API levels in ways that are hard to reproduce in our office. We have issued three patches over the past eighteen months trying to stabilise things. Each time we fix a crash on one device model, we break something on another. We keep a spreadsheet of reported crashes linked to device model and Android version, and we have about 140 entries going back to 2022. We do not have a proper automated test environment; our two Android developers test on six physical devices we own in-house. The crashes affect real work: a farmer in the middle of spraying loses his task list and has to call our support line. We need either a systematic way to reproduce and isolate these version-specific bugs, or a strategy for refactoring the parts of the app that are causing the most failures. Budget for this is modest — we cannot rewrite the whole application from scratch, but we can dedicate one developer full-time for up to six months alongside outside help.

challenges.text: We want to add a water-balance module so farmers can plan irrigation scheduling, but none of our staff understands evapotranspiration modelling or how to couple it with our existing soil-type maps; we need someone to build and validate that calculation engine.
challenges.detail: We have been asked by several larger farm clients to add irrigation scheduling advice to NjivaManager. The basic idea is straightforward: tell the farmer how much water the crop has used since the last rain, how much is left in the soil, and when to irrigate next. But when we sat down to build this we realised quickly that calculating evapotranspiration properly requires knowledge we do not have in-house. We know our soil-type map layers well — we have spatial soil data for most of western Vojvodina built from a mix of Yugoslav-era survey data and our own sampling — and we receive daily weather station data from three agrometeorological stations we maintain near Sombor, Kula, and Odžaci. What we are missing is the calculation engine that converts those inputs into a daily water-balance estimate for a given crop and growth stage. We have read that the FAO Penman-Monteith method is a standard starting point, but none of our staff can implement it correctly, and we do not know how to handle the soil water-holding capacity layer or crop coefficients in a way that connects to our existing parcel database. We want someone to build and validate that engine using real measured data from at least one irrigation season, then hand it to our developers in a form they can maintain. Deadline is before the 2026 irrigation season.

challenges.text: Scratches on polished metal parts: reflections fool our model, and clients only have a few dozen defect photos.
challenges.detail: One of our biggest clients, a pressed-metal parts supplier, wants us to catch surface scratches on polished aluminium brackets. The problem is that polished metal throws reflections everywhere — a scratch looks different depending on the angle of the light, the speed of the conveyor, and even the humidity in the room. Our current model keeps confusing a real scratch with a highlight from the overhead lighting rig. We have tried changing the lighting setup, adding a polarising filter, and retraining with heavier augmentation, but false positives are still too high for the client to trust the system on a live line. The real bottleneck is data: the client has collected about forty confirmed defect images over several months of production. We have tried synthetic augmentation — flipping, brightness shifts, cutout — but the model still does not generalise well to scratch angles it has not seen. We have a budget for a short project, roughly three months, and access to the production line for controlled image capture on two Saturday mornings. A good outcome is a detection rate above ninety percent with a false-positive rate below five percent, measured on a held-out set the client's quality team labels themselves.

challenges.text: Clients want inference on cheaper edge devices than Jetson.
challenges.detail: The Jetson Orin works well, but it costs around three hundred euros per unit, and several smaller clients — plastic injection shops with four or five lines — have told us directly that the hardware cost is the reason they did not sign. They are asking whether we can run on a Raspberry Pi 5 or a low-cost Rockchip board they already have on site. Our current C++ inference runtime is built around CUDA, so it does not run on ARM CPUs without a rewrite, and quantising our models down to INT8 has so far cost us about eight percentage points of accuracy, which is too much to accept. We need to either find a way to hit acceptable accuracy on CPU-only hardware or find a deployment path for boards that have a small NPU but no CUDA support. We have six ML engineers but none of them has deep experience with NPU toolchains like RKNN or Hailo. A good outcome is a deployment option that keeps accuracy within three points of our Jetson baseline and runs at ten frames per second on a device that costs under eighty euros.

challenges.text: We are tendering for EU-funded smart-grid projects in Hungary and Romania but our technical documentation is not meeting the IEC 61968 data-model requirements that the contracting authorities demand; we've lost two tenders in the last 18 months on documentation grounds alone.
challenges.detail: We have been going after EU-co-financed smart-grid tenders in Hungary and Romania for about two years now. The projects are a good fit for what we do, and our pricing has been competitive, but two tenders have been rejected at the technical-documentation stage. The issue the contracting authorities keep citing is that our network data models do not conform to IEC 61968, which is the standard they require for asset and work-management data exchange. Our engineers understand the standard in general terms but we have never had to produce a fully compliant Common Information Model export before. We tried using a consultant for the second tender, but the output still had gaps that the evaluators flagged. We have complete single-line diagrams and asset inventories for every network segment we maintain; the data exists, it just is not structured the way the standard demands. The next tender we are planning to submit closes in the fourth quarter of 2025. A good outcome would be documentation that passes the technical-compliance check without us having to outsource the whole process permanently.

challenges.text: Our switchgear enclosures are rated IP54 but field returns show condensation forming inside in about 8% of outdoor cabinets after two winters; we can't reproduce the failure reliably in our test room and we don't know whether it's a sealing design issue or a material issue.
challenges.detail: Around eight percent of the outdoor distribution cabinets we have installed over the past four years are coming back to us after two winters with condensation on the internal busbar insulation and occasionally on the breaker housings. The cabinets are rated IP54 and built to IEC 61439 part two. We have replaced door gaskets, checked cable-entry glands, and resealed roof joints on the returned units, but the condensation appears again. The problem is that we cannot reproduce it in our test room, which runs humidity cycles but does not replicate the actual thermal cycling that happens when a cabinet sits outdoors in a field in January and then warms up during the day. We are not sure whether the root cause is the door-seal profile, the steel grade we switched to in 2020, the powder-coat process, or something about internal heat dissipation. We have about thirty returned cabinets available for examination and full production records for each batch. Solving this matters to us commercially because two municipal clients have raised the issue formally and it affects our warranty costs.

challenges.text: We have 14 years of maintenance logs from 600+ distribution cabinets, but it's all text in Serbian in a legacy database and nobody has ever extracted anything useful from it; we suspect the data could tell us which cabinet types are most likely to need a repair in the next 12 months.
challenges.detail: Since 2010 our field technicians have been entering maintenance notes into the same database after every visit to our distribution cabinets. We have records covering more than six hundred cabinet locations, with visit dates, fault descriptions, parts replaced, and technician comments, all written in Serbian in free-text fields. Nobody has ever done a systematic analysis of this data. We believe it could show us which cabinet models, installation environments, or age brackets are associated with higher repair rates, and ideally it could let us flag cabinets that are likely to need attention in the next twelve months so we can schedule proactive visits instead of reacting to failures. The obstacle is that the text is unstructured, mixed-dialect Serbian, full of abbreviations our technicians invented themselves, and sitting in a database format that is not easy to connect to modern tools. We have one IT person internally and he manages the network and the SAP system; he does not have time for a project like this. We can provide full data access under a confidentiality agreement. A usable output would be a ranked list of at-risk cabinets updated at least quarterly.

challenges.text: Three of our last five PCB designs failed radiated emissions at a third-party EMC lab on the first submission, typically between 150–450 MHz, which costs us on average €9,000 per re-test visit and delays client projects by six to ten weeks; we need a systematic way to predict and fix emission hotspots during layout review rather than after the fact.
challenges.detail: Three of our last five designs failed radiated emissions on first submission at an accredited lab in Budapest, all showing problems somewhere between 150 and 450 MHz. Each failed visit costs us roughly €9,000 in lab fees and travel, plus six to ten weeks of project delay that we have to explain to the client. We run pre-compliance scans in our own lab before every submission, but we are clearly missing something systematic during layout review. We have tried adding stitching vias around clock traces and tightening the power delivery network on the top two layers, and that helped on one design but not the others. We have HyperLynx licences but our layout engineers mainly use them for impedance checks rather than full emissions prediction. We have the Gerber files, BOM, and pre-compliance scan data for all five boards and would be willing to share them under NDA. Ideally we want a layout checklist or a simulation workflow that our engineers can run themselves before sign-off, not a consultancy that reviews each board for us one at a time.

challenges.text: One of our automotive clients requires that we deliver a functional safety analysis (FMEDA) for a new brake-system sensor interface board to ISO 26262 ASIL-B; our engineers have attended one training course but have never produced a full FMEDA document and the client's deadline is in five months.
challenges.detail: One of our automotive clients, a Slovenian tier-one supplier, has asked us to deliver a formal FMEDA for a brake-system sensor interface board to ISO 26262 ASIL-B. The board handles wheel-speed and brake-pressure signals and feeds a main ECU. Two of our hardware engineers attended a two-day ISO 26262 training course in Zagreb last year and understand the concepts at a high level, but none of us has ever produced a full FMEDA document that includes failure rate data, diagnostic coverage estimates, and the final PMHF calculation. We have the component datasheets and some IEC 62380 failure rate tables, but we are not confident we are applying the right methods for the specific components on this board. The client's project gate review is in five months. We cannot afford to slip that deadline because the contract has a penalty clause. A good outcome would be a completed, client-accepted FMEDA document and, more importantly, our engineers being able to do the next one themselves without outside help.

challenges.text: We are trying to break into the German medical-device market with a contract manufacturing offer, but a Munich distributor told us we need to be listed as a compliant contract manufacturer under MDR Annex IX before they will sign; we have no idea what that audit process looks like or how long it takes.
challenges.detail: We want to offer contract manufacturing services to medical-device companies in Germany. A Munich-based distributor that works with several CE-marked device makers told us directly that they will not put us on their approved supplier list until we can show compliance as a contract manufacturer under MDR Annex IX. We currently hold ISO 13485:2016 certification, which we thought would be enough, but apparently it is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. We do not have anyone internally with direct experience of an MDR Annex IX audit. We do not know whether our existing ISO 13485 documentation covers the technical file and quality system requirements the notified body will check, what gaps are most commonly found in manufacturers at our stage, or how long the whole process typically takes. We have a budget set aside for compliance work this year but we need to understand the scope before we can plan the spend. We are not looking for someone to run the audit for us — we want to understand the process well enough to manage it ourselves.

challenges.text: We want to automate the optical inspection of our assembled boards — we currently have two operators checking solder joints by eye for 6 hours a day — but our component mix changes every two weeks and training a new vision model for every board variant is not practical with our current approach.
challenges.detail: We have two operators spending about six hours a day each doing manual visual inspection of solder joints across our assembly line. As board volume grows and component sizes shrink, manual inspection is becoming a bottleneck and a consistency problem — we had two field returns last quarter that our inspectors should have caught. We looked at off-the-shelf AOI systems and the hardware is affordable, but every vendor we spoke to told us the vision model needs retraining whenever the board mix changes, and our mix changes roughly every two weeks. Manually labelling images and retraining from scratch each time is not practical with our team size. We have a small dataset of images from our current camera setup — roughly 4,000 labelled images of solder joints across eight board types — but no machine learning expertise in-house. We would like an approach where the model can adapt to a new board type with far fewer labelled examples than a full training run requires, ideally something our quality technicians can manage without a data scientist on call every time.

challenges.text: Our optical sorting line was bought secondhand in 2019 and misclassifies dark-coloured HDPE and PP at a rate of about 18%, meaning those bales sell for 40% less to commodity traders because purity is too low; we've tweaked the conveyor speed but it hasn't helped.
challenges.detail: Our optical sorter came from a Dutch facility that had closed; we got it at roughly a third of new price and it handled standard translucent packaging well enough for the first two years. The problem is dark-coloured HDPE containers — motor oil bottles, garden plant pots, black food trays — and dark PP. The machine's NIR camera struggles to read the polymer signal through carbon-black pigment, so those items get routed to reject and end up mixed with general waste. We measured the misclassification rate ourselves by hand-sorting a 200-kilogram sample from the reject stream: 18% of what gets thrown out is actually recoverable HDPE or PP. The commodity traders we sell bales to in Novi Sad and Pécs have dropped their purchase price by 40% on mixed bales because purity sits around 82–84% instead of the 95% they want. We slowed the conveyor from 2.2 m/s to 1.8 m/s and it did not move the needle. We do not have budget for a full new sorter — the expansion bond comes first — but if a software tweak, a secondary sensor, or a sorting-logic change could close even half that gap before end of 2025 it would meaningfully improve our margin.

challenges.text: We're trying to issue a small bond to refinance our sorting hall expansion — 2.5 million EUR — but the two investment funds we approached said our financial reporting isn't structured the way they need it and we don't have a proper credit rating.
challenges.detail: The sorting hall extension we need — a second sorting line, covered unloading bays, and fire suppression — is costed at 2.5 million EUR by the contractor Gradnja Sever d.o.o. from Subotica. We want to issue a corporate bond rather than take a bank term loan because the repayment profile fits our cash flow better. We approached two regional investment funds, Vojvodina Kapital Fond and a private fund based in Novi Sad whose name we are keeping confidential for now. Both said the same thing: our accounts are prepared for tax purposes, not for investor-grade analysis, we have no EBITDA bridge, no debt-service coverage ratio history, and no external credit rating. Our own accountant, Gordana Lukač, does solid work for the tax office but she has not prepared an investor information memorandum before. We have five years of management accounts we can share. We need someone who understands both the numbers side and what waste-sector assets actually look like on a balance sheet. The target is to have documents ready for re-submission to funds by the first quarter of 2026.

challenges.text: The leachate from our temporary storage yard has started seeping toward the site boundary; our last sampling showed COD at 3,400 mg/L and we're worried about the groundwater monitoring wells the inspectorate has ordered us to install.
challenges.detail: The temporary storage yard on the eastern edge of our site has been used for oversized items and pre-sorted residuals for about twelve years. The liner under that area was never designed for liquid retention. This past winter we noticed discolouration along the eastern fence line and we took leachate samples ourselves using our in-house bench: COD came back at 3,400 mg/L, which is well above the threshold that triggers a formal response. The Subotica Environmental Inspectorate conducted a site visit in February and issued an order requiring us to install four groundwater monitoring wells within 120 days and to submit a remediation proposal. We have a hydrogeological sketch from when the site was first permitted in 1993 but nothing more recent. We do not know how far the contamination has moved or which direction groundwater flows under the site at different seasons. We need someone who can interpret the existing data, design the monitoring well network, and help us draft a leachate containment and treatment proposal that the inspectorate will accept — all before the 120-day deadline runs out in late June 2024.

challenges.text: Our platform recommends shift schedules for shift-based clients, but when we run the optimiser on a plant with 340 workers and 28 skill categories it takes 6 hours to produce a two-week plan — clients want a result in under 20 minutes and we don't know how to cut the solve time.
challenges.detail: Naša platforma uključuje optimizator rasporeda smena koji klijentima iz prerađivačke industrije treba da predloži dvonedeljni plan rada. Problem se pojavio čim smo onboardovali Metalik Promet, pogon sa 340 radnika i 28 različitih kategorija veština i sertifikata. Optimizator trenutno radi na jednom serveru i za taj slučaj troši u proseku šest sati. Klijenti iz serijskog pogona ne mogu da čekaju — žele rezultat u manje od 20 minuta, jer planeri smena rade u jutarnjim satima i ne mogu da blokiraju ceo radni dan. Pokušali smo da smanjimo prostor pretrage heurističkim predfilterom, ali dobitak je bio svega 40 minuta. Imamo pristup cloud infrastrukturi i mogući budžet za veću računarsku snagu, ali nismo sigurni da li je pravo rešenje u paralelizaciji, boljem matematičkom modelu ili kombinaciji. Resurse i podatke možemo podeliti s partnerima koji rade pod NDA. Dobar ishod bi bio stabilan algoritam koji daje prihvatljive rasporede u zadatom vremenskom ograničenju, i koji se može integrisati u naš postojeći Python servis.

challenges.text: Our employee wellbeing survey module produces scores that line managers say feel arbitrary; one HR director showed us that two teams with identical scores had completely different absence rates, so the construct we're measuring probably isn't what we think it is.
challenges.detail: Naš modul za dobrobit zaposlenih generiše kompozitni skor na osnovu odgovora iz periodičnih anketa — pitanja pokrivaju radna opterećenja, odnose s kolegama, jasnoću zadataka i slično. Problem je što taj skor ne predviđa stvarne poslovne ishode. HR direktorka u jednoj slovenačkoj kompaniji, Petra Koren iz Primus Logistike, pokazala nam je konkretan primer: dva tima su imala gotovo isti kompozitni skor, ali je jedan tim imao duplo više kratkih odsustva u naredna tri meseca. To znači da meri nešto, ali verovatno ne ono što smatramo dobrobiti relevantnom za radno mesto. Do sada smo pokušavali da revidiramo formulaciju pitanja i promenimo težinske koeficijente, ali bez sistematskog pristupa. Imamo anonimizovane podatke iz anketnih ciklusa i evidencije odsustva za oko 1.800 zaposlenih kod šest klijenta. Hteli bismo da razumemo šta zapravo merimo i kako da redizajniramo instrument ili skor tako da bolje korelira s konkretnim pokazateljima kao što su odsustvovanje i fluktuacija.

challenges.text: We collect keyboard and application-usage metadata as a productivity proxy, but two clients in Slovakia have been contacted by their works councils saying this data collection may breach the Slovak Labour Code and GDPR Article 88 — we need a legal opinion fast or we could lose both contracts.
challenges.detail: Jedan od naših differentiating faktora bila je mogućnost prikupljanja metapodataka o aktivnosti na računaru — koje aplikacije se koriste, u kojim intervalima, bez čitanja sadržaja — kao indikatora angažovanosti. To smo ponudili kao opcioni modul dvama klijentima u Slovačkoj: Hron Distribúcia a.s. i Záruka Finančná. U oba slučaja su ih kontaktovala radnička veća uz pozivanje na odredbe Zákonníka práce i na GDPR član 88. Nismo mi pravnici i ne znamo tačno gde je granica između dopuštenog prikupljanja metapodataka i nedopuštenog nadzora. Pokušali smo da prilagodimo politiku privatnosti i da smanjimo granularnost podataka, ali bez pravnog oslonca to radimo nagađanjem. Ako ne razrešimo ovu situaciju brzo — idealno u roku od mesec-dva — postoji realni rizik da oba klijenta raskinu ugovor, što znači gubitak ugovora vrednih oko 80.000 evra godišnje. Trebamo konkretno pravno mišljenje s praktičnim preporukama, ne samo teorijsku analizu, i ako je moguće predložene izmene u arhitekturi prikupljanja podataka koje bi bile u skladu sa propisima.

challenges.text: When we present our platform to CFOs the conversation always stalls at ROI; we can show engagement scores going up but we have no rigorous way to translate that into a euro figure that a finance director will trust — we lose about one in three deals at this stage.
challenges.detail: Kada predstavljamo platformu finansijskim direktorima, razgovor najčešće stane na pitanju povrata investicije. Možemo da pokažemo da su skorovi angažovanosti porasli, da su ankete popunjene, pa čak i da se nešto promenilo u rasporedima — ali CFO želi da vidi evrski iznos. Jedan od tipičnih komentara: 'Kako znam da tih deset posto veći angažman znači i deset posto manje odsustvovanja, i koliko meni to vredi?' Pokušavali smo da koristimo benchmark podatke iz inostranstva i da ih prilagodimo, ali to je CFO-ima delovalo nepouzdano i previše uopšteno. Imamo podatke o angažovanosti, prisustvu, fluktuaciji i produktivnosti kod klijenata s kojima radimo duže od godinu dana. Budžet za ovaj problem nije definisan, ali je gubitak jednog od tri potencijalna klijenta u završnoj fazi prodaje konkretan i merljiv. Dobar ishod bi bio metodološki osnovan model koji prevodi naše metrike u finansijske pokazatelje — uz pretpostavke koje su transparentne i koje finansijski direktori mogu da provere i ospore, što ih zapravo čini ubedljivijim.

challenges.text: We run eight injection-moulding presses around the clock and we are seeing a 7–9% rejection rate on our PP food-tray line because of warpage that shows up after the parts cool on the conveyor — the reject pile costs us roughly 140,000 dinars a week in material alone, and our process engineers are still tuning cooling-time and hold-pressure by trial and error.
challenges.detail: On our main PP food-tray line we are running a 7 to 9 percent rejection rate caused by warpage that only appears after parts leave the mould and cool down on the conveyor belt. At current volumes that translates to roughly 140,000 dinars a week in wasted raw material, not counting machine time or labour. We have tried adjusting cooling time in ten-second steps and varying hold pressure between 600 and 850 bar, but the results are inconsistent — some weeks improve, the next week is worse again. We log all press parameters through our Fenix DataLog system, so we have six months of time-stamped process data we can share. We also have the part geometry in CAD and the mould cooling-circuit drawings. What we do not have is a way to simulate how different parameter settings will affect final part geometry before we run a full production batch. A good outcome for us would be a clear set of target process parameters — or a simple model we can use ourselves — that brings rejection below 3 percent on this line. We do not have budget for a full mould replacement, so solutions have to work with our existing tooling.

challenges.text: A German retail chain that takes 30% of our crate volume says they will require us to have an ISO 14001 environmental management certificate by January 2026 or they will delist us — we have never done an environmental audit and we do not know where to start with our waste plastics, regrind reuse documentation, or cooling-water discharge reporting.
challenges.detail: One of our largest crate customers, a German retail chain we supply through their regional logistics hub in Pécs, has told us in writing that they will require ISO 14001 certification by January 2026 or they will remove us from their approved supplier list. That customer represents about 30 percent of our crate volume, which is a meaningful share of revenue. We have never done a formal environmental audit and we are starting from zero. The areas we know will be scrutinised are our waste plastic and regrind handling — we do reintroduce regrind into some lines but we do not have a documented procedure that would satisfy an auditor — and our cooling-water discharge, which goes to the municipal industrial drain under a permit we have not reviewed in several years. We also generate solvent waste from the pad-printing station. We need someone to walk through our plant, identify what documentation and monitoring systems we are missing, and give us a realistic gap analysis and action plan. Our target is to have everything in place for a certification audit no later than October 2025, which gives the certifier time to issue the certificate before the January deadline.

challenges.text: We print batch codes and nutrition panels directly onto our trays with pad printing and the ink adhesion fails the cross-hatch tape test about once a week, forcing us to rework or bin a full production lot of 8,000 units — we suspect it is a surface-energy issue with our mould-release agent but we have no way to measure or control it reliably.
challenges.detail: About once a week our pad-printing station produces a full lot — typically 8,000 trays — where the ink fails the cross-hatch tape test. When that happens we either rework the lot, which is slow and not always possible, or we scrap it. The ink adhesion problem started appearing more frequently after we switched to a new mould-release agent supplier about fourteen months ago. Our suspicion is that residue from the release agent is lowering the surface energy of the tray and stopping the ink from bonding properly, but we have no instrument to measure surface energy on our line and we have not been able to confirm this theory. We have tried wiping sample parts with isopropanol before printing and the adhesion improved in informal tests, but we cannot run a full IPA wipe step on every tray in a production run without slowing throughput significantly. We have also tried adjusting the ink viscosity within the range the ink supplier recommends, without consistent improvement. A practical outcome would be either a reliable way to measure and monitor surface energy at the press so we can catch the problem before printing, or a confirmed explanation of the root cause with a process change we can implement permanently.

challenges.text: We applied for an IPARD III grant nine months ago to co-finance a new thermoforming line and we still have not received a decision; meanwhile we signed a supply contract with a Hungarian buyer that requires us to double our tray capacity by Q3 next year and we cannot start the investment without knowing whether the grant will come through.
challenges.detail: We submitted an IPARD III application nine months ago to co-finance a new thermoforming line that would roughly double our tray output capacity. The application is still under review and we have received no decision. In the meantime we signed a supply agreement with a Hungarian packaging distributor, Balaton Pack Kft., that requires us to deliver doubled tray volumes starting in Q3 next year. If the grant is approved it covers 40 percent of the equipment cost and makes the investment financially straightforward. If it is not approved we have to decide quickly whether to finance the full amount ourselves, which is possible but strains our credit position, or to renegotiate the Balaton Pack contract and risk losing the relationship. We are looking for practical advice on how to approach this situation — whether there are ways to get an interim indication of the grant decision, what our legal and commercial options are regarding the supply contract if we need more time, and whether there are alternative financing instruments we have not considered. We are not looking for legal representation, just a factual understanding of the options in front of us.

challenges.text: We introduced hemp-fibre insulation cores into our wall panels two years ago, but some batches absorb moisture during storage and the thermal resistance drops by up to 30 percent before the panels ever reach a construction site; we cannot predict which batches will fail.
challenges.detail: Two years ago we switched from mineral wool cores to hemp-fibre batts because the carbon numbers looked better and customers were asking about it. For about sixty percent of batches it works fine — the panels leave the factory with thermal resistance values that match our datasheet. But the other forty percent absorb enough moisture during outdoor covered storage, sometimes just two or three weeks, that when we test them before dispatch the lambda value has shifted badly — thermal resistance down twenty to thirty percent. We have tried wrapping finished panels in polyethylene film and it helps a little but does not solve it. We do not have a way to predict before storage which batches will be the problem ones. We have temperature and humidity logs from the storage yard and we keep records of which hemp supplier and which delivery lot each batch used, but we have not been able to connect those numbers to which panels fail. We need a reliable way to either predict the problem before it happens or identify what in the incoming hemp material causes it, so we can either reject bad input or change how we store and seal panels. Losing thirty percent thermal resistance before a panel reaches a site is a real liability problem for us.

challenges.text: Our recycled concrete aggregate comes from three demolition contractors and the quality varies a lot — chloride content and residual cement paste fraction change from batch to batch — and this causes compressive strength variability in our panels of plus or minus 20 percent, which is forcing us to over-design and use more virgin cement than we want to.
challenges.detail: We take recycled concrete aggregate from three demolition contractors in the region — Rušenje Partizan d.o.o., Gradnja-Reciklaža Jovanović and a third smaller operator near Zrenjanin. The material quality changes from delivery to delivery. The main variables we measure are chloride content and the fraction of residual cement paste still attached to the aggregate surface. When the paste fraction is high, water absorption goes up and the mix behaves differently in the mould. When chlorides are elevated, we worry about long-term reinforcement corrosion. The combined effect is that our panel compressive strength results scatter across plus or minus twenty percent of our target value even when we use the same nominal mix design. To stay safe we compensate by increasing cement content, which costs more money and hurts the environmental numbers we want to be improving. We have roughly eighteen months of delivery records with our own test data attached — chloride titration results and aggregate grading curves — but we have not built any systematic model that would let us adjust the mix design in advance based on incoming aggregate properties. A good outcome would be a straightforward decision rule our production supervisor can apply when a new delivery arrives.

challenges.text: We want to claim an Environmental Product Declaration for our panels to open the German market, but preparing a full life-cycle assessment in-house is beyond our team; we have production data but no idea how to structure the inventory or which impact categories the German clients will scrutinise.
challenges.detail: Several German residential developers have contacted us in the past year asking whether our panels carry an Environmental Product Declaration. Without one we cannot get onto their approved product lists. We know an EPD requires a life-cycle assessment built to EN 15804, and we know we need a programme operator to verify and register it. We have good production data — electricity meters on each line, cement and aggregate purchase records, transport distances, water use — but we have never structured data into a proper LCA inventory and we do not know which software or databases are standard in this context. Our sales manager attended a one-day seminar in Belgrade last year and came back with more questions than answers. The German clients have mentioned they pay close attention to the global warming potential figure and to the module A1-A3 scope, but we do not fully understand what that means in practice for our product. We have budgeted around eight thousand euros for external support on this, and we would like to have a declared EPD within twelve months. We can provide full access to our production records and our internal test laboratory.

challenges.text: We tendered for a large social-housing project in Novi Sad and lost on price to a competitor importing standard panels from Poland; our production cost per square metre is about 12 percent higher and we have not been able to identify where the inefficiency is coming from in our manufacturing line.
challenges.detail: Last autumn we lost a tender for a four-hundred-unit social-housing development in Novi Sad — Gradski Stanovi projekt, run by a city-linked developer — to a company that imports standard flat panels from a Polish manufacturer. Our submitted price was roughly twelve percent above theirs per square metre of installed wall area. We believe part of the difference is genuine — Polish wage costs are lower — but twelve percent feels too large to be explained entirely by labour arbitrage. We have never done a systematic breakdown of our manufacturing cost per square metre. We track total monthly costs and total panel output, but we do not have line-by-line data on where time and material go: how long each line is actually running versus idle, how much waste aggregate we discard, how many panels are rejected and recast. Our production manager, Slobodan Mirković, has been here since the privatisation and knows the floor well, but he runs on experience rather than measurement. We would like someone to look at our line and tell us honestly where the inefficiency is sitting — whether it is materials waste, energy, cycle time, rework, or something in how we schedule shifts. We can open the factory floor fully to an outside team.

challenges.text: Our voltage-regulation device works well in steady state but when it encounters high-frequency switching transients from nearby industrial variable-speed drives, it trips on overcurrent about once a week per installation — we have oscilloscope captures but no model that predicts when this will happen.
challenges.detail: Naš VR-400 uređaj radi pouzdano u normalnim uslovima, ali kada je u blizini industrijska instalacija s frekventnim regulatorima brzine motora, dolazi do kratkih naponskih prekoračenja koja aktiviraju zaštitu od prestruje. To se dešava otprilike jednom nedeljno po lokaciji, uvek u toku rada teških mašina. Imamo osciloskopske snimke dvadesetak takvih događaja — vidimo šiljke amplitude do 1,4 pu u trajanju od nekoliko mikrosekundi, ali nismo uspeli da odredimo koji parametri tačno dovode do isključivanja. Pokušali smo da ručno podesimo pragove zaštite, što je smanjilo broj isključivanja, ali povećalo rizik od oštećenja opreme. Nemamo fizički model koji bi unapred rekao kada je situacija kritična. Trebalo bi nam nešto između čistog elektromagnetnog modeliranja i analize vremenskih serija iz naših snimaka — neko ko može da poveže te dve stvari i da nam da kriterijum koji možemo ugraditi u firmware. Rok je realan: sledeća serija VR-400 uređaja ide u proizvodnju za šest meseci.

challenges.text: We want to offer a real-time volt-VAR optimisation service across a feeder with 200+ nodes, but our current solver takes 4–6 minutes on a standard server, which is too slow to respond to the 5-minute SCADA update cycle the operators use.
challenges.detail: Nudimo operatorima uslugu optimizacije napona i reaktivne snage duž celog feedera. Problem je što naš trenutni solver, koji radi na standardnom serveru s 16 jezgara, treba četiri do šest minuta da izračuna optimalne setpoint vrednosti za mrežu s više od 200 čvorova. Operatori dobijaju podatke od SCADA sistema svakih pet minuta, što znači da naš rezultat kasni za situacijom na terenu. Probali smo da smanjimo granularnost modela, ali to pogoršava tačnost dovoljno da operatori primete razliku i izgube poverenje u preporuke. Koristimo sopstveni solver baziran na relaksiranoj semidefinitnoj formulaciji. Nismo sigurni da li je usko grlo u samom algoritmu, u načinu na koji učitavamo topologiju mreže, ili u nečem drugom. Nije nam potrebna savršena teorijska rešenost — potrebno je da ciklus bude kraći od tri minuta na istom hardveru, sa tačnošću koja nije lošija od sadašnje.

challenges.text: We are expanding into North Macedonia and need to register our product as certified grid-protection equipment under their national technical regulations, but our legal team has no experience with Macedonian energy law and the process has been stuck for seven months.
challenges.detail: Ulazimo na tržište Severne Makedonije i potrebno nam je da VR-400 bude sertifikovan kao oprema za zaštitu elektroenergetske mreže prema tamošnjim tehničkim propisima. Naši pravnici su iskusni u srpskom i bosanskohercegovačkom zakonodavstvu, ali makedonski regulatorni okvir ima specifičnosti koje nismo predvideli — drugačiji format tehničke dokumentacije, drugačije referentne standarde i zahtev za lokalnom laboratorijskom proverom koji nismo uspeli da razjasnimo. Proces traje već sedam meseci bez konkretnog napretka. Imamo kompletnu tehničku dokumentaciju uređaja na srpskom i engleskom, izveštaje o ispitivanjima iz akreditovane laboratorije u Beogradu i potencijalnog kupca u Severnoj Makedoniji koji čeka da sertifikacija bude završena pre nego što potpiše ugovor. Tražimo nekoga ko razume tamošnji energetski propis ili ko ima kontakte s telima koja mogu da razjasne proceduru — ne advokate opšte prakse, već ljude koji su već prošli kroz sličan proces.

challenges.text: Our field devices send telemetry over 4G but in agricultural areas signal drops cause gaps of 10–40 minutes in the measurement stream; the missing data corrupts our state-estimation results and operators lose confidence in the dashboard.
challenges.detail: Naši tereni uređaji u ruralnim i poljoprivrednim oblastima šalju telemetriju putem 4G mreže, ali signal je nestabilan i povremeno dolazi do prekida koji traju između deset i četrdeset minuta. Tokom tih pauza uređaji čuvaju podatke lokalno, ali kada se veza uspostavi, backend ih prima u nepravilnim naletima, a ne kao uredan vremenski niz. Naš modul za procenu stanja mreže pretpostavlja kontinuirane merne serije i kada naiđe na praznine, ili daje pogrešne procene ili odbija da radi dok operator ručno ne potvrdi status. Imamo bazu podataka s godinu dana takvih prekida i znamo tačno koje lokacije su najproblematičnije. Pokušali smo jednostavno linearno popunjavanje praznina, ali to nije dovoljno — kada se radi o promenljivim teretima kao što su sistemi za navodnjavanje, greška postaje prevelika. Trebaće nam metod koji uzima u obzir kontekst opterećenja i vreme dana, a može da radi u realnom vremenu čim stignu zakasneli paketi.

challenges.text: Our programmatic display network serves 12 million impressions a month but our brand-safety filter blocks roughly 22 % of premium inventory because it over-classifies Serbian news articles as sensitive content; that misclassification is costing us around 9 000 EUR a month in refused bids.
challenges.detail: Our in-house brand-safety filter was built three years ago around a keyword blocklist that was originally written for English-language content and then translated manually. It checks article titles and the first paragraph before deciding whether to allow a bid. The problem is that Serbian news language is dense with words that the filter reads as sensitive — terms like 'napad', 'kriza' or 'protest' appear in perfectly normal local reporting but get flagged the same way a genuine harmful article would. Right now about 22 percent of the inventory we offer to premium buyers gets blocked at the bid-evaluation stage, which translates to roughly 9 000 EUR of refused revenue each month. We have tried expanding the whitelist by hand, but our ad-ops team of three people cannot keep pace with editorial output. We have the full article text available in our ad server at decision time, and we log every blocked impression with its URL and the keywords that triggered the block. A good outcome would be a classifier that understands Serbian-language context well enough to cut that false-positive rate to below five percent without letting genuinely harmful content through.

challenges.text: Our 48 out-of-home LED panels currently show the same playlist regardless of weather, traffic or time of day; we want dynamic content triggers but have no data pipeline connecting traffic counts or weather feeds to our CMS.
challenges.detail: Our 48 LED panels are managed through a Scala-based CMS that schedules playlists in fixed daily blocks — morning, afternoon, evening. The panels themselves are network-connected and can receive new playlist instructions within about two minutes of a push command. What we do not have is any live data feeding into that CMS. We have spoken to the municipal traffic authority in Zrenjanin about accessing their loop-detector counts but the data is available only as a daily CSV export, not a live feed. For weather we have been using a manual check by the scheduling coordinator each morning. Advertisers are increasingly asking for daypart and context-triggered buys — a hot-drinks brand wants to activate only when temperature drops below eight degrees, a petrol station wants higher frequency during morning rush. We would need a lightweight data pipeline that pulls weather and traffic signals in near-real time, applies simple trigger rules we can configure ourselves, and pushes updated playlists to the CMS. We have one developer who could maintain such a system once it is built, but we do not have the in-house capacity to design and build it from scratch.

challenges.text: We commissioned an audience-perception study two years ago, but we have no ongoing way to measure how editorial tone and topic mix on our news portal affects trust scores among different age cohorts; we're flying blind when making programming decisions.
challenges.detail: Two years ago we paid an external research agency to run a telephone survey of 600 Banat residents measuring how much they trusted Banat.rs and what topics they associated with us. The results were useful at the time but they are already dated and we have no way to refresh them without commissioning another expensive study. What we want is a method of continuously estimating audience trust and topic perception from signals we already collect — page dwell time, return visit rate, comment sentiment, share counts across our social pages, and reader letters to the editorial team. We produce roughly 40 articles a day across politics, local economy, culture, sport and emergency services. We suspect that heavy coverage of crime and municipal disputes lowers trust scores among readers over 55 while younger readers respond differently, but we have no data to confirm or challenge that. A usable outcome would be a lightweight dashboard updated weekly that shows how editorial mix and tone correlate with proxy trust indicators, broken down by at least two age cohorts. We have GA4 data going back 18 months and can export comment and social data manually for now.

challenges.text: The TV channel's archive of 35 years of local broadcasts sits on about 14 000 DV and BetaSP tapes in a climate-controlled room; digitising and indexing them is urgent but we have no budget line approved for it and the project estimate came in at 280 000 EUR.
challenges.detail: Since 1987 our camera crews have recorded every significant event in Zrenjanin and the surrounding municipalities. That footage lives on approximately 14 000 DV and BetaSP tapes stored in a dedicated climate-controlled room at our Zrenjanin facility. A specialist firm inspected the tapes last year and estimated that around 18 percent show early signs of binder degradation, meaning the window for safe playback is narrowing. The same firm quoted us 280 000 EUR for full digitisation, quality checking and basic metadata tagging, which is more than our annual capital budget. We do not have approval for that spend and it is unlikely to come in a single budget cycle. We are therefore looking for a way to prioritise which tapes to digitise first, and for a realistic digitisation workflow we could partly run in-house using equipment we purchase or lease incrementally. Beyond preservation, the archive has commercial value — historical footage licences, documentary production, municipal anniversary programming — but none of that can be exploited until the content is searchable. An indexed digital archive with even minimal descriptive metadata would let our archive coordinator, Gordana Nešić, respond to licensing enquiries that currently have to be refused.

challenges.text: We need to detect unusual behaviour on Modbus and BACnet networks without labelled attack data.
challenges.detail: Our EdgeWatch sensor captures all traffic on a customer's Modbus and BACnet segments and sends parsed records to our backend. The problem is that we have almost no labelled examples of actual attacks on these networks. Real incidents are rare, customers do not want us running attack simulations on live plant, and public datasets for OT protocols are thin and often do not match what we see in the field. We have tried writing rules by hand for the most obvious cases — unexpected function codes, register writes outside normal ranges, new devices appearing on the network. That catches some things but misses slow, low-volume probing entirely. We have also looked at statistical baselining but the baselines drift with shift patterns and seasonal production changes, which generates noise our analysts cannot keep up with. What we need is a way to build detection models from unlabelled traffic that can flag genuinely unusual sequences without needing us to say in advance what an attack looks like. We have about eighteen months of raw packet logs from three customer sites, averaging around four gigabytes per day per site. We can share anonymised versions. Our constraint is that any model has to run inference on the edge sensor, which has 512 MB of RAM and a modest ARM core. We need something we can deploy within twelve months.

challenges.text: Clients ask whether our firmware signing will survive quantum computers.
challenges.detail: Our EdgeWatch firmware uses a signing chain built on Ed25519 so that sensors only run code we have authorised. Several customers have started asking pointed questions about whether this will still hold up in ten to fifteen years when practical quantum computers might exist. We are not dismissive of the concern: these are building management systems and factory controllers with expected service lives of fifteen to twenty years, and firmware update mechanisms are exactly the kind of thing that needs to remain trustworthy for the whole lifecycle. We have read the NIST post-quantum standardisation output and we understand that CRYSTALS-Dilithium is the likely replacement direction, but we have not implemented it. Our firmware is written in Rust and the signing and verification code is about two thousand lines. The constraints are real: the sensors have limited flash storage, verification has to complete in under two seconds on boot, and we cannot break compatibility with sensors already deployed in the field without a migration plan. We would like to understand the actual risk timeline more precisely, get a clear migration path mapped out, and have a tested implementation ready before we begin EU Cyber Resilience Act certification talks. Budget for this work is modest — roughly the equivalent of a short-term engineering contract.

challenges.text: Our sensor nodes transmit over LoRa and we are seeing packet loss rates of up to 40% on parcels where the farm has metal-framed poly-tunnels — the signal reflection and multipath interference is killing reliability and clients are calling us every other week.
challenges.detail: We deploy nodes in polytunnels where the frames are galvanised steel tubing every two metres. The LoRa signal bounces off all that metal and by the time packets reach the gateway, we are losing up to four in ten. We have tried moving gateways closer, changing spreading factors, and pointing antennas at different angles, but we do not have a systematic way to measure what is actually happening at each node location before we finalise the installation. We have packet-loss logs from about a dozen affected farms going back eighteen months — that data is sitting on our server. We do not have a radio engineer on staff. We tried buying a better antenna from a catalogue supplier in Budapest but it helped on one farm and made things worse on another. Clients phone us when their dashboard goes blank and we end up driving forty kilometres for something that might be a configuration fix. A good outcome would be a practical installation guideline — antenna placement rules, spreading-factor settings — that our technicians can follow without needing a radio lab.

challenges.text: We produce about 400 nodes per year by hand-soldering and we have no quality control step after assembly — roughly 6% of units come back under warranty within the first three months, which is eating our margin and our reputation.
challenges.detail: We solder every board by hand, two people working on a batch at a time. When volume picked up three years ago we added a second reflow oven for the SMD parts but the through-hole components and final assembly are still manual. We track warranty returns in a spreadsheet and we can see that about 24 units out of every 400 come back in the first three months — usually a cold solder joint, a loose connector, or a sensor that reads out of range from day one. We do a quick visual check before boxing but we have no functional test jig. The returns cost us parts, labour, and a technician visit each time, and growers talk to each other so the reputation damage is real. We have the schematics and firmware for all our current node variants. Budget for a proper fix is limited — we are not going to buy an automated test line — but we could invest in a test jig or a simple protocol if someone helped us design it. We want to get that return rate below two percent.

challenges.text: We want to expand into Hungary and Romania but we have no CE documentation for our sensor enclosures and we have no idea what the process or the cost looks like — it has been sitting on the to-do list for two years.
challenges.detail: We have two growers in southern Hungary and one just across the border in Romania who have asked us to supply and install nodes. We quoted them, they liked the price, but then the question of CE marking came up and we had to say we were not sure. Our enclosures are custom — we machine the lids ourselves and buy the polycarbonate shells from a supplier in Novi Sad — so we cannot just reuse someone else's declaration. We have looked at the RED directive online and it is not obvious which test reports we need or whether our LoRa firmware counts as a radio device that needs a notified body or whether we can self-declare. We have no contacts at a testing lab. We have been sitting on this for two years because every time we start reading the documentation we get pulled back onto installation work. A clear map of the steps, a realistic cost figure, and a contact at a lab that handles this kind of low-power radio device would let us finally move forward. The Hungarian grower checks in with us every few months.

challenges.text: Our ajvar from this season's red peppers has a noticeably bitter aftertaste that we can't explain — the pepper variety is the same as last year, the roasting time is identical, but about 30% of customers who ordered last year are not reordering and three have mentioned the taste difference explicitly.
challenges.detail: This year's ajvar has a bitter aftertaste that was not there last season. We use the same Šorokšar red pepper variety from the same two suppliers, and we roast at the same temperature and time as always. The bitterness is not overpowering but it is noticeable, especially after the jar has been open for a few days. Out of roughly 280 customers who ordered ajvar last autumn, about 85 have not placed a repeat order this cycle, and three wrote to us directly mentioning the taste. We have tried extending the peeling step to remove more of the charred skin, and we tested one batch with a shorter roasting time, but neither fixed it. We do not have laboratory equipment to test for specific compounds. Our guess is something changed in the peppers themselves — maybe the soil, maybe the weather during growing season — but we do not know how to check that or what to do about it in the kitchen. We need to understand the cause before next season's harvest. Budget for outside help is modest, under 500 euros, but we are open to providing pepper and finished product samples to anyone who can analyse them.

challenges.text: We produce about 4 tonnes of jam per year and our sugar use is rising — we are adding 55% w/w sugar to hit a 65 Brix final product, but customers increasingly ask for reduced-sugar versions and we do not know how to reformulate without losing gelling and shelf stability.
challenges.detail: We cook roughly four tonnes of finished jam per year, split across plum, quince, apricot and sour cherry. To reliably reach 65 Brix — which is what keeps the product shelf-stable at room temperature without added preservatives — we currently add sugar at 55 percent by weight of the raw fruit going into the pan. Customers are asking more and more for lower-sugar versions, and a few shops in Novi Sad have told us they would stock a reduced-sugar line if we had one. The problem is that when we tested a batch at around 45 percent added sugar, the jam stayed runny and went mouldy in two jars within six weeks of opening. We know that pectin levels vary by fruit and by ripeness, and that quince behaves differently from plum, but we do not know how to calculate what we would need to add or change to get a stable gel at lower Brix. We would also need to know whether a lower-Brix product could still legally carry a standard best-before date without refrigeration, or whether we would need to change our labelling. We want a clear, practical reformulation guide we can test in our own kitchen with ingredients we can actually buy locally.

challenges.text: We want to sell on a major regional online marketplace but their onboarding requires a food safety management plan and HACCP documentation that we have never written and don't know where to start.
challenges.detail: We have been invited to list our products on Pijaca Direktno, a regional online marketplace for food producers, but their supplier agreement requires a written food safety management plan and a completed HACCP table covering our main product lines. We have never written either document. We do things correctly in practice — we check temperatures, we clean and sanitise, we track batches — but none of it is written down in a way an auditor or a platform reviewer would recognise. We looked at a government template from the Serbian veterinary and food safety authority website but it was written for much larger operations and we could not map it onto what we actually do. We do not want to hire a full-time quality manager. What we need is either a ready-to-adapt template for a small preserve producer, or someone who can spend a day with us going through our process and turning it into the documents the marketplace requires. The deadline is the end of the current quarter because we want to be listed before the summer fruit season begins.

challenges.text: We launched a size-inclusive line last season and returns are running at 34% — almost all customers say the fit was wrong — which is killing our margin because return shipping from Germany or the Netherlands costs us €6–8 per parcel and we're on a 2,000-piece run.
