challenges.detail: When we launched our size-inclusive range last autumn-winter season, we were genuinely pleased with the fabrics and the silhouettes. The response online was warm. Then the returns started coming in. Right now 34% of orders from that line have been sent back, and almost every return note says the same thing: the fit was off. That hurts in two ways. First, we lose the sale. Second, a return parcel from Germany or the Netherlands costs us €6 to €8 in shipping alone, before we even account for re-inspection and repackaging. On a 2,000-piece run, that adds up fast. We adjusted our size chart after the first wave of returns and sent the updated measurements to our photographer for new detail shots, but the return rate barely moved. We think the problem is in how we grade between sizes — our pattern maker has experience up to EU 44 but the extended sizes were extrapolated, not fitted on real bodies. We don't have fit models for larger sizes on our current budget, and flying samples back and forth to a specialist is slow. A good outcome for us would be a reliable way to predict fit issues before we go into production, or at minimum a tool that helps customers choose their size more accurately before they order.

challenges.text: Our Instagram and TikTok content drives traffic but we can't convert it — our webshop session-to-purchase rate is 1.2% and the EU average for fashion is around 3.5%; we've changed the layout twice and hired a photographer but nothing moved the needle.
challenges.detail: Our Instagram account has around 18,000 followers and our TikTok short-form content regularly gets between 20,000 and 80,000 views per clip. People comment, save, and share. Then they arrive on the webshop and most of them leave without buying anything. Our session-to-purchase rate sits at 1.2%. The EU fashion benchmark we've seen cited is around 3.5%, so we're well below where we should be. We've rebuilt the homepage layout twice in the last year, hired a Novi Sad-based photographer for better product imagery, and added a size guide page. None of it changed the number in any meaningful way. Our Klaviyo abandoned-cart flow recovers a small portion, but the abandonment is happening earlier — people aren't even reaching checkout. We look at GA4 data but we're not confident we're reading it correctly or asking the right questions. We don't know whether the problem is trust, pricing presentation, the size confusion discussed elsewhere, checkout friction, or something else. We have the traffic. We don't understand why it doesn't convert, and we don't have budget for a full agency engagement right now.

challenges.text: We want to market our fabrics as 'low environmental impact' but a German wholesale buyer is now asking for a full life-cycle assessment document before they'll list us — we have no idea how to produce one and can't afford a consultancy that quoted us €12,000 for the study.
challenges.detail: A wholesale buyer at a mid-size German retailer called Feldweg Concept Store asked us, before they'll add us to their catalogue, to supply a life-cycle assessment for our core fabric lines — something that quantifies carbon, water use, and chemical inputs from fibre through to finished garment. We understand why they're asking. Their own customers are pushing for it and there's increasing regulatory movement in that direction across the EU. Our fabrics come from two mills we trust and have visited, and we know they use low-impact dyes and don't use certain chemical finishes. But we have no formal documentation of any of this. We approached one environmental consultancy in Novi Sad and one in Belgrade; the Belgrade firm quoted us €12,000 for a full LCA study, which is not something we can absorb this year. We have basic data sheets from our mill partners — fibre origin, dye class, some water consumption figures — but nothing structured. Feldweg has given us an informal deadline of end of Q3 2024 to provide something credible, or they'll move to another supplier. A good outcome is a document or methodology we can stand behind and update as our supply chain changes, without paying consultancy rates we can't afford.

challenges.text: We need a seed investment round of €150,000 to fund the next two collections and a warehouse deposit, but three angel investors passed because we don't have audited financials and our bookkeeping is done in a spreadsheet by the founder's partner who has no accounting background.
challenges.detail: We need €150,000 to cover fabric and production costs for the next two collections and to pay a deposit on a small warehouse space we've identified near Rumenka, which would replace the shared storage arrangement we currently use and give us better control over dispatch times. We've had three conversations with angel investors — two from the Novi Sad startup scene and one introduced through NTP's network — and all three passed at the due-diligence stage. The feedback each time was the same: our financials aren't in order. Our bookkeeping has been handled since founding by the founder's partner, who is organised and careful but has no formal accounting background. Everything lives in Google Sheets. There are no audited statements, no proper profit-and-loss formatted to any standard an investor would recognise, and no clear separation between company and founder cash flows in earlier years. We know this is fixable, but we don't know the fastest path to fixing it in a way that would satisfy an investor rather than just tidy things up for our own use. We're not looking for someone to do the bookkeeping going forward — we can hire for that — we need to understand what the minimum credible financial package looks like and how to get there.

challenges.text: Raspberries for Germany arrive with mould on day 9; buyers want 14 days.
challenges.detail: We ship raspberries from Serbian packing houses to buyers in Germany and the Netherlands. The berries leave Serbia in good condition — our own quality checks confirm that — but by day nine of a typical fourteen-day shelf-life window, a meaningful share of punnets show visible Botrytis mould. Buyers have started issuing penalty deductions and two accounts have threatened to switch suppliers unless we fix this before next season, which means we have roughly eight months. The punnet itself is a standard 125 g rPET shell with a heat-sealed anti-fog lidding film. We have run informal trials with two different film grades and adjusted seal pressures, but mould rates did not drop enough to matter. We suspect the issue is a combination of micro-condensation inside the punnet and an oxygen-transmission rate that is not well matched to berry respiration at 2–4 °C. We have OTR and CO₂TR instruments in the lab and can measure headspace gas composition, but we do not have the modelling background to translate those numbers into a film specification. We also have real shipment data — temperature logs, humidity logs, and destination inspection reports — from the last two seasons. Budget for trials is limited; we can fund materials and lab time but cannot afford a large external testing programme. A good result is punnets reaching day fourteen with mould incidence below one percent, confirmed in controlled simulated-transit tests.

challenges.text: Big retailers will stop taking conventional plastic lidding film by 2028; we need a compostable one that still seals.
challenges.detail: Several large German and Dutch retail chains have told their own-label produce buyers that conventional plastic lidding films will not be accepted from 2028 onward. Two of our three biggest customers are own-label suppliers for those chains, so this is not a distant regulatory issue for us — it is a commercial deadline we have to meet. We need a lidding film that is certified compostable to EN 13432 or an equivalent accepted standard, but that still seals cleanly to our existing rPET punnet tooling at the temperatures and dwell times we run today, and still provides adequate anti-fog performance and a gas-transmission profile suitable for soft fruit. We have done preliminary bench tests with two commercially available PLA-based films. Both sealed, but seal strength was about thirty percent below our current spec and one film showed visible clouding at 4 °C refrigerated storage, which buyers will not accept. We do not have the materials chemistry background to reformulate or identify better candidate polymers, and we are cautious about switching tooling or adding adhesive layers that would compromise compostability certification. We have a budget allocated for a two-year development programme and can run seal, OTR, anti-fog and composting-screen tests in-house. The output we need is a film formulation or a shortlist of available materials that passes all four criteria, backed by enough data to submit for EN 13432 certification by mid-2027.

challenges.text: We size battery storage by rule of thumb — usually 1.2 times the average daily consumption — and about one in five customers ends up with a system that cycles the battery too hard in summer, which degrades it faster than we promised. We need a sizing method we can actually use during a 30-minute site visit.
challenges.detail: When we size a battery we take the customer's average daily electricity use, multiply by 1.2, and pick the nearest product size. That works fine most of the year. The problem comes in July and August on farms that run irrigation pumps or cold storage. The battery ends up doing three or four full cycles a day instead of one, and after eighteen months some of them are already down to seventy percent of their original capacity. We promised ten-year life and we are not going to hit that. We have tried asking customers to shift loads to midday when the panels are producing, but that is hard to enforce and some of them simply cannot change their routines. We have a spreadsheet where we log panel count, battery size, inverter model, and the monthly kWh readings we collect during annual check-ups. We have data from about sixty completed installations going back to 2021. What we need is a simple method — something one of us can run through on a tablet during a thirty-minute site visit — that tells us whether to go up a battery size or recommend a second unit. We do not have budget for custom software development but we could afford a few months of consultancy if the output is a practical tool or a clear decision process.

challenges.text: We can't get financing to stock more than 20 panels and 4 inverters at a time; the bank wants three years of audited accounts and we only have two. Every time a big order comes in we lose two weeks waiting for supplier delivery.
challenges.detail: Our main distributor, Elkotek from Novi Sad, gives us reasonable prices but requires payment within fifteen days. The bank will extend a stock-financing line only to companies with three years of audited accounts and we completed our second audit in March 2024. Until we qualify, we keep a buffer of twenty panels and four inverters in the garage. When a farm or a larger household comes to us needing a ten-kilowatt system with storage, we have to order specially and wait two to three weeks for delivery. In the last twelve months we lost two confirmed orders that way because the customers went with a company from Novi Sad that could start the following Monday. We have looked at factoring and one invoice-finance provider quoted us rates we could not make work. We are not looking for a grant; we are looking for advice on whether there is a financing structure or a procurement approach that a business our size can actually qualify for, or whether there is a cooperative buying arrangement with other small installers in the region that would let us hold more stock collectively.

challenges.text: Our matching algorithm ranks candidates well for software roles but performs poorly for skilled-trades positions like CNC operators or maintenance electricians; hiring managers in manufacturing say the top-10 lists are 'basically random' and we're losing three accounts a month over it.
challenges.detail: The matching engine was trained mostly on IT and office job data because that is what our early customers gave us. When manufacturers started using the platform for roles like CNC machine operators, press-brake setters, or maintenance electricians, the competency ontology we built did not have the right nodes. Skills like 'reads technical drawings' or 'operates Fanuc controller' just get lumped into a generic 'technical skill' bucket and the scoring collapses. We ran an internal audit last autumn and found that for software developer vacancies our top-10 hit rate against hiring-manager selection is around 71 percent; for skilled-trades roles it drops to 28 percent. We've tried manually adding trade-specific tags for a few clients, but it doesn't scale. We have annotated data from roughly 340 completed manufacturing hires we could use for retraining if someone helped us structure it properly. We need a better ontology for industrial trades and ideally a way to learn from the structured interview outcomes so the rankings improve over time. Losing three accounts a month means this needs a working prototype inside six months.

challenges.text: We want to add a short cognitive and personality screening battery to the platform, but we built the current version ourselves by copying items from free online tests; a prospective German client told us our assessment has no documented reliability or validity evidence and they won't use it.
challenges.detail: When we built the screening battery we pulled items from a mix of public-domain puzzle sets and a Creative Commons personality questionnaire. At the time we just needed something functional to demo. Now a prospect in Stuttgart, a mid-size automotive supplier, asked for a technical file showing internal consistency coefficients, test-retest data, and evidence that the scales predict job performance. We have none of that. We ran the battery on about 900 candidates over the past year and we have those response records plus eventual hire or no-hire outcomes for around 600 of them, but nobody on the team knows how to do the analysis or what standards apply. We're also not sure whether we need to rebuild from scratch or whether we can validate what we have. The Stuttgart client has given us a provisional timeline: if we can show them a basic technical report by the end of Q3 this year, the contract stays on the table. Budget for this work is limited, roughly three to five thousand euros for external support, but we can provide full anonymised dataset access.

challenges.text: We process CVs and interview recordings for candidates in Germany and Austria, which means GDPR applies, but we haven't done a Data Protection Impact Assessment and our privacy policy was written by a junior intern; if a client requests an audit we'd fail immediately.
challenges.detail: We store CV files, video interview recordings, and competency scores for candidates who applied to German and Austrian employers. That data sits on AWS servers in Frankfurt, which is good, but our internal processes have not caught up. We never completed a Data Protection Impact Assessment for the video recording feature, which is almost certainly high-risk processing under Article 35. Our privacy policy mentions 'we use your data to match you with jobs' and not much else. We have one part-time person who handles compliance alongside other admin work. A potential enterprise client in Vienna sent us a data processing questionnaire last month and we had to stall because we could not honestly answer the questions about retention periods and sub-processor agreements. We are not looking for someone to write policy documents for us; we need someone to walk through what we are actually doing, tell us where the gaps are, help us run the DPIA properly, and give us a checklist we can work through ourselves going forward. We have a budget of around two thousand euros for this and a hard deadline of before any Vienna contract is signed.

challenges.text: We need to hire a senior backend engineer with experience in vector databases to rebuild our matching engine, but we've been advertising the position for four months and every shortlisted candidate has dropped out when a Frankfurt or Vienna company matched their salary expectation.
challenges.detail: Our current matching engine uses pgvector inside PostgreSQL, which was fine at ten thousand candidate profiles. At 140 000 profiles query latency is becoming a problem and we want to move to a purpose-built vector database and redesign the indexing layer. The person we need has to understand approximate nearest-neighbour search, know at least one dedicated vector store, and be comfortable with our Python stack. We have advertised the role since December 2023 on local job boards, LinkedIn, and through two recruiting agencies. We have reached final-round interviews with four candidates. Two accepted remote offers from companies in Germany before we could make an offer. One accepted, then withdrew after a counter-offer from a Vienna-based firm. One is still in discussion but has signalled he expects a salary we cannot match. Our current budget ceiling for the role is around 3 200 euros net per month. We are open to a part-time arrangement, a fixed-term project contract, or a collaboration with a research group that would let someone apply this work toward a thesis or publication, as long as production code is part of the output.

challenges.text: Our insole pressure sensors drift by up to 8% over a six-month period in daily clinical use; we recalibrate them manually every three months at a service cost of about €180 per pair, and clients are starting to complain that the calibration windows are too infrequent between visits.
challenges.detail: Our insole sensors use capacitive pressure cells that slowly drift as the polymer layers age and compress under repeated clinical use. Over a six-month period we consistently see drift of up to 8% across a sensor pair, which is enough to throw off pressure distribution readings in a meaningful way for post-surgical patients. Right now our service team drives out to each clinic every three months to run a manual calibration routine against a reference plate — that costs us roughly €180 per insole pair per visit in labour and travel, and we have about 60 pairs deployed across 14 sites. Clients have started to flag that three months between calibrations is too long; a few have noticed readings that look suspicious mid-cycle. We have tried logging raw sensor baseline values over time to see if we can predict drift from the data, and we have a 14-month archive of baseline logs from eight deployed pairs. What we want is an on-device or server-side method that can detect drift earlier and either correct it automatically or flag it before it affects a report. Ideally we would reduce service visits to twice a year without reducing data quality. The total budget we can allocate to this is around €25 000 over 12 months.

challenges.text: We want to classify a patient's gait pattern into one of seven rehabilitation progress categories using data from 16 sensor channels at 100 Hz, but our current decision-tree model needs a 90-second walking trial to reach acceptable accuracy; clinicians want a result from a 20-second walk.
challenges.detail: The core clinical value of our StrideSense system is a classification of where a patient sits across seven rehabilitation progress categories — from early compensatory gait through to near-normal symmetrical walking. We get 16 channels of pressure data at 100 Hz from each insole pair, and our current decision-tree model was trained on trials of 90 seconds or longer. At that length it achieves around 84% classification accuracy on our internal validation set, which clinicians find useful. The problem is that many patients, especially those recovering from stroke or with significant fatigue, cannot walk continuously for 90 seconds in the early stages of rehabilitation. Clinicians want a reliable classification from a 20-second walk. When we simply apply our existing model to a 20-second window the accuracy drops to around 61%, which is not good enough to put in a clinical report. We have a labelled dataset of approximately 2 400 trials from real patients collected over five years, including 20-second segments with physiotherapist-assigned ground-truth category labels. We have tried feature engineering on shorter windows but have not had the machine-learning depth in-house to go further. A good outcome would be a model that reaches at least 80% accuracy on 20-second trials without requiring hardware changes.

challenges.text: Three rehabilitation hospitals in Slovenia are asking us to integrate with their Dedalus electronic health record system via HL7 FHIR, but none of our three developers has worked with FHIR before and the integration project has already slipped by four months while we look for a consultant who knows both the standard and Serbian healthcare data conventions.
challenges.detail: Three rehabilitation hospitals in Slovenia — all within our existing customer base — are moving their patient records onto the Dedalus system and have asked us to feed gait session data directly into their electronic health records using the HL7 FHIR R4 standard. This would remove a manual data-entry step that currently takes ward staff around 15 minutes per session and introduces transcription errors. The integration is technically straightforward in principle: we need to map our session output to the relevant FHIR Observation and DiagnosticReport resource types and stand up a FHIR-compliant REST endpoint in our RehabTrack backend. The difficulty is that none of our three developers has worked with FHIR before, and the Slovenian hospitals have specific requirements around patient identifier formats and consent flags that intersect with Serbian healthcare data conventions in ways we do not fully understand yet. We engaged one consultant who backed out after the scoping phase, and the project has now slipped four months beyond the deadline one hospital set for go-live. We have the Dedalus sandbox credentials, we have the FHIR R4 specification, and we have a clear internal API in RehabTrack that a developer could work against. A good outcome is a tested, production-ready FHIR integration delivered within five months.

challenges.text: Patients recovering from stroke show highly asymmetric gait that causes our bilateral symmetry index algorithm to output misleading progress scores — in about 30% of post-stroke cases the score actually improves on paper while the physiotherapist observes functional decline.
challenges.detail: Our SymmetryView module calculates a bilateral symmetry index by comparing step timing, pressure distribution and stance duration between left and right sides. For most orthopaedic patients this works well as a progress indicator. For post-stroke patients it frequently gives wrong signals. Stroke often produces a gait pattern where one side compensates heavily for the other, and a patient can increase their walking speed and reduce their fall risk — genuine functional improvements — while the raw symmetry index gets worse or produces an artificially good score because both sides are moving poorly in a matched way. In roughly 30% of the post-stroke cases we have reviewed with physiotherapists over the past two years, the system score moved in the opposite direction from the therapist's functional assessment. We have about 380 labelled post-stroke sessions where a treating physiotherapist recorded an independent functional rating alongside our system output. We know the bilateral symmetry index alone is not the right measure for this population, but we have not been able to build a replacement metric that the physiotherapists themselves trust and that we can explain clearly in a report. A good outcome would be an alternative algorithm or scoring approach that agrees with physiotherapist functional ratings in at least 85% of post-stroke cases and can be explained to a non-technical clinical audience.

challenges.text: Our bone-fracture detection model hits 91% sensitivity on our test set, but when we deploy it at partner hospitals with older Siemens and Philips scanners, sensitivity drops to around 78% — we lose about 13 percentage points just from scanner-to-scanner variation in DICOM metadata and image reconstruction kernels.
challenges.detail: ClearFrame Bone scores 91% sensitivity on our internal test set, which was built from scans collected on three mid-range Siemens and Philips machines at our main pilot site in Novi Sad. When we deploy at partner hospitals that run older scanner generations — mostly equipment installed before 2015 — sensitivity falls to around 78%. The gap comes from differences in how those scanners encode DICOM headers and apply reconstruction kernels during image processing. The resulting images look similar to the human eye but are statistically different enough to confuse our model. We have tried simple histogram normalisation and CLAHE preprocessing, and we collected roughly 1,200 additional scans from two partner sites to fine-tune on. The drop improved by about 3 points but we are still well below the 88% floor our MDR technical file commits to across deployment environments. We have a dataset of around 14,000 labelled studies in total. Our constraint is that we cannot store scans outside the hospital network, so all additional training has to happen on-site or through federated methods. We need a reliable way to close this gap before our next hospital contract renewal in Q3 2025.

challenges.text: We are trying to close a Series A round of €2.1 million with a German medtech fund, but they want a co-investor from the Western Balkans region and our local bank contacts have no experience structuring equity rounds of this size for software-as-a-medical-device companies.
challenges.detail: We are in advanced talks with Hartmann Medtech Fund, a German investor that focuses on software-as-a-medical-device companies. They have provisionally agreed to lead a €2.1 million Series A but their partnership rules require a co-investor with a presence in the Western Balkans to share deal structuring and local governance responsibilities. We have spoken to three regional banks and two small private equity contacts through the NTP network, but none of them have completed an equity round of this structure for a regulated software product before. The sticking points are the convertible note terms, the MDR-related IP valuation, and the shareholder agreement clauses around regulatory milestones. We have a term sheet draft from Hartmann, legal support from a Belgrade commercial law firm with some tech experience, and a financial model prepared by our CFO, Tatjana Lukić. The round needs to close by the end of Q1 2025 or Hartmann will reallocate the tranche. A good outcome is finding a co-investor or a financial intermediary who has already worked on at least one similar structured deal in the region.

challenges.text: Radiologists at our pilot site spend 40 minutes per shift correcting the bounding-box annotations the model generates, because our active-learning pipeline requeues the same ambiguous edge cases repeatedly instead of escalating them to a senior reviewer.
challenges.detail: Radiologists at our pilot hospital, the Radović General Clinic in Novi Sad, spend around 40 minutes per shift dealing with corrections to bounding-box annotations that ClearFrame generates. The main complaint from their lead radiologist, Dr. Jovan Petrović, is that the same difficult cases — low-contrast hairline fractures, overlapping anatomy at the shoulder and pelvis — keep reappearing in the annotation queue day after day. Our active-learning pipeline scores uncertainty per image and requeues anything below a confidence threshold, but it has no mechanism to distinguish between a case that needs more data and a case that is genuinely too ambiguous for a junior annotator to resolve. As a result, a small pool of about 200 edge cases circulates repeatedly without ever being escalated to a senior reviewer or flagged for exclusion. We have tried raising the confidence threshold, which reduced the queue size but also starved the model of useful training signal. We need a routing layer that can recognise when a case has been seen multiple times without resolution and redirect it automatically. The goal is cutting that 40-minute correction burden to under 15 minutes without reducing annotation throughput.

challenges.text: Our probe electrode corrodes within six to eight weeks in high-clay soils with low pH, which means we have to replace them mid-season at a cost of around €18 per probe; we need a coating or electrode material that survives a full 20-week growing season.
challenges.detail: Elektrode naših sondi izrađene su od nerđajućeg čelika sa tankim platinskim premazom. U zemljištima sa visokim sadržajem gline i pH ispod 5,5 — što je čest slučaj na parcelama u Sremu — elektrode počnu da korodiraju između šeste i osme nedelje. To znači da moramo slati tehničare na teren da zamene sonde usred sezone, što nas košta oko 18 evra po sondi samo za materijal, plus radna snaga i prevoz. Ove sezone imamo oko 600 aktivnih sondi, pa je problem finansijski ozbiljan. Pokušali smo da nanesemo dodatni sloj epoksi laka, ali to menja impedansni odgovor i kvari merenje. Razmatrali smo grafit kao zamenu za metal, ali nismo sigurni kako bi se ponašao u kiselim uslovima tokom dvadeset nedelja. Trebamo ili novi materijal za elektrode ili zaštitni premaz koji elektrohemijski ne ometa merenje, izdrži mehanički pritisak pri umetanju u zbijeno tlo i ne pređe cenovno 4 evra po setu elektroda. Rok za rešenje je pre sledeće sezone setve, dakle do februara 2026.

challenges.text: We are trying to interpret the electrical impedance spectra our probes generate and correlate them with actual root biomass, but our current regression model explains only 51% of the variance when we validate it against destructive sampling — we need a much better signal interpretation approach.
challenges.detail: Naša sonda vraća spektar impedanse na dvadesetak frekvencija svakih sat vremena. Iz tog spektra pokušavamo da izvedemo procenu biomase aktivnog korena u okolini sonde. Trenirali smo linearni regresijski model i nekoliko varijanti ansambla na podacima iz tri sezone, uz destruktivna uzorkovanja kao referencu — fizički smo vadili koren i merili suvu masu. Trenutni model objašnjava 51 odsto varijanse na validacionom skupu. To nije dovoljno za preporuke o đubrenju. Imamo bazu od oko 2.400 vremenskih nizova sa 38 parcela, ali distribucija je neravnomerna — više podataka sa lakših peskovitih zemljišta nego sa teških glina. Nismo sigurni da li je problem u odabiru karakteristika iz spektra, u arhitekturi modela ili u tome što destruktivno uzorkovanje samo po sebi unosi grešku jer ne uzorkujemo tačno tu istu zapreminu tla oko sonde. Dobar ishod bi bio model koji na unakrsnoj validaciji po parcelama dostigne R² iznad 0,80 i može da radi u realnom vremenu na terenskom prijemniku sa skromnim procesorskim resursima.

challenges.text: We want to understand whether root morphology differences between maize hybrids actually affect what our sensor reads, so we can calibrate hybrid-specifically, but we have no agronomic expertise in-house and cannot design a proper field trial ourselves.
challenges.detail: Primetili smo da isti model loše radi na nekim hibridima kukuruza u poređenju s drugima, čak i kada su uslovi tla slični. Pretpostavljamo da razlike u morfologiji korenovog sistema — ugao rasta, gustina lateralnih korenova, prečnik — menjaju odnos između izmerene impedanse i stvarne biomase. Nemamo zaposlenog koji bi mogao da osmisli i sprovede ogled kojim bismo to testirali na naučno prihvatljiv način. Prošle godine smo pokušali da sami postavimo ogled na parceli saradnika Dragana Vukovića u Irigu, ali nismo kontrolisali gustinu setve ni đubrenje, pa podaci nisu uporedivi. Trebamo nekoga ko zna kako se planira i izvodi poljski ogled, ko razume genetiku hibrida dovoljno da odabere reprezentativne genotipove i ko može da nam pomogne da povežemo morfološke parametre korena sa impedansnim potpisom. Rezultat koji očekujemo su kalibracioni koeficijenti specifični za bar pet do deset hibrida koji su najzastupljeniji kod naših korisnika u Vojvodini, sa dokumentovanim protokolom koji možemo da ponovimo.

challenges.text: Our probe produces a continuous data stream of about 500 KB per day per probe, and with 600 probes deployed this season we are already over our cloud budget by 40%; we need on-device filtering or compression that keeps agronomically relevant signals but drops noise before transmission.
challenges.detail: Svaka sonda šalje oko 500 kilobajta dnevno — to su sirovi impedansni spektri, temperatura, vlažnost i dijagnostički metapodaci. Sa 600 aktivnih sondi u sezoni 2024. prekoračili smo planiranu cloud liniju za 40 odsto. Taj trošak ne možemo jednostavno prebaciti na korisnike jer je cena usluge već ugovorena. Pokušali smo da smanjimo frekvenciju uzorkovanja, ali agronomi nam kažu da gubimo dnevne pikove koji su relevantni za stres od suše. Naši RhizoGateway uređaji rade na STM32 mikrokontroleru sa 256 kilobajta RAM-a i ne mogu pokrenuti teške algoritme kompresije. Trebamo pristup filtriranja ili kompresije koji se može implementirati direktno na mikrokontroleru — idealno u C-u ili MicroPythonu — koji čuva agronomski bitne signalne promene, a baca redundantne tačke iz perioda stabilnih uslova. Dobar ishod je smanjenje prenosa za najmanje 60 odsto bez gubitka upozorenja na stresne događaje. Rok je pre sezone 2025., dakle implementacija do aprila.

challenges.text: Our drone flight planning tool re-routes missions in the field, but the algorithm becomes very slow once a single farm exceeds 80 parcels — a pilot with 120 parcels told us last month it took 11 minutes to replan after a no-fly zone appeared, which is completely unusable.
challenges.detail: Our drone mission planner inside CropView lets a pilot draw a farm boundary, mark any temporary no-fly zones — power lines, neighbours' buildings, restricted airspace — and get an optimised multi-parcel flight route back in a few seconds. That works fine for farms with up to about 60 or 70 parcels. The problem starts when a single farm has more parcels than that. Last month one of our larger customers in Vojvodina, who farms 120 parcels across three villages, triggered a no-fly zone update mid-day and the replanning took 11 minutes on his tablet. He nearly aborted the whole flight session. We use a modified nearest-neighbour heuristic today, and we have tried adding a basic time limit with a fallback, but the fallback produces routes that waste 25–30 percent more battery, which is its own problem. We have GPS parcel geometries and elevation data for every farm in our system and the replanning runs on the user's device, not our servers, so the solution needs to stay lightweight enough for a mid-range Android tablet. We need replanning to complete in under 30 seconds for farms of up to 150 parcels.

challenges.text: We collect multispectral imagery at 5 cm resolution, but when we try to automatically delineate individual plant rows in maize and sunflower, our segmentation model produces 15–20% row-skip errors on fields with uneven emergence, and agronomists have to correct it by hand every time.
challenges.detail: When we fly a field with our multispectral drone we get imagery at around 5 cm per pixel. From that we want to automatically count and map individual plant rows — something our agronomists use to estimate stand density, spot gaps and detect early-season stress patterns in maize and sunflower. We trained a segmentation model on roughly 2,400 labelled field images taken in normal, even-emergence conditions, and it performs well when the crop is uniform. The issue is that in real seasons, especially after uneven rain or patchy soil crusting, emergence is irregular and row contrast drops. In those conditions our model skips 15 to 20 percent of rows, and our agronomists correct each image by hand, which takes between 20 and 40 minutes per field. We have collected about 600 images that include patchy emergence but they are not fully labelled yet — annotating them is the bottleneck. We have one engineer dedicated to the model and access to a single GPU workstation. The outcome we want is to get row-skip errors below 5 percent on uneven fields without needing manual correction as a routine step.

challenges.text: We want to expand into Hungary and Romania next year but our legal team says we need separate data-processing agreements and potentially different operator licences for drone flights in each country, and we simply don't have the in-house legal resource to handle that.
challenges.detail: We are planning to sell CropView into Hungary and Romania starting in the second half of next year, and we have already had inbound interest from two cooperatives in those countries. The technical side of the expansion is largely ready — localised weather data, adjusted crop calendars, translations. The blocker is regulatory. Our legal contact here in Serbia has confirmed that operating commercial drone flights in Hungary and Romania each requires separate operator registration, different insurance thresholds and potentially national airspace authority approval processes that can take several months. On top of that, GDPR-aligned data-processing agreements need to be adapted for each jurisdiction because the way we store and process farm location data differs slightly from what a standard Serbian DPA template covers. We do not have a legal team — we have one part-time legal advisor who handles Serbian matters. We need practical help understanding the specific steps and timelines for each country, and ideally template documentation we can adapt rather than starting from scratch. The expansion timeline is fixed because we have committed to a distributor in Cluj-Napoca.

challenges.text: We update our road geometry database by driving survey vehicles ourselves; one full national pass takes four months and costs us around €60,000, which means our maps can be a year out of date when clients use them — new roundabouts and road closures are missing and clients complain.
challenges.detail: Ceo proces ažuriranja mape počiva na tome da naša dva vozila prođu svakim relevantnim putem u Srbiji – to je oko 18.000 kilometara razvrstanih puteva. Jedan kompletan prolaz traje četiri meseca i košta nas oko 60.000 evra samo u gorivom, platama vozača i amortizaciji opreme. Do trenutka kada klijent dobije isporuku, podaci mogu biti i godinu dana stari. Konkretno, Veltron Navigation nam je 2023. vratio reklamaciju zbog tri kružna toka u Nišu i Kragujevcu koji u našoj bazi nisu bili označeni, a bili su pušteni u saobraćaj pre šest meseci. Pokušali smo da pratimo objave JP Puteva Srbije i lokalna saopštenja opština, ali te informacije kasne i nisu strukturirane. Nemamo budžet da udvostručimo broj vozila niti da angažujemo ekipu korisnika kao što rade veliki igrači. Dobro rešenje bi za nas značilo da nekim automatizovanim ili poluautomatizovanim načinom detektujemo promene na terenu pre nego što vozilo uopšte krene, tako da survej prolazi ciljamo tamo gde je stvarno nešto promenjeno – i time smanjimo broj kilometara i troškove.

challenges.text: Three clients want map data in OpenDRIVE format for simulator use, but all our data is in a proprietary binary format and the conversion tool we built in-house produces lane-boundary errors at about 2% of intersections, which is unacceptable for ADAS simulation.
challenges.detail: Tri naša klijenta – sva tri se bave ADAS simulatorima – traže mape u OpenDRIVE formatu. Mi sve čuvamo u KTF formatu, koji smo sami razvili i koji je optimizovan za navigacione uređaje, ne za simulatore. Prošle godine smo napisali alat koji konvertuje KTF u OpenDRIVE, ali kada ga pustimo na složenim raskrsnicama i kružnim tokovima, u oko 2% slučajeva dobijamo pogrešno definisane granice traka – linije se preklapaju ili nedostaje veza između traka. Za navigaciju bi to možda prošlo, ali klijenti koji testiraju ADAS algoritme kažu da takve greške u simulatoru direktno utiču na rezultate testova i da ne mogu da ih koriste. Naš jedini softverski inženjer, Nikola Vranić, utvrdio je da problem leži u načinu na koji mi u KTF-u kodiramo topologiju raskrsnica – neke veze između traka nisu eksplicitno zapisane i alat ih mora rekonstruisati, što ne uspeva uvek. Imamo skup od oko 340 problematičnih raskrsnica gde greška redovno iskrsava. Nemamo internu ekspertizu za formalne specifikacije OpenDRIVE standarda niti za geometrijsku rekonstrukciju topologije. Cilj je alat koji greške svodi na nulu ili ih bar detektuje i prijavljuje pre isporuke.

challenges.text: We have been trying to raise a €400,000 seed round for 18 months; every investor we talk to says the addressable market in the Western Balkans is too small and wants to see a path to selling into the EU, but we do not have the sales connections or the brand recognition to open those doors on our own.
challenges.detail: Od osnivanja smo profitabilni na nivou koji pokriva plate i operativne troškove, ali rast nam je spor jer nemamo kapital za proširenje pokrivenosti i razvoj novih formata. Pre osamnaest meseci odlučili smo da tražimo seed investiciju od 400.000 evra. Razgovarali smo sa pet investicionih fondova – dva iz Srbije, dva iz Austrije i jednim iz Holandije. Svaki put čujemo istu primedbu: tržište Zapadnog Balkana je premalo da bi opravdalo ulaganje te veličine i žele da vide konkretan plan za ulazak na tržište EU. Mi taj plan nemamo jer ne poznajemo kupce u EU, ne znamo ko tamo nabavlja mape za aftermarket segment i nemamo kontakte koji bi nam otvorili prva vrata. Pokušali smo da se javimo na dva evropska tendera za putne podatke, ali oba su zahtevala reference iz EU koje mi ne posedujemo. Budžet za poslovni razvoj nam je minimalan – ne možemo da platimo konsultante ni da stalno putujemo na sajmove. Dobar ishod bi bio konkretan kontakt sa bar jednim potencijalnim kupcem ili partnerom u EU koji bi nam pomogao da izgradimo tu referencu.

challenges.text: Our reading-comprehension exercises work fine in Serbian, but the Hungarian-language versions consistently get poor scores from teachers — we don't know whether the problem is vocabulary level, sentence complexity or the way we sequence tasks, and we have no systematic way to test that.
challenges.detail: Our Serbian reading exercises have been running in classrooms for two years and teachers are generally happy with them. When we released the Hungarian versions last autumn, the feedback was different: teachers in Kanjiža and Senta said the exercises felt too hard, pupils were giving up partway through, and the scores our dashboard recorded were noticeably lower than for equivalent Serbian content. We have session logs showing average completion rates of 58% for Hungarian exercises versus 81% for Serbian ones at the same grade level. The problem is we cannot tell what is causing the gap. Our curriculum specialists rewrote vocabulary lists once already, but the scores barely moved. We do not have a clear method for measuring sentence complexity across the two languages, and we are not sure whether the task sequencing — the order in which question types appear — matters as much as the words themselves. We have the raw session data, the exercise texts, and access to about a dozen teachers willing to give structured feedback. What we want is a way to diagnose where the exercises are failing so we can fix the right thing, not just guess.

challenges.text: Schools want to use our app on the cheap Android tablets they already own, but our 3D interactive scenes lag badly on anything below a Snapdragon 665 — we need to rework the rendering pipeline but nobody on our four-person dev team has done GPU optimisation before.
challenges.detail: Most schools in our target area cannot afford new hardware. The tablets we see most often are low-cost Android devices with processors like the Unisoc T310 or MediaTek MT8167, which are well below the performance level our 3D scenes were designed for. On a Snapdragon 665 the scenes run at a comfortable 30 frames per second; on the cheaper tablets we see frame rates drop to 8–12, which makes the animations look broken and distracts children. We use Unity for the 3D parts of the reading app, but none of our four developers has worked on GPU optimisation before. We have tried reducing polygon counts and lowering texture resolution, and that helped a little, but not enough. We do not know whether the bottleneck is the draw calls, the shader complexity, or something else entirely. We have two devices in the office that reproduce the problem reliably, and we can borrow more from partner schools for testing. We need to either fix the rendering pipeline or redesign those scenes so they run well on modest hardware without looking unfinished.

challenges.text: We applied for an Innovation Fund Serbia voucher in March; we still have no answer after five months and our bridge financing runs out in two months — the accountant says the application had a formal error we can't correct at this stage.
challenges.detail: We submitted an application for an Innovation Fund Serbia small-business voucher in March 2024. It is now August and we have had no decision. Our accountant recently received informal feedback suggesting there was a formal error in the financial attachments, but the fund rules do not allow corrections at this stage of review. The voucher would have covered roughly eight months of development costs. We used a short-term commercial loan as bridge financing while we waited, and that runs out in about two months. We are not in immediate danger, but we will have to pause one development project and possibly not renew two freelance contracts unless we find replacement funding or a paying contract to cover the gap. We are looking at other options: an EU ERASMUS+ project call, direct school licensing deals that we can invoice before year end, and a possible co-development arrangement with another small publisher. We would welcome guidance on which funding paths are realistic in the time we have and how to avoid the same administrative problem on a future application.

challenges.text: We are migrating a Belgian insurance client from COBOL mainframe to a microservices stack, but automated test coverage sits at only 34% and manual regression takes three weeks per release cycle — the client wants monthly releases by Q1 next year.
challenges.detail: We are in the second year of moving a Belgian insurance client off a COBOL mainframe onto a microservices architecture built in Java and running on Kubernetes. The core problem right now is test coverage: automated tests cover only 34% of the migrated codebase, and the gap is filled by manual regression that takes our QA team three full weeks per release. That pace means we ship roughly every two months, but the client has been clear they want monthly releases by Q1 next year. We have two senior QA engineers and four mid-level developers assigned to this, and we have invested in a Jenkins-based pipeline, but writing meaningful automated tests for logic that was originally embedded in decades-old COBOL is slow and error-prone because the business rules were never formally documented. We have partial test data sets and some transaction logs from the old system, but translating those into reliable test cases requires both deep testing expertise and an understanding of financial processing logic. A good outcome would be reaching 75% automated coverage within six months and cutting the manual regression window to under one week.

challenges.text: Hiring senior Java architects in Novi Sad is impossible right now — we have eight open positions, three projects delayed, and the salaries candidates ask for are 40% above our grade bands.
challenges.detail: We currently have eight open positions for senior Java architects, and three active projects are behind schedule because of it. The local market in Novi Sad has tightened considerably over the past two years — candidates with ten or more years of Java experience and any cloud background are being approached by remote-first Western European employers who can offer salaries we are not authorised to match. The gap between what candidates expect and our approved grade bands is roughly 40%. We have tried posting on standard job boards, working with two local recruitment agencies, and running a referral programme, with limited success. We are also looking at whether we can grow architects internally from our pool of mid-level developers, but that takes time we do not have on current project timelines. What would help is either a structured fast-track programme to upskill existing staff, a way to assess which mid-level engineers are closest to readiness, or access to a network of qualified candidates we have not already spoken to.

challenges.text: Our cloud cost for EU clients jumped 28% last quarter because workload autoscaling decisions are made purely on CPU thresholds — we need smarter scheduling that considers time-of-day patterns and cross-service dependencies.
challenges.detail: Our cloud bill for EU client workloads went up 28% last quarter. The main reason is that our autoscaling setup reacts only to CPU utilisation thresholds, which means it scales up aggressively during brief spikes and is slow to scale back down. The workloads we manage for financial clients have very predictable daily and weekly patterns — overnight batch jobs, morning trading peaks, quiet afternoons — but our infrastructure treats every spike the same way. We also have cross-service dependencies that make naive scaling decisions expensive: scaling one service sometimes forces a cascade of unnecessary scaling in downstream services. We have Prometheus metrics and about 18 months of historical usage data across the affected workloads. What we need is a scheduling or scaling approach that incorporates time-of-day patterns and service dependency maps, rather than reacting purely to instantaneous CPU. We are open to tooling, a custom model, or a hybrid approach, as long as it can integrate with our existing Kubernetes and Terraform setup and does not require replacing our current observability stack.

challenges.text: Two of our biggest clients are asking us to provide a carbon footprint report for the IT services we run on their behalf — we have no methodology or tooling to do this and the first deadline is September.
challenges.detail: Two of our largest clients — one in Belgium, one in the Netherlands — have both asked us, within the same quarter, to provide a carbon footprint report covering the IT services we operate on their behalf. This is driven by their own regulatory and ESG reporting obligations. We have no existing methodology for this and no tooling in place. We are not starting from zero on data: we have detailed cloud resource usage logs, data centre power consumption figures from our co-location provider in Amsterdam, and monthly billing records broken down by client and workload. What we are missing is a credible, auditable methodology that maps those inputs to CO2-equivalent figures, ideally one that aligns with a recognised reporting standard so our clients can use the numbers in their own disclosures. The first client deadline is September of this year, which gives us roughly five months. We do not have a sustainability specialist on staff. Budget for getting this done is modest — we are not looking to build a large internal team, but we would fund a focused project or a short consulting engagement to get a working methodology and a first set of reports delivered.

challenges.text: We have 14 ongoing projects and our sprint velocity keeps slipping by about 15% in the third month of every engagement — clients notice, escalate, and we lose renewal bonuses. We think it's a mix of poor estimation and team fatigue but we don't have a model to predict which projects will slip before they do.
challenges.detail: We run fourteen active client projects at any given time, each on two-week sprints. What we keep seeing is a consistent drop in sprint velocity around the third month of an engagement — roughly 15% slower compared to the first eight weeks. Clients track this. Some have renewal bonuses tied to on-time delivery milestones, and we have missed those bonuses three times in the past eighteen months. We think the causes are a mix of initial estimation being too optimistic and team fatigue once the novelty of a new project wears off. We have tried adding buffer to estimates and rotating team members between projects, but without a clear picture of which project is about to slip, we are always reacting rather than preventing. We have our Jira data going back to 2019 — story points, cycle times, team assignments, sick days, client-change-request volume — but no one internally has built a model from it. We need something that flags at-risk projects four to six weeks before the slip becomes visible to the client, so we can intervene. Budget for a working pilot is around €15,000.

challenges.text: Three Danish clients asked us to sign DPA addenda under GDPR Article 28 with sub-processor clauses we've never handled before; our lawyer is in Novi Sad and doesn't know Danish data-authority practice, so every negotiation takes six weeks and has stalled two contracts worth €180k combined.
challenges.detail: Three of our Danish clients have asked us to sign updated Data Processing Addenda under GDPR Article 28, each with sub-processor clauses covering our use of AWS infrastructure and two third-party monitoring tools. Our legal counsel is a single lawyer based in Novi Sad who handles Serbian corporate law well but has no experience with the Danish Data Protection Authority's expectations or the specific standard contractual clause formats Danish companies are currently using. Each negotiation round takes about six weeks because we have to go back and forth, and two contracts worth a combined €180,000 are sitting unsigned. We cannot simply reject the addenda — these are long-term clients and the contracts are real. We also cannot just accept clauses we do not understand. What we need is access to someone who understands both GDPR Article 28 compliance in a practical, operational sense and the specific practice of Danish data authorities, so we can get these documents into a form both sides can sign. Timing is critical: one client has given us a deadline of end of Q2 2025.

challenges.text: We are interviewing for a senior cloud architect role for four months; every suitable candidate we find in Vojvodina gets a competing offer from a remote-first German company within a week of first contact, and we can't match their base salaries.
challenges.detail: We have been trying to hire a senior cloud architect for four months. The role exists because our DevOps practice has grown faster than we expected and the two engineers currently covering cloud architecture are stretched across too many projects. We know what we want: someone with hands-on AWS experience, comfortable with Terraform and container orchestration, who can also talk directly to clients about infrastructure decisions. We have found several strong candidates in Vojvodina and interviewed four people who were genuinely suitable. In every case, within a week of our first contact, they received an offer from a remote-first German or Dutch company at a base salary we cannot match — typically 20 to 30 percent above what we can offer for an in-office or hybrid role in Novi Sad. We have tried adjusting the benefits package and offering flexible hours, but the salary gap is the main issue. We are open to other approaches: a part-time arrangement, a structured knowledge transfer from a more senior external person, or a collaboration that helps us develop the capability internally rather than hiring it fully formed.

challenges.text: Operators want to know which distribution transformers will fail next year; they have dissolved gas analysis results and load data, but no model.
challenges.detail: Several of our distribution operator customers carry out dissolved gas analysis on their oil-filled transformers every one to two years and record the results in maintenance logs. They also have load data from SCADA — hourly active power readings going back between three and eight years depending on the operator. What they do not have is any way to turn those two sources into a ranked list of transformers most likely to fail in the next twelve months. At the moment maintenance teams rely on age and visual inspection, which means they sometimes replace transformers that still had years left and miss ones that are quietly deteriorating. We want to build a predictive failure scoring module inside GridSense Assets. We have cleaned and structured data for roughly four hundred transformers across two operators, including failure event records. We are not looking for a research prototype; we need something that a maintenance planner with no data science background can read and act on. Budget for a collaboration is modest — this would likely be a project or thesis arrangement — and we would need results within about ten months to feed into our 2027 module release.

challenges.text: Rooftop PV is changing feeder loads; operators need a day-ahead forecast per feeder.
challenges.detail: Rooftop solar installations have been growing steadily in the areas our customers serve, and the standard load profiles that operators use for day-ahead planning no longer reflect what actually flows through feeders at midday on a sunny day. Some feeders that used to peak in the evening now show reverse power flow in the afternoon, and our operators are making switching and maintenance scheduling decisions based on forecasts that can be off by thirty percent or more. We have half-hourly smart meter reads for a growing share of customers on those feeders, weather station data from two nearby airports, and satellite-derived irradiance estimates we licensed from a third-party provider. What we do not yet have is a model that produces a per-feeder load forecast twenty-four hours ahead, updated each evening. It needs to run inside our Azure environment on a small virtual machine, produce output in a format our Outage and Network Planner products can consume, and be maintainable by our own engineers once it is handed over. A good outcome is forecast error below fifteen percent mean absolute percentage error on held-out test months.

challenges.text: Our outdoor enclosures are rated IP67 but after one winter season in Vojvodina fields, about 1 in 5 units shows condensation inside the housing that corrodes the PCB connectors; we have replaced 34 units under warranty this year and it is eating our margin entirely.
challenges.detail: Koristimo polietilenska kućišta s IP67 sertifikatom, brtvama od silikona i kablskim uvodnicama, ali posle jedne zime na polju svaka peta stanica pokaže kondenzat unutar kućišta. Vlaga se taloži na konektorima PCB ploče i dovodi do korozije, najčešće na konektoru senzora temperature. Ove godine smo zbog toga zamenili 34 stanice o svom trošku — to su materijal, rad i putni troškovi koji nam direktno jedu maržu. Probali smo da dodamo vrećice silikagela unutar kućišta, ali nakon dva do tri meseca u polju one zasićene više ne pomažu. Sumnjamo da problem nastaje zbog ciklusa zagrevanja i hlađenja: danju sunce zagreje kućište, noću se ohladi i vlaga ulazi kroz mikroporoznosti ili zbog razlike pritisaka. Nemamo opremu niti znanje da precizno odredimo koji put vlaga ulazi. Imamo fotografije 34 oštećene ploče, temperaturne i vlažnosne podatke samih stanica za period u kom su se pokvarile, kao i specifikacije kućnika od dobavljača. Dobar ishod bi bio da shvatimo šta tačno prouzrokuje ulazak vlage i da promenimo konstrukciju ili proces sklapanja tako da problem nestane ili se smanji ispod jednog pokvarenog uređaja na dvadeset.

challenges.text: We power each station from a 20 W solar panel and a 12 V lead-acid battery, but our energy budget calculation was done by hand and two cooperative clients report stations going dark for up to 5 days after cloudy weeks in November; we need a proper sizing model that accounts for Serbian insolation data.
challenges.detail: Svaka stanica napaja se solarnim panelom od 20 W i olovnim akumulatorom od 12 V i 18 Ah. Potrošnju smo procenili ručno na osnovu specifikacija komponenti i nismo uzimali u obzir stvarne uslove insolacije u Vojvodini u novembru i decembru. Dve zadruge — Ratarsko-povrtarska zadruga Ravnica iz okoline Kule i Gazdinstvo Brko iz okoline Apatina — prijavile su da im stanice nisu radile i do pet uzastopnih dana tokom oblačnih perioda u novembru 2023. Imamo izmerene podatke o potrošnji struje iz naše radionice po komponentama, satelitske podatke o sunčevom zračenju koje smo skinuli s javnih portala za poslednjih pet godina za našu oblast, kao i tačne koordinate svih postavljenih stanica. Probali smo da ručno napravimo tabelu u Excelu, ali nismo sigurni da li smo dobro primenili korekcione faktore za ugao panela i starenje baterije. Imamo budžet da jednom promenimo dimenzioniranje za sve buduće serije — ne možemo stalno da menjamo hardver. Dobar ishod je pouzdan model koji kaže koliki panel i baterija trebaju za svaku lokaciju da stanica prebrodi bar sedam oblačnih dana zaredom.

challenges.text: We measure soil temperature and air humidity but farmers keep asking us for an estimated date of first frost at their specific field location, not just the nearest official meteorological station which can be 25 km away; we have two years of our own data but do not know how to build a local microclimate prediction.
challenges.detail: Naši kupci nas sve češće pitaju kada mogu da očekuju prvi mraz na svojoj njivi, jer zvanična meteorološka stanica koja je najbliža njihovom polju ponekad je udaljena i 25 kilometara, a lokalni reljef, blizina kanala ili zaštitni pojasevi drveta mogu da pomere datum prvog mraza i za deset do petnaest dana. Imamo dve pune godine sopstvenih merenja temperature na 47 lokacija u zapadnoj Vojvodini — to su nizovi merenja na svakih 15 minuta. Nikada nismo radili ništa ozbiljnije od proseka u Excelu. Ne znamo koji pristup bi imao smisla — da li je to regresija, da li su to vremenski modeli, da li treba nešto treće. Constraint je da nemamo nikoga u timu ko bi to naučio od nule, pa nam treba pomoć nekoga ko bi uzeo naše podatke i pokazao nam šta se može napraviti i koliko je to pouzdano. Dobar ishod nije savršena tačnost nego neka procena s greškom koja je manja od greške zvanične stanice, i objašnjenje šta model može a šta ne može da uradi, da bismo to mogli pošteno da saopštimo kupcima.

challenges.text: We process payroll for 420 client companies manually in Excel; we make on average three miscalculations per month that result in corrections and one formal complaint per quarter — we know we need automation but none of us are developers.
challenges.detail: Every month we process payroll for 420 client companies using a set of Excel workbooks that our team has built up and patched over the years. The formulas are complicated because Serbian payroll has a lot of moving parts — tax thresholds, contribution rates, benefit deductions, sick-leave calculations — and when a rule changes we update the sheets manually. On average we catch three miscalculations each month before payment, but sometimes one slips through and we have to issue a correction. We get roughly one formal written complaint per quarter. We have tried adding more checking steps and a second pair of eyes on each file, but that just takes more time and we are already at capacity. We have a folder of all our Excel templates and about two years of payroll records in a structured format, so the data is there. We have no developers on staff and our portal developer no longer works with us regularly. We have a rough budget of around four thousand euros for a first phase of anything we build. A good outcome would be a system that runs the core calculations automatically and flags anything that looks wrong before we touch it.

challenges.text: The new amendments to the Serbian Labour Law that came into force in March changed 14 articles we reference directly in our standard contract templates, and we had to update them by hand over two weeks; we need a smarter way to track regulatory changes and flag which templates are affected.
challenges.detail: Our standard service includes preparing employment contracts for clients using a library of about thirty template documents that Miroslav originally drafted. When the Serbian Labour Law was amended this March, fourteen articles that our templates reference directly were changed — things like notice periods, probation rules and grounds for termination. We found out through a legal newsletter we subscribe to, then spent two weeks going clause by clause through every template to update them. We are worried we will miss something next time, or that a client will use an old version without realising it has been superseded. We keep all templates in Word files on a shared drive with version dates in the file names. We have tried a simple spreadsheet that maps each template to the articles it cites, but keeping that spreadsheet updated is itself a manual task that falls to whoever is least busy. We do not have a legal database subscription beyond what is freely available on the government's official gazette website. A good outcome would be something that watches for published changes to the Labour Law and tells us which of our templates probably need reviewing, without requiring us to read every gazette entry ourselves.

challenges.text: Three of our largest clients have asked us to add an employee wellbeing survey module to our portal so they can meet ESG reporting requirements by 2026, but we have no idea how to design a psychometrically valid questionnaire or what to do with the scores.
challenges.detail: Three of our bigger clients — a logistics company, a food processing firm and a retail chain — have told us they need to include employee wellbeing data in their ESG reports from 2026 onward. They have asked us to add a survey module to our client portal so their employees can answer questions and managers can see summary scores. We said yes because we want to keep these clients, but we genuinely do not know how to approach it properly. We are not sure what questions to ask, how to score the answers in a way that means something, or how to present the results without them being misleading. We have read a few things online about workplace wellbeing surveys but the academic papers are hard to follow and most commercial tools are priced for large companies. Our portal is built in PHP and MySQL so adding a new module is technically possible if we can find someone to do the development. We have a deadline of early 2026 for the first reporting cycle. A good outcome would be a questionnaire design and a scoring approach that our clients can actually explain to their auditors, plus a way to show results inside our existing portal.

challenges.text: We pack between 600 and 2,200 parcels per day depending on campaigns; the swing is hard to predict so we either overstaff or rush. If we could forecast daily order volume five days ahead with reasonable accuracy we could plan temporary labour and packaging material orders properly and cut our labour cost overrun, currently about €8,000 a month.
challenges.detail: Our parcel volume swings between 600 and 2,200 boxes in a single day, mostly driven by campaign emails our clients send without always telling us in advance. We currently plan the next day's staffing by looking at the last three days and making a gut call. That works well enough in a flat week, but when a client runs a weekend flash sale we find out at 07:00 on Monday. We have tried asking clients to share their marketing calendars, and some do, but roughly a third do not. We hold about 18 months of daily dispatch records in our WMS database, plus carrier booking timestamps. We also have client email campaign dates where clients shared them. Our constraint is that we use agency temps from two local staffing firms who need 48 hours' notice for more than five extra people, and packaging materials — bubble bags, cardboard dividers — have a three-day lead time from our supplier in Šabac. A forecast that was reliable five days out, even with a margin of ±15%, would let us act in time. The labour cost overrun we can measure directly is around €8,000 per month, mostly overtime and unused temp hours.

challenges.text: Several of our clients ship fragile ceramic and glassware; breakage claims average 2.1% of shipments. We design packaging inserts ourselves without any engineering knowledge, and we suspect the cushioning is wrong for the parcel drop heights that couriers actually produce.
challenges.detail: Two of our larger clients ship hand-thrown ceramic mugs and mouth-blown glass carafes. Our breakage claim rate on those product lines sits at 2.1% of shipments, which sounds small but across roughly 180 ceramic or glass parcels a day it means about four damaged items daily, each triggering a replacement shipment and a refund. We designed our foam and corrugated inserts ourselves by trial and error. We know that drop height matters and that couriers do drop parcels, but we do not have data on actual drop events in the DPD or GLS network. We photograph every packed box before it leaves and we have kept images of returned damaged items for the past eight months — around 340 photos showing which face of the box was crushed or which corner failed. We also have the product dimensions and weights. We have no mechanical engineering background on the team. We are not looking for a full product redesign; we want someone to look at our current insert geometry and tell us specifically what is wrong and what to change. We would be happy to buy a small batch of test packaging to validate any recommendation before we commit to a new stock run.

challenges.text: The EU General Product Safety Regulation that comes into force in 2024 requires us to have a responsible economic operator registered in the EU for all non-EU brands we handle. We currently have none, and our legal advisor in Novi Sad says this is outside her expertise.
challenges.detail: The EU General Product Safety Regulation requires that any product sold to EU consumers by a non-EU brand must have a responsible economic operator with a registered address inside the EU who can be contacted by market surveillance authorities. Several of our clients are Serbian companies with no EU entity. We are registered in Serbia, not in the EU, so we cannot fulfil that role ourselves. Our legal advisor in Novi Sad is competent on Serbian commercial law but has told us directly that EU product compliance is outside what she can advise on. We need to understand which of our client categories — cosmetics, ceramics, textiles, food — have additional sectoral requirements on top of the base GPSR, what documents we must hold on file for each shipment, and what a practical EU-registered operator arrangement looks like, including cost. Our deadline is firm: the regulation is already in force and we have been shipping without this in place. We are a small company so we cannot afford a large international law firm, but we can allocate a defined project budget to get a clear, actionable compliance framework.

challenges.text: We print shipping labels, packing slips and customs invoices on three different printers from two vendors; about 4% of print jobs fail silently and the parcel goes out without a label or with a blank customs form, which triggers returns from German customs. We need a unified, error-checked print workflow.
challenges.detail: We run three printers in the dispatch area: two Zebra ZPL units for shipping labels and one Brother laser for packing slips and customs invoices. They come from different vendors and connect to our WMS through separate drivers. Roughly 4% of print jobs fail without any visible error on the packing station screen — the operator sees a success message but the printer has timed out or run out of ribbon. The parcel moves down the line unlabelled or with a blank customs form. We only discover the problem when the carrier scans nothing at collection or when German customs returns the shipment, which takes two to three weeks and costs us about €14 per returned parcel plus the replacement send. We have tried adding a manual visual check at the sealing station but that catches maybe half the failures because operators are under time pressure. What we want is a print workflow where the system confirms that the printer actually produced output — not just that it accepted the job — and holds the barcode scan on the parcel until all required documents are confirmed printed. We are open to replacing printer drivers, adding middleware or rewriting the print module in our WMS. Our WMS backend is Laravel and we have one in-house developer.

challenges.text: Our route recommendation engine works well on flat terrain but dramatically underestimates physical effort on the Fruška Gora ridge trails — cyclists rated those routes as 40% harder than we predicted, which is causing churn among the athletic segment of users.
challenges.detail: Our route recommendation engine scores trails using a formula that combines distance, road surface type and average gradient. On the flat canal paths of Vojvodina it performs reliably — user effort ratings match our predictions within about 8%. On the Fruška Gora ridge it falls apart. Last season we collected 1,140 completed ride logs from that area along with post-ride effort surveys, and the average rider reported the physical cost as 40% higher than our score suggested. We believe the problem is that our formula treats gradient as a simple average over a segment, so a 6% average across 10 km looks the same whether it is a steady incline or a sequence of short 14% punches with flat recoveries. We tried adding a variance term to the gradient score last autumn, which helped slightly but not enough. We also have wind exposure and trail surface roughness data we are not using well. Our internal team has two developers who work on the engine part-time alongside other duties. We want a model that is accurate enough that users on Fruška Gora routes rate predicted effort within 15% of actual effort, and we need it in production before the spring touring season begins in April 2025.

challenges.text: Our GPS antenna assembly line has a manual calibration step that takes 4.5 minutes per unit and is the bottleneck; we produce 600 units a week but could sell 900 if we could cut that to under 90 seconds.
challenges.detail: Every CycloNav X4 unit we ship goes through a calibration step where a technician attaches the antenna board to a reference oscillator, runs a 4.5-minute signal sweep and adjusts two trim capacitors by hand based on a numeric readout. The step exists because our antenna components arrive with enough batch variation that a fixed factory setting is not reliable. We have three calibration benches and three trained staff. At current throughput we finish about 600 units a week. Sales quotes we received from distributors in the Czech Republic and Austria suggest we could move 900 units a week if stock were available, but adding a fourth bench and a fourth technician only gets us to around 720. We looked at buying pre-calibrated antenna modules from a Taiwanese supplier, but the unit cost increase would reduce our hardware margin from 34% to under 19%, which is not viable. What we want is a way to automate the signal measurement and capacitor adjustment so the step takes under 90 seconds per unit without switching suppliers. We have the three existing benches available for modification and a capital budget of roughly €55,000 for this project.

challenges.text: We are trying to raise a Series A round of €2.8 million from a Vienna-based impact fund but our three-year financial projections have been rejected twice because the reviewers say our unit-economics model is not structured to institutional investor standards.
challenges.detail: We are in discussions with Waldviertel Impact Ventures, a Vienna-based fund, about a Series A round of €2.8 million. The money would go toward expanding our municipal sales team, funding firmware development for a next-generation device and covering a planned move to a larger assembly facility. We submitted a full financial package twice. Both times the fund's analyst returned it saying our unit-economics presentation does not meet the structure they require — specifically, they want a clear separation of hardware margin, subscription gross margin and professional services margin, along with cohort-based customer lifetime value calculations for both the tour operator and municipality segments, and a sensitivity table for three hardware volume scenarios. Our current financial model is an Excel workbook our office manager built over the years. It tracks overall revenue and costs accurately but mixes the revenue streams together and was not designed to answer the specific questions institutional investors ask. We have a part-time bookkeeper and a tax accountant who visits quarterly; neither has experience structuring investment-grade materials. The fund has indicated they will review a third submission if we resubmit before the end of Q1 2025.

challenges.text: Municipalities that license our trail portal want to embed it in their official tourism websites with full white-label branding, but our current map rendering pipeline takes 3–4 seconds to load a 50 km trail segment on mobile, and page-abandon rates on municipal sites are already at 67%.
challenges.detail: Twenty-three of the 28 municipalities that license our TrailPortal have asked for the white-label embed option, which lets them drop a fully branded interactive trail map into their own tourism website. The technical problem is load time. When a visitor opens a 50 km trail segment on a mobile device the map takes between 3 and 4 seconds to appear, measured on a standard 4G connection. We ran an analysis using session logs from four municipal sites and found a 67% page-abandon rate before the map finishes loading. The rendering bottleneck appears to be the way we pre-load the full trail geometry and all associated point-of-interest data in a single request before drawing anything on screen. We use Mapbox GL JS for rendering and our own Django API for data delivery. We tried reducing the resolution of trail geometry for mobile viewports, which cut load time to about 2.6 seconds but introduced visible staircase artifacts on curves that municipalities found unacceptable. Several municipalities have told us directly that they will not renew their licenses unless the mobile experience improves before the summer 2025 tourist season. A target of under 1.2 seconds to first meaningful paint is what we need to pass the threshold their web teams are measuring.

challenges.text: Our spraying drones apply pesticide at a flat 120-litre-per-hectare rate regardless of crop density, and agronomists are telling us that we are over-applying in sparse zones by as much as 35% — we need the drone to adjust flow rate on the fly based on the canopy it sees beneath it.
