challenges.detail: Trenutno sve naše letelice za prskanje rade na fiksnoj normi od 120 litara po hektaru, bez obzira na gustinu sklopa ispod njih. Naši agronomi-partneri su izmerili da u proređenim zonama, gde je sklop suncokreta ili pšenice slabiji zbog suše ili slabijeg klijanja, prekoračujemo optimalnu dozu i do 35 odsto. To je direktan gubitak preparata i potencijalni problem sa ostacima. Pokušali smo da ručno delimo parcele na zone prema prethodnoj NDVI karti i da za svaku zonu planiramo poseban let sa drugačijom brzinom, ali to je sporo i sklono greškama. Ono što nam treba je sistem koji tokom leta čita optički signal sa kamere ispod letelice i u realnom vremenu prilagođava protok pumpe. Imamo telemetriju i PWM regulaciju na pumpama, ali nemamo algoritam koji bi to vezao za trenutnu gustinu krošnje. Hardver je tu, nedostaje nam softversko i algoritamsko rešenje. Rok nam je sledeća sezona prskanja — april 2025. Dobar ishod bi bio smanjenje prekoračenja doze ispod 10 odsto u proređenim zonama.

challenges.text: We flew 9,400 hectares last season but our flight path planning is still done manually in QGIS by one person — during peak season in May we are turning away clients because planning is the bottleneck, not aircraft or pilots.
challenges.detail: Prošle sezone prekrili smo 9.400 hektara, ali svaki let i dalje planira ručno jedan čovek u QGIS-u. Kolega Stevan Bačić radi brzo, ali u maju, kada se poklapaju tretman fungicidom pšenice i prvo prskanje suncokreta, nije fizički moguće isplanirati sve naloge na vreme. Procenjujemo da smo u maju 2023. odbili ili odložili narudžbine za oko 1.200 hektara čisto zbog tog uskog grla. Pokušavali smo da uvedemo šablone ruta po tipičnim oblicima parcela, ali vojvođanske parcele su dovoljno različite da šabloni ne funkcionišu dobro. Imamo sve GIS podatke, ortofoto i katastarske granice za naše uobičajene klijente. Trebamo alat ili skriptu koja iz granice parcele i agrotehničkih parametara (vrsta useva, zadana norma, brzina vetra) automatski generiše optimizovanu rutu i izvozi je u format koji ArduPilot čita. Budžet za alat je umeren, ali nam je važno da Stevan može da ga koristi bez naprednog programiranja.

challenges.text: We raised a Series A of €2.1 million last year and the lead investor is now pushing us to show a clear path to profitability in the Hungarian and Slovak markets within 18 months — we need a proper financial model and go-to-market analysis but we don't have anyone internally who can build it.
challenges.detail: Zatvorili smo Seriju A od 2,1 milion evra prošle godine, a vodeći investitor, fond Pannonia Ventures iz Budimpešte, sada traži konkretan plan profitabilnosti za mađarsko i slovačko tržište u roku od 18 meseci. Imamo operativne podatke iz naše pilot-zone u Mađarskoj — leteli smo oko 600 hektara za dva klijenta u sezoni 2023 — ali nemamo sistematski model troškova i prihoda koji uzima u obzir logistiku prekograničnog rada, regulatorne razlike, sezonalnost i lokalnu konkurenciju. Interno, niko od nas nema iskustvo sa finansijskim modelovanjem na nivou koji investitor očekuje. Pokušali smo da popunimo Excel tabelu, ali ona nije povezana i ne odgovara na scenarije. Trebamo osobu ili tim koji razume i poslovni razvoj i specifičnosti agro-usluga — ne generalnog konsultanta — da nam pomogne izgraditi model, definisati ciljne segmente i odrediti cenovnu strategiju. Rok je prezentacija investitoru u februaru 2025.

challenges.text: After a heavy rain the drone landing gear and underbelly pick up clay-heavy Vojvodina soil and the residue clogs the spray nozzles within one sortie — we are stopping flights to clean every 45 minutes in wet conditions and that is unacceptable.
challenges.detail: Vojvođansko zemljište posle kiše postaje lepljivo i glinasto, i letelice za prskanje, koje lete nisko — između jednog i tri metra visine — skupljaju taj mulj na stajnom trapu i donjem delu trupa. Za 45 minuta leta u vlažnim uslovima dolazi do začepljenja mlaznica u meri koja zahteva kompletno čišćenje pre sledećeg sortija. U praksi to znači da umesto osam sortija dnevno realizujemo četiri do pet, što nam prepolovljava kapacitet baš kada su tretmani najurgentniji — odmah posle kiše, kada je i insekatski pritisak najveći. Isprobali smo zaštitne poklopce od gume na stajnom trapu, ali oni povećavaju masu i menjaju centar težišta. Razmatrali smo keramičke premaze na mlaznicama, ali nismo sigurni koji materijal bi bio otporan na kombinaciju pesticida i abrazije. Nismo još probali izmenu geometrije stajnog trapa niti usmeravanje vazdušnog strujanja da odbija čestice. Rešenje mora biti retroaktivno primenljivo na postojeću flotu bez strukturnih izmena na trupu letelice.

challenges.text: Our treated greywater consistently fails the manganese and iron limits set by the new Serbian industrial discharge regulation — we're seeing 0.18 mg/L manganese where the limit is 0.10 mg/L — and we don't know whether the problem is in our coagulation step or something upstream in the client's process.
challenges.detail: Serbian regulation SR-IED-2023 lowered the allowable manganese in treated discharge to 0.10 mg/L and iron to 0.30 mg/L. Our own analysers, confirmed by an accredited external lab in Zrenjanin, are reading 0.18 mg/L manganese at the outlet of our coagulation stage across three different client sites. We have already tried increasing coagulant dose by 30 percent and dropping pH from 7.4 to 6.9 during coagulation, without meaningful improvement. We have inlet samples showing that the raw greywater entering our plant contains between 0.04 and 0.07 mg/L manganese, so something in the process is either releasing additional manganese or preventing its removal. We suspect the issue may be connected to our filter media or to manganese cycling in our holding tanks, but we have not been able to confirm this. We have on-site analytical kit and can pull samples at every process stage. The deadline is real: one large laundry client faces a reinspection in five months. A good outcome is a root-cause finding with a specific process change we can implement at existing installations without replacing major equipment.

challenges.text: We currently size every new recycling unit by hand using spreadsheets and conservative safety factors, which means we over-engineer by roughly 25–30% on capital cost and lose bids to cheaper competitors; we need a fast, reliable simulation tool we can run during a sales call.
challenges.detail: When we respond to a tender or meet a potential client, we need to give a system size and a capital cost figure quickly. At the moment our lead engineer, Tomislav Grulović, works through a spreadsheet model that was built in 2015 and applies fixed safety factors of 1.3 to 1.4 on every key component. We have compared our installed systems against their design specs and consistently find we have oversized tanks by 20 to 35 percent and pumps by a similar margin. On bids we have lost in the last two years, the winning price was on average 22 percent lower than ours. We have hydraulic flow data, effluent quality profiles, and operational logs from all forty-plus installations, so there is a reasonable dataset to work from. We do not have software engineers in-house. The tool needs to be usable by a sales engineer who is not a modelling specialist, ideally on a laptop during a client meeting. Budget for development is limited to around 15,000 EUR. A good outcome is a tool that produces a reliable system configuration and cost estimate in under 30 minutes from a standard set of client inputs.

challenges.text: Three food-plant clients have asked us to handle their process sludge as part of the same contract, but we have no licence to transport or treat hazardous waste and the permitting process through the Vojvodina Provincial Secretariat has already taken 14 months with no end in sight.
challenges.detail: Three of our food-processing clients have asked us to incorporate their process sludge — primarily from flotation units and centrifuge discharge — into our service contract. In principle this would make us a more complete partner and improve client retention. In practice we hold a water-treatment operating licence but have no authorisation to collect, transport, or treat waste classified as hazardous under Serbian waste law. We submitted a permit application to the Vojvodina Provincial Secretariat for Environmental Protection in February 2023. As of today we have received two requests for supplementary documentation and one notification of a changed case officer, but no decision. We do not have a dedicated regulatory specialist on staff; our compliance work is handled by our office manager, Snežana Korać, who is not a lawyer. We are not sure whether the delay is procedural, whether our application has a substantive gap, or whether a different licensing route exists. A good outcome would be either a clear path to obtaining the licence within a realistic timeframe, or a legally sound partnership arrangement with a licensed waste handler that would let us offer the service under contract.

challenges.text: Biofilm builds up inside our stainless steel holding tanks within six to eight weeks of commissioning, raising our clients' microbiological counts above 100 CFU/mL and forcing emergency chlorination that damages the downstream reverse-osmosis membranes; we need to understand which microbial consortia are responsible and how to suppress them without continuous biocide dosing.
challenges.detail: Across several installations, mainly food-plant clients that handle vegetable or poultry washwater, we are seeing visible biofilm inside our 10 to 20 cubic metre stainless-steel holding and buffer tanks within six to eight weeks of commissioning. When we swab and send samples to a commercial microbiological lab in Novi Sad, total plate counts come back above 100 CFU per mL, occasionally as high as 800 CFU per mL. Our current response is a shock chlorination cycle, typically dosing to 5 mg/L free chlorine and holding for two hours. This brings counts down temporarily but the chlorine residual then enters the reverse-osmosis stage and we are seeing accelerated membrane degradation — two membrane sets replaced early in the last 18 months at a combined replacement cost of around 9,000 EUR. We do not know whether the biofilm is driven by one dominant species, a stable consortium, or something specific to the food-waste load coming from these clients. We have not done any sequencing or detailed microbiological characterisation. We want to understand what is growing and why, so we can consider non-chemical or low-frequency chemical suppression strategies that do not harm the membranes. Budget for investigation is around 8,000 EUR.

challenges.text: Baterije u stanicama zimi traju upola kraće nego leti, pa voćari moraju da ih menjaju usred sezone.
challenges.detail: Naše stanice koriste litijumske baterije kapaciteta 3,6 V / 14 Ah. Leti jedna baterija traje između četrnaest i šesnaest meseci, što je sasvim prihvatljivo. Problem nastaje zimi: ispod nule baterija gubi kapacitet brže nego što smo predviđali, pa na nekim lokacijama traje svega šest do sedam meseci. Voćari moraju da idu na parcelu usred januara ili februara, po mrazu i snegu, i menjaju baterije – baš u periodu kada su stanice najpotrebnije za detekciju mraza. Pokušali smo da smanjimo frekvenciju slanja podataka s jednog merenja na petnaest minuta na jedno na trideset minuta, ali voćari su se žalili da gube preciznost upozorenja. Razmatrali smo i mali solarni panel, ali naši testovi su pokazali da u decembru i januaru u Vojvodini panel ne isporučuje dovoljno energije zbog kratkog dana i oblačnosti. Imamo log podatke o naponu baterija sa svih aktivnih stanica u poslednjih dve i po godine, razvrstane po lokaciji i temperaturi. Budžet za ovaj problem je ograničen – ne možemo drastično podići cenu stanice. Dobar ishod bi bio da stanica preživi celu zimsku sezonu, od novembra do marta, bez zamene baterije.

challenges.text: Voćari ručno broje leptire na feromonskim klopkama; hteli bismo da kamera na klopci to radi sama.
challenges.detail: Voćari koji koriste feromonske klopke za praćenje štetočina – pre svega jabučnog savijača i breskvine mušice – moraju svake sedmice da fizički dođu do klopke, izvade lepljivu podlogu i prebroje uhvaćene leptire. Taj podatak im govori da li treba da prskaju ili ne. Problem je što je to zamorno, podložno greškama, a neki voćari preskače preglede. Mi bismo hteli da na klopku montiramo malu kameru koja bi snimala podlogu jednom dnevno i automatski prebrojala insekte. Već imamo prototip napajanja za kameru koji se uklapa u naš postojeći sistem baterija i LoRaWAN prenosa, ali prenos slike je skup po pitanju potrošnje energije i zauzima previše propusnog opsega LoRaWAN mreže. Nismo sigurni da li da obradu radimo lokalno na uređaju ili da šaljemo slike u cloud. Nemamo iskustva sa računarskim vidom niti sa optimizacijom modela za male mikrokontrolere. Imamo oko dvesta fotografija lepljivih podloga koje su nam dali voćari tokom ove sezone – to bi moglo da posluži kao početni skup podataka. Rok koji smo sebi postavili je da imamo funkcionalni prototip pre sajma u proleće 2026. godine.

challenges.text: Our welding robots drift by up to 2 mm over a single shift due to thermal expansion of the fixture, and we recalibrate manually every four hours — that alone costs us roughly 800 production minutes per week across three customer sites.
challenges.detail: On three of our active customer sites we run welding cells where the fixture steel heats up during the shift and the robot's reference points drift. Over eight hours we can see up to 2 mm of positional error accumulate, which is enough to push weld starts off the joint edge on tight-tolerance brackets. Right now our technicians stop the cell every four hours, run a reference point check, and manually jog the robot back to calibrated position. Across three sites that adds up to roughly 800 lost production minutes every week, and it also means we need a technician physically present more than the contract requires. We have tried using the robot's own built-in thermal compensation parameters but the drift is mostly in the fixture, not the robot arm, so those settings do not help much. We have temperature sensors on one fixture as a trial but we have not found a reliable way to turn that temperature reading into an automatic positional correction the robot controller will accept. We want an automatic, closed-loop correction that runs without stopping the cell. Our budget for a pilot solution on one site is around 15,000 euros. A good outcome is cutting manual recalibration to once per shift or less.

challenges.text: We quote every new cell integration from scratch; our estimators spend 10–15 days per tender and we still lose about 30% of bids because our price is unpredictable — sometimes we over-quote, sometimes we bleed money.
challenges.detail: Every tender we respond to starts from a blank sheet. Our estimators — two people with fifteen years of experience each — pull numbers from memory, old project folders, and a shared spreadsheet that has grown into something nobody fully trusts. A single quote takes between ten and fifteen working days and involves going back to suppliers for updated prices on motors, safety fencing, cable trays, and robot hardware. We win roughly seven out of ten bids on smaller repeat-type jobs where we know the scope well, but on new cell types or unfamiliar industries we lose about three in ten, and when we win those, the margin is often worse than forecast because we missed something in the estimate. We have looked at commercial ERP systems but the ones aimed at our size of company do not understand how robot cell projects are structured. What we actually need is a way to build a historical cost database from our thirty years of completed projects and use it to generate a first-pass estimate quickly, then let the estimators refine it. We have project records going back to 2005 in digital form. A good outcome would be cutting tender preparation time to under five days and reducing price variance on comparable projects.

challenges.text: We want to expand to Germany and Austria but our CE documentation for machine safety is incomplete and we've had two audit failures this year; a local lawyer can't help because the Machinery Directive interpretation requires technical expertise we don't have in-house.
challenges.detail: We have two customers in Germany we are in early discussions with, and at least three Austrian fabricators have asked for a quote in the last eighteen months. Every time we get close, the question of CE marking and full Machinery Directive documentation stops the conversation. We have had two third-party audit failures this year — one on a safety distance calculation for a perimeter guarding layout, and one on incomplete risk assessment documentation for a two-robot coordinated cell. Our current compliance approach is that our safety officers write the documentation in-house and we hire a local lawyer to review contracts, but the lawyer cannot review the technical content of a risk assessment. Fixing the audit failures took us three months each time, and we lost one German prospect during the second delay. We need someone who understands both the technical requirements of EN ISO 10218-2 and the practical way German and Austrian notified bodies interpret the Machinery Directive in practice. We are not looking for a consultant who charges by the hour indefinitely — we want to build the internal capability so our own team can produce compliant documentation without outside help for routine projects. We have budget for a structured engagement up to roughly 20,000 euros over twelve months.

challenges.text: Our procedural level generator produces playable layouts but they feel repetitive after about two hours — players on Steam are leaving reviews saying the maps all look the same, and our 30-day retention has dropped to 18% this quarter.
challenges.detail: Our procedural level generator has been part of our pipeline since 2021. It assembles playable maps from a library of hand-crafted tile sets and follows a set of rules we wrote to keep layouts fair and navigable. For the first hour or so, most players find the results interesting. The problem is that the underlying logic does not vary the structural patterns enough — corridors and rooms start repeating in ways players notice. We track this through Steam reviews and our own Firebase retention data. This quarter our 30-day retention sits at 18%, down from 27% the same quarter last year. We have tried expanding the tile library and adjusting the weighting rules by hand, but the improvement was small. We have not yet tried machine-learning approaches because no one on the current team has that background. We have around two months before our next major content update, and we would like a working improvement in place by then. A good outcome is retention climbing back toward 25% and fewer Steam reviews mentioning repetitive maps.

challenges.text: We want to add lip-sync animation to our characters automatically from dialogue audio files, but our current tool requires animators to keyframe every phoneme by hand — it's adding three weeks to every localization pass when we release in a new language.
challenges.detail: We currently release our games in English, German, and French. Each new language adds a full localization pass that includes redoing lip-sync animation for every speaking character. Our animators keyframe phoneme shapes by hand using Spine 2D, matching the audio timing from the recorded dialogue. For a single language this takes roughly three weeks of animator time. We have looked at one commercial auto lip-sync tool but it produced output that did not match our character style well enough — the mouth shapes felt mechanical and our art director rejected the results. We have the raw audio files organized by character and line, and we have a clean set of phoneme-to-mouth-shape mappings that our animators use as a reference. What we need is a way to read an audio file, identify phoneme timings automatically, and output keyframe data in a format Spine 2D can import. Cutting that three-week pass down to under a week would let us release in two additional languages per year. Budget for tooling is modest but we can discuss a longer arrangement if the approach works.

challenges.text: We've been trying to close a co-development deal with a Dutch publisher for eight months and the contract negotiation keeps stalling on IP ownership clauses — we need someone who actually understands cross-border intellectual property agreements in the EU games industry.
challenges.detail: We have been in talks with a Dutch publisher, Grachtwerk Media B.V., for eight months over a co-development agreement for our next major PC title. The commercial terms — advance, royalty split, marketing spend — were agreed relatively quickly. What keeps stalling the deal is the IP ownership section. Grachtwerk wants a reversion clause that would give them full rights to the game if we miss two consecutive milestones, and they want the clause to cover derivative works including sequels and ports. We are not willing to hand over the franchise permanently over a scheduling issue. We have tried negotiating through email with the help of a local general-practice lawyer, but that lawyer has no background in cross-border creative IP under EU law and the conversations go in circles. We need someone who has actually worked through IP agreements in the European games industry, knows how similar clauses have been handled in comparable deals, and can help us reach a version of this contract that protects our core rights. We would like the deal closed within the next three months.

challenges.text: Farmers want a yield estimate per parcel by mid-June, but our maps only show crop vigour.
challenges.detail: Our crop health maps are genuinely useful for spotting stress or uneven emergence, but by late May every season our customers start asking the same question: how many tonnes per hectare should I expect on parcel 14 by harvest? Right now we cannot answer that. We have NDVI and a red-edge chlorophyll index going back five seasons for most customer parcels, and we have the operation logs — sowing date, seed variety, fertiliser amounts — for about 60 percent of those parcels. What we do not have is a reliable link between those signals and final yield. We tried fitting a simple linear regression between peak June NDVI and the combine yield-monitor data that a handful of customers shared with us, and the correlation was weak enough that we would be embarrassed to publish a number to a farmer. The deadline that matters is mid-June, because that is when forward grain contracts are still being adjusted. A good outcome would be a per-parcel yield range — not a single point estimate — that is honest about its uncertainty and accurate enough that a farm manager would actually use it to make a sales decision. We have two data scientists on staff but neither has a background in crop modelling, and we cannot afford to spend the whole 2025 season on something that does not ship for 2026 planting.

challenges.text: Ground truth for soil moisture costs too much: probes are expensive and we can't place them on every parcel.
challenges.detail: Soil moisture is probably the single variable that would most improve both our health maps and any future yield estimate, but we have no affordable way to collect it at field scale. We looked at commercially available capacitance probes: a basic setup with a data logger and cellular modem costs roughly 600 to 900 euros per installation point, and a single 500-hectare farm might need eight to twelve points to capture the soil variability across parcels. That is not something most of our customers will pay for on top of their software subscription. We experimented with one customer, Zlatko Petrović near Kikinda, who agreed to install four probes on his farm last season, and the data was useful, but four points on 480 hectares left large gaps. We have also looked at deriving relative moisture estimates from SAR backscatter in the Sentinel-1 archive, but our data scientists ran into well-known problems with surface roughness and crop cover confounding the signal, and we do not have the expertise to untangle that properly. A practical outcome would be either a low-cost proxy for field-level moisture that we could derive from existing satellite data, or a smarter sensor placement strategy that gets acceptable coverage with two or three probes instead of ten.

challenges.text: Our mono-material PE-based pouch has excellent seal integrity at room temperature but oxygen transmission rate jumps from 12 to over 80 cc/m²/day at 38°C — which rules us out of any Mediterranean or Middle-East export customer. We need to identify whether this is a coating formulation issue or a structural one in the film layering.
challenges.detail: Razvili smo mono-materijalnu PE kesicu koja dobro funkcioniše na sobnoj temperaturi — OTR nam je oko 12 cc/m²/dan, što je prihvatljivo za kategoriju suve hrane. Problem nastaje čim idemo na 38°C: merenja koja smo radili u eksternoj laboratoriji u Beogradu pokazuju da OTR skače na više od 80 cc/m²/dan. To praktično znači da ne možemo da izvozimo u toplijе klimatske zone. Probali smo da povećamo debljinu EVOH sloja, ali to komplikuje mono-materijalnu reciklabilnost. Nismo sigurni da li je problem u načinu na koji nanosimo premaz, u redosledu i debljinama slojeva u ekstruziji, ili u nečem trećem. Imamo podatke sa tri serije merenja OTR-a (temperatura 23°C i 38°C, RH 50% i 85%), kao i specifikacije ekstrudera. Budžet za rešavanje ovog problema je ograničen — možemo da finansiramo materijale i testiranje, ali ne i dugotrajan projekat. Dobar ishod bi bio jasna dijagnoza uzroka i barem jedan modifikovani recept filma koji drži OTR ispod 20 cc/m²/dan na 38°C.

challenges.text: We are trying to validate that our packaging meets the EU's upcoming recyclability criteria under the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation, but we cannot find a local lab that can certify the recyclate quality class. The two Belgian labs that can do it quoted us €22,000 for the test campaign, which is more than our monthly revenue.
challenges.detail: EU Uredba o ambalaži i ambalažnom otpadu (PPWR) uvodi obavezne kriterijume reciklabilnosti koji će postati uslov za nabavku za mnoge prehrambene brendove sa kojima razgovaramo. Da bismo dokazali usaglašenost, potrebno nam je zvanično testiranje kvaliteta reciklata prema priznatoj metodologiji — konkretno, certifikacija koja pokazuje u koji razred reciklata ulazi naš materijal. U Srbiji ne postoji laboratorija koja to može da uradi na način koji je priznat prema EU regulatornom okviru. Kontaktirali smo dva belgijska laboratorijska centra — dobili smo ponude od 18.000 i 22.000 evra samo za test kampanju, što je više od naše mesečne prihode. Imamo uzorke gotove ambalaže i znamo tačnu strukturu filma. Rok je pritisak — kupci počinju da postavljaju pitanja već od 2025. godine. Dobar ishod bi bio pronalazak puta da dođemo do validiranih rezultata po ceni koja je realna za firmu našeg obima, ili razvoj interne metodologije koja je usklađena sa PPWR kriterijumima.

challenges.text: Our sealing layer is an mLLDPE and we get a narrow process window — seal strength is acceptable between 130–138°C but outside that range it either fails to bond or makes the film impossible to peel for end users. Our customers want a wider process window so they can run their vertical form-fill-seal lines faster.
challenges.detail: Naš zaptivni sloj je od mLLDPE granulata koji nabavljamo od dobavljača iz Austrije. Prozor za zaptivanje koji smo postigli je uzak — između 130 i 138°C dobijamo prihvatljivu čvrstоću spoja, ali ispod 130°C veza nije pouzdana, a iznad 138°C film se deformiše toliko da ga krajnji korisnik ne može normalno otvoriti. Problem je što naši kupci koji pakuju na VFFS (vertical form-fill-seal) mašinama rade brže od onog što naš materijal može da podnese, jer brzina trake zahteva kraće vreme kontakta na nešto višim temperaturama. Probali smo dva različita mLLDPE tipa i jedan blend sa LDPE — bez značajnog poboljšanja. Imamo podatke o čvrstoći spoja (N/15mm) za više kombinacija temperature i vremena kontakta, kao i DSC krive za sve tri formulacije koje smo testirali. Dobar ishod bi bio prozor od najmanje 20°C, idealno između 125 i 145°C, uz zadržanu mogućnost lakog otvaranja.

challenges.text: We have no in-house printing capability and all our pouches are gravure-printed externally in Hungary, which adds 10–12 days to every order and makes short runs uneconomical. We want to understand whether digital inkjet printing directly on our film is technically feasible at the ink adhesion and food-contact compliance level before we invest in equipment.
challenges.detail: Trenutno svu štampu radimo gravurno kod partnera u Mađarskoj. Svaka narudžbina ide dva puta preko granice, što dodaje 10 do 12 radnih dana na svaku isporuku. Za male serije to je ekonomski neisplativo — troškovi štamparskih cilindara se ne mogu pokriti narudžbinom manjom od 15.000 metara. Sve više kupaca traži kratke serije sa promenljivim dizajnom. Razmišljamo o digitalnom inkjet štampanju direktno na naš film, ali imamo konkretne nedoumice: da li inkovi koji se koriste na PE filmovima imaju dovoljnu adheziju bez posebnog premaza, i da li ti inkovi ispunjavaju zahteve kontakta sa hranom prema EU regulativi 10/2011? Nismo još uložili ni evro u opremu — pre toga želimo da razumemo tehničku izvodljivost. Imamo uzorke filmova svih naših aktuelnih struktura i možemo da obezbedimo testne substrate. Dobar ishod bi bio jasna tehnička preporuka: da li je inkjet na PE izvodljiv za naš slučaj upotrebe, i ako jeste — koji tip tintе i eventualno koji predtretman površine.

challenges.text: Our maintenance team replaces diesel engine components on a fixed 500-hour schedule regardless of actual wear. Last year we had four unplanned engine failures mid-route; each one cost us around €14,000 in towing, delays and penalties. We collect vibration and temperature data from sensors already fitted to the engines but no one on staff knows how to use that data to predict failures before they happen.
challenges.detail:
We run twelve barges and every one of them gets its engine serviced at 500 hours, no matter what. The manual says 500 hours, so that is what we do. The problem is that four times last year an engine gave out mid-route anyway, and each incident cost us around €14,000 when you add up emergency towing, port fees, cargo delay penalties and overtime for the repair crew. That is €56,000 we did not plan for.

We already have vibration sensors and temperature probes on the main propulsion units — they were fitted during a retrofit in 2019 as part of a fuel efficiency project that never fully got off the ground. The sensors log data to a small onboard computer and we download it to USB when the barge comes into the workshop. The files are mostly CSVs. Nobody on staff has the background to do anything useful with them beyond checking whether a reading is obviously out of range.

We would like a way to look at that data and get a warning — even a rough one — that a specific engine is trending toward a problem before it actually fails. We are not looking for perfection; catching two out of four failures in advance would already pay for a reasonable project. We have two years of historical sensor logs we can share.

challenges.text: Canal water levels are dropping more often in late summer; two years ago we had to reduce barge loads by 30% for six weeks because we couldn't predict low-water events early enough to reroute cargo to trucks in time. We need a reliable 10-to-14-day low-water forecast for the DTD canal so we can plan load factors and pre-book truck capacity.
challenges.detail:
The DTD canal system is getting shallower in late summer more often than it used to. Two summers ago we had a six-week stretch where loaded barges could not safely draw more than 1.8 metres, which forced us to cut loads by about 30%. Because we did not see it coming early enough, we scrambled to book extra trucks at spot-market rates, which cost significantly more than pre-booked capacity would have.

The public hydrology services publish water-level readings and some short-range outlooks, but nothing reliable beyond three or four days, and nothing specific to the narrower canal sections where shallow water hits us first. We tried using regional rainfall forecasts ourselves but the connection between upstream rain and canal depth at our critical points is not something our dispatchers can judge reliably.

What we need is a forecast with a 10-to-14-day horizon that tells us, at the canal sections we care about, whether we are likely to face draft restrictions. That would give us enough time to call our truck subcontractors, pre-book capacity at normal rates and redistribute cargo across the combined fleet. Even a probabilistic forecast — 'there is a 70% chance of restrictions at Bečej by August 14' — would be far more useful than what we have today.

challenges.text: We employ 312 people and the payroll and HR administration still runs on spreadsheets. We are losing roughly two full working days per month just reconciling overtime records, and our HR manager is about to retire. We need to hire or buy a solution, but every ERP vendor we spoke to wants a six-figure licence up front.
challenges.detail:
HR and payroll for 312 employees — drivers, barge crews, mechanics, office staff — runs entirely on spreadsheets. Our HR manager, Gordana, has been here for 22 years and she retires in October. She is the only person who knows exactly how the overtime calculations work for canal crew rotations, which follow a different schedule from truck drivers, who in turn differ from workshop staff.

Right now we lose roughly two full working days every month just reconciling overtime records between department supervisors and the central payroll sheet. Errors get caught late, people are paid incorrectly and corrections carry into the next month.

We spoke to three ERP vendors last year. Each one quoted a licence fee between €80,000 and €140,000 before implementation and customisation, which is not something we can absorb in a single budget year. We are open to a modular or cloud-based solution, an open-source system with paid support, or even a custom-built tool if the ongoing cost is reasonable. The hard deadline is that Gordana leaves in October and whoever replaces her should not inherit a spreadsheet system that only she understands.

challenges.text: Our route optimisation engine re-solves the whole timetable overnight; when a bus breaks down at 7 AM and we need a new schedule by 7:15, the solver takes 40 minutes and dispatchers end up doing it by hand on whiteboards.
challenges.detail: TrasaNet's scheduling engine works well for overnight batch runs — it typically produces a full network timetable for a 120-bus system in about 35 minutes, which is fine when planners have hours to review the output. The problem is disruption during operations. When a vehicle breaks down or a driver calls in sick at 7 AM, we need a revised schedule for the affected lines in under fifteen minutes or dispatchers lose confidence in the tool and fall back to marker boards. Right now our solver re-optimises the full network from scratch every time, which takes around 40 minutes even on a stripped-down problem. We have tried restricting the solver to only the affected lines, but vehicle and driver constraints are coupled across the whole network so partial re-solves produce infeasible results about a third of the time. We have two backend engineers who work on the solver, and we have historical logs of roughly 1,400 past disruption events with the manual solutions dispatchers chose. We are not looking for a perfect academic solution; we need something that fits inside the existing Java codebase and produces a result dispatchers will actually trust within 15 minutes. A pilot on one customer network by the end of 2025 would be a realistic target.

challenges.text: We are collecting AVL data from 340 buses — GPS pings every 10 seconds — but we have never used it to predict travel times; three Romanian municipalities are asking for passenger information screens that show live ETAs within 90 seconds of reality.
challenges.detail: Since 2021 we have been collecting GPS pings from 340 buses every ten seconds through DataBridge AVL. The raw data sits in a PostgreSQL time-series table — roughly 2.8 billion rows at this point — and we have done almost nothing analytical with it beyond basic replay and delay logging. Three Romanian customers, the Timișoara Metropolitan Authority, the Alba Iulia Transit Office and the Reșița City Bus Consortium, have signed letters of intent for PassengerView screens at stops, but their contracts require displayed ETAs to be within 90 seconds of the bus's actual arrival at least 85 percent of the time. Our current PassengerView simply projects the published timetable plus a crude offset based on the last known GPS position. On a clear day that works. In peak-hour traffic, roadworks or bad weather it drifts badly. We have one data engineer on staff who knows Python well but has no background in time-series modelling. The AVL data includes timestamp, vehicle ID, line ID, stop sequence, door-open events and odometer. We do not have weather data integrated yet. The Romanian contracts have a twelve-month implementation window starting from go-live approval, which we expect in Q3 2024.

challenges.text: The Hungarian side of our cross-border service requires licensing under Hungarian transport law and GDPR data-residency rules that differ from Serbian regulations; our legal team has spent eight months on this and we are still not cleared to go live.
challenges.detail: Our Debrecen-area customer, the Hajdú Cross-Border Transit Consortium, operates routes that cross from Serbia into Hungary and back. Technically TrasaNet handles the scheduling without issues. The problem is legal. Hungarian transport licensing requires that certain operational records be stored on servers physically located in Hungary or the EU, while Serbian personal data law has its own requirements for driver and passenger data that conflict with the Hungarian interpretation of GDPR controller obligations. We have been working with an external legal firm in Novi Sad and a Hungarian transport law consultant since last spring. Eight months in, we have a 140-page analysis but no agreed data architecture that satisfies both regulators simultaneously. The Hajdú Consortium is losing patience — they have already delayed their new timetable season once. What we need is a concrete technical design: which data categories sit on which servers, how synchronisation works across the border, and how we log access in a way that satisfies both audit regimes. We have budget for implementation once the design is approved. Our internal team can build it; the gap is the compliant architecture specification, not the coding.

challenges.text: Our cold-pressed pumpkin seed oil goes rancid within 4 months on shelf, but competitors manage 9–12 months; we lose about 15% of each batch to returns and we have no idea what oxidation pathway is hitting us fastest.
challenges.detail: Our cold-pressed pumpkin seed oil hits a peroxide value above the acceptable threshold somewhere between three and five months after bottling, depending on the batch. We bottle into dark glass and we do a nitrogen flush, but the flush equipment is basic — a single nozzle above the fill point — and we are not sure how much residual oxygen we are actually leaving in the headspace. We have measured peroxide value on fresh oil and it is consistently below 5 meq/kg, which is fine, but by month four we are seeing values above 15. We have tried adding a small amount of rosemary extract as a natural antioxidant on two batches but saw no clear improvement. We do not have gas chromatography equipment and we have never done a fatty acid profile breakdown or a tocopherol content analysis in-house. Our lab technician, Vesna Marković, handles the routine checks but has no specialist oxidation training. We spend roughly 180,000 RSD per year on returned and written-off stock from this issue alone. A good outcome would be identifying the main oxidation pathway — whether it is enzymatic, photo-oxidative, or related to trace metals — and getting a clear set of process changes we can actually implement without buying major new equipment.

challenges.text: We press roughly 400 kg of oil per shift and the filter press is the bottleneck — it clogs every 90 minutes and cleaning takes 25 minutes each time, costing us almost a full shift per week.
challenges.detail: Our filter press handles the crude oil after pressing and it is the single point in the line that limits how much we can produce per shift. The press has eighteen plates and it clogs with seed meal fines roughly every ninety minutes of operation. Each cleaning cycle takes about twenty to twenty-five minutes — manually opening the press, removing the filter cloths, scraping residue, rinsing, and reassembling. Across a six-day working week that adds up to roughly one full eight-hour shift lost purely to cleaning. We have tried pre-filtering through a vibrating sieve before the oil reaches the press, which reduced clogging frequency slightly but did not solve it. We have also experimented with different filter cloth grades from two suppliers — one domestic, one sourced from Hungary — but the improvement was marginal. The crude oil temperature coming off the press varies between 28°C and 38°C depending on ambient temperature and seed moisture, and we suspect this variability affects the viscosity and therefore the filtration rate, but we have not been able to test this properly. We are open to continuous filtration alternatives or a redesigned pre-clarification stage. Budget for equipment is limited — we could justify up to around 20,000 euros if the payback is under two years.

challenges.text: We want to enter the German organic retail market but our current EU organic certification application has been sitting with the certifier for 11 months and we cannot figure out how to move it forward.
challenges.detail: We applied for EU organic certification through a certified body, Öko-Control GmbH based in Germany, eleven months ago. The application covers our pumpkin seed and camelina oil lines. We have submitted our farm supplier list, our cleaning and separation protocols, and our input material declarations. Since the initial submission we have had two rounds of written questions from the certifier and we have answered both, but the file has been sitting without a decision for the last five months. We suspect the sticking point is our shared production line — we press conventional sunflower on the same equipment — and the parallel processing protocol we submitted may not have been detailed enough. We have one person, our export coordinator Ivana Đurić, handling all correspondence, but she does not have a background in organic regulation and is finding it difficult to interpret what exactly the certifier needs. We have a tentative agreement with a German importer, Naturkost Havel GmbH, that they will place a trial order once certification is granted, but they have indicated they cannot wait past the end of this calendar year. A good outcome is either getting the certificate issued or getting a concrete list of what we still need to fix and a realistic timeline.

challenges.text: Our ground-penetrating radar surveys on urban roads return raw B-scan images that our operators interpret visually; we miss about one in five utility pipes because operators disagree on what they see, and one missed gas pipe last year caused a major incident on a construction site.
challenges.detail: Every GPR survey on an urban road produces a stack of B-scan slices, and right now a trained operator sits down and draws lines on screen based on what looks like a hyperbola. Two operators looking at the same scan will sometimes disagree on whether a feature is a gas pipe, a water main, a cable duct, or just a tree root. We estimate we miss roughly one in five utilities this way, based on comparing our maps against later excavation findings on twenty completed projects over the past three years. Last spring a crew on a road-widening job in Subotica hit an undetected medium-pressure gas pipe; the incident shut the site for nine days and cost us and the contractor a combined settlement we do not want to repeat. We have tried stricter operator checklists and mandatory second-pass review, which helped a little but did not close the gap. We have raw B-scan files going back to 2017 on an internal server, roughly 4 terabytes, much of it from sites where the ground truth is now known from excavation. What we want is a reliable automated detection layer that flags probable pipe locations and gives the operator a confidence score, so disagreements can be escalated rather than silently dropped.

challenges.text: We have twelve years of GNSS base-station data from our network of five permanent reference stations across northern Vojvodina, but we are not using it for anything beyond standard RTK corrections; we suspect there is value in the data for subsidence monitoring or infrastructure deformation tracking, but we don't know how to start.
challenges.detail: Since 2012 we have logged continuous RINEX observation data from five permanent reference stations placed across northern Vojvodina, mainly Subotica, Kanjiža, Senta, Ada, and Bečej. The stations were built to provide RTK corrections for our field crews and for a handful of licensed subscribers, and that is still their primary job. But twelve years of daily position solutions sitting on a RAID array feels like a resource we are not using. We have heard that networks like this can detect millimetre-level ground movement over time, which would be directly relevant to monitoring road embankments, canal levees, and the older building stock in our area, some of which sits on unstable loess. We downloaded one academic paper on GNSS time-series analysis and quickly ran into processing steps we did not understand. We have the raw RINEX data, station metadata, and antenna calibration logs. We do not have geodetic software licences beyond what we use for RTK processing, and we do not have staff with a background in time-series statistics. A practical outcome would be a pilot report showing whether any of our five stations show a detectable trend, with a workflow we could apply ourselves going forward.

challenges.text: Cross-border projects with Hungarian clients require us to produce deliverables in the Hungarian unified national projection system (EOV), but our Serbian-licensed surveyors are not certified under Hungarian geodetic regulations, which means we must always subcontract the final certification to a Hungarian firm at a cost of roughly 8 percent per project.
challenges.detail: Hungarian infrastructure clients need deliverables in the EOV projection with Hungarian cadastral reference numbers and a certification stamp from a surveyor licensed under the Hungarian chamber of civil engineers. Our Serbian-licensed staff cannot provide that stamp, even when every measurement was taken by us with our own instruments. The practical result is that on every cross-border project we subcontract the final certification package to a small Hungarian geodetic firm based in Szeged, Térkép és Terep Kft., and we pay them roughly eight percent of project value for review and stamping work that adds no technical content. Over the last financial year that came to approximately 14 000 EUR in margin we handed over. We have looked at whether one of our surveyors could pursue Hungarian chamber registration, but the process requires a Hungarian university degree or a separate recognition procedure that our legal team estimates would take two to three years. What we are looking for is either a faster regulatory path we have not found yet, or a technical and documentation workflow so clean and standardised that it reduces the review time the Hungarian firm charges us for, even if we cannot eliminate the subcontract entirely.

challenges.text: Our digital-twin models for Italian factory clients run 15–20× slower than real time because the physics solvers aren't parallelised — operators can't use them for live decision support and three prospects declined for exactly this reason.
challenges.detail: Our digital-twin models for Italian factory clients are built around finite-element and finite-difference solvers written in C++. On a modern workstation they run at roughly 1/15th to 1/20th of real time, meaning a ten-minute process takes three hours to simulate. That was acceptable when clients used the models offline for planning, but over the past two years clients have started asking for live decision support — they want to run what-if scenarios while the plant is operating. We cannot do that at current speed. We have tried reducing mesh resolution and simplifying boundary conditions, but accuracy drops to a level clients reject. We have not yet attempted GPU acceleration or domain decomposition for parallel CPU runs, partly because none of our current developers have done that kind of work before. Three serious prospects in the Lombardy region have cited simulation speed as the reason they did not sign. We need the solver to run at or above real time on a server with up to 32 CPU cores or a mid-range GPU. We have the solver source code, the test cases and two Italian client environments we could use for benchmarking.

challenges.text: A French aerospace supplier wants us to add vibration fatigue analysis to our mechanical digital twin, but we have no in-house expertise in structural dynamics — we'd need to either hire or partner fast because the tender closes in 90 days.
challenges.detail: A French aerospace supplier, Atelier Delambre SAS, is putting out a tender for an extended digital-twin platform that would include vibration fatigue analysis of structural components — brackets, housings, mounting frames. We have a mechanical digital twin running for them already, covering static loads and thermal behaviour, and they want to extend it rather than start over with a different vendor. The problem is that vibration fatigue is a specialised area. It involves frequency-response analysis, S-N curve databases, possibly Rainflow counting for variable-amplitude loads, and knowledge of aerospace fatigue standards that none of our engineers currently hold. We have looked at adding a commercial fatigue solver as a licensed module but the integration work and licensing cost are a problem at this stage. The tender deadline is 90 days from now. We would need a partner or consultant who could either build the module with us or advise our developers intensively over that period. The deliverable is a working prototype that Atelier Delambre can evaluate; it does not need to be fully certified at that stage.

challenges.text: We visualise simulation results in a 3D web viewer but rendering complex factory layouts with 200,000+ mesh elements crashes browsers on mid-range company laptops — about 40% of our end users can't view the full model.
challenges.detail: Our 3D web viewer is built on Three.js and renders factory geometry exported from CAD as mesh files. For simple layouts with under 50,000 elements it works well on ordinary laptops. When we load full factory models — 200,000 elements or more — the browser runs out of memory or the frame rate drops below one frame per second on mid-range machines. We know this because we collected browser performance logs from 60 end users at three client sites; about 40 percent of those users are on laptops with integrated graphics and 8 GB of RAM. We have tried geometry instancing for repeated objects and LOD switching based on camera distance, and those changes helped somewhat but not enough for the worst cases. We have not yet tried progressive mesh loading, geometry compression formats like Draco or KTX2, or offloading rendering to a server-side renderer and streaming video to the client. We are uncertain which of these directions gives the best result without requiring a full rewrite of the viewer. A good outcome would be that users on 8 GB integrated-graphics machines can navigate the full model without crashing.

challenges.text: Our Slovenian clients are asking us to include a worker ergonomics assessment module in the digital twin — we know nothing about ergonomics standards and don't know whether this is an engineering or a medical problem.
challenges.detail: Two of our Slovenian manufacturing clients — both running assembly lines with significant manual handling — have asked whether their digital twin can include an ergonomics assessment layer. The idea is that when a workstation layout or process sequence changes in the model, the system would flag potential ergonomic risk. We have had two conversations with their health and safety teams and we understand the general request, but we do not know enough to scope it. We do not know whether the relevant standards are ISO, EN or something sector-specific. We do not know whether a software model of posture and movement is a medical device under current EU regulation or an engineering tool. We do not know what input data the model would need — motion capture, video, manual measurements — or what a defensible output looks like. We need someone who understands both the standards and the practical measurement side to help us decide whether this is feasible for us to build, what it would require, and how to respond to the clients with a realistic offer. The Slovenian clients are long-standing accounts and we do not want to lose the relationship by giving a vague or wrong answer.

challenges.text: Our platform generates executable workflow scripts from user-drawn diagrams, but users in logistics companies keep building loops that deadlock under real load — support tickets about frozen workflows went from 12 to 67 per month in six months.
challenges.detail: FlowDeck lets users draw diagrams that become running automations. The engine walks through steps and fires actions — send email, update shipment status, call a carrier API. The problem is that users keep building loops with no safe exit: a step that waits for a carrier confirmation can loop back to itself if the confirmation never arrives, and under real production load those loops pile up and starve the worker pool. Six months ago we were getting about 12 support tickets a month about frozen workflows. Last month we had 67. We added a basic loop counter that kills a workflow after 100 iterations, but that just breaks legitimate retry logic and upsets customers. We have tried documenting best practices and adding warnings in the canvas, but users ignore them. We have all the execution logs and the diagram graphs for every frozen workflow — roughly 340 documented incidents. What we actually need is either a way to detect deadlock-prone patterns before a workflow goes live, or a smarter runtime that can detect starvation and handle it without killing the workflow. We have one senior backend engineer who can own this full-time starting next quarter. We need a workable solution before our next client renewal cycle in Q3 2025.

challenges.text: German logistics clients want their dispatchers to see a live map of vehicle positions and predicted ETAs inside our platform, but integrating GPS telemetry from five different telematics vendors is taking our team six months per vendor.
challenges.detail: Several of our German clients want their dispatchers to see where vehicles are and get predicted arrival times directly inside FlowDeck, without switching to a separate tracking tool. We built FlowDeck Live to provide that view. The technical problem is that the telematics market in Germany and the Benelux is fragmented — each carrier or fleet operator uses a different vendor, and every vendor has a different API design, authentication method, data format, and polling behaviour. We have finished integrations with two vendors so far and each one took our team roughly six months. We have three more on the list that clients are actively waiting for. At that pace we will not close the remaining integrations before the end of 2025, and two clients have told us directly that they will not renew if the map feature does not cover their carriers. We have tried reading vendor documentation and contacting developer support, but the documentation quality varies widely and support response times are slow. We have two developers who can work on integrations part-time. What we need is either a faster integration methodology, a normalisation layer that reduces per-vendor work, or access to someone who already knows these vendor APIs.

challenges.text: We pitch to EU clients in English but our two founders speak with heavy accents and lose deals at the demo stage — we need professional sales training and presentation coaching, not more engineering.
challenges.detail: Both of our founders run sales demos for prospective clients in Germany and the Benelux. The platform itself performs well in demos — prospects generally like what they see. The problem is that after demos with competitors, we are losing deals at a rate that our pipeline data does not fully explain by product gaps alone. We have collected feedback from three lost deals and in each case the client mentioned communication clarity as a factor. Our founders are strong engineers and know the product well, but English is not their first language and the accent and pacing make it harder for German and Dutch procurement teams to follow a 45-minute technical demo. We do not need help with the product. We need structured coaching on spoken presentation delivery, handling objections in a second language, and running demos that move a cautious logistics buyer toward a decision. We have a modest budget — roughly €4,000 — and would prefer a programme that can be delivered in short sessions over two to three months rather than a single workshop. A good outcome is that both founders can run a full demo confidently and close at a higher rate than the current 18 percent.

challenges.text: Our web portals need to support Hungarian, Slovak and Serbian simultaneously, and machine-translated UI strings often sound unnatural or confuse users — we had one Slovak client ask for a full refund over mistranslated checkout labels.
challenges.detail: We maintain portals and shop fronts in Hungarian, Slovak and Serbian at the same time. For a while we tried speeding up the translation step by running UI strings through a machine translation service and then having our translators do a light review. That broke down badly last year when a Slovak grocery client's checkout page rendered 'shipping address' as something closer to 'delivery declaration' — a handful of customers thought they were signing a customs form and abandoned their carts. One client demanded a refund for the entire integration project. We have since gone back to full human translation, but that adds four to seven days to every release and costs us roughly 300 to 500 euros per project depending on volume. We have two part-time translators on staff, but they are already at capacity. What we want is a way to catch mistranslations or awkward phrasings automatically before a build goes to the client, something that works specifically on short UI strings in these three languages. We are not chasing perfect literary quality; we just need a reliable filter for embarrassing errors. Budget for a working tool or integration is under 8 000 euros.

challenges.text: We want to add a product recommendation widget to our e-commerce clients' stores, but with only 500–2,000 transactions per client the collaborative filtering models we tried give worse results than simple best-seller sorting.
challenges.detail: Several of our e-commerce clients have asked us to add a 'you might also like' widget to their product pages. We tried building a standard collaborative filtering model last autumn using transaction logs from three clients. The largest dataset had 1 900 completed orders over eighteen months; the smallest had around 520. The models we trained gave recommendations that were either obvious — recommending the best-sellers regardless of what the user was viewing — or simply wrong, suggesting unrelated items because the purchase co-occurrence matrix was too sparse to be useful. We ended up shipping nothing and telling the clients to wait. Simple best-seller sorting actually outperformed the model in our A/B test on the one client where we got far enough to test. We do not have the budget or the traffic to wait for larger datasets. We want to understand whether there is a sensible approach — maybe content-based signals from product descriptions or category metadata, maybe some kind of hybrid — that would give meaningfully better results than a best-seller list on catalogs this small. A working prototype for one client would be enough to start. We can give a collaborator full read access to anonymised transaction and product catalogue data.

challenges.text: We need a line of credit to buy out a competing studio in Subotica, but our bank says our retained earnings are too low and wants three years of audited accounts — we only have two.
challenges.detail: There is a small development studio in Subotica, five people, that we have been in informal talks with for several months. Acquiring them would give us capacity we need and remove a local competitor that has been undercutting our quotes. The asking price is manageable, but we need a line of credit to cover it without draining our operating reserves. Our bank has so far declined because we can only produce two years of fully audited financial statements — they want three as a minimum condition. Our retained earnings are real but modest; we have never needed external financing before. We are exploring whether a development grant, an NTP-linked instrument or a guarantee scheme could bridge the gap or give the bank enough comfort to proceed. We would also consider a silent equity partner for a minority share if the terms were straightforward. We want to close this within twelve months before the other studio finds a different buyer.

challenges.text: We are designing more timber-frame residential buildings because clients are asking for them, but our engineers trained on reinforced concrete and we keep having to outsource the structural calculations for glulam connections, which adds two to three weeks to each project and cuts our margin by about 18 percent.
challenges.detail: Over the past two years roughly one in three new residential projects we take on involves a timber frame or glulam elements. Clients see these buildings in magazines or talk to neighbours who had one built and they come to us expecting us to handle it. Our engineers are solid on reinforced concrete and masonry but timber connection design, especially glulam moment connections and notched joints, is not something we built internal skill for. Every time we hit that part of a project we subcontract the connection calculations to a specialist in Novi Sad. That adds between two and three weeks to the delivery timeline and we pay around 1,200 to 1,800 euros per project for it, which on a typical small house project eats about 18 percent of our fee. We have tried to train our junior engineers using manuals and one attended a two-day Eurocode 5 seminar last year, but without dedicated software and someone to check their work the first few times we are not confident enough to sign off on it ourselves. What we want is a reliable calculation workflow our engineers can actually use, not just a course.

challenges.text: Several of our older buildings designed in the 1990s are now being sold or refinanced and banks are demanding seismic vulnerability assessments, but doing a full assessment by hand for a four-storey masonry building takes our senior engineer almost a week and we have a backlog of eleven buildings right now.
challenges.detail: Banks and notaries have started asking for seismic vulnerability reports before they process sales or refinancing on buildings put up before 2000. We understand why but for us it means a lot of manual work. Our senior engineer, Zoran Petrović, does these assessments almost entirely by hand using a method we adapted from national guidelines, walking the building, measuring wall thicknesses, checking floor connections and then running calculations in a spreadsheet we built ourselves. For a typical four-storey unreinforced masonry block that is between four and five working days of his time. We currently have eleven buildings waiting. Zoran cannot take on new design work while he is doing assessments and that is creating delays across other projects. We have looked at commercial software packages but the ones we found are priced for larger consultancies or research institutes. We have drawings and field notes for all eleven buildings and good data on local ground conditions. A faster, structured workflow that could bring assessment time down even to two days per building would clear our backlog within two months and let Zoran return to design work.

challenges.text: We lost two experienced structural engineers in the last eighteen months to firms in Germany and Austria and cannot fill the positions locally; the salary we can offer is simply not competitive with what Western European firms advertise, even remotely.
challenges.detail: In the last eighteen months two of our experienced engineers left for positions in Germany and Austria. One had eight years with us. We have advertised through the usual job boards and through the civil engineering faculty notice board without success. The candidates we see are either very junior, still in their final year, or they are experienced and expecting salaries we cannot match. A Western European firm offering remote or hybrid work can pay two to three times what we can offer and candidates know it. We have one open position now and another that will open when our current site supervisor retires at the end of 2025. We are willing to invest in mentoring and in covering licensing exam fees. We are also open to part-time or project-based arrangements if that is what it takes to bring in specific expertise on timber and seismic work. This is not a short-term crisis we can manage by working overtime; it is a structural problem for the firm that will affect our ability to take on projects within two years if nothing changes.

challenges.text: Our platform lets users upload financial reports in five languages but the automatic cross-language consistency checker produces about 30% false positives when the same budget line is named differently in Hungarian and Croatian — clients stopped trusting it and switched back to manual checks.
challenges.detail: Our consistency checker compares budget line labels and figures across documents uploaded in different languages. The core problem is that Hungarian and Croatian grant terminology does not map one-to-one: a line called 'személyi jellegű kiadások' in Hungarian might appear as 'troškovi osoblja' or 'izdaci za zaposlene' in Croatian depending on which managing authority issued the template. Our current approach uses a bilingual glossary we built manually, plus a spaCy similarity model we fine-tuned on about 1,200 labelled pairs. That gets us to roughly 70% precision, but the 30% false-positive rate means clients get flagged warnings on correct reports. We ran a small test with three clients last autumn where we raised the similarity threshold — false positives dropped but we started missing real errors. We have about 4,000 labelled budget-line pairs collected from real submissions and two developers with NLP experience who can work on this. We cannot spend more than two to three months of developer time on a solution that might not hold, so we need a more principled approach before we invest further. A good outcome would be consistent precision above 90% on our existing test set.

challenges.text: We need to raise a €400k seed round by Q1 next year to fund the next 18 months of development, but we've only spoken to two regional angel investors and neither has moved in three months.
challenges.detail: We need roughly €400,000 in seed funding to cover eighteen months of development, one additional senior developer, and the cost of obtaining legal opinions on e-signature compliance across three jurisdictions. Our current runway is about seven months based on subscription revenue of around €11,000 per month and a small grant we received from the Provincial Secretariat for Economy last year. We have spoken to two angel investors — one based in Novi Sad, one in Budapest — and both expressed interest initially but neither has responded to follow-ups in the past three months. We have not yet approached any VC funds or EU innovation programmes such as EIC Accelerator, partly because neither of us has done a fundraising process before and we are unsure how to prepare the materials. We are also open to grant instruments if the timelines are realistic. The hard constraint is Q1 next year: if we do not close something by then, we will need to reduce the team.

challenges.text: EU clients want a built-in audit trail that is legally admissible as an electronic record in any member state, and we have no idea how to structure our database logging to satisfy that requirement across different national e-signature laws.
challenges.detail: Several clients — particularly the municipalities — have asked whether our audit trail would hold up if a managing authority challenged a submission and the case ended up in an administrative or legal proceeding. Right now we log every document upload, field edit, user action, and export to a PostgreSQL table with timestamps and user IDs. We hash each log entry and chain the hashes, similar to a simple linked structure. What we do not know is whether that structure, combined with a qualified electronic timestamp or signature, actually satisfies admissibility requirements in Serbia, Hungary, and Croatia as electronic records. Each country has transposed the eIDAS regulation differently, and Serbia is not an EU member state, which adds another layer. We have read the eIDAS regulation text and looked at one Croatian technical standard, but we do not have legal or technical expertise in this area. We cannot afford a full legal review in three countries at our current stage, so we are looking for guidance on the technical requirements first — what the database structure and signing process should look like — so we can then get a targeted legal opinion rather than an open-ended one.

challenges.text: We scan patients with a structured-light scanner and generate the orthosis geometry in CAD, but the automatic fitting algorithm adds about 3 mm of clearance everywhere as a safety margin — experienced orthotists say this is too conservative and causes pressure sores in roughly 1 in 8 devices, which come back for rework at an average cost of €180 each.
challenges.detail: When we scan a patient's limb and generate the orthosis shell in OrthoFlow Studio, the software automatically adds a 3 mm clearance offset around the entire geometry before sending the file to print. The idea was to prevent the shell from pressing directly on bony prominences, but in practice it is far too uniform — a flat section of the shin needs almost no clearance, while a malleolus might genuinely need some. Our senior orthotists have been telling us this for two years. The result is that roughly one in eight finished devices comes back to us for rework because the patient develops a pressure point or the fit is loose enough to cause pistoning. We log every return and the average cost to correct and reprint is about €180 per item. Across last year's output that adds up to a significant sum. We have the scan data and the rework logs for roughly 1,400 devices going back to 2019, and we can map which zones on which device types come back most often. What we need is a smarter offset rule — or ideally a way to vary the clearance based on local geometry and tissue type — so that we can cut that one-in-eight rate down considerably. We have no hard deadline but want to pilot something within twelve months.

challenges.text: We print in PA12 nylon and the finished parts look fine visually, but we're failing fatigue tests at around 180,000 cycles when the spec requires 500,000 — we've tried adjusting infill density from 60% to 80% with no consistent improvement and we don't understand why.
challenges.detail: We print load-bearing components in PA12 nylon on four FDM machines and we run every batch through a fatigue test on our in-house servo rig before shipping. The test protocol calls for 500,000 cycles at the relevant load. We are consistently failing somewhere around 180,000 cycles, and the fractures almost always initiate at layer boundaries rather than in the bulk material. We increased infill density from 60% to 80% and saw no reliable improvement — some batches got marginally better, some got worse. We have tried adjusting print temperature by plus or minus 10°C and slowing the print speed on the final outer perimeters, again with no consistent result. We keep print logs for every job — temperature, speed, layer height, humidity in the print room — but we do not have the materials science background to know which parameters actually drive inter-layer bonding strength in PA12 specifically. We also don't know whether the problem is in the filament storage (we keep it in a drying cabinet at 65°C), the machine calibration or the geometry of the test piece itself. We need someone to look at our process data and our test results and tell us what is actually driving the failures, then work with us on a fix. Budget is modest — we are not buying new machines — but we are open to process changes.

challenges.text: We want to expand into the German market — three orthopaedic supply chains have asked us for quotes — but our export pricing is based on guesswork because we don't know what the real logistics and customs costs add up to, and our last two tenders came in 18% above what the buyer expected.
challenges.detail: Three orthopaedic supply companies in Germany have approached us for quotes on batches of custom orthotic shells and prosthetic sockets. This would be our first real export outside the former Yugoslav markets and we want to take it seriously. The problem is that our export pricing is built on rough estimates — we know our production cost well enough, but we have no reliable model for what freight, customs classification, VAT handling, packaging compliance and delivery lead time actually add to the final price when shipping to Germany. On our last two submitted tenders we came in about 18% above what the buyer expected, and in both cases we lost the contract. We don't know if the gap was in logistics costs, in the customs duty rate we assumed, or somewhere else entirely. We have the tender documents and the buyer feedback from both lost bids. We need a clear cost breakdown model that we can apply to future quotes — ideally a simple tool our sales coordinator can use — so that we stop pricing ourselves out of a market where we believe our product quality is competitive. We have a part-time export coordinator with general trade experience but no specific knowledge of medical device export to EU markets.

challenges.text: We want to introduce real-time process monitoring on our four FDM printers — specifically layer-delamination detection — but we only have a basic webcam on each machine and our team has never worked with computer vision before.
challenges.detail: Layer delamination is our most common print defect and it is almost always invisible from the outside until the part is loaded in use or on the fatigue rig. We want to catch it during the print rather than after. Each of our four FDM machines has a basic USB webcam mounted to watch the bed, installed two years ago mostly for remote monitoring. We generate about 12 hours of footage per machine per day and nobody watches it — there is simply no time. We believe the footage contains useful information: delamination often causes a visible warping or edge-lift on the layer being deposited, and sometimes a colour change where the material is not fusing correctly. But our production team has never done any image processing work and we have no data science background in-house. We also have no labelled dataset of what a delamination event looks like on camera, though we could go back through footage from batches we later found to be defective and try to create one. The constraint is that we cannot replace the webcams with something expensive right now — if the approach works, we would invest in better hardware in a second phase. A good outcome would be an alert system that flags a possible delamination event and pauses the machine so an operator can check, even if there are false positives in the early stages.

challenges.text: We are cutting and bending 3 mm galvanized steel all day, and our press-brake operators are writing down bend angles by hand on paper sheets — we lose about 2 hours per shift just on rework because someone misread a spec or the worn tooling shifted the springback by 3–4 degrees. We need a way to compensate for springback automatically so first-part-good rate goes above 95%.
challenges.detail: Radimo pretežno sa galvanizovanim limom debljine 3 mm i svakodnevno se borimo sa preskočnim uglom — opruga materijala koji se vraća posle savijanja. Naši operateri press-kočnice beleže uglove na papirnim listovima i ručno podešavaju kompenzaciju na osnovu iskustva. Problem je što se alatni set istroši, gornja matrica malo popusti, i odjednom isti ugao daje odstupanje od 3 do 4 stepena u odnosu na prethodni dan. Rezultat: komada koji ne odgovaraju mernoj toleranciji šaljemo nazad na savijanje, ponekad i dva-tri puta. Procenili smo da gubimo oko dva sata po smeni samo na tu vrstu dorade. Imali smo jednog mlađeg tehničara koji je pokušao da napravi Excel tabelu za kompenzaciju, ali nije uzimao u obzir promene temperature u hali niti stepen istrošenosti alata. Kupili smo jedan digitalni kutomer, ali operateri ga ne koriste redovno jer usporava tok. Hteli bismo da dođemo do automatskog sistema koji čita stvarni ugao na mašini i predlaže korekciju pre nego što se komad skine sa alata — da stopa prvog dobrog dela bude iznad 95 procenata bez zavisnosti od ličnog iskustva operatera.

challenges.text: We have 14 welding stations and our energy bill jumped 38% last year; we know TIG and MIG arcs draw a lot but we have no idea which stations or which parts of the shift are burning the most — we just get one monthly invoice from the utility and we can't justify a retooling plan without knowing where the waste is.
challenges.detail: Imamo 14 zavarivačkih stanica i prošle godine je račun za struju porastao za 38 odsto u odnosu na godinu pre. Znamo da TIG i MIG lukovi troše znatno, ali ne možemo da kažemo koja stanica troši najviše niti u kom delu smene dolazi do najvećih vršnih opterećenja. Sa distributera dobijamo jednu mesečnu fakturu za celokupnu halu — u njoj nema nikakve podele po potrošačima.
