Pokušali smo da pratimo vreme rada po dnevnicima, ali zavarivači nisu dosledni u beleženju. Bez konkretnih podataka ne možemo da kažemo finansijskom direktoru koliko bismo uštedeli ako prebacimo dve najstarije stanice na noviji aparat sa inverterskom tehnologijom ili ako uvedemo raspored smena koji razmazuje vršne sate. Jedini kapital koji smo spremi da uložimo odmah jeste postavljanje mernih uređaja — ali ne znamo koji tip podmerne opreme kupiti niti kako da iz tih podataka izvučemo korisne zaključke koji bi opravdali konkretnu investiciju u rok od godinu dana.

challenges.text: We want to hire two CNC programmers who know SolidWorks CAM but there is nobody with that profile in Zrenjanin, and the two candidates from Novi Sad we interviewed want salaries we simply cannot pay right now.
challenges.detail: Firma raste i već smo kupili licencu za SolidWorks, ali nam nedostaju CNC programeri koji znaju da rade u SolidWorks CAM okruženju i koji razumeju specifičnosti savijanja i rezanja lima. U Zrenjaninu jednostavno nema kandidata sa tim profilom — proverili smo na Infostud-u i direktno kontaktirali bivše studente koji su radili praksu kod nas, ali niko od njih nije koristio CAM moduo. Dva kandidata iz Novog Sada su imala odgovarajuće znanje, ali su tražili platu koja je za 40 odsto iznad onoga što trenutno možemo da ponudimo u skladu sa sistematizacijom radnih mesta. Razmišljamo o alternativama: prekvalifikacija nekog od postojećih tehničara, saradnja sa školom tehnike u Zrenjaninu ili forma povremene usluge od spoljnog saradnika. Nemamo budžet za dugoročno visoko plaćenu poziciju, ali nam treba neko ko može da odradi programiranje za bar dva nova tipa dela mesečno i da obučava ostatak tima u hodu.

challenges.text: Our zinc-bath hot-dip galvanizing line produces a rough 'ash inclusion' surface defect on roughly 1 in 20 batches when the steel has higher silicon content; customers in the agricultural-equipment sector are rejecting those parts and we are taking a 12% scrap rate on affected runs.
challenges.detail: Naša toplo-pocinkovalna linija radi na temperaturi cink-kupatila oko 450 stepeni Celzijusa. Problem nastaje kada čelik u šarži ima viši sadržaj silicijuma — otprilike svaka dvadesetа šarža izlazi sa hrapavim uključcima pepela na površini, što stručno zovemo 'pepelasti uključci' ili ash inclusion. Kupci iz segmenta poljoprivrednih mašina — posebno oni koji naručuju konzole i okvire za kombajne — takve delove odbijaju jer vidljivi defekt stvara utisak loše korozivne zaštite, čak i kada je funkcionalna zaštita i dalje adekvatna. Na pogođenim šaržama imamo oko 12 odsto škarta, što direktno ide na naš trošak jer smo mi ti koji ocinkujemo. Pokušali smo da pre uranjanja primenimo fluksno sredstvo na bazi amonijum-hlorida u većoj koncentraciji, ali to nije rešilo problem konzistentno. Ne vršimo hemijsku analizu ulaznog materijala jer nemamo opremu za to, pa ne možemo unapred da izdvojimo šarže sa problematičnim silicijumom. Hteli bismo da pronađemo pouzdan i jeftin način da identifikujemo rizične šarže pre pocinkavanja ili da prilagodimo parametre procesa kada je silicijum povišen.

challenges.text: Our forklift-operator training simulator needs to model realistic load physics — right now a pallet on the forks behaves like it's glued on, and clients in the warehousing sector say their trainees are surprised by real load shift when they move to actual machines.
challenges.detail: In our StackSim Pro simulator, pallets on the forklift forks are currently treated as a rigid attachment to the mast — they do not shift, tip, or slide regardless of acceleration, cornering speed, or load height. Clients running warehouse-training programmes have told us their trainees consistently under-estimate how unstable an elevated load is, and that this is causing near-miss incidents when those trainees move to real machines for the first time. We have tried adjusting PhysX joint parameters and adding a simple centre-of-mass offset model, but the results either look physically wrong or introduce jitter that breaks immersion. We have access to a test forklift at a partner warehouse in Šid that we can use for reference recordings. The constraint is performance: the simulator must run at 60 fps on a mid-range workstation used in training centres, so any physics solution cannot be computationally expensive. We would like a model that captures at least the most dangerous failure modes — forward tip when stopping hard with a high load, and lateral slip when cornering — and that a qualified trainer would consider realistic enough to pass a client review.

challenges.text: We want to track trainee gaze during simulated tasks to identify where attention breaks down before an error occurs — we have the eye-tracking hardware but no one on the team knows how to turn scanpath data into a meaningful performance score.
challenges.detail: We have integrated Tobii eye-tracking glasses into our StackSim Pro and LiftSim setups. The hardware works and we can export raw gaze coordinates and fixation events as CSV files. What we cannot do is turn those files into anything actionable. Right now an instructor watches a replay and makes a judgement call, which is inconsistent and slow. We want a scoring method that can flag, for a given task segment, whether a trainee's gaze pattern is associated with elevated error risk — for example, not checking the load before lifting, or fixating on the forks rather than the path ahead. We have about 14 months of archived session data: roughly 340 recorded sessions across two simulator titles, each with matched outcome data showing whether an error event occurred. We have a Python environment and someone who can run scripts, but no one with a background in signal processing or behavioural data modelling. The output needs to be a numeric score or a simple flag that the TraceBoard dashboard can display — it does not need to be publishable research, it needs to work reliably enough that a trainer trusts it.

challenges.text: Our biggest construction-sector client wants the simulator to render believable dust, smoke, and concrete-particle effects in real time on mid-range laptops — our current particle system tanks the frame rate below 30 fps as soon as more than two machines are working simultaneously.
challenges.detail: Construction-sector clients expect to see realistic environmental effects — dust raised by earthmoving, diesel exhaust, concrete spray from cutting tools, and smoke from site equipment. Our current implementation uses Unity's built-in particle system, and it performs adequately with a single machine running. The moment a second or third machine is active, the combined particle count drops frame rate below 30 fps on the laptops our clients deploy in training rooms — typically machines with integrated or entry-level discrete graphics. We cannot require clients to upgrade their hardware; that has been a non-starter in every sales conversation. We have tried culling particles aggressively by distance and reducing emitter rates, but the visual result then looks sparse and clients push back. We have a dedicated graphics programmer who is competent in Unity's shader pipeline but has not worked with GPU-instanced particle systems or compute-shader approaches before. We are looking for a technical approach that keeps visual density in the acceptable range while fitting within the hardware budget of those machines. A target of stable 45 fps with three machines active, on a laptop with an integrated graphics chip from the last four years, would satisfy client requirements.

challenges.text: We need to certify our crane-operator simulator module against a European vocational training standard and the certification body is asking for a formal validation study with a control group — we have no budget to run this ourselves and don't know which institution would accept it as a research collaboration.
challenges.detail: We are in conversation with a certification body about validating our LiftSim crane-operator module against a European vocational training standard for equipment operators. The body has indicated they will accept a formal validation study in place of a longer field trial, provided the study uses a control group design and is conducted by an institution that can sign off on the methodology. We do not have the budget or the staff capacity to design and run such a study ourselves — our team is engineers and artists, not researchers. We also do not know which institutions have run this type of study before and would be interested in it as a research collaboration rather than a paid contract. The timeline matters: the certification would unlock a public-procurement category that our largest construction client has asked us to meet before their next framework tender, which closes in approximately 18 months. A good outcome would be a signed collaboration agreement with an institution willing to design the study, recruit participants, and produce a report that meets the certification body's documentation requirements.

challenges.text: Our sensor nodes run on coin-cell batteries and we promise 5-year lifetime, but field data from two Austrian clients shows 28% of units drop below threshold voltage before 30 months — we have no model that predicts which units will fail early so we can adjust the BOM before the next production run.
challenges.detail: Our VN-4x nodes are sold with a five-year battery life guarantee under a defined duty cycle. We size the power budget carefully and the median unit in the field is fine, but last year two Austrian integrators — Brauer Systemtechnik and Feldergruppe — sent us field data showing that 28% of units from two specific production batches (Q3 2022 and Q1 2023) had dropped below 2.0 V before 30 months. We pulled production records and we have component lot numbers, reflow temperature logs, and cell supplier certificates for those batches. We also have cell voltage telemetry from about 1,400 live units. What we do not have is a model that can look at early voltage-drop curves or production metadata and tell us which units are likely to fail ahead of schedule. If we could identify that pattern, we could change the cell supplier or adjust the BOM before we run the next 5,000-unit batch in Q4 2024. We have the data; we do not have the statistical or machine-learning background to build something reliable from it in time.

challenges.text: We are sampling a new sub-GHz mesh radio stack from a Taiwanese supplier, but our internal RF team of two people cannot do a full regulatory pre-compliance test for CE RED before we commit to 10,000 units — last time we skipped this step we had to respin the antenna matching network and lost four months.
challenges.detail: We are evaluating a new sub-GHz mesh radio module from a Taiwanese supplier, Suncore Wireless, as a potential replacement for the module we have used since 2018 — the old part is going end-of-life. The Suncore module looks good on paper and samples have worked on the bench, but before we commit to a 10,000-unit order we need to do a pre-compliance check against CE RED radiated emissions and receiver blocking requirements. Our RF team is two engineers. They are capable people, but running a proper pre-compliance campaign — antenna matching verification, conducted and radiated spurious checks, duty-cycle compliance — takes equipment and time we do not have in-house. We rented chamber time once before and did it ourselves, but we missed an antenna matching issue that only showed up in the accredited lab, and that respun the whole antenna network and delayed the product launch by four months. We want someone with RF measurement experience to either run the pre-compliance tests with us or review our test plan and point out where we are likely to have trouble before we book the accredited lab.

challenges.text: Our gateway firmware does TLS 1.2 for cloud uplink, but two enterprise clients in Germany are now asking for a written cryptographic audit report as part of their supplier onboarding — we have no budget to hire a specialist security consultancy and our own developers say it would take three months to do it themselves.
challenges.detail: Our VG-10 gateway uses TLS 1.2 with mutual authentication to push data to client cloud endpoints. That has been acceptable to most integrators, but two German enterprise clients — both in manufacturing — are now requiring a written cryptographic audit report as part of their supplier security onboarding process. They want documented confirmation of cipher suite choices, certificate management practices, key storage, and update signing. Our own developers know how the implementation works, but they are not security specialists and they estimate it would take them roughly three months to produce a report that would satisfy an enterprise procurement team. We do not have budget to hire an outside security consultancy. What we need is someone who understands embedded TLS implementations and can either help us write the audit report or review what our developers produce and flag anything that would not hold up to scrutiny. Both client contracts are on hold until this is resolved and we are already past the informal deadline one client gave us.

challenges.text: We do final board-level functional testing manually on a custom jig — one technician tests roughly 180 boards per shift, error rate is 1.2%, and we are missing subtle intermittent faults that only show up after 48 hours of thermal cycling; we need an automated test coverage analysis and a smarter jig that catches these outliers without doubling test time.
challenges.detail: Final functional testing of our boards is done on a custom jig built in 2019. One experienced technician can test roughly 180 boards per shift. Our recorded error rate at this stage is 1.2%, which sounds low but at our volumes means 50 to 60 boards per month leaving with a defect we missed. More concerning is that our jig only checks static electrical parameters — power rails, communication bus responses, RF carrier detect — and misses intermittent faults that only appear after thermal stress. We know this because we have had field returns where the board passed jig testing but failed after a few weeks in a warm enclosure. We added a 48-hour thermal cycling step for a period but it created a bottleneck and we dropped it. We want to understand where our current test coverage is actually weak, and we want a smarter jig or test sequence that catches outliers — specifically marginal solder joints and components that drift under heat — without doubling test time per board. The solution has to fit into our current production layout and be operated by the same technician.

challenges.text: Our game is set in 1920s Vojvodina and we want the dialogue to feel period-authentic in both Serbian and Hungarian, but our playtesters say some phrases sound modern and out of place — we have no linguist on the team and Google Translate is clearly not good enough for this.
challenges.detail: Our game is set in Vojvodina between 1922 and 1929, and characters speak Serbian, Hungarian, and occasional German depending on their background and social setting. We want the dialogue to feel like it belongs to that time and place — not stiff, not modern, but natural in the way people actually spoke. Right now we write first drafts in contemporary Serbian, then attempt a rough Hungarian pass using a mix of bilingual dictionaries and machine translation. Playtesters who grew up speaking Hungarian in Subotica keep flagging phrases that feel like they were written by someone who learned the language from a textbook or a phone app. We have tried asking friends informally, but none of them have the historical knowledge to know whether a phrase was in use in 1924 versus today. We have roughly 18,000 words of dialogue in Serbian and around 9,000 in Hungarian at current draft stage, and both scripts will grow. We have a small localization budget — a few hundred euros — and a target Early Access build for mid-2025. A good outcome would be a systematic review of both language scripts by someone who understands early twentieth-century registers in both languages, plus a short style guide we can apply ourselves going forward.

challenges.text: We are building 3D environments based on real Vojvodina architecture from the interwar period — manor houses, mills, farmsteads — but we only have a handful of photographs and our environment artist is reconstructing layouts by guesswork, which slows us down badly.
challenges.detail: A large portion of the game takes place in interwar Vojvodina buildings — a manor house near Sombor, a working watermill, timber-framed farmsteads, a railway station waiting room, a village church. Ervin, our environment artist, is skilled at modelling and texturing but he is reconstructing these spaces almost entirely by intuition. We have around thirty archival photographs, most of them from the 1930s or 1940s and shot from the outside. We have no floor plans, no dimensions, no interior photographs for most locations. Ervin estimates that roughly forty percent of his modelling time is spent guessing structural details and then revising after someone points out an obvious anachronism or error. We have looked at museum catalogues and a few published regional history books, but we have not found anything that gives us usable technical documentation. Each major interior environment takes around three weeks to reach a presentable state; we think that could be closer to ten days if we had reliable reference material. A good outcome is either access to documented sources — measured drawings, survey records, photographic archives — or a structured way to consult with someone who has worked with this type of vernacular architecture.

challenges.text: Our platform collects clickstream and in-store sensor data and tries to infer customer mood and intent in real time, but the model we trained on Belgian retail data drops from 84% to 61% accuracy when deployed for a Romanian grocery chain — the shopping behaviour patterns are just different and we don't know how to adapt without retraining from scratch each time.
challenges.detail: Naš model za prepoznavanje raspoloženja i namere kupaca treniran je uglavnom na clickstream podacima i podacima senzora iz belgijskih maloprodajnih objekata. Kada smo ga primenili za jednog rumunskog klijenta — lanac supermarketa sa oko 60 prodavnica — tačnost je pala sa 84% na 61%. Razlog je, pretpostavljamo, u različitom ponašanju kupaca: drugačiji obrasci kretanja, drugačija struktura kupovine, drugačija raspored prodavnica. Pokušali smo da primenimo jednostavnu rekalibraciju modela na malom skupu rumunskih podataka, ali to nije dalo značajno poboljšanje. Problem je što svaki put kada dođe novi klijent iz druge zemlje, ne možemo sebi priuštiti da model treniramo od početka — to traje mesecima i košta previše. Trebamo pristup koji nam omogućava da model brzo prilagodimo novom tržištu sa ograničenom količinom lokalnih podataka, a da pri tom zadržimo ono što smo naučili iz belgijskog skupa. Imamo pristup rumunskim podacima od klijenta, ali je skup relativno mali — oko šest sedmica snimanja iz 12 prodavnica.

challenges.text: A Belgian telecom client wants us to add a churn-prediction score to every customer record and show it on their CRM, but their data protection officer is asking for a full algorithmic impact assessment and documentation of feature importance in a form that satisfies the EU AI Act transparency requirements — we've never written one.
challenges.detail: Jedan od naših belgijskih telekomunikacionih klijenata, kompanija s oko 400.000 pretplatnika, želi da u svom CRM sistemu prikazuje skor verovatnoće odliva za svakog korisnika. Tehnički smo to u stanju da isporučimo — model već imamo. Međutim, njihov službenik za zaštitu podataka traži potpunu dokumentaciju: kako model donosi odluke, koje su varijable najvažnije, kako se to uklapa u zahteve EU AI Akta koji se tiče transparentnosti algoritama koji utiču na poslovne odluke prema fizičkim licima. Mi nikada nismo pisali ovakav dokument. Pokušali smo da koristimo SHAP vrednosti za objašnjenje modela, ali nismo sigurni kako to da prevedemo u format koji je prihvatljiv za pravni i compliance tim klijenta, a ne samo za tehničare. Rok koji nam je klijent dao je kraj prvog kvartala sledeće godine. Ako ne isporučimo dokumentaciju, ugovor vredan oko 180.000 evra godišnje pada u vodu.

challenges.text: Our R&D team is testing a new in-store footfall heatmap feature using overhead cameras, but the people-counting model confuses partially occluded shoppers with shelving units — in stores with tall gondola shelving the error rate reaches 22%, which makes the heatmaps useless.
challenges.detail: Razvijamo novu funkciju unutar CXCore platforme koja generiše toplotne mape kretanja kupaca u prodavnicama na osnovu snimaka nadglednih kamera. Koristimo YOLO-based model za detekciju i brojanje osoba. U prodavnicama s niskim policama model radi dobro — greška je ispod 5%. Međutim, čim u prodavnici postoje visoke gondole, kupci koji prolaze iza njih bivaju delimično zaklonjeni, i model ih meša sa delovima polica ili ih potpuno propušta. U takvim uslovima stopa greške dostiže 22%, što znači da heatmape više nisu pouzdane ni za kakvu poslovnu odluku. Testirali smo dosnimavanje u dve prodavnice s takvim rasporedom, i prikupili smo oko 8.000 anotiranih frejmova sa delomično zakrivenim osobama. To je za sada sve čime raspolažemo. Tražimo pristup koji bi poboljšao detekciju u ovim uslovima bez potrebe za skupim ponovnim anotiranjem u svakom novom tipu prodavnice. Postoji i vremenski pritisak — jedan od rumunskih klijenata čeka upravo ovu funkciju i planira pilot u 10 prodavnica u aprilu.

challenges.text: We want to expand into the German market but our current sales team has no German-speaking enterprise sales experience; we've been trying to hire a country manager for seven months without success and the two candidates we made offers to both declined.
challenges.detail: Planiramo ulazak na nemačko tržište već dve godine, ali nam nedostaje ključna karika — neko ko poznaje tržište, govori jezik i zna kako se prodaje enterprise softver nemačkim kompanijama. Naš sadašnji prodajni tim odlično funkcioniše za Belgiju i Poljsku, ali nema iskustva s nemačkim korporativnim okruženjem. Objavili smo oglas za poziciju country managera za Nemačku pre sedam meseci. Imali smo šestoro kandidata koji su stigli do završnih razgovora, dvojici smo poslali ponudu — oba su je odbila, jedan zbog preseljenja, drugi zbog konkurentske ponude. Naš HR tim nema kapacitet da pokrije ovaj problem sam. Razmatramo alternativne modele: angažovanje sales konsultanta na projektnoj osnovi, partnerstvo s nekom lokalnom konsultantskom firmom koja već ima kontakte u nemačkom enterprise segmentu, ili kombinovanu strategiju. Budžet za ovu poziciju postoji i nije prepreka — problem je pronalazak odgovarajućeg profila.

challenges.text: We use drone-mounted LiDAR to capture as-built data on bridges and overpasses, but converting the raw point clouds into usable structural models still takes our engineers three to four weeks per site — we need that down to under five days or we lose competitive bids.
challenges.detail: Every bridge inspection we win starts the same way: a drone flight that produces a point cloud of between 200 and 600 million points. Cleaning that cloud, registering it to a coordinate system, segmenting structural elements and then rebuilding it as a usable Revit model currently takes three to four weeks of engineer time per site. We have tried semi-automatic segmentation scripts in CloudCompare and experimented with one commercial point-cloud-to-BIM tool, but both still require heavy manual correction and our team ends up rebuilding large portions by hand. We have two licensed BIM engineers and one junior geodesist dedicated to this pipeline. The problem is competitive: public tenders in Serbia and Bosnia now expect turnaround times we cannot meet without either hiring staff we cannot afford or finding a smarter processing approach. A target of five working days per average-sized bridge — roughly a two-span overpass with a total deck area under 800 m² — would let us bid on at least four additional contracts per year. We are open to automation tooling, a trained ML model or a hybrid workflow, as long as the output is a clean IFC or Revit file a structural engineer can work with directly.

challenges.text: Our proptech spin-off product — a web platform that gives municipal clients a live cadastral and utility-network overlay — is seeing 40-second load times when a user queries more than 50,000 parcels at once; three pilot municipalities have complained and one is threatening to cancel the contract.
challenges.detail: KatastarVid is a browser-based platform we built for municipal clients who want a single map view of cadastral parcel boundaries, underground utility routes and ownership status. Three pilot municipalities are live: Inđija, Srbobran and Bač. The platform performs well for small queries, but when a user draws a bounding box over a dense urban area and pulls more than roughly 50,000 parcels the response time climbs past 40 seconds. We have already added PostGIS spatial indexes and moved to vector tiles for the front-end layer, but the bottleneck appears to be somewhere in how we join cadastral geometry with the utility-network attribute tables on the fly. We have no dedicated backend developer on staff — the platform was built by a GIS analyst and a part-time contractor who has since moved on. The municipality of Bač has put us on notice that they will not renew their annual licence if performance does not improve before the contract review in September 2025. The platform needs to support at least 200,000 parcels at acceptable load times before we can pitch it to larger cities. Budget for technical improvement is modest but we can allocate it with a clear scope.

challenges.text: We won a EU-funded project to assess foundation soil conditions along a 12 km road corridor in Srem, but our current geotechnical models rely only on borehole logs every 500 m and we're seeing unexpected settlement predictions — we need a way to interpolate subsurface stratigraphy more reliably between boreholes.
challenges.detail: We are mid-way through an EU-funded project to evaluate soil conditions along a 12-kilometre road corridor in Srem, between Ruma and Šimanovci, ahead of a planned road widening. Our standard approach is to commission boreholes at 500-metre intervals, log the stratigraphy by hand and run PLAXIS models from those logs. On this corridor we are hitting a recurring problem: the settlement predictions between adjacent boreholes vary more than the geology should explain, which suggests we are missing lateral discontinuities — probably old river channels or clay lenses — between drill points. We added four extra boreholes in the worst section and it helped locally but the project budget does not allow full densification along the whole corridor. We have GPR data for the top two metres and a set of archive borehole logs from a 1980s road survey that cover some of the same alignment. What we need is a more robust method for building a continuous stratigraphic model from sparse, unevenly distributed point data. The final geotechnical report is due to the project client, Srem Regional Development Agency, by February 2026, and the modelling work needs to be complete several months before that.

challenges.text: We have been trying for eight months to get our updated geodetic-services licence approved by the Republic Geodetic Authority after a regulatory change in 2023; the paperwork is stuck and we can't legally sign off on cadastral surveys in the meantime, which is blocking roughly 15% of our planned revenue this year.
challenges.detail: Following a 2023 amendment to the Law on State Survey and Cadastre, all geodetic companies in Serbia were required to reapply for their practising licences under a revised classification scheme. We submitted our application to the Republic Geodetic Authority in March 2024 with what we believed was a complete package. Eight months later the application is still marked as pending. We have received two requests for supplementary documentation, both of which we answered within the required deadlines, but no substantive response has followed. Without the updated licence we are legally barred from signing off on cadastral surveys and submitting them to the cadastre registry. This blocks a category of work that represents approximately 15 percent of our planned revenue for 2025. We have engaged a regulatory consulting firm, Jurisprojekt d.o.o. from Belgrade, to help navigate the process, but progress has been slow. We are not looking for legal advice here — we have that covered. What we lack is any insight into whether there is a technical or procedural angle we are missing, or whether others in the sector have found a faster route through the same bottleneck.

challenges.text: We are connecting more and more small prosumer solar installations — sometimes 20 to 30 on a single rural LV feeder — and our field teams report voltage rising above 253 V at the far end of the feeder on sunny afternoons, which is causing nuisance tripping and complaints from neighbours who do not even have solar; our network planning tool was designed for one-way power flow and simply does not handle this.
challenges.detail: Over the past two years we have connected roughly 340 rooftop solar systems to rural low-voltage feeders across our service territory, and the density is increasing fast — some feeders in the Srem and Banat areas now have 20 to 30 small generators on a line originally built for 80 households drawing power, nothing more. On sunny afternoons in spring and summer our field teams measure voltages of 256 to 261 V at far-end service points, which is above the 253 V upper limit. Neighbours without solar are experiencing nuisance disconnections of sensitive appliances. We have tried adjusting on-load tap changers at the local transformers, but that just shifts the problem — lower voltage at the source end means the far-end problem gets worse at night. Our current planning tool, which we have used since 2009, runs only unidirectional power-flow calculations. We have an export of the feeder topology in QGIS and metering data from about 60 percent of affected customers. We need a simulation or decision-support tool that handles bidirectional flow and can recommend practical interventions — reactive power setpoints, tap changes, or simple curtailment thresholds — that our engineers, who are not power-systems academics, can actually apply in the field within a normal project schedule.

challenges.text: We installed 18,000 smart meters in the last contract cycle and the utility is asking us to provide a report showing the carbon footprint of their entire low-voltage network operation — we have no methodology, no internal expertise, and the tender for the next phase explicitly requires an ISO 14064 compliant calculation.
challenges.detail: The utility we work with on the largest ongoing metering contract has received pressure from its regulator to report greenhouse gas emissions from network operation, and they have passed that requirement down to us as the contractor responsible for the installed asset base. The next tender, which opens in early 2025, explicitly requires ISO 14064-1 compliant reporting covering the LV network assets we manage — roughly 18,000 meter points, associated cable runs, transformer stations and the maintenance activities tied to them. We have energy consumption figures from the metering data we already collect, and we have purchase records for materials and vehicles. What we do not have is any internal person who understands how to build an emission-factor model, how to handle Scope 1, 2 and 3 boundaries in a network operations context, or how to get an external verifier to sign off the result. We looked at one commercial software package but the licensing cost was around 12,000 euros per year, which is hard to justify for a single reporting obligation. We need a methodology we can own and maintain ourselves, documented clearly enough that a technically literate project engineer can run the annual calculation without starting from scratch each time.

challenges.text: Our civil crews have to dig exploratory trenches to locate old underground cables before every excavation because the as-built drawings from the 1970s and 1980s are either missing or wrong by up to 4 metres — last year we had two cable strikes that cost us a combined 340,000 dinars in repairs and project delays.
challenges.detail: A significant portion of the underground cable network in the municipalities we work in was installed between 1965 and 1990, and the documentation from that era is unreliable. Paper drawings were digitised in the early 2000s but the spatial accuracy is poor — offsets of two to four metres are common, and in some streets the cables simply do not appear on any drawing at all. Before every excavation our civil crew spends between half a day and two full days digging exploratory pits, and last year we had two cable strikes despite that precaution. The combined cost in emergency repairs and project overruns was around 340,000 dinars. We own a Radiodetection RD8100 cable and pipe locator and use it routinely, but in areas with multiple parallel cables the signal discrimination is difficult and the instrument alone has not prevented strikes. We have started a programme of updating the QGIS asset registry when we are on-site, so new and recently touched infrastructure is now recorded well. The unsolved problem is the legacy network in areas where we have not done recent work. We are interested in any detection or probabilistic mapping approach that could reduce the number of exploratory pits and give our site engineers a clearer confidence interval on cable position before they break ground.

challenges.text: We want to move into battery energy storage system (BESS) integration for industrial clients but we cannot find electricians or commissioning engineers in Vojvodina who have any hands-on experience with lithium iron phosphate battery management systems — the two people we tried to hire in the last six months both took offers in Germany.
challenges.detail: Several of our larger industrial clients — a food processing plant near Zrenjanin and a cold-storage operator in Novi Sad — have approached us about installing battery energy storage systems to reduce their peak demand charges and provide backup capacity. We see this as a natural extension of our existing electrical contracting work, and we have a commercial agreement in principle with a LFP battery system supplier based in Slovenia. The technical barrier is that none of our current staff has hands-on commissioning experience with battery management systems, cell balancing, protection relay coordination for storage, or the communication protocols that tie a BESS to an energy management system. We advertised two positions in the last six months — one commissioning engineer and one experienced electrician with storage background — and both candidates who reached the offer stage accepted positions in Germany instead, citing salary levels we cannot match. We are willing to invest in training existing staff but need a structured programme with real hardware, not only classroom instruction. A good outcome would be having two or three of our engineers competent enough to commission a 200 to 500 kWh LFP installation under supervision by mid-2025, so we can deliver the first client project before the end of that year.

challenges.text: Our platform generates 3-D urban models from cadastral footprints and building heights, but the models look obviously wrong in historic city centres where buildings have irregular roof forms — clients in Austria and Slovenia have flagged this as a dealbreaker for public consultation sessions.
challenges.detail: We build 3-D building models by extruding cadastral footprints to a single height value taken from a national building register. That approach works fine for postwar residential blocks and modern commercial buildings, but it falls apart in historic centres where you have mansard roofs, gabled attics, stepped facades, and irregular floor plates that were never captured in any structured dataset. When we showed a demo to a planning office in Graz and another in Ljubljana, both teams said the models looked too wrong to show to the public — residents would dismiss the whole tool. We have tried writing procedural rules to guess roof type from building age and footprint shape, and the results are inconsistent. We have also looked at deriving roof geometry from aerial lidar point clouds, but we do not have reliable lidar coverage for most of our target cities, and processing the data we do have is not something our team knows how to do at scale. We need a method that produces visually plausible historic rooflines from the data we actually have, or a clear workflow for ingesting lidar where it exists. Getting this right would unblock at least three pending contracts.

challenges.text: We want to add a pedestrian comfort layer to the simulation — showing wind speed and shadow patterns at street level — but our team has no background in microclimate modelling and the CFD tools we tried take eight hours per scenario, which is too slow for interactive planning sessions.
challenges.detail: Several of our municipal clients have asked for a comfort layer that shows pedestrians where wind is strong or shade is absent at street level. We see this as a genuine product gap and we want to add it to ZoneSim within the next twelve months. The problem is that nobody on our team has a background in fluid dynamics or microclimate simulation. We ran trials with two open-source CFD packages and one commercial solver, and the fastest run we achieved was about eight hours for a single wind direction on a small neighbourhood model. That is fine for an overnight batch job, but our platform is designed around interactive what-if sessions — planners expect to change a building height and see something updated within a minute or two. We have read about machine-learning surrogate models that approximate CFD outputs much faster, but we do not know how to build or validate one, and we are not sure what training data we would need or how much. We have budget set aside for one senior hire or a focused external collaboration. A good outcome would be wind and shadow estimates accurate enough to rank scenarios relative to each other, delivered fast enough to feel interactive.

challenges.text: Spatial plans in Serbia are legally referenced to the national geodetic datum and our EU clients work in ETRS89; the coordinate transformation introduces visible misalignment of up to three metres in some regions, and we do not fully understand why.
challenges.detail: Serbia's official spatial data is referenced to the MGI 1901 Balkans datum, while all of our EU clients work in ETRS89. We use the GDAL Proj library to do the transformation and we apply the standard published parameters, but in some areas we see residual offsets of up to three metres when we overlay our transformed data against a reference layer our Slovenian client provided. Three metres is enough to put a building outline on the wrong side of a property boundary, which causes real problems in planning reviews. We have tried applying a national grid shift file we found on the Serbian geodetic authority website, but the offset does not fully disappear in certain regions, particularly in areas with older cadastral records. We do not know whether the remaining error comes from incorrect transformation parameters, from inconsistencies in the source cadastral data, or from something we are doing wrong in our pipeline. We have a set of ground-control points our GIS specialist collected from public sources that could be used to test any proposed fix. Resolving this is a prerequisite for expanding into new EU markets.

challenges.text: We are trying to close a Series A round with a Vienna-based proptech fund and they want audited financial statements for the past three years, but our accountant has produced them in the Serbian statutory format and the fund's lawyers say they cannot use them without an IFRS restatement.
challenges.detail: We are in active negotiations with a Vienna-based proptech investment fund, Riedler Ventures, and they have requested three years of audited financial statements prepared under IFRS. Our accountant, who has worked with us since we were founded, produces statutory reports in the format required by Serbian law, which follows local accounting standards rather than IFRS. The fund's lawyers reviewed the Serbian statements and said they cannot use them as the basis for due diligence without an IFRS restatement — specifically they want IFRS 15 revenue recognition treatment for our SaaS subscription contracts and IFRS 16 for our office lease. We contacted two large audit firms and received quotes that were higher than we expected for a company our size. We are also under time pressure: the fund has given us a soft deadline of the end of Q3 2024 to deliver compliant financials or they will move on. We need to understand what an IFRS restatement actually involves for a SaaS business of our scale, find a realistic path to getting it done in time, and keep the cost proportionate to a Series A of the size we are targeting.

challenges.text: Our cobots slow down or stop entirely when a human worker gets within the safety envelope, which cuts throughput by up to 35% on mixed human-robot assembly lines; clients are starting to complain that promised cycle times aren't being met and two contracts are at risk of penalty clauses.
challenges.detail: Na mešovitim linijama gde kobot i radnik dele isti prostor, naši UR10e i UR16e roboti prelaze u zaštitni režim smanjene brzine čim radnik uđe u definisanu zonu. Ovo je standardna funkcija SafeMove protokola, ali u praksi znači pad takta od 30 do 35 posto. Na liniji za pakovanje u pogonu jednog od naših klijenata u Subotici, obećani takt je bio 18 ciklusa po minuti, a realni prosek je 12. Klijent ima pravo na penale po ugovoru počev od trećeg kvartala 2024. Pokušali smo da prepravimo zone detekcije i smanjimo radijuse, ali to je kompromitovalo sigurnosnu dokumentaciju. Imamo podatke iz log fajlova robota za poslednjih šest meseci i snimke kamera na liniji. Idealno bi nam bilo tehničko rešenje koje razlikuje namerni prolaz radnika od slučajnog ulaska u zonu — bez menjanja sertifikovane sigurnosne arhitekture — i koje bi takt vratio na obećanih 18 ciklusa.

challenges.text: We reprogram each new workcell from scratch and it takes our engineers an average of 11 days per installation; we've turned down four projects this quarter alone because we simply don't have the engineering hours, and at our current day-rate that is roughly €38,000 in lost revenue.
challenges.detail: Svaka nova robotska ćelija počinje od praznog projekta. Naši inženjeri troše u proseku 11 radnih dana po instalaciji samo na programiranje — sekvence kretanja, I/O mapiranje, HMI ekrane, parametre sigurnosti. Imamo tri iskusna integracionog inženjera i dva juniora. Pokušali smo da napravimo interni šablon u URScript-u za tipične pick-and-place aplikacije, ali šablon se pokazao previše krutim za razlike u geometriji hvatača i rasporedu paleta. Rezultat je da smo u prvom kvartalu 2024. odbili četiri upita jer nismo imali kapaciteta, što je po našoj internoj kalkulaciji oko 38.000 evra propuštenog prihoda. Ne tražimo gotov softverski paket — tražimo metodologiju ili alat koji bi nam skratio programiranje na ispod pet dana po ćeliji, uz zadržavanje fleksibilnosti za varijante.

challenges.text: A German Tier-2 automotive supplier wants us to provide a full CE Declaration of Conformity package under the new EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 before they will sign a €620,000 framework agreement, and we have never prepared this documentation for the German market before.
challenges.detail: Dobili smo ozbiljan upit od nemačkog Tier-2 dobavljača u automobilskom sektoru — firma se zove Dresdner Baugruppen GmbH — koji želi da potpiše okvirni ugovor vrednosti 620.000 evra za isporuku tri zavarivačke ćelije. Uslov koji su postavili je kompletan CE paket po Uredbi EU 2023/1230 o mašinama, uključujući tehničku dokumentaciju na nemačkom jeziku, procenu rizika po ISO 12100, analizu upravljačkih funkcija po EN ISO 13849-1 i Izjavu o usklađenosti. Do sada smo radili CE dokumentaciju za srpsko i bosanskohercegovačko tržište po starijim direktivama, ali nikada za nemački tržišni ispit u ovom obimu. Imamo inženjera koji je prošao jednodnevni seminar o mašinskoj direktivi pre tri godine, ali to nije dovoljno. Rok koji nam je klijent dao za dostavu dokumentacije je oktobar 2024. Potrebna nam je stručna pomoć u pripremi i validaciji kompletnog tehničkog dosijea.

challenges.text: The welding robot on our flagship cell leaves inconsistent bead width — varying between 3.8 mm and 6.1 mm on the same joint — when the steel workpiece temperature drifts during long production runs, and we have no sensor feedback loop to compensate in real time.
challenges.detail: Naša zavarivačka ćelija sa Mitsubishi MELFA robotom i Fronius TPS izvором pokazuje neujednačenu širinu zavara na istom spoju — merenja pokazuju raspon od 3,8 do 6,1 mm tokom iste serije. Problem se pojavljuje isključivo na dugim production run-ovima, obično posle 40 do 50 minuta rada, kada temperatura čeličnog radnog komada poraste zbog akumulirane toplote. Naši inženjeri su pokušali da fiksiraju parametre struje i brzine žice, ali to ne pomaže jer je promenljiva sam komad, ne samo zavarivačka oprema. Nemamo senzorski povratni kup koji bi prilagođavao parametre u realnom vremenu. Imamo podatke merenja širine zavara iz vizijskog sistema Keyence IV3 za poslednjih 200 serija i temperature snimane termoparom na šablonu. Tražimo rešenje koje bi koristilo te podatke da automatski koriguje parametre Fronius izvora tokom rada, bez zaustavljanja linije.

challenges.text: Three of our best-selling moisturisers have a shelf life of only 14 months, which is too short for some German and Austrian distributors who need at least 24 months to cover their warehouse cycle. We've tried increasing the preservative load but it pushes us over the EU Cosmetics Regulation limits and changes the smell.
challenges.detail: Three of our moisturisers — the Intensive Lavender Night Cream, the Chamomile Daily Fluid and the Rose Hip Hand Barrier Cream — currently pass stability testing at 14 months but start showing signs of microbial and oxidative change before 24 months. Austrian and German distributors tell us they need a minimum 24-month shelf life to allow for warehouse rotation and retail display time. We have already pushed the broad-spectrum preservative blend (phenoxyethanol plus ethylhexylglycerin) to the upper boundary of what EU Cosmetics Regulation allows, and going further is not an option. When we tried adding a secondary antioxidant at a higher dose, the top-note fragrance profile changed enough that our Austrian distributor flagged it with consumers. We have three ICH-compliant stability chambers in-house and can run accelerated and real-time studies ourselves, but our formulation team does not have deep expertise in water-activity control, emulsion architecture redesign or alternative preservation systems such as ferment-based or pH-driven approaches. A good outcome for us would be reaching a confirmed 24-month shelf life without reformulating the scent profile and without adding any ingredient that requires a new safety assessment under EU rules. Budget for external support is flexible if there is a clear plan.

challenges.text: We extract lavender and chamomile in-house using a 1980s steam-distillation vessel, and our yield is about 20% lower than benchmarks we see from Turkish and Bulgarian competitors. We suspect the raw material pre-treatment and distillation time profiles are suboptimal but we've never done a systematic study.
challenges.detail: Our steam distillation vessel was installed in 1983 and has never been subject to a proper process study. We run lavender at roughly 90 minutes and chamomile at 110 minutes, based on procedures written by staff who retired years ago. When we compare our oil yield per kilogram of dry herb against published figures from Bulgarian and Turkish producers — and against one Romanian cooperative we briefly partnered with — our yields come in about 20 percent lower across both crops. We harvest lavender from our own plots near Palić and buy chamomile from three growers in Bačka Topola, so raw material quality should be comparable. We suspect the issues are in how we pre-treat the plant material before loading the still — moisture content, particle size, packing density — and possibly in our temperature ramp profile during distillation. We have a GC-MS unit and can analyse oil composition, and we log batch weights and times, but we have never done a designed experiment varying these parameters systematically. We need someone to help us design that study, interpret the results and tell us whether the vessel itself needs modification or whether process changes alone will close the gap.

challenges.text: Our new sunscreen line needs SPF validation testing before we can put SPF 30 or SPF 50 on the label, and every accredited lab we've contacted in Serbia says they don't do in-vivo or in-vitro SPF testing — the nearest option is Budapest and they quoted us 9,000 EUR per SKU.
challenges.detail: We have developed two mineral sunscreen formulas — one at SPF 30 and one at SPF 50 — using zinc oxide as the only UV filter, which means they fall under the EU Cosmetics Regulation as cosmetics rather than medicines. Before we can put the SPF claim on the label we need validated SPF testing, either in-vitro (ISO 24443) or in-vivo (ISO 24444). We contacted five laboratories in Serbia and none of them holds the accreditation or equipment for either method. The closest accredited option we found is a contract lab in Budapest that quoted us 9,000 EUR per SKU, meaning 18,000 EUR for both products, plus travel and coordination time. That is not impossible but it is a large outlay before we know the products will pass. We would prefer to find a way to do preliminary in-vitro screening closer to home before committing to full validated testing, or to find a Serbian or regional partner institution that has the spectrophotometric equipment needed for the ISO 24443 method and might be interested in developing that capability formally. Our launch timeline for the sunscreen line is the first half of 2026.

challenges.text: We've seen a 30% rise in returns of our hand-cream jars from pharmacy chains because the injection-moulded PP lid warps in summer heat during transport, causing the seal to fail. Our packaging supplier says the tooling is fine but we think the wall thickness distribution is wrong.
challenges.detail: Since April last year we have seen a sharp rise in returns of our 50 ml hand-cream jar — the polypropylene screw-top with the white lid — from two pharmacy chains, Farmeko Plus and Zelena Lekarnica. The complaint is always the same: the lid arrives warped enough that the inner sealing ring no longer sits flush, and the cream either dries out or leaks slightly. This happens after transport in summer, when vehicles and warehouse loading bays can reach 45–50 degrees Celsius. Returns are running at about 30 percent on affected batches, which is damaging our relationship with both chains. Our packaging supplier, Plastforma d.o.o. from Novi Sad, inspected the tooling and says the mould is within specification. We believe the problem is in the wall thickness distribution around the lid rim — it looks uneven to the eye and we think thinner sections deform under thermal load while thicker sections hold, which creates the warp. We do not have access to mould-flow analysis software or coordinate measuring equipment to prove this. We need someone who can measure the geometry of existing lids, model the thermal behaviour and tell us concretely whether the tooling needs adjustment, whether a different PP grade with a higher heat deflection temperature would solve it, or both.

challenges.text: We collect accelerometer and gyroscope data from players' phones during training, but our movement-pattern model was trained on professional-athlete datasets from Western Europe and the injury-risk scores it produces for our amateur users in Serbian regional leagues are uncorrelated with the actual injury events coaches report — we have 340 players worth of data now and need to retrain.
challenges.detail: Our injury-risk model uses accelerometer and gyroscope readings to estimate how much mechanical stress a player's body is absorbing during a session. The model we shipped was adapted from open datasets built on GPS and wearable data from semi-professional and professional players in Germany and the Netherlands. Those players train on better pitches, follow structured programmes, and generally have lower baseline injury rates than the amateur players in Serbian regional leagues we actually serve. When we compare our risk scores week-by-week against the injury log coaches fill in after each session, there is no meaningful correlation. We have tried recalibrating the output thresholds manually but that made things worse for some clubs and no better for others. We now have 340 players with between four and thirty-two weeks of continuous data each, plus a hand-coded injury event log covering 47 confirmed muscle and joint injuries. We need help retraining or fine-tuning the model on this local dataset, understanding whether the raw features we extract are even the right ones for this population, and setting up a simple validation loop so we can measure whether changes actually improve predictions before we push them to production. The next competitive season starts in August and we want a better model in clubs' hands by then.

challenges.text: Coaches tell us the dashboard is hard to understand — they spend more time figuring out what the charts mean than actually coaching, and our 30-day retention is only 19% among coaches over 40 years old.
challenges.detail: The dashboard shows training load as an acute-to-chronic workload ratio plotted over a rolling four-week window, colour-coded by risk band. It made sense to us when we built it because we had read the sports science literature. Coaches have not read that literature and do not want to. In user interviews we ran in February 2024, coaches over 40 consistently told us they open the dashboard, look at the charts for a minute, feel confused, and go back to their notebook. Our 30-day retention for that age group is 19 percent, compared to 61 percent for coaches under 35. We have tried adding a short tooltip glossary and a two-minute onboarding video. Neither moved the number. We think the underlying issue is that we are presenting the same information model we use internally instead of translating it into the questions coaches are actually asking, which are things like: who should I go easier on today, and who has been underworked this week. We have one designer on a part-time contract and no dedicated UX researcher. We want to reach at least 45 percent 30-day retention across all age groups before we approach new clubs this autumn.

challenges.text: We need to hire two senior backend engineers to handle the real-time data pipeline before the next season starts in August, but every candidate we approach is immediately counter-offered by companies in Belgrade or remotely for EU salaries we simply cannot match at our current funding stage.
challenges.detail: Right now our real-time data pipeline is held together by two developers who also handle mobile features, bug fixes, and customer support requests. As squad numbers grow and more clubs start simultaneous evening sessions, the pipeline drops events and we have to backfill from device logs the following morning. We need two senior backend engineers who understand real-time streaming, database performance under write-heavy load, and ideally some experience with time-series data. Every person we have interviewed seriously has either already accepted a remote role for a company in Western Europe or received a counter-offer from a Belgrade fintech within a week of talking to us. Our current salary range tops out at around 2,200 euros net per month, which is below what those offers look like. We are not in a position to close that gap with cash alone before our next funding round, which we hope to close in late 2024. We are open to other arrangements — part-time contracts, project-based work, co-supervision agreements — anything that gets reliable senior technical hands on the pipeline before August.

challenges.text: Our protective jackets are tested to EN ISO 11612 but we keep failing the vertical flame spread test on the collar seam — roughly 3 out of every 10 sample batches — and we can't pinpoint whether it's the thread, the interlining adhesive, or the dye chemistry on that specific fabric blend.
challenges.detail: We have been producing flame-retardant jackets certified to EN ISO 11612 for about six years. The fabric itself — a 280 g/m² para-aramid and cotton blend we source from a supplier in Novi Pazar — passes the vertical flame spread test without any problem on flat panels. The issue appears specifically at the collar seam, and only on certain batches. Roughly 3 in 10 sample batches we send to the testing lab in Belgrade come back with a failure on vertical flame spread at that seam. We have tried switching from polyester sewing thread to a meta-aramid thread on the collar, and that reduced failures but did not eliminate them. We have not yet changed the interlining adhesive, which is a standard polyamide hot-melt type, because we use it on several other products and changing it creates a chain of re-testing costs. Our dyeing supervisor, Gordana Petrić, suspects the dye fixative we apply after dyeing might be leaving a residue that behaves differently at the seam where two fabric layers and the interlining overlap. We have no lab equipment to isolate which material is the problem. A good outcome would be a clear diagnosis — is it the thread, the adhesive, or the dye chemistry — so we can fix one variable at a time without re-testing the entire product range from scratch. We have a budget of around €8,000 for this and we need a resolution before our EN certificate renewal in Q3 2025.

challenges.text: Our dyeing unit uses roughly 18,000 litres of water per shift, and the municipal wastewater utility just told us we'll face a 40% surcharge starting next year unless we bring our effluent COD below 180 mg/L — right now we're averaging around 420 mg/L and we have no treatment step at all.
challenges.detail: Our dyeing unit runs one shift per day, five days a week, and it consumes roughly 18,000 litres of water per shift. All of that goes directly to the municipal sewer. We received a formal notice from the Zrenjanin municipal wastewater utility in October 2023 telling us that our effluent COD average of around 420 mg/L is well above the 180 mg/L threshold they will start enforcing with a 40% surcharge from January 2025. We have measured our own COD a few times using a portable photometer and the readings are consistent with what the utility found. We do not have any treatment step at all — no screen, no neutralisation tank, nothing. Our yard has a concrete area of about 180 square metres adjacent to the dyeing unit where we could install something, but we cannot afford to stop production for more than two weeks for a construction phase. We spoke to one local environmental engineering firm, Eko-Pro d.o.o. from Novi Sad, which proposed a coagulation-flocculation unit at a quoted cost of €55,000, which is more than we can spend as a single capital item right now. We would prefer a phased or lower-cost approach — even a partial COD reduction that gets us to 220–250 mg/L in the short term would delay the surcharge trigger and give us time. We have someone internally, our maintenance technician Bojan Stanković, who can run and maintain simple equipment if it is documented clearly.

challenges.text: We want to break into the German and Austrian B2B market for certified PPE but we have no idea how to register our EN-certified products under the EU PPE Regulation 2016/425, find a notified body, or handle the technical file — our accountant handles all paperwork and she's overwhelmed.
challenges.detail: We currently sell our EN-certified protective jackets and high-visibility workwear to industrial clients in Serbia and Romania through direct sales visits by our commercial manager, Svetlana Đorđić. Several of those clients have German or Austrian parent companies, and on two occasions procurement managers from those parent companies have asked us directly whether we could supply their German facilities. Both times we had to say we did not have the EU documentation in order. Our products are tested and certified by a Serbian testing institute, which is acceptable for the Serbian market, but for placing PPE on the EU market under Regulation 2016/425 we understand we need a notified body, a technical file, a Declaration of Conformity, and proper CE marking. We do not know how to select a notified body, what the technical file needs to contain, or what the practical timeline and cost looks like. Our accountant, Mirjana Kovač, currently handles all product documentation alongside her regular finance duties and is not in a position to take on a regulatory project of this size. We are not looking for a lawyer — we need someone who has done this before for a garment manufacturer and can walk us through it step by step. Ideally we would start with two product categories, the EN ISO 11612 jacket and the EN ISO 20471 Class 2 vest, and have them properly registered within 12 months.

challenges.text: We cut roughly 2,400 metres of fabric per week by hand with straight-knife cutters, and our fabric utilisation is sitting at about 71% — we're throwing away almost a third of every roll, which at current fabric prices costs us around €3,200 a month in waste alone.
challenges.detail: Every week we cut approximately 2,400 metres of fabric across all our product lines. We do this by hand using straight-knife cutting machines, with fabric laid up manually on two cutting tables each 18 metres long. Our marker-making is done partly by hand on paper and partly using Gemaks software, which our pattern technician Dragana Ilić has been using for about three years. Our current fabric utilisation is around 71%, which we calculated by weighing cut waste against total fabric consumed over a 12-week period in late 2023. At current fabric prices — averaging around €10.50 per metre across our main materials — the waste comes to roughly €3,200 per month. We know that automated nesting software can typically bring utilisation to 85% or above for simple garment shapes, and even a move to 80% would recover about €1,500 per month. We have looked at two automated cutting system vendors who visited us in 2022 and 2023, but both quoted full automated cutting table systems at €120,000 to €180,000, which is not feasible. We are more interested in whether better nesting software alone — without buying a new cutting table — could make a significant difference on our existing equipment. Dragana is willing to learn new tools. We would like to pilot something within six months and measure the actual utilisation change before committing to any software licence cost above €3,000 per year.

challenges.text: Our LED driver produces a total harmonic distortion of around 19% at partial load, which disqualifies us from EN 61000-3-2 Class C compliance and has already caused us to lose two Hungarian municipal tenders worth a combined €280,000; we need to reduce THD below 8% without increasing board size.
challenges.detail: Naš trenutni LED driver radi s ukupnim harmonijskim izobličenjem (THD) oko 19% pri parcijalnom opterećenju, što znači da ne zadovoljava EN 61000-3-2 Klasu C. To nije teorijski problem – izgubili smo dva mađarska komunalna tendera ukupne vrednosti oko 280.000 evra jer komisija traži odgovarajući sertifikat. Pokušali smo da dodamo pasivni LC filter na ulazu, ali to podiže cenu i zauzima prostor koji nemamo na ploči formata 85×50 mm. Simulacije u LTspice-u pokazuju poboljšanje, ali ne dovoljno. Raspolažemo izmerenim oblicima struje sa osciloskopa za različite radne tačke i kompletnom šemom. Ograničenje je da ne smemo povećati gabarit ploče niti znatno rasti troškovi komponenti. Sledeći tender za koji smo zainteresovani je u prvom kvartalu 2025. godine, tako da nam je vremenski okvir kratak. Dobra solucija bi bila topološka izmena ili upravljačka strategija koja THD spušta ispod 8% bez promene gabarita.

challenges.text: We are developing an adaptive spectral tuning algorithm for grow-light applications that should adjust red/blue/far-red ratios based on a plant growth model, but none of our team has a biology background and we do not know which photomorphogenic parameters to optimise for or how to validate the model.
challenges.detail: Razvijamo modul za rasvetu u zaštićenim uzgajalištima koji treba da automatski podešava odnos crvene, plave i daleke crvene svetlosti u zavisnosti od faze rasta biljke. Ideja je da algoritam čita senzorske podatke i prilagođava spektar, ali nismo sigurni koje biološke parametre da postavimo kao ciljne vrednosti niti kako da proverimo da li model uopšte funkcioniše. U timu nemamo nikoga s biološkim ili agronomskim obrazovanjem. Pronašli smo nekoliko naučnih radova o fitohromu i kriptohromu, ali ne znamo kako da odaberemo koji su relevantni za konkretne kulture koje naši potencijalni kupci gaje – trenutno su to rukola, bosiljak i krastavac. Imamo hardversku platformu s četiri nezavisno dimabilna kanala i mogućnost beleženja podataka o rastu u kontrolisanim uslovima u maloj stakleničkoj komori površine oko 4 m². Ono što nam treba je neko ko može da nam kaže koji merljivi pokazatelji rasta su dovoljno pouzdani za validaciju modela i kako da postavimo eksperiment.

challenges.text: Our luminaire controller runs a small Cortex-M4 MCU and needs to execute a local scheduling and dimming optimisation for up to 64 nodes; the current greedy algorithm causes visible flicker synchronisation artefacts at 3 a.m. low-load periods and we do not know how to formally model the problem.
challenges.detail: Naš mrežni kontroler upravlja do 64 svetiljke istovremeno i treba lokalno da izračuna raspored i nivo zatamnjivanja za svaki čvor bez stalne veze s oblakom. Trenutni algoritam prolazi kroz čvorove sekvencijalno i postavlja nivo osvetljenosti po redosledu – to radi dobro pri punom opterećenju, ali u periodima malog saobraćaja oko 3 ujutru primećujemo vidljive artefakte sinhronizacije treperenja jer se promene gomilaju. Zabeležili smo pojavu na logu i vidimo da do problema dolazi kada više čvorova istovremeno menja nivo za više od 15%. Cortex-M4 nema puno slobodnih resursa, a komunikacija između čvorova ide kroz RS-485 sa vremenskim okvirima od 10 ms. Nismo sigurni kako formalno da opišemo ovaj problem – ne znamo da li je to problem raspoređivanja, upravljanja redom čekanja ili nešto treće. Hteli bismo rešenje koje možemo da implementiramo u C-u na postojećem hardveru bez zamene mikrokontrolera.

challenges.text: We applied for a €150,000 Horizon Europe EIC Accelerator grant eight months ago and have heard nothing; our accountant says our books are not structured the way EU auditors expect and we may have to return pre-financing if we ever receive it.
challenges.detail: Pre osam meseci podneli smo zahtev za EIC Accelerator grant od 150.000 evra i do danas nismo dobili konačan odgovor. U međuvremenu naš računovođa nam je skrenuo pažnju da naše poslovne knjige nisu organizovane na način koji EU revizori očekuju – troškovi istraživanja i razvoja nisu jasno odvojeni od operativnih troškova, a nema ni odgovarajuće dokumentacije o internim časovima rada po projektima. Ako dobijemo odobrenje i prefinansiranje, postoji realan rizik da ćemo morati da vraćamo sredstva jer ne možemo da dokažemo namjensko trošenje. Nemamo iskustva s EU projektima i nismo imali savetnika koji bi nas vodio kroz ovaj proces. Ono što nam treba je neko ko razume finansijsko upravljanje EU projektima i može da nam pomogne da uspostavimo ispravan sistem praćenja troškova pre nego što novac eventualno stigne.

challenges.text: Our phycocyanin purity after the first chromatography pass sits at around 70%, but buyers in the German nutraceutical market need 95%+ purity with documented heavy-metal content below EU limits; every extra purification step we try costs more than we can recover in margin.
challenges.detail: Our phycocyanin comes off the first chromatography column at roughly 70% purity, measured as the ratio of absorbance at 620 nm to 280 nm. German nutraceutical buyers — we currently supply one small-batch formulator in Hamburg on a trial basis — will not sign a repeat order unless we can consistently hit 95%+ and hand over a batch report showing lead, cadmium, arsenic and mercury all below the EU limits in Regulation 2023/915. We have tried adding a second ion-exchange pass, but the yield loss in that step drives our cost per gram past the price the Hamburg buyer is willing to pay. We have also tested ammonium sulphate precipitation before the column, which helped yield but not purity. Our lab has an ICP-MS for metal testing, and we track every cultivation input, so contamination is not the problem — the problem is selectivity in the separation. We have a rough budget of around €8,000 for process development before the next harvest season and we need a validated, repeatable protocol, not just a one-off lab result.

challenges.text: Our outdoor raceway pond loses 30–40% of its productivity in October–March compared to summer — we tried supplemental LED lighting but the electricity cost wiped out the revenue gain — and we need a smarter way to manage the light-temperature trade-off through the cold months.
challenges.detail: Between October and March our outdoor raceway pond drops to roughly 60–70% of its summer volumetric productivity. We installed a ring of 660 nm and 440 nm LED bars last winter and ran them for 14 hours a day. The algae responded — cell density improved by about 15% — but the electricity bill for that period cancelled out almost all of the pigment revenue gain. The core issue is that we do not have a good model for how much light is actually useful versus wasteful given the water temperature, which drops to around 8–12 °C in the pond during cold months and slows metabolism regardless of photon supply. We have been logging temperature, PAR sensor readings and cell-density OD measurements three times a day since September 2022, so we have roughly 18 months of paired data sitting in a spreadsheet. What we want is a way to schedule the LED output dynamically — or to figure out whether heating the pond a few degrees would be more cost-effective than more light. We do not have a greenhouse structure yet, and building one is not in the current budget.

challenges.text: We are selling direct to two cosmetics companies now but we have no formal distribution agreement, no exclusivity clauses and no IP assignment clause in our supply contracts — one buyer has already asked us to sign their standard terms, which we think are unfair but we can't afford a lawyer to review them.
challenges.detail: We supply phycocyanin to two cosmetics companies — one in Ljubljana and one in Düsseldorf — under informal arrangements: a price list, a product spec sheet and email confirmations. No framework contract, no minimum order commitment, no clause about what happens if we cannot deliver, and no agreement about who owns any formulation data we share during technical discussions. The Düsseldorf buyer recently sent us their standard supplier agreement and asked us to sign before the next order. We read through it ourselves and found clauses that appear to assign them the right to audit our facility on 48 hours' notice, require us to indemnify them against any regulatory action in any jurisdiction and give them a perpetual licence to use our product specifications. We do not have an ongoing relationship with a commercial lawyer and a single contract review in Serbia costs more than we have budgeted for legal in the whole quarter. We need either a reviewed and negotiated version of that contract or a template supply agreement of our own that we can offer as an alternative, specifically covering pigment supply, exclusivity limits and IP boundaries.

challenges.text: Same-day deliveries with narrow time windows: our planner takes too long when orders change during the day.
challenges.detail: Same-day delivery has grown from about 8 percent of our order volume in 2021 to nearly 34 percent this year, and it has exposed a real limit in how our planner works. The problem is re-optimisation speed. When a new batch of orders arrives at noon for a 2–5 pm window, the planner has to reconsider routes for drivers who are already out. Right now that recalculation can take four to nine minutes on a fleet of thirty vehicles, and by the time it finishes the situation has moved on again. We have tried warm-starting the solver from the previous solution and tightening the time limit, but solution quality drops noticeably. We have also experimented with splitting the fleet into smaller sub-problems, which helps speed but creates awkward zone boundaries. What we need is an approach that can return a usable, near-optimal route update in under sixty seconds for fleets up to fifty vehicles, with order sets changing every fifteen to twenty minutes. Our three-person optimisation team has the solver infrastructure and the historical order data — roughly eighteen months of timestamped dispatch logs — but we do not have the research time to explore fundamentally different algorithmic directions. A good outcome is a recalculation that completes in under a minute and keeps total driving distance within five percent of the overnight-batch baseline.

challenges.text: Retail clients ask us to forecast store demand so deliveries match it.
challenges.detail: Three of our larger retail clients, including Sunce Retail, have asked us to help them predict how much stock each store will need so that replenishment deliveries are sized and timed more precisely. At the moment we plan routes based on confirmed orders from the warehouse system, but by the time an order is confirmed the store shelf is already thin or the van is over capacity. The clients want us to suggest delivery quantities and timing two to three days ahead, not just optimise the routes once orders exist. We have access to two years of delivery records showing what was delivered to each store, on what day, and in what quantity. The retail clients can share their point-of-sale data if there is a clear data-sharing agreement. What we do not have is any forecasting model or the in-house skills to build one. Our data team can prepare and pipe data but has not done demand forecasting before. A working outcome would be a simple model that produces store-level daily demand estimates with reasonable accuracy, surfaced inside RouteWise Planner so dispatchers can see suggested order sizes before the warehouse confirms. Budget for this is modest — it is a client retention play rather than a funded project — so a lightweight, interpretable model is more useful than a complex one.

challenges.text: Bus schedules change seasonally and parcel volumes on each route swing by up to 60% week to week; right now the owner manually decides which parcels go on which bus the evening before, and we miss the optimal loading about 30% of the time, leaving capacity unused or making customers wait an extra day.
challenges.detail: Every evening our owner Tibor sits down with the next day's bus timetable printout and a spreadsheet of pending parcels and tries to figure out which parcel goes on which bus. The problem is that bus schedules change twice a year and sometimes mid-season, and the number of parcels waiting for any given route can jump or drop by 60% compared to the week before — seasonal markets, holidays, a web shop running a sale. About 30% of the time the loading decision turns out to be wrong: either a bus leaves with space we could have used, so a parcel waits an extra day, or we overload a manifest and have to pull something at the last minute. We keep about 90 days of historical parcel-volume data per route in our PostgreSQL database, and we have the bus timetables in a structured format. What we have tried is colour-coded spreadsheet rules, but they don't handle the combinations well. We want a tool — something Tibor or a dispatcher can actually use on a laptop the evening before — that suggests a loading plan and flags when a route is near capacity. We are not looking for something that requires a data scientist to maintain. A reasonable budget would be under 8 000 EUR for a working prototype.

challenges.text: We have a small web shop integration but our tracking page is only in Serbian and Hungarian. We want to expand to B2B clients in Austria and Germany but we have no one to maintain a German-language customer interface and none of our three developers speak German.
challenges.detail: Our tracking page and merchant integration are entirely in Serbian and Hungarian, which covers our current customers well. But we have been approached by two small Austrian mail-order companies and a spare-parts distributor in Bavaria who ship regularly to customers in Vojvodina, and all three said they would use us if they could manage their accounts and read tracking updates in German. None of our three developers speak German well enough to write interface copy or handle error messages, and we do not have budget for a full-time translator on staff. What we have tried is running the interface through a machine-translation service and asking a friend of the family who speaks German to check it, but the result was inconsistent and some of the logistics terminology was wrong in ways that confused the test users. We need the German interface to stay correct as we update the platform, which happens roughly once a month. Our developers can build the infrastructure for language strings and localisation; the gap is the ongoing linguistic accuracy and someone who understands both German business expectations and what our service actually does. We would like to have a working German interface ready before the autumn shipping season.

challenges.text: At our Subotica hub we handle about 800 parcels a day and the floor space is 140 m². Congestion at the inbound belt slows throughput by about 25% during the 07:00–09:00 peak. We've looked at reorganising the floor but every layout we try on paper seems to make something else worse.
challenges.detail: Our Subotica sorting hub is 140 square metres, which was adequate when we were handling 400 parcels a day. Now we are at around 800 and we expect that to grow. The real problem is the morning peak between 07:00 and 09:00, when the overnight parcels from partner drop-off points arrive at the inbound belt at the same time as the first bus departures need their manifests ready.
