Throughput drops by about 25% in that window because the inbound and outbound flows cross in the middle of the floor. We have tried sketching new floor layouts on paper — moving the inbound belt to the east wall, splitting the staging area — but every arrangement we draw seems to fix the crossing problem and create a new one somewhere else, like blocking the fire exit or making the scan station too far from the dispatch table. We do not have budget to hire a logistics consultant, and we are not in a position to close the hub for more than one weekend to reorganise. We have detailed floor measurements and a rough count of how many parcels move through each zone per hour during the peak. A good outcome would be a concrete, tested layout recommendation we can actually implement.

challenges.text: We run 1,400 blood samples a day across three analysers and our middleware flags about 60 samples daily for manual technician review, but we estimate at least half of those reflex reviews are unnecessary — that alone costs us 2.5 extra technician-hours every shift.
challenges.detail: We run roughly 1,400 blood samples through our three analysers every working day. Our middleware is set up with a rule set that flags results outside certain delta-check and absolute-value thresholds, and on a typical day about 60 samples come back requiring a technician to physically look at the slide or re-run the sample. From our own internal tracking over the last six months, we can see that around 30 of those 60 flags each day end up confirming the original result — the review changes nothing. That adds up to about 2.5 technician-hours per shift that are spent on reviews that do not improve the result. We have tried tightening and loosening individual threshold values manually, but without a structured way to evaluate the combinations, we have not made meaningful progress. We have a full year of flag-and-outcome data in our LIMS export that we have never fully analysed. A good outcome for us would be a revised rule set, or a lightweight decision-support layer, that brings unnecessary reflex reviews down by at least 40% without increasing the rate of missed abnormal results.

challenges.text: Our new veterinary microbiology line is growing fast — revenue up 40% in two years — but we keep getting inconclusive antimicrobial susceptibility results for Enterococcus strains coming from poultry farms, and we have no in-house expertise to investigate why.
challenges.detail: Our veterinary microbiology line has grown 40% in revenue over the past two years, driven mainly by poultry farms in the Subotica and Senta areas. The recurring problem is that Enterococcus strains from poultry samples keep coming back with inconclusive or borderline susceptibility results on our standard card-based system. The breakpoints we are using are based on human clinical guidelines, and we suspect they are not the right reference point for veterinary isolates, but we do not have anyone on staff who has worked with veterinary-specific interpretive criteria or EUCAST veterinary breakpoint tables in a practical setting. We have contacted two external consultants in the past year; one did not respond and the other gave us a generic answer that did not help us resolve the interpretation problem. We have archived isolates going back 18 months that could be used for any follow-up work. What we need is someone who can tell us specifically why these strains are producing the results they are and what a more reliable testing protocol would look like for routine use in our lab.

challenges.text: We need to upgrade our laboratory information management system to comply with the new national e-health interoperability standard by Q1 next year, but the two developers we have don't know HL7 FHIR and vendor quotes are 120,000–180,000 EUR, which is way over our IT budget.
challenges.detail: Serbia's national e-health programme requires all accredited reference laboratories to support HL7 FHIR-based data exchange with the national health information platform by the end of Q1 next year. Our current LIMS, Deltasoft LabCenter 5.2, has an API, but it is not FHIR-compliant and the vendor has quoted us between 120,000 and 180,000 EUR for a full upgrade or migration to their newer platform. That is several times our annual IT budget. The two developers we employ internally are experienced with the Deltasoft system and with SQL, but neither has worked with FHIR before and they have not had time to go through any formal training while keeping our current systems running. We have looked at open-source FHIR middleware options and at one smaller domestic vendor, but we have not been able to evaluate whether any of these are realistic without someone who understands both FHIR implementation and the constraints of a production laboratory environment. The deadline is fixed and there is no provision for an extension.

challenges.text: Clients ask whether our firmware signing will survive quantum computers — we've been telling them 'we're looking at it' for eighteen months and that answer is wearing thin; we need a concrete migration path to post-quantum algorithms in our HSM product line.
challenges.detail: Several of our larger clients — two national-level agencies and one payment network operator — have started asking formally, in writing, whether the RSA and ECDSA signing operations inside our KL-HSM line will hold up once capable quantum hardware appears. We first acknowledged the question eighteen months ago and said we were evaluating options. That answer no longer satisfies procurement officers who are planning five- to ten-year infrastructure cycles. We have one engineer who has read the NIST post-quantum standardisation documents and done some prototype work with ML-DSA (formerly Dilithium), but we have not touched the firmware architecture to accommodate larger key material or different signature flows. Our HSM firmware runs on a constrained microcontroller with limited flash and RAM, so a straight drop-in is not possible. We need a migration plan that tells clients which firmware version will support post-quantum algorithms, what the performance trade-offs are, and how hybrid classical/post-quantum operation will work during transition. A good outcome is a documented roadmap and at least one working proof-of-concept integration inside twelve months.

challenges.text: Our PKI certificate issuance platform handles about 380,000 certificates a year and the database query time on revocation checks has climbed to 900 milliseconds on peak days — clients in the payment sector are complaining that OCSP responses are too slow.
challenges.detail: CertiCore issues certificates for clients in banking and payment processing, and those clients rely on our OCSP responder to get fast revocation answers during transaction authorisation flows. Twelve months ago, average OCSP response time was under 200 milliseconds. On peak days now it sits around 900 milliseconds, occasionally spiking past a second. The database behind the responder is PostgreSQL, running on two physical servers in our data room. The revocation table has grown to about 2.1 million rows and our indexing strategy was designed when the table was a tenth of that size. We ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the worst queries and found sequential scans on certificate serial lookups under certain join conditions. We added a composite index three months ago and saw a modest improvement that did not hold. We have not tried partitioning or caching layers yet, partly because our database administrator left in late 2023 and has not been replaced. We have the query logs, schema, and a non-production copy of the database available for analysis. A good outcome is sustained OCSP response times below 150 milliseconds at peak load without replacing the existing hardware.

challenges.text: We're trying to raise a Series A round of about €4 million to expand into the German and Austrian government markets, but every VC we've spoken to wants three years of IFRS-consolidated financials and we've been reporting under Serbian GAAP only.
challenges.detail: We have had serious conversations with two venture capital firms about a €4 million Series A to fund sales operations and certification work in Germany and Austria, where government PKI procurement cycles are opening up. Both investors asked for three years of IFRS-consolidated financial statements as a precondition for due diligence. We have been reporting under Serbian GAAP since the company was founded, and our accounts are audited annually by a local firm in Novi Sad. We do not have IFRS statements, and we do not have in-house staff who know how to prepare them. We understand a full IFRS restatement for three years is a substantial piece of work involving fixed-asset revaluation, deferred tax treatment, and possibly revenue recognition adjustments on our multi-year managed-service contracts. We have set aside a rough budget of €30,000–€40,000 for this exercise and have a self-imposed deadline of the end of the current calendar year, because we want to re-approach investors in Q1 2026. A good outcome is audited IFRS-compliant statements for 2022, 2023, and 2024 that can be handed to investors without qualification.

challenges.text: Our hardware security module enclosure needs to pass tamper-evidence tests for Common Criteria EAL4+ certification, but our in-house mechanical team keeps seeing micro-fractures in the epoxy potting layer under thermal cycling between -10°C and 60°C.
challenges.detail: Common Criteria EAL4+ requires that our KL-HSM enclosure demonstrate tamper evidence under physical stress, including thermal cycling. Our target operating range for the certified product is -10°C to 60°C. During evaluation preparation, our mechanical team has been running thermal cycle tests and consistently finding micro-fractures in the epoxy potting layer after 50 to 80 cycles. The fractures appear near the corners of the PCB substrate and at points where metallic fasteners meet the potting compound. We have tried two different epoxy formulations from our current supplier, adjusted pour temperature, and varied curing time, but the cracking pattern persists. We do not have materials science expertise in-house; our mechanical team is competent at enclosure design but has no background in polymer behaviour under cyclic thermal stress. The certification timeline is a constraint: we have a pre-evaluation agreement with an accredited laboratory and the physical testing phase is scheduled to begin in seven months. We have physical samples, test data from the last four test runs, and the enclosure drawings available. A good outcome is an enclosure that passes 200 thermal cycles without visible fracturing.

challenges.text: Our spraying drone deposits 80% of the target dose on average, but drift measurements on windy days (above 3 m/s) show we miss up to 35% of the intended strip, and one large client in Bačka is threatening to switch supplier after two suboptimal fungicide runs this spring.
challenges.detail: Our drones deposit an average of 80% of the target dose on the intended strip under calm conditions, but on windy days (above 3 m/s wind speed) drift measurements show we miss up to 35% of the strip width. This spring we had two fungicide runs on a 400-hectare client farm in Bačka during less-than-ideal wind conditions; the client is now in talks with a competitor. We have tried adding GPS-guided variable-altitude logic and reducing flight speed, but the core problem is that our nozzle design and spray physics are not optimised for wind rejection. We have weather data from 12 field seasons, spray trials from 2023, and a budget of about 45,000 EUR for equipment and consultancy. A good outcome is to reduce drift loss to under 15% in winds up to 4 m/s, documented by independent field trials that we can show to clients.

challenges.text: We have 14 agronomists on staff who write prescription maps manually by overlaying yield maps and soil surveys; this takes two to three days per farm per season and we simply cannot service more than 40 clients this way — we need to automate prescription generation.
challenges.detail: We have 14 agronomists on staff who spend two to three days per farm per season manually overlaying yield maps, soil boring data, and satellite images to write prescription maps. This blocks us from taking on more than 40 clients; new enquiries arrive every week but we cannot service them. We have tried hiring two junior agronomists but they still need three weeks of field training and supervision. We own all the raw data (soil surveys in shapefile format, yield maps from combine sensors, Sentinel-2 archives), and we have a small in-house software team who maintain our flight logs database. The constraint is that we lack a formal algorithm and validation protocol. A good outcome is a semi-automated system that an agronomist can review and refine in one day per farm, cutting our per-client labour by 60%.

challenges.text: We raised a Series A round 18 months ago but our investors are now pushing for a formal EBITDA improvement plan before the next tranche, and our internal finance team has no experience building the kind of three-year financial model with scenario analysis that the investors' term sheet requires.
challenges.detail: We closed a Series A investment 18 months ago (2.1 million EUR from two Serbian VC funds) on the condition that we hit EBITDA breakeven by Q4 2025. Our investors now require a three-year financial model with scenario analysis (revenue growth, margin cases, capital requirements for fleet expansion) before they release the second tranche. Our finance team (two staff, both with accounting background) have built a simple P&L spreadsheet but have never created a formal cash-flow forecast or run sensitivity scenarios. We have clean historical data for the last four years and a rough operational plan, but no experience with investor-grade financial documentation. The deadline is end of Q2 2025. A good outcome is a presentation-ready Excel model or similar tool that shows credible paths to profitability, stress-tested against 20% lower client retention and 30% slower acquisition.

challenges.text: A pharmaceutical client must remove drug residues (diclofenac, carbamazepine) that our biological step doesn't catch.
challenges.detail: One of our pharmaceutical clients — a generics manufacturer in Sremska Mitrovica — must meet a discharge limit for active pharmaceutical ingredients before their permit renewal in late 2026. Right now our MBR system handles the biological oxygen demand fine, but two compounds keep showing up above the limit in effluent samples: diclofenac and carbamazepine. Both are well-known hard-to-degrade molecules, and our standard aerobic biology simply does not break them down enough. We have done some reading on ozonation and activated carbon polishing, but we have no in-house experience with either. Our process engineer ran a small-scale ozone contact test last autumn and got inconsistent results — partial removal some days, almost none others. We suspect the matrix is interfering but we do not know why. Our lab can measure the compounds by HPLC if we send samples to an external lab, which costs money and takes a week. Budget for a technical study is modest — around 15 000 EUR — and we cannot afford a large pilot rig without external co-funding. A good outcome would be a validated small-scale method we can build into a compact polishing stage that fits within the existing footprint at that client's site.

challenges.text: Membranes in dairy plants foul quickly and need cleaning every week.
challenges.detail: At two dairy plants we service — one near Temerin, one outside Bečej — our MBR membranes are fouling much faster than the design assumptions. We scheduled cleaning cycles every two weeks, but in practice the operators are forced to do a full CIP clean every five to seven days because transmembrane pressure spikes. A full CIP uses roughly 200 litres of citric acid and caustic solution per unit and takes the system offline for four to six hours. That adds up to significant chemical cost and lost treatment capacity over a year. We have tried adjusting aeration intensity and sludge retention time, but the fouling rate has not changed much. Dairy wastewater has high fats, proteins, and sugars, and we think the combination is forming a gel layer the biology is not breaking down fast enough. We do not have the tools or know-how to characterise the foulant properly. Our service records go back three years and show a clear seasonal pattern — fouling is worst in summer, which might point to temperature effects on the biology or on the fat chemistry. A good outcome would be a reliable explanation of what is causing the fouling and a practical change — to pre-treatment, aeration, or membrane material — that pushes cleaning intervals back to at least twelve days.

challenges.text: Our cold-process soaps sometimes develop a white powdery layer called soda ash within 48 hours of unmoulding — it doesn't affect quality but about 15% of bars look unsellable and we have to rebatch them, wasting roughly 8 working hours a week. We've tried covering the moulds and using sodium lactate but nothing works consistently.
challenges.detail: About fifteen out of every hundred bars we unmould develop a white dusty coating on the surface within a day or two. We know it is soda ash — unreacted sodium carbonate coming to the surface — and we know it does not change how the soap performs on skin, but it looks bad and customers notice. We cannot sell those bars at full price at the market so we chop them up and rebatch them, which means reheating, remoulding and re-curing. That process takes roughly eight working hours every week across two people. We have tried spraying the tops of the loaves with isopropyl alcohol right after pour, covering the moulds with cardboard and a blanket to keep the heat in during the gel phase, and adding sodium lactate at one percent of the water weight to speed unmoulding. None of these steps has brought the rate below about twelve percent consistently. The problem is worse in winter when our workroom gets colder. We do not have the budget for a climate-controlled curing room — we are talking about a small converted garage. A good outcome for us would be a reliable protocol we can actually follow with the equipment we have, or a clear explanation of which variable is causing the inconsistency so we can target it.

challenges.text: We use shea butter and cocoa butter as our main base materials and their price has gone up 40% in the last two years, which is squeezing our margin below 18%. We'd like to explore locally sourced Vojvodina plant-oil alternatives — sunflower, hemp, pumpkin seed — but we don't know how their fatty-acid profiles will affect product texture and skin feel.
challenges.detail: Two years ago we were paying roughly 4.20 euros per kilogram for shea butter and around 5.10 for cocoa butter. Today both are closer to six euros, and our supplier in Budapest has flagged that prices may keep climbing. Those two ingredients make up about half the weight of our body-butter line and around twenty percent of our soap recipes. Our margin on body butter has dropped to under eighteen percent and if costs rise another ten percent we are at break-even on that product. Vojvodina has good sunflower, hemp and pumpkin-seed oil production and we can source those oils locally at prices that have stayed much more stable. The problem is we do not know enough about fatty-acid composition to know whether a reformulation will hold together properly, feel good on skin, or go rancid faster. We have one trial batch of a sunflower-heavy body butter we made last spring and it separated after three weeks. We need help understanding what is going wrong chemically and what a realistic reformulation path looks like. We have the production capacity and the willingness to test, but we need guidance on the science side.

challenges.text: We sell about 1,200 units a month through our webshop but our abandoned-cart rate is 71% and we don't know whether it's the checkout flow, the photos, or the product descriptions. We've never done any structured customer behaviour analysis.
challenges.detail: Our webshop turned over about 14,400 units in 2023, so roughly 1,200 units a month. The average order value is around 1,350 dinars. The problem is our abandoned-cart rate, which our WooCommerce dashboard shows sitting at seventy-one percent. We do not know what is driving it. We have three guesses: the checkout has too many steps for mobile users, the product photos do not show texture clearly enough to make someone trust a soap they cannot smell, or the descriptions do not answer the questions people have before buying. We have not done any structured testing. We do not use heatmaps, session recordings or A/B testing tools. We do not have a person on the team who knows how to set those things up. Our budget for fixing this is modest — we could justify spending money if we had a clear plan and some evidence about what is actually wrong. A good outcome would be a tested change that brings the abandoned-cart rate below fifty percent within six months.

challenges.text: Our nature-interpretation app lists 210 species but the automatic species identification from guest photos is wrong about 35% of the time for birds and insects, which embarrasses guides in front of guests and has led to three formal complaints from ornithologist clients this season.
challenges.detail: TrailSense lets guests photograph something they see on the trail and get a species name back instantly. It works reasonably well for plants — maybe one wrong answer in ten — but for birds and insects we are getting it wrong about one in three times. We built the identification feature ourselves using a pre-trained image classification model we found through an open-source repository, and we have not touched the model since 2021. The problem is that the photos guests take in the field are low resolution, poorly lit, and often show just a wing or a tail. We have accumulated roughly 14,000 labelled guest photos over three seasons and our guides have manually corrected about 4,200 of them, so we have a corrections dataset sitting unused. Three guests who were experienced birdwatchers wrote formal complaints this season after the app confidently misidentified species on their tour sheets. We want accuracy for birds and insects to reach at least 80 percent under real field conditions. We have a small cloud budget — around €400 per month — and we cannot take the feature offline during the main season, which runs April to October.

challenges.text: We want to add a carbon-footprint score to each tour package so that sustainability-conscious agencies in the Netherlands and Scandinavia can use it in their own marketing, but we have no validated methodology for calculating transport, catering and accommodation emissions at the per-guest level.
challenges.detail: Several of our Dutch and Scandinavian agency partners have started asking for a carbon-footprint figure they can print on their brochures and put on their booking pages. Right now we have nothing to give them. We did try to use a generic online calculator last winter but the numbers it produced did not account for the fact that most of our transport is shared minibuses, that our catering suppliers are all within 40 km, or that our accommodation partners use wood pellet heating. We collected fuel receipts and mileage logs for all of 2023 and we have supplier invoices that show roughly what food was served per tour. What we do not have is a clear methodology that an external auditor would accept. We are not aiming for a formal certification right now — that is too expensive — but we need a calculation approach that is transparent enough that an agency in Utrecht or Aarhus can explain it to their own clients without embarrassment. A spreadsheet tool our guides could update after each tour would be a realistic outcome.

challenges.text: Our trails cross three protected natural areas and getting annual permits renewed takes six to eight months of back-and-forth with provincial and national inspectorates — last year we lost the entire spring season on one trail because the permit renewal was delayed, costing us roughly €34,000 in cancelled bookings.
challenges.detail: We operate trails inside three protected natural areas managed by different bodies — one provincial and two under national oversight. Each body has its own forms, its own inspection calendar and its own interpretation of what documents we need to resubmit versus what carries over from the previous year. In 2023 a permit for our Deliblato Sands spring trail was held up from February until late May because one inspectorate asked for a supplementary impact assessment that had never been requested before and that nobody in the office could find a template for. We lost all April and May bookings on that trail — roughly €34,000 in revenue — and had to refund six agency partners. We have kept records of every submission, every request for additional documents and every inspector contact since 2015, so there is a paper trail. What we need is either a clearer map of what the requirements actually are and how to anticipate changes, or some kind of early-warning system so we start renewals earlier and can flag when a request seems unusual. We have no legal department and our office manager handles this alongside other duties.

challenges.text: We have GPS track logs from 4,800 guided tours over seven years but we use them only for navigation; we suspect there are patterns in where guests slow down, photograph and linger that could help us redesign tour itineraries and set better pricing tiers, but nobody on our team knows how to analyse spatial movement data.
challenges.detail: Every tour we run is logged with a Garmin device carried by the guide. We export GPX files after each tour and store them on our server, organised by trail and date. We have 4,800 files going back to 2017. We also have timestamped photo metadata from TrailSense that shows where and when guests took pictures, and brief guide notes that record when a group stopped and for how long. We have never done anything with this data except use the tracks for navigation and occasionally to check whether a guide followed the planned route. What we suspect is that certain spots — a particular bend in the trail, a viewpoint, a pond edge — consistently cause groups to slow down and cluster, and that this information could tell us which parts of a tour guests actually value, which segments feel like filler, and maybe even whether premium pricing for certain routes is justified by what guests actually experience. None of us knows how to work with spatial data beyond drawing a line in QGIS. We would like to start with one trail as a pilot and see whether the analysis produces anything actionable before we invest more time.

challenges.text: Too many false atrial fibrillation alarms when patients move.
challenges.detail:
Our motion artefact problem is straightforward to describe and hard to fix. When a patient moves quickly — walking fast, reaching overhead, rolling over in bed — the electrode contact changes momentarily and the raw signal looks enough like atrial fibrillation that our current classifier flags it. Right now roughly one in four AF alerts that land in the clinician portal turns out to be a motion artefact once the cardiologist looks at the raw trace. That rate is too high; clinicians have told us they are starting to ignore low-confidence flags entirely, which defeats the purpose of automatic detection.

We have a three-axis accelerometer on the patch and we log its data alongside the ECG at 50 Hz, so we have the raw material to do better. Our dataset currently holds about 1,400 completed patient recordings, each tagged by one of two reviewing cardiologists as true AF, other arrhythmia, or noise. The problem is that our two biomedical engineers are occupied with hardware revisions for the next device generation and neither has deep experience with time-series classification beyond what they have read. We have no budget for a large external contract — somewhere in the range of €15,000–25,000 is what we can move without board approval. We need a false-positive rate below ten percent without missing confirmed AF events. A working prototype model integrated into our Python pipeline by the end of 2025 would be a good outcome.

challenges.text: We need a clinical validation study in Serbia before CE marking.
challenges.detail:
CE marking under MDR requires clinical evidence, and for a class IIa active device like ours the notified body has made clear that a post-market clinical follow-up plan is not enough on its own at this stage. We need a prospective study in which patients wear the CardioTrack patch alongside a predicate device simultaneously, and a clinician adjudicates the results. The study needs to be run in Serbia, partly because that is where our existing clinical relationships are and partly because running it abroad would cost more than we can justify before we have revenue to match.

We have a clinical liaison, Milena Ðorić, who has contacts at two private cardiology practices in Novi Sad, but neither practice has experience running a formal clinical investigation under the MDR-aligned Serbian Medical Devices Act framework. We need someone who understands how to write a clinical investigation plan, navigate the ethics committee application, and help us manage data collection in a way that will satisfy our notified body, TÜV SÜD. Target enrolment is around 120 patients over six months. We have set aside roughly €30,000 for the study itself, not including device costs. We need ethics approval and the first patient enrolled before the end of Q1 2026, or our 2027 CE mark timeline slips by at least a year.

challenges.text: Our vibration sensor on the gearbox generates 4 kHz raw signals; we are currently sending everything to the cloud and the data bill is already €18,000 a month at only 200 trucks — we cannot scale to 2,000 trucks without compressing or filtering at the edge first.
challenges.detail: Right now every sensor node streams raw 4 kHz accelerometer data straight to AWS. At 200 trucks that costs us roughly €18,000 a month just in ingestion and storage. We have run the numbers and scaling to 2,000 trucks without changing the architecture would push that above €180,000 a month, which kills the unit economics completely. We have experimented with simple threshold-based filtering on the node — only transmitting when amplitude crosses a set level — but that throws away the low-amplitude early-warning signatures we need for predictive work. We also tried downsampling to 500 Hz before transmission, but our data science team found that the bearing-fault sidebands we rely on sit between 1 and 3 kHz, so downsampling removes exactly the information we care about. What we need is something smarter on the device itself: extract the relevant features or compressed representation at the edge and send only that. Our Cortex-M4 nodes have headroom — they are not running anywhere near full capacity — but our team does not have deep expertise in edge ML compression. We have a budget of around €40,000 for this work and we need a solution we can push as an OTA firmware update within nine months.

challenges.text: We can detect that something is wrong with the drivetrain about 80% of the time, but our model cannot tell a worn differential from a failing wheel bearing — fleet managers need a specific fault code, not just a warning light, or they won't pay for the subscription.
challenges.detail: Our current fault-detection model flags anomalies with about 80% recall across our labelled dataset of 340 confirmed fault events collected from customer trucks over two years. The problem is that it outputs a single binary alert — something is wrong — rather than identifying which component has failed. Fleet managers at Nordtrans Spedition told us directly that a vague warning is not worth paying a subscription for; they need something equivalent to a fault code, like 'rear differential wear' or 'nearside front wheel bearing fatigue', so they can order the right part before the truck comes in. We have tried training separate binary classifiers for each fault class but our labelled dataset per fault type is thin — we have 80 worn-differential cases and only 34 wheel-bearing cases, for example. We also lack balanced negative examples for each class. We have the raw signal archives going back to 2019, all stored in S3, and we have maintenance records from two customers that we could use to build more labels if someone helped us structure that work. A good outcome is a model that outputs a ranked fault-code list with a confidence score, achieving at least 75% top-1 accuracy per fault class on a held-out test set.

challenges.text: We collect location and driving-behaviour data continuously from trucks; two German fleet operators have told us that before they sign, they need a data processing agreement that satisfies their works council and the German Betriebsrat co-determination rules around employee monitoring, which our Serbian lawyers have never dealt with before.
challenges.detail: We collect GPS position, speed, acceleration and braking events at one-second intervals from every truck in a customer's fleet. For our Polish and Austrian customers this has not been a problem. But two German prospects — both mid-sized logistics operators — have said that their works council will not permit deployment unless we can show them a data processing agreement and an operational protocol that explicitly covers the rights of employed drivers under German co-determination law, specifically the rules their Betriebsrat can invoke around electronic monitoring of individual workers. Our Serbian legal team is experienced with GDPR in general but has never negotiated with a German Betriebsrat or drafted the kind of annex to a works agreement that these customers need. We had one conversation with a German law firm in Frankfurt but their quote for the full engagement was €25,000, which we found high for what we hope is a reusable template. What we actually need is a reusable data processing framework and a standard addendum that we can adapt for each German customer, so we are not starting from zero every time. Getting this right would unlock at least two signed contracts worth a combined annual recurring revenue of around €180,000.

challenges.text: Our sensor housing is rated IP67 but after 18 months on trucks operating in winter conditions in Poland, about 4% of units show corrosion on the PCB, which we believe is caused by thermal cycling cracking the potting compound seal — we need to understand the failure mechanism before we can fix the next hardware revision.
challenges.detail: Starting about six months ago we began seeing corrosion on the main PCB of sensor units returned from trucks operating in northern Poland through the winter. The failure rate is around 4% of units after 18 months in the field. The housing is rated IP67 and passes our in-house water-immersion test, but the returned units show moisture ingress at the cable entry gland and at one corner of the potted cavity. Our working theory is that the temperature swings these trucks experience — from minus 25°C overnight in a Polish depot to plus 60°C near the gearbox casing when running — are causing micro-cracking in the epoxy potting compound, and that the cracks are opening a path for condensation. We have cross-sectioned four returned units and can see discolouration in the potting near the gland, but we do not have the equipment or the expertise to characterise the crack morphology properly or to confirm whether it is the potting, the gland seal or the bond between the two that is the primary failure point. We have a batch of 30 returned units available for destructive testing. We need to identify the failure mechanism clearly enough to specify a fix for the next hardware revision, which is scheduled to go to manufacturing in about twelve months.

challenges.text: Our lithium-ion cell sorting relies on open-circuit voltage only and we're sending about 22% of still-usable cells to shredding because we can't distinguish genuinely degraded cells from ones that are just deeply discharged; this is destroying our margin on black mass recovery.
challenges.detail: When a battery pack arrives at our facility, our technicians measure open-circuit voltage on each cell they extract. Cells below a set threshold go straight to the shredder for black mass recovery. The problem is that a cell sitting in a discharged device for months can read exactly the same voltage as a cell that has genuinely lost capacity. We have no way to tell them apart quickly on the floor. Our internal count for the last two quarters shows that roughly 22% of cells flagged for shredding actually have usable remaining capacity when we send a sample to Halvard's lab for spot-checking. Each kilogram of cells sent to shredding instead of being resold or reused is money we don't recover. We've looked at adding a brief pulse-discharge test but our current bench equipment is too slow for the volume we handle. A good outcome for us would be a triage method fast enough to keep up with manual disassembly pace, cheap enough to run per cell rather than per batch, and reliable enough to reduce that 22% figure to under 5%. We do not have a dedicated lab, but we have bench space and are willing to invest up to around €30,000 in equipment if the approach is validated.

challenges.text: Our collection point cabinets run on 4G and we're seeing about 8% of fill-level and weight sensor readings drop out every week; we don't know if it's the modems, the firmware or network coverage gaps, and we're making wrong collection decisions as a result.
challenges.detail: Our 340 field cabinets each send fill-level readings from an ultrasonic sensor and a weight reading from a platform load cell, transmitted over 4G every four hours. On any given week about 8% of those readings simply do not arrive. When we look at the raw logs we can see that some cabinets miss one reading and then recover, while others go silent for several days. We have three possible causes and no clear way to separate them: modem hardware failures, firmware bugs in the data-push code, or genuine coverage gaps in parts of rural Hungary and northern Romania. We have tried pushing a firmware update six months ago that added retry logic, which reduced the dropout rate from about 11% to 8%, but progress has stalled. The practical damage is that our logistics planner, Milena Ćirković, sometimes dispatches a collection vehicle to a cabinet that is barely half-full while a nearby cabinet overflows because it stopped reporting. We need a diagnostic approach that helps us classify the failure mode per cabinet so we can fix the right thing, rather than replacing hardware blindly. Budget for tooling or a short pilot is roughly €8,000.

challenges.text: Disassembly output per worker has stayed flat at around 18 kg/hour for two years; we've watched the workflow but don't know how to redesign the station layout or the sequence of operations to get closer to the 28 kg/hour our Dutch partner achieves.
challenges.detail: Our disassembly floor has ten workstations. Each station handles a mix of device types: phones, tablets, small household electronics. For the past two years our average output has stayed at about 18 kilograms of separated material per worker per hour regardless of which devices are coming in. Our Dutch downstream partner, Halvard Material Group, reports roughly 28 kg per worker per hour at their Dordrecht facility on a comparable device mix. We have visited their site once and came back with notes but no clear picture of exactly what we should change. The differences we noticed were in station layout, the sequence in which parts are removed, and the way tools are arranged, but we did not have a structured way to measure which of those factors actually drives throughput. We have tried rearranging one station as a test but did not measure before and after consistently enough to draw conclusions. We have timestamped video of about 40 hours of floor work that we collected internally. A concrete target for us is reaching 24 kg per worker per hour within 12 months without adding headcount or significant capital equipment. We are open to a structured process study if someone can tell us what data to collect and how to act on it.

challenges.text: We want to hire two experienced electronics engineers to build an in-house testing bench but the salaries candidates are asking for in Novi Sad are above what we budgeted, and the ones we can afford keep leaving for larger firms in Belgrade after six months.
challenges.detail: We want to build an in-house testing bench that would let us characterize battery cells, diagnose sensor faults from our field cabinets, and prototype small improvements without relying on external labs. To do that we need at least two electronics engineers with hands-on experience in embedded systems and battery measurement. We have posted the roles twice in the past 14 months. The candidates with the right skills ask for salaries between €2,400 and €2,900 net per month in Novi Sad, which is above our approved budget of €1,900 net. We have hired two people at the lower figure and both left within six months, one for a hardware company in Belgrade and one for a German firm that agreed to remote work. We are not looking for advice on salaries alone; we are also open to thinking about whether a shared resource model, a structured internship-to-hire track, or a part-time arrangement with an external specialist could give us the technical capacity we need while we grow revenue. Our constraint is that we need this capacity in place within the next 18 months to meet our own product roadmap.

challenges.text: We can't tell how healthy a used battery module is without a full test cycle that takes 20 hours.
challenges.detail: Every used battery module that comes into our workshop needs a state-of-health number before we can assign it to a cabinet. Right now the only way we trust is a full charge-discharge-charge cycle on our test rigs. At a 0.2C rate on a 50 Ah module that runs close to 20 hours per channel, and we only have four channels. When a bus dismantler offers us a batch of 120 modules we can physically test maybe 30 of them before we have to decide whether to buy the rest. We have tried using the open-circuit voltage curve as a shortcut but it gives us too wide a spread — we have seen modules with identical OCV that differed by 18 percent in usable capacity. We also tried a short 10-minute pulse test based on a paper we found, but our false-pass rate was still around 12 percent, which is too high when a two-year capacity warranty is on the line. We have accumulated about 2,400 completed test records with full voltage, current and temperature traces stored in our SQLite database, plus the corresponding end-of-life capacity figure for each module. What we want is a method — probably a faster partial test combined with some kind of model — that can estimate remaining capacity within plus or minus 5 percent in under two hours per module. We have no budget for additional test hardware this year. A working method would let us screen full incoming batches and double our throughput without adding rigs.

challenges.text: Our depot sorting is still done by hand: two sorters misplace roughly 3–4% of parcels per shift, which costs us about 180,000 RSD a month in redeliveries and customer refunds. We need a way to read and route labels automatically even when they are crumpled, printed poorly, or in Hungarian.
challenges.detail: Every parcel that arrives at our depot gets sorted by hand onto one of 22 district shelves. Two sorters on the morning shift handle about 1,800 parcels between 6 a.m. and 10 a.m. The error rate sits around 3 to 4 percent, which means 55 to 70 parcels a day end up on the wrong van. Most of those need a redelivery attempt the next day, and a share result in customer refund claims. We calculated the direct cash cost at roughly 180,000 RSD per month across redelivery fuel, driver overtime, and refunds. We tried sticker-based colour coding by district in 2022, but sellers print labels in all kinds of conditions: thermal paper that has rubbed against other parcels, addresses typed in Hungarian with diacritics, hand-written add-ons. Our Zebra scanners read clean 1D barcodes fine, but they cannot parse anything else. We want a system that can read the destination from a label image and light up or beep the correct shelf, even when the print quality is poor or the text is in Hungarian. We have a camera we bought for testing and about 14,000 parcel label photos archived. Budget is not fixed but we cannot absorb a six-figure hardware investment in year one.

challenges.text: We have 34 drivers and dispatch is still done by one person on the phone every morning. When three or more orders cancel or are added after 10 a.m. we just can't re-optimise in time, and drivers end up doing 15–20% more kilometres than they should.
challenges.detail: Each morning our one dispatcher, Nenad Vukić, calls every driver, assigns stops verbally, and sends a printed stop list by WhatsApp. On a normal day with fewer than 30 changes after 10 a.m. he manages well enough. But during sales events or bad weather we regularly see 80 to 100 post-cutoff changes, and Nenad simply cannot recalculate 34 routes in real time while also answering driver questions. The result is that drivers stick to the morning plan even when it no longer makes sense. We measured an average of 17 percent excess kilometres during the four weeks of November 2023 peak compared to October. At our fuel cost that is a material monthly loss. We have tried using a free routing website for small batches, but it tops out at 25 stops and does not talk to our dispatch console. We need something that can ingest our order list, accept late additions and cancellations, and produce updated route assignments within a few minutes so Nenad can push them to drivers before they leave the next stop. It does not need to be a finished product on day one; a working prototype we can test with a subset of drivers is a realistic first milestone.

challenges.text: We want to expand into Slovakia and Romania but do not have anyone on staff who understands the cross-border VAT and customs documentation for B2C parcels under the EU OSS scheme. Every consultant we talk to quotes us six months of work.
challenges.detail: Several of our seller clients have customers in Romania and Slovakia, and three of them have asked us to extend delivery there as early as mid-2025. We understand the road network and we could arrange subcontractor partners in Timișoara and Košice. The blocker is paperwork. B2C parcel shipments across EU borders under the OSS VAT scheme require customs declarations, IOSS registration checks per shipment, and country-specific labelling rules we do not currently know. One of our sellers was fined in Romania last year for incorrect CN22 forms, which scared the others. We spoke to two logistics consultants; both estimated six months of preparation and fees above 800,000 RSD. That timeline would push expansion past the window when our clients need it. We want someone who can map exactly what documentation and system changes are required, help us build a checklist and template set we can operate ourselves, and flag which parts genuinely need a licensed customs agent versus what we can handle in-house. We are not looking for someone to run our compliance forever, just to stand it up correctly the first time.

challenges.text: We're seeing surface-fatigue spalling on the output gear of our RA-40 planetary gearbox after about 9,000 operating hours — our design spec says 20,000 — and it only happens in installations where the robot makes frequent rapid direction reversals, not in continuous-duty applications.
challenges.detail: Our RA-40 planetary gearbox carries a 20,000-hour design life. In continuous-duty installations — conveyor drives, for example — we see no unusual wear. The problem shows up only where the robot reverses direction frequently, say 40 to 80 reversals per minute. In those applications we are seeing surface-fatigue spalling on the output-stage ring gear at around 9,000 hours, less than half the rated life. We have pulled failed units and measured hardness, case depth and surface finish — all within spec on the drawing. We changed the output bearing preload on one batch as a test and saw no improvement. We do not have the in-house capability to model the transient load spikes that come from rapid reversals, and we do not have a test rig that can replicate the duty cycle at accelerated speed. What we need is someone who can help us understand whether the failure is driven by contact stress during the reversal transient, by lubricant film breakdown at low sliding speeds, or by something in the geometry. A good outcome would be a design or process change we can validate on a test rig within about six months, before the next production run.

challenges.text: We machine about 1,200 actuator housings per month and our scrap rate on the final bore tolerance is running at 4.1%, up from 1.8% two years ago; we think tool wear is the root cause but we haven't been able to prove it because we don't log tool age systematically.
challenges.detail: We machine roughly 1,200 actuator housings per month and the final bore tolerance is H6 on diameters between 40 mm and 120 mm. Two years ago our scrap rate on that feature was 1.8%. It is now running at 4.1% over the last six months, which costs us in material, machining time and delivery delays. Our strong suspicion is tool wear — we use indexable boring bars and we change inserts on a fixed cycle, not on a condition basis — but we have no systematic log of insert age per spindle, so we cannot prove it statistically. We have tried tightening the replacement interval across the board, which cut scrap briefly but drove consumable costs up more than the scrap saving was worth. We have a Mitutoyo air-gauge on the final inspection station and we record every result, so we have a large dataset of bore measurements against date and machine number but not against tool identity. What we want is a way to connect the measurement data we already have to tool condition, so we can replace inserts based on actual wear state rather than a fixed schedule.

challenges.text: A large German robotics OEM has asked us to supply 4,000 units per year with PPAP documentation; we've never done PPAP before and our quality manager estimates it will take eight months just to understand what's required, which is too slow for the customer's timeline.
challenges.detail: Robotik Augsburg GmbH — a fictional German robotics OEM — has offered us a contract for 4,000 gearbox subassemblies per year starting in the second half of 2025. The condition is full PPAP documentation at level three. We have never submitted a PPAP package. Our quality manager, Dragana Vukić, has read the AIAG reference manual and her estimate is that understanding the requirements, running the capability studies, preparing the control plans and getting the first submission approved will take eight months if we work through it ourselves. The customer wants preliminary documentation in four months. We have ISO 9001 in place and we do first-article inspection routinely, so we are not starting from zero, but the specific PPAP elements — process FMEA, MSA studies, initial process capability indices — are new to us. We are not looking for someone to write the documents for us; we need structured guidance and a realistic project plan so our own team can build the competence and meet the customer's deadline.

challenges.text: Our lubricant supplier changed the base-oil formulation last year and now our sealed gearboxes are showing elevated operating temperatures — up 11°C on average — but we can't tell whether the thermal problem is in the lubricant viscosity, the seal friction, or both.
challenges.detail: Our sealed gearboxes leave the factory with a specified lubricant fill, and for years we used Termol GX-220 synthetic gear oil from our local supplier. Last year the supplier reformulated the product — same name, different base-oil blend — without a formal change notice. We only found out when a customer reported elevated temperatures. We have since measured operating temperature on twelve units in the field and eleven units on our internal run-in stand; average temperature is up 11°C compared to our historical baseline at the same load and speed. We have measured the viscosity of the new lubricant and it is slightly higher at 40°C than the old specification but within the tolerance band printed on the datasheet. We replaced the shaft seals on four test units with identical parts from a different seal supplier and saw a small reduction — about 2°C — that may or may not be significant. We do not have a way to separate the thermal contribution of lubricant churning losses from seal friction losses under controlled conditions. A good outcome is a clear answer: which factor dominates, what is the fix, and whether we need to re-qualify the gearbox thermal rating.

challenges.text: Our vibration-based anomaly detection on CNC milling machines works well in the lab but on the factory floor ambient noise from neighbouring machines creates so many false positives that operators just switch the alerts off — we need a smarter signal-separation approach.
challenges.detail: Our vibration-based anomaly detector was trained on data recorded in a quiet test cell using a single CNC milling machine. In that setting it catches spindle wear and tool chatter with a false-positive rate below three percent. When we deployed it at our pilot site in Győr, the machine sits on a shared concrete floor next to two punch presses and a conveyor belt. The background vibration from those machines looks, to our current model, like low-level anomalies almost continuously. Operators started ignoring the alerts after about a week. We have tried a simple high-pass filter and a short-window FFT threshold, but both still let through too much floor-transmitted noise. We have roughly eight weeks of raw accelerometer logs from the Győr site — about 400 GB — plus clean lab recordings for comparison. Our signal-processing engineer can dedicate roughly half her time to this over the next three months. We are not looking for a perfect academic solution; we need something we can ship as a firmware update to an edge device with 4 GB of RAM. A good outcome is getting the false-positive rate back below five percent in a noisy multi-machine environment.

challenges.text: We want to apply for an EU Horizon EIC Accelerator grant but the application requires a certified financial audit for the last two fiscal years and we've never done one; our accountant says it will take four months and cost more than our current monthly burn.
challenges.detail: We have been shortlisted for a pre-screening call with an EIC Accelerator evaluator in October and the written application deadline is January. One hard requirement is a certified statutory audit covering fiscal years 2022 and 2023. We have clean bookkeeping — our accountant Marta Vekić has kept tidy records since day one — but we have never been through a formal audit. Two audit firms we contacted in Subotica quoted four to five months and fees between eight thousand and eleven thousand euros, which is roughly our entire monthly operating cost. We cannot delay the application because the next call opens a full year later. What we need is either a realistic path to completing a credible audit faster and at lower cost, or clarity on whether an alternative financial document — a reviewed engagement, for example — would satisfy the EIC requirement. We have all transaction records, bank statements, and tax filings readily available in digital form. A good outcome is submitting the application on time with documentation that will not be rejected at the eligibility check.

challenges.text: The camera on our quality-control unit needs to be re-calibrated every time it is moved to a new production cell, and our Hungarian pilot clients don't have technicians who can do it — each recalibration visit costs us two person-days and kills our margin.
challenges.detail: Our quality-control camera unit uses a fixed focal-length lens and a calibration target we built in-house. Getting accurate pixel-to-millimetre measurements requires a full intrinsic and extrinsic calibration every time the unit is moved to a different position on the line. This takes about three hours on-site and requires someone who understands camera geometry. Our pilot clients in Hungary have maintenance staff but no one comfortable with calibration software. That means one of our engineers drives to the site, which costs us roughly two person-days including travel. We have had six such visits in the past four months alone. We have tried a simplified single-image calibration procedure using a printed A3 target, but the reprojection error is too high for the tolerances our clients need — they are checking metal parts to plus-or-minus 0.3 millimetres. We have budget for a small hardware change if the unit cost stays below two hundred euros per device. A good outcome is a calibration workflow that a factory maintenance worker can complete in under thirty minutes using only a smartphone or a simple printed target, with no specialist knowledge required.

challenges.text: Our refrigerated trailers consume about 6.2 litres of diesel per hour just for the reefer unit, regardless of outside temperature or load volume. We've heard that smarter pre-cooling and setpoint management could cut that by 20–25%, but we have no way to model or test it without risking product temperature excursions for our pharmaceutical and food clients.
challenges.detail: Svaki naš frigo agregat troši oko 6,2 litra dizela na sat bez obzira na to da li prevozimo punu prikolicu smrznutih riblje štangle za Hamburg ili pola prikolice lekova na 2–8°C za Budimpeštu. Godišnje to iznosi otprilike 310.000 litara samo za rashladne jedinice, što je blizu 40% ukupne potrošnje goriva. Čitali smo da pametno pred-hlađenje pre utovara i dinamično upravljanje setpointom mogu da smanje tu potrošnju za petinu do četvrtine, ali nismo u poziciji da eksperimentišemo dok vozimo insulinska analoga ili svež sir. Nemamo simulacioni alat kojim bismo modelovali različite scenarije punjenja i ambijentalne temperature. Probali smo da dobijemo tehničku podršku od distributera opreme, ali oni su nam ponudili samo standardni servisni ugovor. Idealno rešenje bi bila neka vrsta modela ili softvera koji bi nam rekao koji setpoint i koji raspored pred-hlađenja da primenimo za određeni tip tereta i rutu, a da ne riskujemo ekskurziju temperature.

challenges.text: Drivers on the Germany run are governed by EU Regulation 561/2006 tachograph rules, but our dispatcher still calculates driving-time compliance by hand on a spreadsheet. We've had two infringement notices in 18 months, each costing €3,200 in fines, and we're worried the next inspection will be worse.
challenges.detail: Rute Zrenjanin–Minhen ili Zrenjanin–Hamburg spadaju u najtaksi scenarije po EU Uredbi 561/2006: vozači menjaju države, uzimaju odmore na parkinzima u Austriji ili Mađarskoj, a ponekad se raspored menja u poslednji čas zbog zakašnjelog utovara. Naš dispečer Slobodan Marinković vodi sve to u Excel tabeli koja ima skoro sto redova po vozaču nedeljno. U poslednjih godinu i po dobili smo dve inspekcijske kazne ukupno 6.400 evra – obe zbog greške u obračunu kumulativnog vremena vožnje. Pokušali smo da kupimo gotov TMS softver, ali ono što smo pogledali ili košta previše za licencu ili ne podržava srpsku regulativu. Tražimo alat ili metodu koja bi dispečeru u realnom vremenu pokazala koliko ko sme još da vozi, i koja bi ga upozorila pre nego što dođe do prekršaja, ne posle.

challenges.text: About 1 in 20 of our groupage loads arrives with a cold-chain temperature excursion recorded by the datalogger, but we can't tell whether the breach happened at the shipper, at a transfer hub, or during line-haul. Without knowing where the break occurred we can't fix the process or defend ourselves in damage claims.
challenges.detail: Od svakih dvadeset grupažnih pošiljki, statistički jedna stigne sa zabeleženom temperaturnom ekskurzijom na dataloger izveštaju. Problem je što taj izveštaj pokazuje kada je temperatura izašla izvan opsega, ali ne i gde se to desilo. Naša prikolica preuzima robu od tri do pet pošiljalaca po turi, prolazi kroz cross-dock u Budimpešti i menja vozača na granici. Svaki od tih aktera ima razlog da kaže da je ekskurzija nastala kod nekog drugog. Imamo CSV datoteke sa svim merenjima na svakih pet minuta, imamo GPS podatke o poziciji vozila, i imamo dokumente o preuzimanju tereta. Ali nemamo način da sve to automatski povežemo i ukažemo na tačku u lancu gde je najverovanije nastao problem. Platili smo jednu štetu od 14.000 evra prošle godine iako smo bili uvereni da greška nije naša. Dobar ishod bi bio sistem koji nam za svaki incident generiše izveštaj sa procenom gde je ekskurzija nastala, potkrepljenu podacima.

challenges.text: We are trying to refinance the depot expansion through a Serbian development bank loan but the application requires a five-year audited cashflow projection in a format our accountant has never prepared. Two banks have already rejected the application on formal grounds.
challenges.detail: Planiramo proširenje hladnjačkog magacina za još 1.200 m² kako bismo mogli da prihvatamo sezonske viškove kapaciteta za klijente iz prehrambene industrije. Dva razvojna kredita smo već pokušali – oba su odbijena jer naša petogodišnja projekcija novčanog toka nije bila u formatu koji banka traži: trebalo je odvojeno prikazati operativni, investicioni i finansijski tok sa pretpostavkama koje su eksplicitno navedene i proverljive. Naša knjigovodstvena firma Kosović i Marković radi sa malim privrednicima i nikada nije pravila ovakav dokument. Rok za sledeću rundu prijava je septembar 2025. godine. Nemamo godišnji budžet za konsultantsku kuću, ali smo voljni da platimo razumnu cenu za konkretan, primenjiv model koji naš računovođa može da popuni i odbrani pred bankom.

challenges.text: Our churn-prediction model for a telecom client tops out at 71% recall, and every percentage point we miss costs the client roughly €180,000 in lost revenue per quarter — we've tried XGBoost and basic neural nets but we're stuck.
challenges.detail: We have been running a churn-prediction model for a telecom client for about fourteen months. The model flags subscribers likely to cancel within the next 30 days so the client's retention team can call them first. Right now we are hitting 71% recall on the holdout set, and the client has worked out that each percentage point of recall we recover is worth roughly €180,000 per quarter in revenue they keep. We have tried XGBoost with extensive feature engineering — call-drop rates, recharge intervals, customer-service contacts — and we tried a straightforward feed-forward neural network, but neither moved recall past that ceiling. The training set has about 2.1 million subscriber records over 18 months, with a churn rate of around 6%, so class imbalance is a real issue. We have tried SMOTE and class-weight adjustments without much gain. The client gives us a monthly data refresh. We cannot share the raw data externally but we can work with a collaborator under NDA on anonymised samples or synthetic data. The client wants to see a meaningful recall improvement within one business quarter, and budget for this specific problem is set at around €12,000.

challenges.text: We invoice in euros but pay salaries in dinars; with the exchange rate moving 8% in six months our margin forecast was off by nearly a full point and the board is asking us to hedge, which none of us knows how to do properly.
challenges.detail: Roughly 60% of our invoices go out in euros — mainly to clients in Slovenia, Croatia, and increasingly Germany — while all 38 salaries and most local costs are in Serbian dinars. Over the first half of 2024 the EUR/RSD rate moved about 8% against us, which knocked nearly a full percentage point off our net margin compared to what we had told the board at the start of the year. We track the exposure on a spreadsheet, which is clearly not enough. The board has asked us to put a hedging policy in place before the next annual budget cycle, which is October. Nobody on our finance team has practical experience with currency forwards, options, or any structured product. We bank with two local commercial banks and we are not sure which instruments they actually offer to a company our size, or what the transaction costs look like at our volume. A good outcome is a written hedging policy we can present to the board, an understanding of which instruments are realistic for a 38-person consultancy, and ideally a connection to someone who can implement it without us needing to hire a treasury specialist.

challenges.text: Clients in Germany and Austria are now asking for a data-processing agreement and a transfer-impact assessment before they sign; our standard contract template is Serbian law and we have no one in-house who can produce the EU-compliant paperwork fast enough.
challenges.detail: Two potential clients — one logistics broker in Hamburg and one mid-size retailer in Graz — have both paused contract negotiations until we can give them a signed data-processing agreement that meets GDPR requirements and a transfer-impact assessment covering data flows from the EU to Serbia. Our current standard contract is written under Serbian law and covers data handling in a general way, but it does not address the specifics those clients need: Article 28 DPA clauses, the transfer mechanism given that Serbia does not yet have an adequacy decision, and the TIA documentation. Both clients have their own legal teams who will review whatever we send. We have a Serbian lawyer we use for general commercial matters, but she does not work in EU data law. We have looked at template libraries online but the documents are either too generic or too large-enterprise in their assumptions. The Hamburg client has indicated they could sign within three weeks of receiving acceptable paperwork. We need someone who can produce documents that will actually pass review, not just a checklist. We would consider a short fixed-fee engagement for this, somewhere in the range of €2,000 to €4,000 for the full package.

challenges.text: We have a logistics client running 14 regional warehouses and they want a real-time inventory allocation engine, but order volumes spike 4x during promotions and our current rule-based system can't rebalance fast enough — we need something that plans ahead.
challenges.detail: One of our longer-standing logistics clients operates 14 regional warehouses across Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, distributing fast-moving consumer goods. They currently use a rule-based allocation system we built for them in 2021, which distributes stock according to fixed regional quotas updated weekly. The problem is promotions: when a retailer runs a campaign, order volumes at two or three of the warehouses spike by a factor of four within 48 hours, and the rule-based system cannot redistribute stock in time. The result is stockouts at the busy locations and excess at quieter ones. The client wants a system that can look at incoming orders, current stock positions across all 14 sites, and a promotional calendar, and decide in near-real-time how to reallocate. Historical order data going back three years is available, well-structured, and lives in a PostgreSQL database we already manage. The seasonal and promotional patterns are reasonably predictable — the client gives us the promotional calendar two weeks in advance. The constraint is that reallocation instructions feed into a warehouse management system that processes movements in batch windows of about 20 minutes, so true real-time is not necessary, but the planning horizon needs to be at least 48 hours out. The client has approved a budget for this project and we are targeting a working pilot before the peak November–December period.

challenges.text: About 40% of our subscribers photograph receipts instead of uploading PDFs; our current OCR misreads amounts on thermal paper about 22% of the time, which causes wrong VAT calculations and angry support tickets.
challenges.detail: Around 40 percent of our subscribers submit receipts as photos taken on a phone rather than scanned PDFs. Thermal paper receipts are the main problem — the contrast is low, the paper curls, and the print fades. Our current setup uses Tesseract with some post-processing we wrote ourselves, and it misreads the total amount or VAT amount on roughly one in five thermal receipts. That sounds manageable until you realise a wrong number flows straight into a VAT return, and then we get a support ticket, sometimes an angry phone call, and occasionally a subscriber who files an incorrect declaration with the Tax Administration. We have tried image pre-processing — grayscale conversion, adaptive thresholding, deskewing — and it helped a little but not enough. We do not have a labelled dataset of Serbian receipts large enough to train anything more sophisticated ourselves. We have budget for a short project engagement and we can contribute staff time for testing and integration. A good result would be getting the error rate below five percent on thermal paper without slowing down the upload flow for the user.

challenges.text: We want to automatically categorise expense line items to the correct Serbian account plan (Kontni plan) codes, but the free-text descriptions merchants type are inconsistent and our rule-based system requires constant manual updates.
challenges.detail: Every expense a subscriber enters has a free-text description — the merchant name, maybe a note the user typed, sometimes just whatever appeared on the receipt. We need to map each line item to the correct four-digit code in the Serbian Kontni plan so the ledger balances correctly and the annual accounts are valid. Right now we maintain a keyword lookup table: if the description contains 'gorivo' we map it to fuel, and so on. The table has about 2,000 rules and a part-time staff member spends maybe three days a month updating it when new edge cases come in from support tickets. The coverage is still poor for anything slightly unusual, and the system has no way to learn from corrections. We have eighteen months of anonymised transaction data — roughly 800,000 line items with the correct Kontni plan codes that our accountant reviewer assigned. That is the main resource we can offer. We want something that can suggest the right code with a confidence score so that low-confidence items can be flagged for human review rather than silently miscategorised.

challenges.text: Our biggest growth bottleneck is that accountants actively advise their small-business clients against self-service tools like ours — we need a channel strategy to either partner with accountants or reach clients directly without alienating them.
challenges.detail: A significant number of small-business owners in Serbia rely on a trusted accountant for everything, and many of those accountants tell their clients that self-service tools create errors and compliance risk. Some of that concern is genuine and some of it is about protecting a fee relationship. Either way, it means potential subscribers hear negative things about us before they ever see the product. We have tried running online ads, going to small-business trade fairs, and offering a two-month free trial, and while those tactics bring in some users, we keep hitting a ceiling. We are not sure whether the right move is to build a version of the product designed for accountants to use on behalf of multiple clients — turning them from competitors into resellers — or to find a direct channel that does not trigger their resistance. We do not have a sales team; this is partly a strategy question and partly a product and pricing design question. We want to grow from 1,400 to around 3,000 subscribers within two years without taking on investment that would change how we run the company.

challenges.text: Error mitigation on today's noisy quantum hardware for molecular simulation.
challenges.detail: The quantum processors we use today make a lot of mistakes. When we run a molecular simulation circuit — even a fairly small one representing ten or twelve qubits — the noise introduced by the hardware pushes our energy estimates far enough off that our clients cannot use them with confidence. We have tried zero-noise extrapolation and a basic version of probabilistic error cancellation, but both approaches increase the number of circuit shots we need by a factor of ten to thirty, which drives up cloud compute costs quickly. We have about twelve months of runway, so we cannot just throw money at more shots indefinitely. What we need is a smarter mitigation strategy that keeps shot counts manageable while getting our energy estimates within chemical accuracy — roughly one and a half millihartree of the reference values we calculate with classical tools. We have clean benchmark datasets for three small molecules, a working Qiskit codebase, and four physicists who understand the problem deeply but have not found a practical solution yet. A good outcome would be a repeatable mitigation routine that runs within our existing cloud budget and passes our accuracy threshold on all three benchmark molecules.

challenges.text: We are seeing a 15% return rate on our flagship SP-400 spirometer because the plastic turbine blades warp slightly after about 800 measurement cycles at high humidity; the deformation is under 0.3 mm but it shifts flow calibration enough to trigger out-of-spec results.
challenges.detail: The SP-400 uses a small turbine assembly with four injection-moulded polycarbonate blades to measure airflow. After roughly 800 measurement cycles in environments where relative humidity stays above 70 percent — which is common in occupational health clinics and factory medical rooms — the blades develop a measurable warp of 0.2 to 0.3 mm. That is enough to shift the flow calibration curve outside the tolerance band we guarantee, which triggers an out-of-spec flag when the device is returned for its annual service check. Our current return rate on this issue is around 15 percent of the installed SP-400 base, and each return costs us roughly €85 in labour and parts plus the cost of a loan unit. We have already tried switching blade wall thickness and adjusting the mould cooling cycle with our current plastics supplier, Vojvođanplast from Novi Sad, but the improvement was marginal. We have also tested a glass-fibre-reinforced grade of the same polymer, which reduced warping but introduced a surface roughness that affected flow readings in a different way. We have samples, measurement logs, and return-history data going back to 2019. Our target is to get the blade geometry stable to within 0.05 mm after 2,000 cycles at 80 percent humidity. We have a budget of around €15,000 for materials testing and prototyping and would need a working solution within 12 months to incorporate it into the 2026 production run.

challenges.text: Our occupational health clients want an automated report comparing a worker's spirometry trend over three years against age- and height-adjusted reference norms; right now a technician does this manually for each patient and it takes about 12 minutes per report, adding up to nearly 30 hours of labour per week.
challenges.detail: Occupational health regulations in Serbia and Bosnia require employers to track lung function trends for workers exposed to dust, fumes, or chemicals. Our clients need a report that takes a worker's spirometry readings over three or more years and shows whether their FEV1, FVC, and FEV1/FVC ratio are changing faster than expected for someone of their age, sex, and height, using accepted reference equations such as the GLI-2012 norms. Right now our PulmoTrack software stores all the raw measurement data but has no module to do this comparison automatically. A trained technician at the clinic pulls the data, opens a spreadsheet template we supply, enters the reference values by hand, and writes a short narrative summary. We have timed this process: it averages 12 minutes per patient. Across our occupational health client base, that adds up to roughly 400 reports per month, or close to 80 hours of technician time. Clients have started asking whether competitor products offer automated reporting, and two have mentioned they are evaluating alternatives. We have three years of anonymised measurement records for approximately 4,200 patients that we could use for development and testing. Our PulmoTrack application is Java-based and runs on Windows; any new module needs to fit that environment or be accessible from it. We have one in-house software developer, Dragan Ilić, who handles maintenance but does not have capacity for a project of this size. A working automated report module, validated against our existing manual outputs, within nine months is what we are looking for.

challenges.text: We assemble 200 to 300 units per month on a mixed-model line with three operators, but scheduling which variant to build on which shift is done on paper and we routinely end up with stockouts on one SKU and overstock on another, tying up roughly €40,000 in unnecessary inventory.
challenges.detail: We build four variants of the SP-400 — differing in connectivity options and mouthpiece configurations — and two variants of the SP-200, for a total of six SKUs on one mixed-model assembly line with three operators working two shifts. Production volumes run between 200 and 300 units a month depending on orders. Scheduling which variant to build on which shift is currently managed by our production coordinator, Bojana Marić, using a printed weekly plan and a whiteboard. The problem is that demand for each variant is not uniform and not easy to predict more than two weeks out, and our current approach does not account for component lead times or shared subassembly constraints well enough. In practice, we end up short on one or two SKUs almost every month while accumulating buffer stock on others. Our finance team estimates the excess inventory tied up by this imbalance averages around €40,000 at any given time. We track orders and shipments in an older version of a Serbian ERP system, MikroERP, which exports to Excel. We have 30 months of order history by SKU. We are not looking for a large enterprise software replacement; we want a scheduling or planning tool or method that our coordinator can run each week without specialised training, ideally integrated with or at least feeding from our existing Excel exports. A reasonable budget for this is €8,000 to €12,000, and we would want something usable within six months.
