challenges.text: We finance retrofits on the basis of guaranteed energy savings, but for facilities with variable production — like a sunflower-oil press that runs flat-out October to February and idles the rest of the year — our baseline model overestimates savings by 15–20% and we end up absorbing the shortfall ourselves.
challenges.detail: Our guaranteed savings contracts are built on a baseline: we measure a facility's energy use over a reference period, adjust for weather and production volume, and promise the client a fixed saving. The problem shows up with seasonal processors — a sunflower-oil press is the clearest example. That facility runs three shifts from October through February and is nearly idle the rest of the year. When we build a baseline from twelve months of meter data and then normalise it against production tonnes, our model consistently overshoots the real savings by 15 to 20 percent once the retrofit is in place. We absorb that gap ourselves under the contract terms. We have tried splitting the year into operating and idle seasons and recalibrating separately, but the idle-period consumption is so irregular — weekend runs, maintenance heating, occasional small orders — that it introduces more noise than it removes. We have about three years of hourly meter readings for this site and two others with similar patterns. A good outcome would be a normalisation method we can apply at contract-signing that keeps our savings estimate within five percent of actual over a full contract year. We need something we can explain to a client in a one-page annex.

challenges.text: We've done 130 energy audits but they all live in PDF reports; when a client asks us to compare their facility to similar ones we have to read through dozens of documents by hand. We need a structured way to extract and benchmark key performance indicators across our whole portfolio.
challenges.detail: Every audit we have done since 1997 was written up as a PDF and filed. That is 130 documents, ranging from eight pages to over sixty, covering compressed-air systems, industrial boilers, refrigeration plant, lighting, motor drives, and building envelopes across a wide range of facility types. When a prospective client asks how their energy intensity compares to similar operations, or when a project manager wants to know what savings we typically see from variable-frequency drives on refrigeration compressors, someone has to open reports one by one and copy numbers into a spreadsheet. It takes days and the results depend on whoever does the searching remembering which facilities are actually comparable. We have tried building a summary spreadsheet twice; both times it was out of date within six months because nobody had time to maintain it. What we need is a way to pull the key figures — energy intensity per tonne of product, savings by measure type, baseline consumption by end use — out of those PDFs and into something queryable, ideally something the audit team can update when a new report is filed without specialist help. Budget for this is modest; we are not looking to build a data warehouse.

challenges.text: Two large clients want us to model how adding a 500 kW rooftop PV array will interact with their existing compressed-air and refrigeration loads during peak summer demand — they specifically want to know whether they can drop a grid connection tariff band, but we don't have the simulation tools to answer that confidently.
challenges.detail: Two of our larger clients — a cold-storage and distribution facility and a packaging manufacturer — want to add rooftop PV, both around 500 kW. They are not asking us to fund the PV; they want to know whether the generation will reliably reduce their peak import enough to move them into a lower grid connection tariff band under the current distribution network operator tariff schedule. The answer depends on how the PV output interacts with their existing large loads: the cold-storage site has a bank of ammonia compressors that cycle on fifteen-minute intervals, and the packaging site has compressed-air peaks tied to shift schedules. A few percentage points difference in coincidence between peak load and peak generation determines whether the tariff reduction happens or not, and that is worth roughly 18,000 euros per year to each client. We have fifteen-minute interval meter data going back two years for both sites and we have the compressor and air-system specifications on hand. What we lack is a simulation environment that can model PV generation against a realistic load profile with that level of time resolution and then map the result onto a stepped tariff structure. We need outputs we can put in front of clients and, if needed, show to the distribution network operator.

challenges.text: Our LoRa nodes send a packet every 15 minutes, but in dense corn canopy from July onward we see 30–40% packet loss even at maximum transmission power, and farmers are missing irrigation alerts during the hottest part of the season.
challenges.detail: From roughly mid-July to the end of August, corn plants in Vojvodina reach full canopy height, sometimes above two metres, and the crop stands in dense blocks of several hectares. During that window we see 30 to 40 percent of our data packets failing to reach the base station, even when nodes are set to maximum transmit power. We have moved antennas higher on the mounting stakes, tried changing the spreading factor, and staggered transmission times to reduce collisions, but the loss rate stays stubbornly high. The problem is worst on farms where the base station sits inside the same field rather than on an elevated edge position. Those are also the farms that most need reliable irrigation alerts, because they tend to be larger. We log every failed packet with a timestamp, so we have a clear picture of when the losses happen and on which nodes. What we do not have is the radio engineering knowledge to work out whether the fix is a different antenna geometry, a mesh relay approach, a different frequency plan, or something else. Any solution has to work with hardware we can still assemble here in Zrenjanin at a cost that does not push the node price above what cooperatives will pay.

challenges.text: We are still printing single-colour labels on our enclosures with a desktop printer and laminating by hand; distributors in Austria and Germany are asking for CE-marked labelling and multilingual quick-start cards, and our current process cannot scale past 200 units a month.
challenges.detail: Right now one person spends roughly half a day per week printing product labels on a desktop colour laser printer, laminating them by hand, and folding the quick-start card we include in each box. That process works at 150 units a month but falls apart above 200. We have two distributors in Austria and one in Germany who want to stock our nodes as a local product, but they have asked us clearly that they need CE marking visibly on the enclosure, a Declaration of Conformity in the box, and a quick-start card in at least German, English, and Serbian. Our current label does not have the CE mark because we have not gone through that process, and the card is Serbian only. We understand CE marking requires us to go through electromagnetic compatibility and environmental protection testing, and we have a rough budget of around five thousand euros set aside for that process. Beyond the certification itself, we need a repeatable way to produce compliant labels and multilingual inserts in batches of 300 to 500 units without adding headcount. A good outcome is a certified product with a professional label produced at a per-unit cost we can absorb.

challenges.text: We have 11 years of sensor readings paired with manual farm-book records, but we have never done anything analytical with that archive; we believe there is a pattern linking our microclimate data to local pest pressure but we do not have the people or tools to find it.
challenges.detail: Since 2013 we have stored sensor readings from our deployed nodes in a PostgreSQL database. That is soil moisture, soil temperature, air temperature, relative humidity, and leaf wetness, logged every 15 minutes from roughly 800 to 1,200 nodes depending on the year. Alongside that, several of our long-term customers have shared their paper farm books with us, and we have digitised the key entries: spray dates, pest observations, yield estimates. We have always suspected there is a usable link between the microclimate patterns we measure and the timing of aphid pressure or fungal outbreaks in the weeks that follow, but we have never tested that properly. We have one person, Milica, who knows Python well enough to clean the data but not to build any kind of predictive model. We have no experience with machine learning tools and no budget to hire a data scientist on a salary. The archive is messy: node IDs changed when we replaced hardware, some farms have gaps of weeks, and the farm-book records use inconsistent terminology. A good outcome would be even a simple rule or threshold that a farmer could act on, confirmed with enough data that we feel confident recommending it.

challenges.text: Our CYP2C19 and CYP2D6 panel works well in the lab, but we're getting allele dropout in about 3% of samples with degraded DNA — typically saliva collected at pharmacy kiosks — and we don't yet understand whether it's the extraction protocol, the PCR design, or the sample transport conditions.
challenges.detail: We run about 120 samples a week, and roughly three or four of those come back with at least one allele that we cannot confidently call — what the field calls allele dropout. It happens almost exclusively in saliva samples collected through pharmacy kiosks rather than in-clinic buccal swabs. Our suspicion is that the problem sits somewhere in a chain of three things: how the sample is collected into the stabilisation tube, how long it sits at room temperature before a courier picks it up, and whether our extraction protocol is well matched to low-input or partially degraded DNA. We have tried two different extraction kits alongside our standard Chelex method, and we have tightened the courier pickup window from 48 hours to 24 hours, but the dropout rate has not moved much below 3%. We have a freezer of the affected samples set aside and a full record of collection timestamps and courier logs. What we need is someone who can help us design a systematic experiment across those three variables and tell us which one is doing the damage, so we can fix the protocol before we expand to more pharmacy sites later this year.

challenges.text: Our bioinformatics pipeline for calling star alleles from short-read sequencing data takes 4–6 hours per batch of 24 samples on our current cloud setup, which costs us about 9 EUR per sample in compute — that's killing our margin at the price point pharmacies will pay.
challenges.detail: Our bioinformatics pipeline takes a batch of 24 samples from raw sequencing reads to a final star-allele call in roughly four to six hours. We run two batches a day on weekdays, and the cloud compute bill is working out to about 9 EUR per sample. At the price point pharmacies are willing to pay — which is genuinely constrained by what they can charge patients under Serbian out-of-pocket pricing — that compute cost alone is a serious problem before we even account for lab consumables and staff time. We wrote the pipeline ourselves in Python using Snakemake, and it works correctly; the issue is that we have not optimised it for cost or speed. We have looked briefly at spot instances to cut the hourly rate, but we have not properly profiled which steps are the bottleneck. We think alignment and the star-allele calling step are the heavy consumers, but we are not certain. A good outcome would be getting compute cost below 3 EUR per sample and ideally cutting total run time to under 90 minutes, without touching the clinical accuracy of the calls.

challenges.text: We want to explain our test results to patients in plain language through a mobile app, but our current PDF reports are written for physicians — in user testing, 7 out of 10 patients said they didn't understand what the result meant for them.
challenges.detail: Right now, when a patient's result is ready, we send a PDF to the pharmacy or clinic and they pass it along to the patient. The PDF is written for the prescriber — it lists allele names, predicted metaboliser status, and drug-specific dosing flags in clinical language. In a small round of user testing we ran last autumn with 20 patients recruited through a partner pharmacy in Novi Sad, 14 out of 20 said they could not explain in their own words what their result meant for how they should take their medication. Seven out of ten, roughly. We want to build a simple mobile app — probably a lightweight web app that works well on a phone — where a patient can enter a short code, see their result explained in plain Serbian or English, and get a clear answer to the question they actually care about, which is: does this affect any medicine I am currently taking? We have a designer on a part-time contract and we can write the clinical content ourselves. What we are missing is help structuring the information in a way that is genuinely clear to someone with no medical background, and guidance on how to test whether it actually works before we release it.

challenges.text: Our clients in the automotive supply chain generate time-series sensor logs at 10 ms intervals from assembly lines, and our current anomaly-detection pipeline flags roughly 22% false positives per shift, which means floor managers have started ignoring the alerts entirely — we need a fundamentally better approach to separating real drift from normal process variation.
challenges.detail: Radimo s nekoliko klijenata u automobilskom dobavnom lancu čije montažne linije šalju senzorske logove svakih 10 milisekundi. To je ogroman obim podataka, i naš trenutni sistem za detekciju anomalija — zasnovan na statičkim pragovima i jednostavnim z-score pravilima — generiše oko 22% lažnih uzbuna po smeni. Pošto se to ponavlja svaki dan, menadžeri na terenu su počeli da ignorišu upozorenja. Posledica je da prave greške prolaze nezapaženo dok ne postanu skupi problem. Probali smo da ručno podešavamo pragove po liniji, ali procesi variraju zavisno od smene, temperature u hali i tipa materijala, pa statički pragovi nikad nisu dovoljno precizni. Imamo istorijske logove za poslednjih 18 meseci i znamo koji su alarmi bili lažni — tu labelu smo prikupili ručno od tehničara. Budžet za rešenje ovog problema je otvoren ako vidimo konkretan plan, a cilj je da lažne uzbune svedemo ispod 5% bez povećanja broja propuštenih stvarnih grešaka.

challenges.text: We landed a contract with a Slovenian logistics operator worth €280,000 annually, but the deal requires us to demonstrate GDPR-compliant data residency and an ISO/IEC 27001 certification within six months — we have no in-house legal or compliance staff and every external firm we approached quoted over €40,000 just for the gap analysis.
challenges.detail: Potpisali smo ugovor s logističkim operaterom iz Slovenije — firma se zove Velox Spedition d.o.o. — vredan 280.000 evra godišnje. Uslov ugovora je da u roku od šest meseci demonstriramo GDPR-usklađeno čuvanje podataka na teritoriji EU i da dobijemo ISO/IEC 27001 sertifikat. Nemamo ni pravnika ni osobu zaduženu za compliance unutar firme. Kontaktirali smo tri spoljne konsultantske kuće — jednu iz Beograda i dve iz Zagreba — i sve tri su ponudile cenu iznad 40.000 evra samo za analizu raskoraka između naše trenutne prakse i standarda. To je za nas previsoko s obzirom na rok i na to da još nismo naplatili ni prvu fakturu od novog klijenta. Imamo dokumentovane interne procedure, koristimo cloud infrastrukturu kod jednog evropskog provajdera, i voleli bismo da nekome damo pristup toj dokumentaciji i tehničkim sistemima kako bismo zajedno napravili plan koji možemo izvesti ispod 20.000 evra ukupno.

challenges.text: About 60% of our project hours are spent cleaning and reconciling data from clients who deliver Excel files in 15 different formats with mixed date conventions, inconsistent unit labelling and duplicate rows — we estimate we lose €120,000 a year in billable capacity just on this pre-processing step.
challenges.detail: Većina naših klijenata dostavlja podatke u Excel fajlovima. Na papiru to zvuči jednostavno, ali u praksi svaki klijent ima svoje konvencije: datumi su nekad DD.MM.YYYY, nekad MM/DD/YY, nekad samo naziv meseca na srpskom ili engleskom. Jedinice za masu, dužinu i vreme nisu označene konzistentno ili uopšte nisu označene. Dupli redovi su česti jer se izveštaji prave ručnim kopiranjem iz više izvora. Imamo pet klijenata koji redovno šalju fajlove u 15 različitih formata i struktura, a novi projekti donose nove varijante. Naši inženjeri podataka troše otprilike 60% radnog vremena na ovo pre nego što uopšte počnu analizu. Procenili smo da to iznosi oko 120.000 evra godišnje u izgubljenoj naplatnoj kapacitetu. Pokušali smo da napišemo skriptove za svaki format posebno, ali to je neodrživo jer se formati menjaju bez najave. Cilj nam je sistem koji može da prepozna format, predloži mapiranje i zatraži potvrdu samo za nejasne slučajeve, bez potrebe da inženjer sedi pored njega.

challenges.text: Three of our largest clients are asking for natural-language interfaces so their non-technical staff can query dashboards in plain Serbian — our prototype works acceptably in English but the model makes systematic errors on Serbian business vocabulary, especially domain-specific terms from finance and procurement, and we don't have the annotated corpus to fine-tune it ourselves.
challenges.detail: Trojica naših najvećih klijenata — svi u prerađivačkoj industriji — tražili su da njihovi zaposleni koji ne razumeju tabele i SQL mogu da postavljaju pitanja dashboardu na srpskom jeziku i dobiju odgovor. Napravili smo prototip koji koristi jezički model i dobro radi na engleskim upitima. Problem nastaje čim se pojave srpski termini iz finansija i nabavke — 'trebovanje', 'nalog za isporuku', 'fakturna vrednost', 'devizni kurs na dan knjiženja' i slično. Model ili ne prepoznaje termine ili ih mapira na pogrešne kolone u bazi. Nismo imali resurse da skupimo i anotiramo sopstveni korpus srpskog poslovnog jezika. Tražili smo od klijenata da nam pomognu s prikupljanjem primera, ali to ide sporo jer nemaju ko da to uradi. Imamo oko 4.000 parova pitanje-odgovor na engleskom koje smo sami napravili, i 600 na srpskom koje su zaposleni kod klijenata uneli tokom pilota. To nije dovoljno za fine-tuning. Rok koji su klijenti postavili je kraj prvog kvartala sledeće godine.

challenges.text: Porosity in 316L parts fails customer pressure tests in about 1 of 12 builds.
challenges.detail: Roughly once every twelve builds, a batch of 316L parts comes out of the machine and fails a customer's hydrostatic or pneumatic pressure test. The failure is always subsurface porosity — gas pores or lack-of-fusion voids that the surface finish hides completely. We have tried adjusting laser power, scan speed, and hatch spacing manually, and we keep a log of every parameter set we have used over the past two years. The log now has about 340 build records with density measurements and pass/fail notes, but we have not been able to find a clean pattern that tells us in advance which builds will fail. We own an Olympus metallographic microscope and we do Archimedes density checks on coupons in every build, but coupon density does not always predict what happens in the actual part geometry. We do not have CT scanning in-house and sending parts out costs us time and money we cannot recover from small orders. A good outcome would be a reliable in-process or post-process indicator — or a parameter selection method — that gets the fail rate below one in fifty without slowing build times significantly. We have the full build logs available and could share coupon cross-sections.

challenges.text: Four printers, many small orders: we schedule builds by hand.
challenges.detail: We currently receive between eight and twenty separate customer orders per week, most of them involving two to thirty parts. Each order specifies a material, a deadline, and sometimes a preferred surface finish. We have four machines that each take between four and eighteen hours per build, and parts from different customers can often be nested together in one build if their material and parameter requirements match. Right now, one of our application engineers spends a full morning every Monday — and smaller chunks of time on Wednesday and Friday — manually matching orders, estimating fill rates in Magics, and writing a build plan in a spreadsheet. When a rush order arrives on Tuesday it often means redoing the whole week's plan. We lose machine utilization this way: our average platform fill is around 61 percent when we estimate it could be above 75 percent with better nesting decisions. We have looked at generic scheduling software but nothing accounts for the geometry-dependent nesting logic that Magics uses. A good outcome is a tool or workflow that takes our open orders as input and proposes a build sequence and nesting grouping automatically, or at least ranks combinations by estimated fill rate.

challenges.text: Our decortication line damages long fibres, which lowers the price we get.
challenges.detail: Our decorticator is a hammer-mill design that we bought second-hand in 2019. It does a reasonable job of separating the woody core from the bast, but the hammers are rough on the long fibres. We see breakage that shortens usable fibre length from an average of around 60 cm down to 30–35 cm by the time it comes off the line. Long-line fibre above 50 cm commands about 20–25% more per kilogram from our Slovenian converter than the short stuff does. Last season we processed roughly 18 tonnes of bast, and by our estimate we lost somewhere between 3 and 4 tonnes of material into the short-fibre tow category that should have stayed in the long-fibre grade. That is a real revenue gap. We have tried slowing the feed rate and adjusting the clearance between the drum and the casing, which helped a little but did not solve it. We have no engineering staff in-house. Our budget for any fix is limited — we are thinking in the range of 8,000 to 15,000 euros for consultancy and trials combined, not for a full equipment replacement. A good outcome would be a clear diagnosis of where in the line the breakage is happening and a practical set of adjustments or low-cost modifications we could test in the 2025 harvest season.

challenges.text: Our pose-estimation model works well in the clinic demo room but in patients' homes — with bad lighting and cluttered backgrounds — joint-angle errors jump from ±3° to ±11°, which is clinically unacceptable for knee rehabilitation protocols.
challenges.detail: In our clinic demo room we get joint-angle errors of roughly plus or minus three degrees, which is within the tolerance most knee rehabilitation protocols allow. When the same patients use the app at home the error jumps to plus or minus eleven degrees. We have looked at the failure cases and the main culprits are dim ceiling lights in the evening, busy backgrounds like bookshelves and furniture, and patients who wear loose tracksuit bottoms that hide the knee contour. We tried adjusting the MediaPipe confidence threshold and adding a simple brightness check that asks the patient to move to better light, but the accuracy improvement was modest. We do not have the budget to require patients to buy a ring light or a plain backdrop. We need a way to make the pose-estimation step more robust to realistic home conditions, either by improving keypoint detection under noise or by building a correction layer on top of the raw keypoints. A good outcome for us is getting back to plus or minus five degrees in at least eighty percent of real home sessions, which is the threshold our clinical advisors say would be acceptable for guiding knee flexion targets.

challenges.text: We have 34 patients generating daily session videos but no physiotherapist can watch them all — we need an automated way to score exercise quality and flag deviations, but we only have 34 annotated sessions to train on so any model we try overfits immediately.
challenges.detail: We currently have thirty-four patients who complete daily sessions, which means roughly two hundred and thirty video sessions per week. One physiotherapist can realistically review twenty to thirty sessions per week in detail, so the rest are either skimmed or missed. We want an automated quality score — something like a pass, needs attention, or stop flag per session — so the physiotherapist only watches the flagged ones. The problem is that we only have thirty-four fully annotated sessions, labelled by Dragana and Nikola using Label Studio. Every classifier we have tried, including simple decision trees on the angle time-series and a small LSTM, overfits to those thirty-four examples within a few training epochs. We cannot annotate faster because each session takes about twenty-five minutes to label properly. We have the raw video for all two hundred and thirty sessions; we just do not have labels for most of them. We are open to transfer learning, self-supervised approaches, or rule-based baselines — whatever would give reliable enough results to put in front of a physiotherapist without causing alert fatigue. Budget for compute is small; we use a shared cloud instance.

challenges.text: We applied for a UNICEF Innovation Fund grant and a domestic Innovation Fund voucher at the same time and were told we can't receive both for the same project — we need legal advice on how to restructure the IP ownership between the family business and a potential spin-off entity so we can access both funding streams.
challenges.detail: We applied in the same calendar quarter for a UNICEF Innovation Fund grant, which requires us to be the sole IP owner and operate as a legal entity with a social-impact mandate, and for a domestic Innovation Fund proof-of-concept voucher, which in our case was filed under the family preduzetnik registration. The funding bodies told us the same project cannot receive both instruments simultaneously under the current registration structure. We believe both funding streams are genuinely compatible with what we are building, but the legal form is the obstacle. We need someone who understands Serbian company law and technology IP structures to advise us on whether forming a separate d.o.o. entity, assigning or licensing the platform IP to it, and keeping the preduzetnik for clinical services would satisfy both funders' eligibility rules without triggering a tax event or breaking the existing patient-data agreements we have signed. We have a deadline of end of Q3 2025 to resubmit to the Innovation Fund. We cannot afford a large commercial law firm; we need targeted advice from someone who has done this kind of restructuring for early-stage technology businesses in Serbia.

challenges.text: Our insurance-underwriting scoring model is challenged by regulators in three countries because auditors cannot follow why a specific applicant was declined; we need to show a clear, auditable reason for every individual decision or we lose the contract.
challenges.detail: Our underwriting scoring model for one insurance product is currently under review by financial-services regulators in Serbia, Croatia and Romania at the same time. The core problem is that the model gives an overall score and a decline flag, but it does not produce a human-readable explanation that a compliance officer or an aggrieved applicant can follow step by step. We have added SHAP values to the output, but regulators say that feature-importance numbers are not the same as a documented decision trail. We have tried templated text generation that picks the top three SHAP features and wraps them in a sentence, but auditors say the sentences are inconsistent and sometimes technically accurate but practically meaningless. The model itself scores about 178,000 new applications per month. We have full access to training data, model weights, feature pipelines and audit logs. Our constraint is that any explanation layer must run within the existing Kubernetes pipeline and return a result in under 400 milliseconds. We have budget for a structured engagement and need a working prototype within four months before the next regulatory review cycle.

challenges.text: We process health-insurance claims in bulk and about 3.2% of records contain diagnosis codes that don't match the procedure codes — our rules catch the obvious ones but nuanced clinical inconsistencies slip through and cost one client €420,000 in reimbursements last year.
challenges.detail: One of our health-insurance clients processes around 95,000 claims per month through our platform. We have a rules engine that flags obvious mismatches — for example, a paediatric procedure code billed against an adult diagnosis — but clinical coding is far more subtle than that. Last year, roughly 3,000 claims per month passed our rules and were reimbursed, but post-audit reviews identified about 3.2% of the total as clinically inconsistent, meaning the combination of diagnosis code, procedure code, medication and patient history does not form a coherent clinical picture. That translated to €420,000 in incorrect reimbursements for one client in a single year. We have a labelled dataset of approximately 240,000 historical claims, each reviewed by a human clinical coder and marked correct or inconsistent. We also have access to standard ICD-10 and procedure code taxonomies. We have tried gradient-boosted classifiers and they improve recall slightly but the false-positive rate is still too high for the client to act on every flag without manual review. We want to reduce the error rate by at least 60% without dramatically increasing manual review workload.

challenges.text: We're trying to hire two senior MLOps engineers but the market is completely dry — every candidate we interview either wants remote work for a Western company or is already at a bank; we've had the roles open for nine months.
challenges.detail: We have had two senior MLOps engineer positions open for nine months without filling them. The roles require hands-on experience running Kubernetes-based ML pipelines, familiarity with MLflow or a comparable model registry, and the ability to mentor mid-level engineers. We have interviewed 23 candidates over that period. Most credible candidates either want fully remote contracts with salaries pegged to Western European rates, which our current salary band does not reach, or they are already inside large banks or telecoms where job security and benefits are strong. We are open to flexible arrangements but our core infrastructure runs on on-premises hardware in our Novi Sad data centre, so fully remote operation is not practical for these specific roles. We are also open to a structured knowledge-transfer arrangement with an external research group as an interim measure while we continue recruiting, if it helps us reduce the operational load on existing staff.

challenges.text: Our ISOBUS terminals currently support only four tractor brands via proprietary CAN bus adapters, and dealers keep losing sales because the terminal won't talk to Belarusian MTZ and Chinese YTO tractors that dominate the Serbian market below 100 HP — reverse-engineering every new variant is costing us three to four months per model.
challenges.detail: Our FieldDesk terminal connects to tractor electronics through CAN bus adapters we build ourselves. Right now we support four brands — two Western European, one domestic, one Ukrainian — and each adapter took our two embedded engineers between three and four months to develop, mostly through trial and error with borrowed machines and oscilloscopes. The problem is that MTZ tractors from Belarus and YTO tractors from China together make up a large share of the sub-100-horsepower market in Serbia and across the region, and our dealers are telling us they are losing orders specifically because the terminal will not pair with those machines. We have tried using publicly available documentation, but CAN message structures vary between production batches and model years, so what we document for one serial range breaks on the next. We have one oscilloscope rig in-house and two engineers who can do this work. We need a faster method — whether that is a smarter logging and classification approach, some kind of adaptive layer, or a better workflow — that gets us to a working adapter in weeks rather than months. A good result would be a reliable adapter for current MTZ and YTO variants delivered before the spring sales season.

challenges.text: Our variable-rate application maps are built from soil sampling data that is often two to three years old, and the actual within-season crop response to fertiliser varies a lot — we want to incorporate current-season plant sensing data so the controller adjusts rates based on what the crop actually needs right now.
challenges.detail: Our prescription maps are built from soil analysis — nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, pH — that farms collect every two or three years. That is the standard in this region. The maps are spatially detailed enough, but they tell us about soil history, not about what the crop needs right now in this season. A field that had good nitrogen last autumn might have had a wet spring this year and the nitrogen has moved; a crop that looks uniform on the soil map might show stress in one corner that no one has measured. We want to bring in current-season plant data — whether from satellite imagery, drone flights, or ground sensors — so that the VRS-7 controller can adjust application rates against what the crop is actually showing, not just what the soil showed two years ago. We have the spatial data infrastructure and the controller architecture to accept adjusted rate maps; the gap is in knowing how to translate a vegetation index or a sensor reading into a nitrogen rate correction that is agronomically sound and not just a number. We want a method that a practical agronomist can explain to a farmer.

challenges.text: We want to enter the German market this year but our largest dealer there told us we need to show conformity with the new EU machinery regulation 2023/1230 before they will list us — our legal team in Serbia doesn't have EU machinery law experience and external EU counsel is quoting us €35,000 just for the gap analysis.
challenges.detail: We have a signed letter of intent from Drecker Landtechnik GmbH, a dealer in Baden-Württemberg, to list the FieldDesk terminal and VRS-7 controller in their catalogue for the 2025 season, but they have told us clearly that they will not proceed until we demonstrate conformity with EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230, which replaced the old Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC. Our product was CE-marked under the old directive, and we do not know exactly where the gaps are under the new regulation — we assume there are gaps in risk assessment documentation, software safety provisions, and possibly in the way we document modifications made by dealers during installation. We have a two-person quality and documentation team in Novi Sad with no experience in EU machinery law. We have spoken to two law firms in Germany and one in Austria; the cheapest gap analysis quote was €35,000 and none of them had specific experience with agricultural electronics. We have a budget set aside for this, but we want to understand what we are actually buying before we spend it. A good outcome is a clear list of what needs to change in our technical file and a realistic timeline to get there before the Agritechnica trade fair in November 2025.

challenges.text: We log 180 gigabytes of field operation data per month from 340 active terminals but we have no way to detect when a controller is behaving abnormally — a miscalibrated flow sensor can under-apply nitrogen for an entire season before anyone notices, and by then the yield damage is done.
challenges.detail: Every FieldDesk terminal that has a mobile data connection sends operational logs back to our Farm Portal servers. At 340 active terminals we collect about 180 gigabytes per month — GPS tracks, flow sensor readings, section control events, application totals, error flags. We store all of it in PostgreSQL. Right now, the only anomaly detection we do is threshold alerting: if a flow reading goes to zero or above a hard ceiling, the system flags it. That catches failures. It does not catch slow drift — a flow sensor that reads 8 percent low, consistently, across a full season. That kind of miscalibration means a farm under-applies nitrogen on every pass, and the yield loss only becomes visible at harvest, long after anything can be done. We have the historical data going back several years for most terminals. We have one data analyst on staff who handles reporting. We do not have anyone working on time-series modelling or anomaly detection. We want a way to detect terminals that are behaving differently from their own baseline or from comparable terminals in similar operating conditions, and to alert the dealer or the customer early enough that they can recalibrate before the damage is done.

challenges.text: Our string inverters start clipping at about 11 AM on clear summer days even though total irradiance looks fine — we think partial shading from nearby structures is the root cause, but we have no reliable way to model exactly how a shadow moves across a non-flat roof and what that does to the I-V curve of each string throughout the day.
challenges.detail: Na nekoliko naših lokacija sa složenim krovovima — uglavnom industrijske hale sa ventilacionim kućištima, antenama i susednim objektima — primetili smo da string inverteri ulaze u clipping već oko 11 ujutru, i to čak i kada ukupna osunčanost prema piranometru izgleda normalno. Sumnjamo da delimično zasenčenje pojedinih modula u stringu drastično ruši ukupnu I-V karakteristiku, ali nemamo alat koji bi nam pokazao kako tačno senka nekog dimnjaka ili nadstrešnice putuje po kosom krovu u toku dana i šta to znači za svaki string posebno. U PVsystu smo pokušali da modelujemo senčenje, ali softver pretpostavlja ravne površine i ne može da uhvati dinamiku pokreta senke po složenoj geometriji krova. Imamo tlocrtne nacrte objekata i GPS koordinate svake lokacije. Nemamo resurse za skupu lidarsku snimku. Željeli bismo konkretan proračun — po satu, po stringu — koji bi nam rekao gde da presložimo nizove ili ugradimo optimizere, i to pre sledeće sezone.

challenges.text: We have 5-minute production data from 140 installed sites going back three years, but our maintenance team still reacts to faults after the inverter alarms — we want to flag degrading modules two or three weeks before they trip, and right now nobody on our team knows how to build that kind of predictive model.
challenges.detail: Od 140 lokacija prikupljamo podatke na svakih pet minuta — napon, struja, snaga, temperatura invertera — i sve to čuvamo u InfluxDB bazi koja sada ima oko tri godine istorije. Naš servisni tim trenutno reaguje tek kad inverter sam javi alarm, što znači da je modul već u kvaru ili blizu njega. Želimo da vidimo degradaciju ranije — recimo dve do tri nedelje unapred — kako bismo mogli da planiramo posetu terenu i izbegnemo iznenadne gubitke u produkciji. Probali smo da ručno pratimo odnos stvarne i očekivane produkcije po lokaciji, ali bez uzimanja u obzir vremenskih uslova i sezonskih varijacija to daje previše lažnih uzbuna. Niko od naših inženjera nije radio mašinsko učenje, a nemamo budžet za spoljnog konsultanta koji košta kao velika IT firma. Prihvatljiv ishod bi bio model koji jednom nedeljno prođe kroz podatke i označi lokacije koje zahtevaju pažnju, sa obrazloženjem zašto.

challenges.text: Three clients in Germany and Austria are asking us to certify our monitoring platform under EU Cyber Resilience Act requirements before they will sign multi-year O&M contracts — we have a lawyer but she has no background in the technical annexes and we cannot afford a big consultancy.
challenges.detail: Dva klijenta u Nemačkoj — Feldmann Agrarenergie GmbH i Bruckner Industriewerke — i jedan u Austriji traže od nas da naša platforma za daljinski nadzor bude usklađena sa zahtevima EU Akta o sajber otpornosti pre nego što potpišu višegodišnje O&M ugovore. Ukupna vrednost tih ugovora je značajna za naš obim poslovanja. Imamo pravnicu koja prati regulativu, ali tehnički aneksi akta — zahtevi za dokumentaciju o ranjivostima, procese ažuriranja softvera, izveštavanje o incidentima — su van njenog domena. Nismo ni blizu tome da angažujemo veliku konsultantsku kuću. Ono što nam treba je neko ko razume i tehničku stranu i pravni okvir i ko može da nam pomogne da mapiramo naše trenutno stanje na konkretne zahteve akta, identifikuje praznine i predloži šta tačno treba da promenimo u arhitekturi platforme i u procesima. Rok koji smo dobili od klijenata je kraj prvog kvartala 2025. godine.

challenges.text: Dust and bird droppings on panels at our agri-PV sites in Bačka cut output by an estimated 8–12 % between cleanings, but sending a crew every two weeks costs more than the lost energy — we need to know when soiling actually crosses the threshold that justifies a wash, not just clean on a calendar.
challenges.detail: Na našim agri-FN lokacijama u Bačkoj — trenutno sedam aktivnih, sa panelima postavljenim iznad aktivnih njiva — prašina i izmeti ptica između dve posete za čišćenje smanjuju produkciju procenjeno osam do dvanaest posto. Trenutno šaljemo ekipu na teren svakih četrnaest dana bez obzira na stanje panela. Taj raspored ne odgovara stvarnoj potrebi: posle kišnog perioda paneli su čisti i dolazimo bespotrebno, dok posle dve suve i vetrovite nedelje zaprljanje može biti i veće. Imamo meteorološke podatke sa stanica na tri od tih lokacija i produkcione podatke na pet minuta. Nemamo senzore za merenje prašine ni kamere na svim lokacijama. Željeli bismo model koji proceni stepen zaprljanja na osnovu dostupnih podataka — produkcija u odnosu na očekivanu, količina padavina, smer vetra — i koji nam kaže kada zaprljanje verovatno prelazi prag koji opravdava trošak izlaska na teren. Ušteda i od jedne nepotrebne posete mesečno po lokaciji već bi pokrila razvoj takvog alata.

challenges.text: Our ERP connectors break every time a German client upgrades their SAP instance — we spend roughly 600 developer-hours a year on reactive patches instead of new features, and three clients have already threatened to leave.
challenges.detail: Svaki put kada neki od naših nemačkih klijenata nadogradi SAP instancu — a to rade otprilike dva puta godišnje — naši konektori prestanu da rade kako treba. Greške se pojavljuju na nivoima mapiranja podataka i autentifikacije, i svaki put moramo da šaljemo jednog ili dvojicu inženjera da ručno analiziraju šta se promenilo u novoj verziji. Prošle godine smo izbrojali oko 600 programerskih sati samo na ovakve zakrpe, što je ekvivalent tri meseca rada jednog seniora. Tri klijenta su jasno rekla da razmišljaju o prelasku kod konkurencije ako se situacija ne promeni. Probali smo da napišemo bolje testove i da pratimo SAP release note-ove unapred, ali bez strukturiranog načina da detektujemo šta će se promeniti pre nego što se promeni, i dalje reagujemo umesto da planiramo. Nemamo interni alat koji bi automatski proveravao kompatibilnost konektora sa novom verzijom SAP-a pre nego što klijent izvrši nadogradnju. Željeli bismo rešenje koje nam daje makar 80 posto pokrivenosti automatskim testiranjem kompatibilnosti i smanjuje reaktivne intervencije za bar polovinu.

challenges.text: We store EU client data in our Novi Sad data centre, but since mid-2023 four Dutch clients are asking for documented GDPR Article 28 processor agreements that our legal team cannot draft fast enough — we lost one contract already.
challenges.detail: Od sredine 2023. godine, četiri naša holandska klijenta traže formalne ugovore o obradi podataka u skladu sa GDPR članom 28 — takozvane Data Processing Agreement-e. Naš pravni tim trenutno čine jedan interni pravnik i jedna administrativna saradnica, i prosto ne stižu da prate tempo novih zahteva uz sve ostale obaveze. Pokušali smo da koristimo gotove predloške koje smo našli online, ali klijenti ih odbijaju jer nisu dovoljno specifični za naš konkretan slučaj — naročito što mi podatke čuvamo u Srbiji, a ne unutar EU. Jedan ugovor smo već izgubili direktno zbog ovog razloga, a još dva su trenutno u zastoju dok dokumentacija nije završena. Razumemo da je osnovno pitanje to što Srbija nije na listi trećih zemalja sa adekvatnom zaštitom prema EU standardu, pa moramo da primenjujemo Standardne ugovorne klauzule. Trebamo nekoga ko razume i pravni okvir i tehničku stranu naše infrastrukture i ko može da nam pomogne da izgradimo standardizovan proces koji ćemo moći sami da primenjujemo ubuduće, bez angažmana eksternog advokata za svaki novi klijent.

challenges.text: Our analytics product generates PDF and Excel reports for clients, but the layout breaks on non-Western paper formats and brand guidelines vary per client — a senior designer spends two days per new client just on report templates.
challenges.detail: Naš analitički proizvod generiše izveštaje u PDF i Excel formatu, i to radi sasvim dobro kada klijent koristi A4 format i standardne fontove. Problem nastaje čim klijent ima specifične zahteve — drugačiji format papira, drukčije zaglavlje, boje prema internom brendu, ili dodatne kolone koje mi nismo predvideli u osnovnom šablonu. Svaki takav novi klijent zahteva da naš senior dizajner Tijana Đorđević provede dva do tri radna dana na prilagođavanju šablona u Jasper Reports-u. Imamo trenutno dvadeset i tri aktivna klijenta sa analitičkim modulom i stopa rasta novih je oko četiri do pet godišnje. To znači da trošimo između deset i petnaest dizajnerskih dana godišnje samo na onboarding šablona, što nije skalabilno. Razmišljali smo o tome da napravimo konfiguracioni interfejs gde bi klijent sam birao opcije, ali nismo imali kapaciteta da to realizujemo interni. Dobar ishod bi bio alat ili engine koji omogućava da se šablon definiše konfiguracijom, a ne ručnim kodiranjem, uz podršku za bar pet različitih papirnih formata i uvoz brend-palete putem JSON-a ili CSV-a.

challenges.text: Our analysts are drowning in alerts — we get roughly 4,200 SIEM events per day per client and maybe 12 of those are real; we need a way to rank and cluster alerts automatically so the team isn't spending 80% of their shift chasing noise.
challenges.detail: We ingest roughly 4,200 SIEM events per day for each client we monitor. After manual triage, typically around 12 of those turn out to need any real attention. The rest are false positives, misconfigured services, or known-benign behaviour that our rules have not yet learned to suppress. Right now our analysts make those judgement calls by hand, which means a meaningful share of every shift goes toward reading events that will never become incidents. We have tried writing suppression rules and tuning thresholds ourselves, and that helps at the margins, but it does not scale as we add clients. We have 18 months of labelled alert data sitting in Elastic — events marked by analysts as true positive, false positive, or inconclusive — which we have never used for anything systematic. We do not have a data scientist on staff. We would want something that runs close to our existing stack, does not require sending client data to an external cloud, and gives analysts a ranked queue each morning rather than a flat firehose. A good result would be cutting noise by 60 percent without missing any confirmed incident class we have seen in the past two years.

challenges.text: We want to offer clients a threat-intelligence feed tailored to Serbian and regional threat actors, but extracting structured indicators from Serbian-language dark-web forums and local hacker communities is something none of our analysts have time for.
challenges.detail: A growing share of the threats we see against Serbian clients originate from, or are discussed in, Serbian and regional-language online communities — forums, Telegram channels, paste sites, and a small number of dark-web boards that use Serbian Cyrillic. Our analysts read Serbian, but they do not have time to monitor these sources manually and then convert what they find into structured indicators — IPs, domains, file hashes, TTPs — that can go into MISP and be pushed to client sensors. We have tried using generic commercial threat feeds, but those feeds are tuned for Western European and North American targets and miss a lot of the regional activity we care about. We have collected roughly eight months of raw scraped text from publicly accessible parts of some of these communities, stored as plain text files, but it has never been processed in any structured way. The constraint is that some of this text is informal, uses slang, and mixes Latin and Cyrillic script inconsistently. A good outcome is a pipeline that runs at least daily, extracts indicators with acceptable precision, and feeds them into our existing MISP instance with minimal analyst review per batch.

challenges.text: Three of our largest potential clients — a bank, an energy distributor, and a hospital — are asking for NIS2 compliance gap assessments before they sign contracts, and we don't have a lawyer on staff who understands both the EU directive text and Serbian transposition law.
challenges.detail: Three organisations we have been in commercial discussions with for over a year — a regional bank, an energy distributor, and a private hospital network — have each told us they will not finalise a managed security contract until they have a formal NIS2 compliance gap assessment. NIS2 was transposed into Serbian law through amendments that our legal counsel, who handles our standard commercial contracts, openly says are outside his expertise. We have looked at hiring a consultant but the few firms in Serbia with the relevant knowledge are expensive and slow — quotes we received ranged between 8,000 and 14,000 EUR per assessment, and turnaround times of three to four months. We believe we could offer these assessments ourselves if we had a structured framework mapping NIS2 articles to Serbian transposition language and then to technical controls we already know how to audit. We have the technical audit capability; what we lack is the legal mapping layer. If we could produce assessments that are defensible and accurate, we would run the first three for the waiting clients and then add it as a standard service offering. Timeline pressure is real: at least one of the three clients has mentioned a competitor.

challenges.text: Our anti-cheat system flags about 900 accounts a day but our manual review team can only process 200 — legitimate players are getting banned and posting about it, and we've had a 7% drop in daily active users in the last quarter that we attribute partly to trust issues.
challenges.detail: Naš sistem BehaviorWatch v2 trenutno označava oko 900 naloga dnevno zbog sumnjivog ponašanja — ubrzanog kretanja, neprirodno visokih stopa pogodaka i koordinisane zloupotrebe ekonomije igre. Problem je što naš tim za ručnu proveru ima kapacitet za svega 200 slučajeva dnevno. Ostatak se ili automatski banuje ili čeka danima u redu. Imamo podatke iz poslednjih 18 meseci o svim označenim nalozima — oko 2,3 miliona zapisa o događajima — ali nemamo dovoljno stručnjaka koji bi napravili bolji model za automatsko odlučivanje. U poslednjem kvartalu dnevna aktivna baza igrača pala je za 7%, a na našim forumima i Discord serverima igrači eksplicitno navode lažne banove kao razlog napuštanja. Probali smo da fino podešavamo pragove u BehaviorWatchu, ali svaki put kad smanjimo lažne pozitive, propustimo više stvarnih varanja. Cilj nam je sistem koji tačnije razlikuje legitimne igrače od prevaranata, uz jasno objašnjenje zašto je određeni nalog označen — da moderatori mogu brže da odluče. Imamo budžet za šestomesečni projekat i resurse za deljenje anonimizovanih podataka.

challenges.text: Server costs jumped 40% last year because our matchmaking spins up full instances for as few as two players — we know there's a smarter way to allocate cloud resources dynamically but we don't have the backend expertise in-house to redesign it.
challenges.detail: Svaki put kad igrač pokrene sesiju, naš matchmaking sistem podiže celu serversku instancu — bez obzira da li čeka dvoje ili dvadeset igrača. To znači da plaćamo punu cenu EC2 instance i za sesije koje nikad ne dostignu minimum potreban za igru. Lani su nam troškovi AWS-a porasli 40% uprkos tome što baza igrača nije rasla u istom tempu. Znamo da rešenje leži u dinamičkom raspoređivanju resursa — podizanju i gašenju instanci prema stvarnoj potražnji — ali naš backend tim je fokusiran na funkcionalnosti igara i nema iskustva s orkestriranjem kontejnera ili serverless arhitekturama. Pokušali smo da angažujemo freelancere, ali svaki put dobijemo inicijalni predlog koji ne uzima u obzir specifičnosti naše NetCore biblioteke. Podaci o opterećenju servera po satu dostupni su nam za celu 2023. godinu. Rok koji smo sebi dali je pre sledećeg velikog ažuriranja u oktobru 2025. Dobar ishod bi bio smanjenje mesečnih troškova za najmanje 25% bez degradacije iskustva igrača.

challenges.text: We want realistic crowd audio in our stadium-themed game modes — right now we loop the same 12-second clip and players in focus groups rate the atmosphere as 'fake' within minutes of playing.
challenges.detail: ArenaForge ima stadionske modove u kojima se utakmice igraju pred virtuelnom publikom od desetina hiljada gledalaca. Zvučni dizajner Milena Draganović snimila je kvalitetnu biblioteku od 47 audio klipova reakcija publike, ali ih trenutno kombinujemo u petlji od 12 sekundi zbog ograničenja u zvučnom sistemu igre. Igrači u focus group sesijama koje smo organizovali u februaru i aprilu 2024. — ukupno 34 učesnika — naveli su 'lažan' ili 'dosadan' zvuk publike kao treću po redu smetnju u iskustvu igranja. Pokušali smo ručno da variramo redosled klipova po šablonu, ali mozak igrača veoma brzo prepoznaje obrasce. Ono što nam treba je sistem koji generiše ili kombinuje zvuk publike u realnom vremenu na osnovu onoga što se događa u igri — golovi, bliske situacije, greške — a da pri tom ne zahteva previše procesorske snage na klijentskom računaru. Imamo svu audio građu i podatke o igračkim događajima. Budžet za ovaj segment je manji nego za ostale, ali je važan za kvalitet atmosfere u igri.

challenges.text: We are trying to hire three senior network engineers in Novi Sad and have had the positions open for eleven months — the candidates we want all have competing offers from remote-first companies in Germany or the Netherlands.
challenges.detail: Već jedanaest meseci tražimo tri iskusna mrežna inženjera koji bi radili na NetCore biblioteci i serverskoj infrastrukturi u Novom Sadu. Oglasi su bili postavljeni na tri platforme, radili smo s jednom lokalnom i jednom beogradskom agencijom za zapošljavanje, i organizovali smo dva dana otvorenih vrata u kancelariji. Stiglo nam je dovoljno prijava, ali kandidati koji su prošli tehničku proveru redovno odbijaju ponudu jer im konkurentske firme iz Nemačke i Holandije nude rad od kuće i veće plate u eurima. Naš model rada podrazumeva najmanje tri dana nedeljno u kancelariji zbog prirode timskog rada na engine-u. Plate koje možemo da ponudimo su konkurentne za srpsko tržište, ali ne i u poređenju s remote ponudama iz Zapadne Evrope. Razmatramo relokacione pakete, hibridni model rada i programe internog školovanja, ali svaka od tih opcija ima svoja ograničenja. Ako ne popunimo ova mesta do kraja 2025, biće ugrožen razvoj sledećeg naslova.

challenges.text: Our automated essay-grading feature scores short factual answers decently, but as soon as students write longer argumentative texts — anything over 200 words — the agreement with human graders drops below 60%, which is not good enough for any of our university clients.
challenges.detail: ScoreAssist handles short factual questions well enough — a sentence or two, right or wrong, our model scores consistently. The problem starts when students write longer argumentative responses, anything above roughly 200 words. We measured inter-rater agreement between our model and human graders on a dataset of 4,200 essays collected from three university partners over two academic years. For short answers we sit above 80% agreement. For longer texts we drop below 60%, which our clients have told us, plainly, is not acceptable for anything that counts toward a grade. We have tried fine-tuning a multilingual BERT-based model on the same dataset and the number improved slightly but not enough. Our training data covers Serbian, Bosnian, and Croatian text, which adds complexity because none of the large pre-trained models handle these variants especially cleanly. We have one data scientist and one ML engineer working on this part-time alongside other duties. We need to reach at least 75% agreement with human graders by the end of the calendar year, because two university clients have renewal decisions in January.

challenges.text: Live virtual classrooms on our platform crash or stutter for groups above 35 participants — our infrastructure team traced it to inefficient media server load balancing, but we lack the expertise to redesign the WebRTC architecture and every outside vendor we approached quoted over €80,000.
challenges.detail: VirtualRoom works acceptably for small groups. Below 35 participants, video and audio are stable. Once a session goes above that number — a typical university lecture group — we start seeing dropped frames, audio desync, and in the worst cases a full server crash that kicks everyone out. Our infrastructure team traced the root cause to the way we distribute media streams across our Janus Gateway instances. The load balancing logic was written in 2019 for much smaller sessions and has not been redesigned since. We know what needs to change at a high level, but none of our current engineers have hands-on experience redesigning a WebRTC media server architecture at this scale. We spoke to three outside vendors who do this kind of work commercially. The lowest quote we received was €83,000. That is outside our budget for a single infrastructure project this year. We are running on an on-premises cluster at NTP, so a pure cloud migration is not straightforward either. Institutions are asking for lecture groups of up to 120 people. That is the target we want to hit.

challenges.text: We want to add a burnout-risk early-warning feature that flags students who are likely to disengage, but our current logistic regression model has a precision of only 54% on the validation set, which means teachers get too many false alerts and stop trusting it.
challenges.detail: InsightDash includes a feature that is supposed to flag students who are at risk of disengaging before it becomes a dropout. The idea came from several school counsellors who told us they always notice the warning signs too late. We built a logistic regression model trained on login frequency, assignment submission timing, quiz scores over time, and forum participation. On our validation set the precision sits at 54%, meaning more than four in ten alerts sent to a teacher are for students who are actually fine. Teachers at two pilot schools told us they stopped looking at the alerts after a few weeks because they did not trust them. We have behavioural log data going back four years across roughly 60,000 students. We store it but we have not done serious feature engineering beyond the obvious signals. We do not have a dedicated researcher on this — it has been handled by one of our backend engineers who has some ML background. We want to reach a precision of at least 72% without sacrificing recall below 65%, and we want a model we can explain to a teacher in plain language.

challenges.text: Two of our four senior backend engineers received better offers and left in the last quarter; we are now three months behind on our product roadmap and cannot find replacements willing to relocate to Novi Sad at the salaries we can currently offer.
challenges.detail: Between October and December last year, two of our four senior backend engineers accepted positions elsewhere — one moved to a product company in Vienna, the other to a remote role with a Dutch firm. Both cited salary as the main reason. We are now running the backend team at half its intended capacity. The roadmap impact is real: a permissions rework that was supposed to ship in November is still unfinished, and a new API layer for our CorpPath module has been pushed to an unknown date. We have posted job listings on several platforms and received applications, but the candidates with the right Java and distributed systems background are either asking for salaries we cannot currently match or are not willing to be based in Novi Sad. We are not opposed to a hybrid arrangement but we need people who can be on-site regularly given how much institutional knowledge transfer is required right now. We are open to a structured collaboration with a university or research group that could provide junior-to-mid level engineering support while we stabilise the team.

challenges.text: Our static code analysis pipeline flags about 900 warnings per release and our team spends roughly 60% of sprint time triaging them manually; we need a way to rank which warnings actually matter for safety-critical paths so we can cut that effort in half.
challenges.detail: Koristimo Polyspace Bug Finder kao osnovu naše statičke analize i pri svakom releazu dobijamo oko 900 upozorenja. Nemaju sva ista težinu – neka su tehničke sitnice koje ne utiču ni na šta, a neka mogu biti ozbiljan problem u delu koda koji je na kritičnom putu. Problem je što naš tim trenutno nema automatizovan način da ih razvrsta po važnosti, pa inženjeri prolaze kroz listu ručno i na osnovu iskustva odlučuju šta zaslužuje pažnju. Procenili smo da to oduzima oko 60% vremena po sprintu. Pokušali smo da napišemo interne skripte koje filtriraju po tipu upozorenja, ali to nije dovoljno precizno – isti tip upozorenja može biti kritičan u jednom kontekstu i potpuno bezopasan u drugom. Imamo istorijske podatke o tome koja upozorenja su u prošlim releasima zaista dovela do grešaka ili zahtevala izmene koda. Tražimo pristup ili alat koji bi mogao da koristi te podatke i kontekst koda da rangira upozorenja po verovatnoj opasnosti po bezbednosno-kritične putanje. Cilj je da skratimo vreme trijažiranja za polovinu, bez povećanja broja inženjera.

challenges.text: Our biggest German customer now requires ISO 26262 ASIL-B certification for the brake-assist module by Q3 next year, and we have no one in-house who has run a full functional safety process before; we are looking at hiring a consultant but the quotes we have received are between €120,000 and €180,000, which is too much for our size.
challenges.detail: Naš klijent Kern Antriebssysteme GmbH zahteva da modul za asistenciju pri kočenju koji isporučujemo dobije ASIL-B sertifikaciju prema ISO 26262 do trećeg kvartala sledeće godine. To nam je prvi projekat te vrste – do sada smo se kretali ispod praga koji formalno zahteva funkcionalne bezbednosne procese, pa niko u timu nije prošao kroz ceo taj postupak. Znamo teoriju, ali nemamo praktično iskustvo sa izradom HARA analize, definisanjem bezbednosnih zahteva, praćenjem do implementacije i pripremom dokumentacije za reviziju. Kontaktirali smo tri konsultantske firme i dobili ponude između 120.000 i 180.000 evra za vođenje procesa, što premašuje naše mogućnosti. Raspolažemo kompletnom tehničkom dokumentacijom modula, istorijatom izmena i test izveštajima. Ono što nam nedostaje je neko ko poznaje proces iznutra i može da nas provede kroz njega uz prenos znanja, kako bismo sledeći put bili samostalniji. Rok je fiksan jer je definisan ugovorom sa klijentom.

challenges.text: Our HIL test bench runs on a single dSPACE MicroAutoBox that cost us €55,000; when we take on smaller vehicle platform projects the bench setup cost alone kills the margin and clients walk away.
challenges.detail: Naš HIL test benč zasnovan je na jednom dSPACE MicroAutoBox II uređaju koji smo kupili 2019. godine za 55.000 evra. Za projekte srednje i veće veličine, taj trošak se amortizuje kroz ugovorenu vrednost. Problem nastaje kada dobijamo ponude za manje projekte – razvoj softvera za manji kontroler u niše voznoj platformi – gde je budzet projekta 30.000 do 50.000 evra. Postavljanje benča za novu platformu zahteva hardverske adaptere, dodatne licence i vreme inženjera, što lako dostigne 15.000 do 20.000 evra samog troška pre nego što napišemo i jednu liniju koda. Klijenti, obično manji tier-2 dobavljači, ne žele da plate taj overhead i odlaze. Razmišljali smo o virtuelizaciji ili softverskim HIL alternativama, ali nismo pronašli rešenje koje zadovoljava naše zahteve za tačnošću simulacije u realnom vremenu a da ne zahteva sličan hardverski ulog. Cilj je da smanjimo trošak postavljanja benča za nove platforme tako da manji projekti postanu finansijski izvodljivi.

challenges.text: Utilities lose 30–40% of water; they have pressure sensors in a few zones but can't say where the leak is.
challenges.detail:
Non-revenue water is the number-one cost problem for every utility we work with. Across our four active customers the figure sits between 30 and 40 percent of total input volume, and the utilities' boards ask about it at every annual review. The honest answer right now is that we can tell them how much water is missing at the district metered area level, but we cannot tell them where in the pipes it is going.

Each utility has pressure loggers in a handful of fixed zones—typically between eight and twenty sensors per network—and they send readings every fifteen minutes via GPRS. We store all of that in PostgreSQL and we can plot pressure traces on the map. What we do not have is a method that takes those sparse sensor readings, combines them with the EPANET hydraulic model and the consumption data we already hold, and produces a ranked list of probable leak locations that a crew can actually go and check.

We have tried a basic threshold alarm—flag a zone when overnight pressure drops below a set point—but it generates too many false positives and crews have stopped trusting it. Budget for this work is modest, roughly the cost of one external engineer for six to nine months. We want a working prototype tested against one utility's real data by the end of 2026, in time to build it into the leak module we are planning to ship in 2027.

challenges.text: Forecasting daily water demand for pumping plans.
challenges.detail:
Every utility we support runs its pumping stations on a fixed daily schedule that was designed years ago and has barely changed since. Pump operators decide how long to run each station based on experience and a look at the reservoir level in the morning. That works most of the time, but it means pumps run during expensive peak-tariff hours when they do not need to, and occasionally a reservoir drops lower than it should because demand was higher than expected.

To give operators something better we need a reliable 24-hour-ahead forecast of demand at the district metered area level. We have between two and four years of hourly meter aggregates for each network, plus billing records that tell us household count and connection type per zone. We know that day of week, public holidays and school terms matter. We suspect temperature and rainfall matter too but we have not modelled it.

What we have tried so far is a simple seven-day rolling average, which a junior developer put together last year. It reduces obvious errors but it is not good enough to hand to a pump operator as a planning tool. We do not have a data scientist on staff and we do not have the time to build that expertise internally. A good outcome would be a forecasting component that integrates with HidroLogik Net and gives a mean absolute percentage error below eight percent on a held-out validation set from one of our existing customers.

challenges.text: We produce roughly 600 packaging variants a year and our senior designer spends two days per project manually fitting artwork into structural dielines; we need a way to automate or semi-automate that layout step so turnaround drops from five days to two.
challenges.detail: We produce around 600 packaging variants every year, and the bottleneck is always the same step: taking finished artwork and fitting it into the structural dieline for that specific SKU. Our senior designer Jovana Petrović does almost all of this manually in Illustrator and Esko ArtPro. On a straightforward rectangular box it takes half a day. On a shaped carton or a multi-panel sleeve it can take two full days. That means our average packaging turnaround is five days from approved artwork to print-ready file. Clients, especially the larger retail ones, are now expecting three days or less. We have looked at scripting some of the repetitive placement steps inside Illustrator, and Dragan built a few basic actions, but the dielines vary too much in anchor points and bleed zones for a simple macro to handle reliably. We have also looked at one commercial plug-in but it assumed flat rectangular formats only. What we want is something that can read a dieline structure, identify the printable panels, and place and scale artwork into those panels with minimal manual correction, ideally reducing Jovana's involvement to a review step rather than a build step. Our constraint is that the solution has to produce files that our existing offset and digital print vendors can accept without extra conversion work.

challenges.text: Clients are asking for colour consistency guarantees across offset, digital and large-format print, but our colour profiles drift between vendors and we have no systematic measurement process; we lost one retail contract last quarter because of visible hue shifts on shelf.
challenges.detail: Colour consistency has become a commercial problem for us. Last autumn we lost a shelf-ready packaging contract with a Croatian household goods retailer, Jadran Domić, because their store audit found a visible hue shift between the offset-printed outer carton and the digitally printed shelf talker for the same product line. Both files left our studio with the correct Pantone references, but somewhere between the two vendors the profiles diverged and nobody caught it before production. We own an X-Rite spectrophotometer and we do measure colour on press proofs, but we have no consistent protocol for recording and comparing those readings across vendors over time. Each project lives in its own folder and there is no shared baseline to flag when a vendor's output is drifting. We need a measurement and tracking process, and possibly a simple database or dashboard, that lets us compare spectral readings across jobs, vendors and substrate types, and alerts us when a reading falls outside an agreed tolerance. We are not looking for a full quality-management system, just something practical that two people can run without dedicated technical training. Budget for tooling is modest, under three thousand euros, and we would rather build something lightweight than license an enterprise platform.

challenges.text: We want to hire a mid-level 3D motion designer but the three candidates we interviewed in the last six months all wanted Berlin-level salaries; we simply cannot close the gap on our current rates.
challenges.detail: We want to bring a mid-level 3D motion designer onto the team permanently. The demand is clear: more clients want product visualisations and animated packaging reveals for digital channels, and we are currently outsourcing that work to a freelancer in Ljubljana, which means slower turnaround and no institutional knowledge building inside the studio. We interviewed three candidates over the past six months. All three had the right skills in Cinema 4D and After Effects. All three declined our offers. The salary gap compared to what studios in Berlin or Amsterdam are paying is simply too large for us to close on current revenue, especially given our existing salary structure. We do not want to create internal pay inequity. We are exploring whether a structured remote or hybrid arrangement might widen the candidate pool, or whether a part-time role with a path to full-time is realistic. We are also open to the idea of a work-study or residency arrangement with a graduating student if the right supervision structure exists, but we have not yet found a formal route into that kind of partnership.

challenges.text: One of our agri-food clients collects temperature, humidity and CO₂ readings every five minutes across 22 storage silos, but the time-series database is growing at 40 GB per month and our queries for monthly reports already take 45 minutes — we can't afford cloud and need a smarter on-premise approach.
challenges.detail: Jedan naš klijent, prerađivač voća i povrća, ima 22 silosa u kojima senzori mere temperaturu, vlažnost i CO₂ svakih pet minuta, cele godine. Koristimo TimescaleDB na njihovom lokalnom serveru — mašina sa 32 GB RAM-a i 4 TB diska koji je već popunjen skoro do pola. Baza raste oko 40 GB mesečno i sada nam upiti za mesečne izveštaje traju 45 minuta, što znači da ih ne možemo pokretati tokom radnog vremena. Pokušali smo sa boljim indeksima i sa chunk politikom u TimescaleDB, što je malo pomoglo, ali nije dovoljno. Nemaju budžet za cloud rešenje niti za novi server u narednoj godini. Trebalo bi nam da naučimo kako da agresivnije komprimujemo starije podatke, kako da zadržimo samo ono što je statistički korisno za dugoročne izveštaje, a da operativni podaci i dalje budu brzo dostupni. Dobar ishod bi bio da mesečni izveštaj ne traje duže od pet minuta i da baza ne prekorači raspoloživi disk u narednih godinu dana.

challenges.text: The brewery client wants a dashboard that predicts fermentation completion time within ±2 hours, but fermentation curves shift with each new grain batch and our fixed regression model drifts badly after about three batches without manual recalibration.
challenges.detail: Pivara sa kojom sarađujemo želi dashboard koji im govori kada će fermentacija biti gotova — sa greškom ne većom od dva sata. Fermentacija traje između četiri i osam dana zavisno od serije. Problem je što svaka nova serija žita menja krivulju fermentacije dovoljno da naš regresioni model počne da greši već posle dve-tri serije i mora ručno da se rekalibrira. Milica je to radila jednom mesečno, ali to znači da između kalibracija ima perioda loših predikcija. Imamo istorijske podatke za oko 180 serija u poslednjih pet godina — temperatura vrenja po satima, specifična gustina, pH, i informacije o seriji žita. Pokušali smo da dodamo batch identifikator kao kategorijsku promenljivu, ali to ne pomaže dovoljno za serije sa novim dobavljačima. Ono što nam treba je pristup koji se sam ažurira kada stignu novi podaci sa vrenja, bez da neko sedne i ponovo trenira model. Nismo sigurni koji je pravi put — da li online učenje, da li nešto drugo — i tu nam treba savet i pomoć u implementaciji.

challenges.text: We only have two people who can write code and one of them is Milica who is going on maternity leave; we have three active contracts and won't be able to deliver all of them on time — we need to either hire or subcontract within the next six weeks.
challenges.detail: Milica odlazi na porodiljsko odsustvo u roku od šest nedelja i ona je jedina u timu koja samostalno piše Python kod i održava naše TimescaleDB i Grafana instalacije. Dragan i ostala tri člana tima mogu da rade sa podacima u Excelu i Metabasu, ali ne mogu da preuzmu razvojne zadatke. Trenutno imamo tri aktivna ugovora sa rokovima isporuke: novi moduo za izveštavanje komunalnog preduzeća, ažuriranje pivarske kontrolne table i novi projekat sa prerađivačem šećerne repe koji tek počinje. Bez Milice, realno možemo da isporučimo jedan od tri projekta na vreme. Tražili smo freelancera lokalno, ali nismo našli nikoga raspoloživog u kratkom roku. Budžet za angažovanje nije velik — u pitanju su ugovori srednje vrednosti. Otvoreni smo za podizvođača koji razume TimescaleDB i Python i koji može da uđe u projekat bez dugog uvođenja. Rok je čvrst: sva tri ugovora imaju isporuku pre kraja tekućeg kvartala.

challenges.text: We're producing about 12 novel organic reference standard compounds per month for clients, but our NMR interpretation and mass-spec data reporting is done manually and takes one senior chemist nearly half their working week. We need a faster pipeline but can't afford a €50,000 commercial LIMS solution right now.
challenges.detail: We produce around twelve new reference standard compounds every month. For each one, we generate raw NMR files and mass-spec data that need to be interpreted, written up, and formatted into a client-facing certificate of analysis. Right now that work falls almost entirely on one of our senior chemists, Nikola Vranić, and it takes him roughly two days out of every four-day working week. We have tried using shared Word templates to speed up the writing part, but the bottleneck is really the interpretation step and pulling numbers from different instrument software exports into a single document without making transcription errors. We looked at one commercial LIMS platform earlier this year and the quote came back at around fifty thousand euros for a licence and setup, which is not realistic for us at this size. What we need is something more modular—ideally a tool or a workflow that can parse our instrument output files, flag key peaks, and pre-populate a structured report template that a chemist then reviews rather than builds from scratch. If we could cut that reporting time by sixty percent, Nikola could get back to synthesis work and we could comfortably take on three or four more standard compounds per month without hiring.

challenges.text: Two of our synthesis routes for beta-lactam intermediates generate halogenated solvent waste streams totalling about 800 litres per month, and our hazardous-waste disposal contract costs us 4,200 EUR monthly. We want to redesign those steps to use greener solvents but we're not sure which alternatives are compatible with the reaction conditions.
challenges.detail: Two of our synthesis routes for beta-lactam intermediates use dichloromethane and chloroform at the extraction and purification stages. Together those steps generate roughly eight hundred litres of halogenated waste per month. We have a disposal contract with a licensed hazardous waste handler and it costs us about four thousand two hundred euros a month, which is a significant line item for a company our size. We know greener alternatives exist—2-methyltetrahydrofuran and ethyl acetate come up in the literature—but the beta-lactam ring is sensitive and we have not been able to confirm whether those solvents are compatible with the specific temperature and pH conditions in our routes without running a proper screening programme. We have tried substituting ethyl acetate in one extraction step on a small scale and saw acceptable yield but a drop in purity that we could not immediately explain.
