We do not have a dedicated process chemistry resource; our chemists are focused on delivering client orders. A practical solvent substitution study that accounts for our actual reaction parameters would let us make a decision with real data rather than guesswork. Reducing that waste stream by half would save us over twenty-five thousand euros a year.

challenges.text: We want to apply for an INOVACIJE fund grant from FREN to scale up one of our synthesis lines, but we've never prepared a project budget in the required format and we have no one internally with grant-writing experience.
challenges.detail: We have a synthesis line for a class of protected amino acid intermediates that we believe has real commercial potential if we can scale it from our current fifty-millilitre batch size to one-litre and eventually ten-litre runs. The FREN INOVACIJE fund looks like the right mechanism to finance that scale-up, but the application requires a detailed project budget in a specific format, a technical feasibility section, and an impact narrative that we have no experience writing. We have read through the published guidelines and found them straightforward in principle but difficult to fill out in practice because we have never framed our work in the way grant evaluators expect. We have the technical data to support the application—yield data, purity results, a basic cost-per-gram calculation—but translating that into a compliant budget document and a convincing case for reviewers is a different skill. We would like help from someone who has worked through at least one FREN or similar national fund application before and can guide us on what level of detail is expected, how to structure the milestones, and how to present the commercial rationale without overstating things.

challenges.text: Our inverters generate fault codes we can't interpret fast enough — last quarter we had 11 sites sitting at reduced output for more than 48 hours before a technician even arrived. We need a way to diagnose the fault remotely and dispatch only when truly necessary.
challenges.detail: Our inverters — mostly from two manufacturers, Voltaro and SunBridge — push fault codes to SolarPulse every thirty seconds. The codes cover everything from ground faults to MPPT drift to communication dropouts, and the manuals list over 200 distinct codes per model. Right now our monitoring team looks at the raw code, checks the manual, and makes a judgement call. Last quarter that process was too slow on 11 occasions: sites sat at reduced output for more than 48 hours before a field technician arrived. In four of those cases the technician arrived, reset a parameter remotely, and left in under 20 minutes — meaning the dispatch was unnecessary. We have two years of time-stamped fault logs, inverter metadata, and metered output data we could use to build something smarter. We want a system that looks at a fault code in context — time of day, recent weather, which inverter string, history of that unit — and tells the monitoring team either 'safe to wait and try a remote reset' or 'dispatch now'. Budget for a pilot is modest; we'd want to see something working on real data within six months.

challenges.text: We promised clients a performance guarantee of P90 annual yield, but our irradiance estimates for flat rooftops in Vojvodina are off by up to 12% compared to actual metered output — shading from HVAC units is the main culprit and we can't model it quickly enough at the proposal stage.
challenges.detail: When we put together a proposal for a new rooftop installation we run the site through PVsyst using a standard meteorological dataset and a simplified shading scene. For ground-mounted sites that works reasonably well. For industrial rooftops it does not, because large HVAC units, ventilation stacks, and parapet walls cast moving shadows we don't have time to model accurately at proposal stage — a full detailed scene can take a senior engineer half a day. The result is that our P90 yield guarantees have been off by up to 12% on some sites, which creates uncomfortable conversations with clients at the annual review. We do drone surveys before construction begins, so we have point-cloud data for most of our existing rooftops. We also have three or four years of metered output for many of those sites. What we want is a faster way to go from a drone scan or even a simple rooftop photograph to a shading estimate that is good enough for a proposal — not a research-grade simulation, just something that reduces the error to under 4% without taking half a day of engineer time.

challenges.text: Three of our biggest clients want us to integrate our monitoring data with their ERP systems, but every client uses a different API standard and our two developers are already overloaded on the core platform.
challenges.detail: Three long-standing clients — a flour mill, a packaging company, and a refrigerated logistics operator — have asked us to feed SolarPulse data directly into their ERP systems so their energy managers can see solar yield alongside consumption data without logging into a separate tool. In principle our REST API can export any data we hold. In practice, one client uses SAP with a custom connector, one uses a local ERP called OptiManager that expects a specific XML schema, and the third is moving to a cloud platform with its own webhook format. Each integration is a separate small project. Our two developers maintain the core SolarPulse platform and handle the normal release cycle; taking on three bespoke integration jobs on top of that would push the next platform release back by at least a quarter. We are not looking to hire a dedicated integration engineer for what may be a one-time effort. A reusable adapter layer or a low-code integration approach that our developers could configure without writing a full custom connector each time would be the ideal outcome.

challenges.text: Our kefir-analogue drink shows live cell counts of 10^8 CFU/ml at bottling but drops to under 10^5 CFU/ml by day 21 in the fridge, which kills our 'live cultures' marketing claim and we have had two retail listings pulled as a result.
challenges.detail: When we fill bottles of our oat-base kefir analogue we are consistently measuring 10^8 CFU/ml, which is a good number and what we put on the label. By day 21 of refrigerated storage — still well inside the 35-day best-before date — counts have fallen below 10^5 CFU/ml in repeated tests across multiple batches. That is a three-log drop and it means our 'live cultures' claim no longer holds at the point a customer actually drinks the product. Two retail partners in Germany pulled our listing after their own lab checks confirmed the drop. We have tried adjusting fill temperature and reducing headspace oxygen, and we switched to a slightly thicker bottle wall last autumn, but the trend persists. We have 18 months of CFU data at bottling and at days 7, 14 and 21 for roughly 40 batches. We do not currently know whether the main factor is oxygen permeation through the PET bottle, pH falling too low during extended cold storage, nutrient depletion, or something about the oat base itself. Budget for a proper investigation is around €15,000–20,000 and we need a solution in place before the spring retail review cycle in February 2025.

challenges.text: We are scaling from 200-litre pilot tanks to 2,000-litre production vessels and the fermentation profile is completely different — pH drop timing is off by 6–8 hours and texture is inconsistent batch to batch.
challenges.detail: We ran our kefir analogue and our pepper spread successfully at 200-litre scale for two years before deciding to move to 2,000-litre vessels in mid-2023. The larger tanks have the same jacketed temperature control and the same inoculation rate by volume, but the fermentation behaves differently in practice. For the kefir analogue, the pH drop that used to happen around hour 10–12 is now happening at hour 16–20, sometimes later, and on three batches it stalled entirely above pH 4.6, which forced us to dump the batch on safety grounds. For the spread, texture varies noticeably between batches — some are acceptable, some come out grainy and lose water during shelf life. We think the issue is related to mixing dynamics, heat distribution or dissolved oxygen levels in the larger vessel, but our current sensor setup does not give us enough data to be sure. We have pH and temperature logs but no dissolved oxygen readings and no mixing speed data. We are not in a position to run many more test batches before the cost becomes serious — each failed 2,000-litre batch costs us roughly €3,200 in raw materials alone. A good outcome would be a revised process protocol that we can reliably reproduce.

challenges.text: We need a seed investment of €400,000 to buy a second filling line and none of the three banks we approached would lend to a company with only 5 years of history and a product range that changes seasonally.
challenges.detail: We have a second filling line identified — a semi-automatic monoblock filler-capper suited to our 330 ml bottles — priced at €310,000 from a supplier in Slovenia, with installation and commissioning taking the total to roughly €400,000. Adding this line would let us run two-shift production and fulfil the larger HoReCa contracts we have been offered but cannot currently accept. We approached three banks in 2023 and 2024. All three declined, citing our company age of under six years, seasonal revenue variation and the absence of significant fixed-asset collateral. We have a clean credit record, five years of audited accounts showing consistent growth, and letters of intent from two distributors. We have looked at the IPARD III programme and at the Vojvodina development fund but the application process and timelines are long and neither our accountant nor anyone on our current team has experience navigating them. We are open to equity investment, a convertible loan or a structured grant co-financing arrangement. The filling line needs to be operational by Q1 2026 to meet a supply agreement deadline.

challenges.text: Our labels for Germany carry health-related phrases like 'supports gut balance' and we have received two warnings from a German legal firm saying these phrases may breach EU Regulation 1924/2006; we need to know exactly which claims we can keep.
challenges.detail: Several phrases on our German-market labels and website have been flagged. The specific phrases include 'supports gut balance', 'aids digestive comfort' and 'contributes to a healthy intestinal environment'. A legal firm in Hamburg sent us formal warning letters in October 2023 and March 2024 stating that these phrases may constitute unauthorised health claims under EU Regulation 1924/2006 and the associated list of permitted claims. We have not yet changed the labels because we are not sure which phrases, if any, can be retained in a modified form versus which need to be removed entirely. We also do not know whether nutrient-function claims for any of our ingredients — live cultures, fibre from oat base — would provide a compliant route to communicating the product's properties. We have the two warning letters, our current label text in German and Serbian, the ingredient and nutrition declarations, and the lab data on our culture strains. We cannot afford a full external legal retainer at the moment but we could fund a focused written opinion and label review. We need clarity before we reprint labels for the autumn 2024 production run.

challenges.text: We built a document-search module for accounting files that our clients use daily, but when the same accounting concept appears in both Slovenian and German within the same corpus the keyword search either misses half the results or returns junk; we've looked at off-the-shelf solutions but nothing handles mixed Slovenian-German legal vocabulary out of the box.
challenges.detail: Our document-search module indexes scanned and exported accounting files — invoices, contracts, correspondence — that our clients have accumulated over many years. The problem is that these files mix Slovenian and German freely: a Slovenian accountant writing to an Austrian supplier might use 'DDV' in one sentence and 'Mehrwertsteuer' in the next, both meaning the same tax concept. Our current search is straightforward SQL full-text search with a fixed keyword list. When a user searches for 'DDV' they miss every German variant, and the other way around. We built a small synonym table by hand — roughly 140 term pairs — but it covers maybe sixty percent of the cases we actually see. We have tried two off-the-shelf search libraries and neither had a multilingual legal dictionary that covered Slovenian tax and accounting vocabulary. We have a corpus of roughly 80,000 documents sitting on client servers that we could use for testing if a solution required it. Our clients notice the missed results and complain about it at least once a month. We have no dedicated budget for this yet but we are prepared to spend three to six months of junior-developer time on a working solution, or to pay a modest fee for a usable component we can embed. A good outcome is a search that returns relevant results regardless of which language the term appears in, without requiring our clients to learn any new interface.

challenges.text: One of our Austrian clients moved to a cloud accounting platform last year and now wants us to migrate their 12 years of legacy desktop data; we quoted 200 hours but we're already at 340 hours and still not done — every legacy export format is slightly different.
challenges.detail: One of our Austrian clients, a four-person office in Linz, switched from our desktop application to a cloud platform last year. They want all twelve years of their historical data — client records, invoices, journal entries, attachments — moved into the new system. We agreed on a fixed-price contract based on a sample of their exports, which looked consistent. In practice every annual backup from 2008 to 2016 uses a slightly different field structure, some years have attachments stored as relative paths that no longer resolve, and two years of data were exported from an intermediate system that added its own non-standard columns. We are now at 340 hours against a 200-hour quote and still have roughly three years of data left to clean. We have written about fifteen Python scripts to handle specific quirks, but each new batch of files tends to introduce at least one more. The client is patient but has a hard deadline of end of September because their auditor wants a full archive available before the annual review. We have no extra staff to assign. What we need is either a smarter way to detect and handle format variations automatically, or a second pair of experienced eyes on the pipeline to help us stop discovering surprises one file at a time.

challenges.text: Our iron and manganese removal units at three municipal plants keep failing to meet the 0.05 mg/L manganese limit after heavy rainfall events; we've tried adjusting aeration rates but the problem returns within 48 hours and we're facing regulatory fines.
challenges.detail: At three of our municipal plants — Bačka Palanka, Temerin and Srbobran — we run standard cascade aeration followed by pressure sand filtration to remove iron and manganese from groundwater. Under normal conditions we hit the required limits without difficulty. The problem is that after heavy rainfall, typically anything above 30 mm over two days, manganese in the raw water spikes and our treated water starts coming out above the 0.05 mg/L limit. We have tried increasing aeration contact time, raising pH with lime dosing and extending filter run times, but within 48 hours of a rainfall event the exceedance is back. Our operators keep manual log sheets and we have SCADA data going back three years that show the pattern clearly. We have not had the manganese speciation analysed — we do not know whether we are dealing with dissolved Mn2+ or colloidal forms. Regulatory inspectors have issued two warnings in the last 12 months and fines are next. We need someone who can look at our raw water chemistry and filter configuration and tell us concretely what to change. Our budget for a solution is around 15,000 EUR per site if it comes to equipment changes.

challenges.text: We won a tender in Zrenjanin to upgrade a 12,000 m³/day drinking water plant but the EU co-financing requires a full Environmental Impact Assessment and hydrogeological model of the aquifer before the end of Q3 — we don't have the in-house expertise and the consultants we called quoted 90,000 EUR.
challenges.detail: We signed a contract with the City of Zrenjanin to upgrade a drinking water plant that currently handles 12,000 cubic metres per day. The upgrade is co-financed by an EU instrument and the grant agreement requires us to submit a full Environmental Impact Assessment and a validated hydrogeological model of the Banat aquifer before the end of Q3 this year. We have the raw borehole logs, historical pumping test data and water level records from the waterworks operator going back to 1987, but we have never built a numerical groundwater model and we do not have a licensed environmental consultant on staff. We called three outside firms; the cheapest quote was 90,000 EUR, which wipes out our project margin. The deadline is fixed — the grant disbursement schedule depends on it. We are looking for a collaboration where we provide all the primary data and field access, and a partner provides the modelling and report authorship. We can offer co-authorship on the EIA, access to our site and data archive, and a fair fee — realistically in the 25,000 to 35,000 EUR range.

challenges.text: We're seeing accelerated corrosion on our stainless-steel pipe welds in the Sremska Mitrovica network — we're replacing about 200 metres of pipe per year unexpectedly and we can't explain why the corrosion is so much worse there than in other towns.
challenges.detail: In our Sremska Mitrovica distribution network we are replacing roughly 200 metres of AISI 316L stainless steel welded pipe every year due to pitting and crevice corrosion at or near the weld seams. The same pipe specification and the same installation teams work in Bačka Palanka and Apatin without this problem. The Mitrovica water has higher chloride content — around 180 mg/L versus 60–80 mg/L elsewhere — and a slightly lower pH, but our corrosion rate there still seems worse than chloride levels alone would explain. We have kept records of every replacement segment: location, installation year, pipe batch number, failure type. We suspect localised galvanic effects or microbially influenced corrosion but we have not had any microbiological or metallurgical analysis done on the failed pipe sections. We have three removed pipe segments in storage that have never been analysed. Continuing to replace 200 metres a year is costing us roughly 40,000 EUR annually in materials and labour, not counting customer complaints during shutdowns. We want to understand the root cause before deciding whether to switch pipe material, change the welding procedure or apply cathodic protection.

challenges.text: Our field crews spend roughly 30% of their time travelling between maintenance sites in scattered villages; we have GPS logs for every vehicle but nobody has ever analysed them to build a better schedule.
challenges.detail: Our field maintenance teams cover scattered villages across four districts, driving company vans between pump stations, meter reading points and repair call-outs. We estimate they spend about 30% of working time in transit, which is roughly 26 person-days lost per month across the fleet. We have GPS logs from our eight service vehicles going back two years — timestamped coordinates at one-minute intervals, tied to job tickets in our service management spreadsheet. Nobody has ever done anything with this data beyond checking whether a van was where it should be. We believe a better daily routing and scheduling system could cut travel time significantly, but we do not have the internal skills to build one or to even assess what kind of tool would fit our workflow. Our dispatchers currently assign jobs by phone the morning of each day. We are not looking for an expensive off-the-shelf logistics platform — our jobs have constraints that standard delivery-route tools do not understand, such as required time windows at certain pump stations and crew certification requirements for different job types. We want to start with an analysis of the existing GPS and job data to see what is actually possible before committing to any software.

challenges.text: Our LiDAR point clouds for urban areas are enormous — a single city-block survey runs to 80 GB — and clients want classified, feature-extracted outputs delivered within 48 hours of the flight, but our current processing pipeline takes five to seven days on our own hardware.
challenges.detail: A single block-level LiDAR flight in a dense urban area — the kind we routinely run for city infrastructure departments — produces raw point clouds in the range of 80 GB. After noise filtering, ground classification, building extraction, and vegetation separation, we need to hand the client a clean, attributed dataset. Clients have started asking for delivery within 48 hours of the flight window closing, and we understand why: they are tying our data to field crews and construction schedules. Our problem is hardware. We run a local processing cluster with twelve workstations, and a full urban dataset takes between five and seven days end-to-end. We have experimented with splitting jobs manually across machines, but coordination overhead eats up the time we save. We looked at one commercial cloud processing platform last year and the per-job cost at our volumes would exceed what most of our municipal contracts allow. What we need is either a faster automated pipeline — something that parallelises the LAStools and PDAL steps intelligently — or a cost model for burst cloud compute that makes financial sense below a certain dataset size. A good result would be consistent 36-to-48-hour turnaround on datasets up to 120 GB without adding permanent hardware cost.

challenges.text: We integrate cadastral data from five different municipalities and the data schemas are inconsistent — parcel IDs don't match, coordinate reference systems differ, and topology errors cause overlaps that our clients notice in the final maps.
challenges.detail: We work regularly with cadastral data supplied by five different municipal cadastre offices, and each one has developed its own internal conventions over the years. Parcel identifiers use different formatting rules — some include leading zeros, some do not, some embed the cadastral municipality code differently. Coordinate reference systems vary between older Gauss-Krüger zones and newer ETRS89 realisations, and the transformation parameters used locally do not always match the official ones. The result is that when we merge layers from two or more municipalities into a single project dataset, we get topology errors: overlapping parcel polygons, gaps along administrative boundaries, and mismatched ownership attributes. Clients notice these in the final maps, and correcting them manually after the fact costs us roughly two to three working days per project. We have built some FME workspaces and PostGIS validation scripts to catch the most common errors, but the rules are not systematic enough to run unattended. We have not found an off-the-shelf tool that handles the specific Serbian cadastral identifier conventions. A good outcome would be a semi-automated validation and harmonisation workflow that we can run as a standard step in every project, with a clear log of what was changed and why.

challenges.text: Two EU-funded project bids were rejected last year because our consortium agreement templates didn't comply with Horizon Europe partner liability clauses; we don't have an in-house lawyer and the consultants we hired gave us conflicting advice.
challenges.detail: We have tried twice to join EU-funded research and infrastructure consortia, once under a Horizon Europe call for smart-city spatial data and once under an Interreg call covering cross-border environmental monitoring. Both bids were rejected at the administrative compliance stage, not on technical merit. The feedback in both cases pointed to problems with how partner liability and financial responsibility were written into our consortium agreement. We do not have a lawyer on staff, and the two external consultants we engaged gave us different readings of the same Horizon Europe guidance document — one told us a certain indemnity clause was standard, the other said it exposed us to unlimited liability. The process cost us roughly four months of preparation time and a noticeable share of our business development budget. We are currently preparing a third bid for a Western Balkans spatial infrastructure project and we need someone who has direct experience reading and drafting Horizon Europe consortium agreements, specifically for SME partners in associated countries. We are not looking for general legal advice — we need someone who knows these specific document types and can work with us on a fixed-scope, fixed-fee basis before the next submission deadline.

challenges.text: We designed our game mechanics intuitively, but we have no evidence they actually build mathematical reasoning skills — two schools tried the kits last year and the teachers said the kids had fun but their test scores didn't noticeably improve, and we need real evidence before we can pitch to the Ministry.
challenges.detail: We built the game mechanics by instinct — Milena drew on her classroom experience and we iterated through maybe thirty playtesting sessions with children from our own networks before going to market. Last school year two primary schools in the Zrenjanin area each ran a six-week enrichment programme using the BrojOtkrij kit, with a combined group of about sixty children. The teachers reported that the children were engaged and asked to keep playing, which felt encouraging. But when we compared end-of-term test results for those groups against comparable classes who did not use the kit, there was no clear improvement in arithmetic scores. We do not know whether the mechanics are simply not targeting the right cognitive steps, whether six weeks is too short, or whether the test being used just measures something different from what our game develops. We have the raw observation notes from those sessions and the teachers filled in a short feedback form we designed ourselves. We have no controlled data and no way to analyse what we do have rigorously. Before we can approach the Ministry of Education about any kind of broader rollout or endorsement, we need to be able to show that the kit actually builds mathematical reasoning in a measurable way. A good outcome would be a clear testing protocol we can run next school year and a method for interpreting what we find.

challenges.text: The cardboard components of our kit warp in humid conditions — three batches shipped to schools in Srem last autumn arrived unusable after two weeks in storage, and we had to replace them at our own cost, which wiped out margin on that entire run.
challenges.detail: Our kits are printed and assembled by a small print shop in Zrenjanin that uses standard 2mm grey board and a matte laminate cover layer. In dry indoor conditions the components hold their shape well — we have kits in homes from 2021 that still look fine. Last autumn we shipped fifteen School Enrichment Packs to five schools across the Srem district. The packs were delivered in early October and stored in school storage rooms, which are typically unheated and poorly ventilated. By the end of October, teachers reported that game boards were warping badly — corners lifting, cards bowing — and in three of the five schools the components were not flat enough to play with. We replaced those three batches entirely at our own cost. The print shop suggested we try a heavier laminate or a different board stock, and we asked them to quote for both. The heavier laminate adds roughly 18% to per-unit material cost, and the alternative board stock they found adds about 22%. Either option would push our School Pack margin below a level we can sustain at current volume. We have not yet tested moisture-barrier packaging, coating alternatives, or different adhesives. We need a practical solution that keeps the per-unit material cost increase below 10% or that solves the humidity problem through the packaging rather than the component itself.

challenges.text: We want to add a companion app that listens to a child reading a problem aloud and checks whether they understood it correctly, but the child-speech recognition models we tested have word-error rates above 40% for Serbian-speaking children aged 8 to 10.
challenges.detail: We want to add a feature to our web portal where a child reads a maths problem aloud and the app checks whether they have understood the key numbers and the operation being asked. The idea is not to replace reading but to catch the specific moment when a child misreads '47' as '74' or skips the word 'minus' entirely. We spent about two months testing this using the Web Speech API and two open-source models we found documented online, running tests with eight children aged 8 to 10 from families we know. The word-error rates were very high — above 40% in every case — and the errors were not random. The models struggled most with Serbian number words spoken by younger children, particularly numbers above twenty, and they frequently misrecognised short function words that carry the actual mathematical meaning of a sentence. We cannot build a useful feature on that accuracy. We do not have the data or expertise to train or fine-tune a speech model ourselves, and we cannot afford a commercial speech API that charges per-call at our volume. A good outcome would be a working prototype with word-error rate below 15% for Serbian-speaking children in our age range, running either in-browser or on a small server we manage ourselves.

challenges.text: Our biggest customer — a Slovenian industrial bakery — is asking us to guarantee consistent falling number above 280 seconds and wet gluten content within a 1% band per delivery lot, but our current blending is done by feel and we overshoot or undershoot about 30% of loads, causing expensive reformulation on their side.
challenges.detail: Our Slovenian customer, an industrial bakery we call Pekarna Gorenjka in our internal files, places orders of 40–80 tonnes per delivery and their production line is calibrated tightly. They now require a falling number above 280 seconds and wet gluten within plus or minus 0.5 percent of target per lot — effectively a 1 percent band. We measure both values in our lab using standard equipment, so the data is there. The problem is that blending decisions happen on the floor based on the miller's read of the incoming wheat lots, and we overshoot or undershoot the spec on roughly 30 percent of outgoing loads. When we miss, their team has to reformulate, which costs them time and generates complaints that land on our commercial director's desk. We have tried adjusting blend ratios by hand after seeing the lab result, but by that point the load is largely mixed. We have two wheat storage silos with NIR sensors and four without. A good outcome would be a blending decision tool — it does not have to be complicated — that takes our incoming grain analysis data and tells the miller what ratio to draw from which silo to land inside the spec. Budget is modest; we are looking at something practical within six months.

challenges.text: We are running six roller mills dating from 1988 and unplanned bearing failures cost us an average of 14 hours of downtime and 60,000 dinars per incident last year — we had nine such incidents — but we do not have vibration sensors on any of the machines and do not know where to start.
challenges.detail: Our six roller mills were installed in 1988 and the frames and bearings are original. Last year we counted nine unplanned bearing failures. Each one stopped production for an average of 14 hours while we waited for a fitter and parts, and the direct repair cost averaged 60,000 dinars per incident. We do not have any vibration monitoring on these machines at all. Our maintenance team, which is three people, does visual and acoustic checks during shift walkthroughs, but that catches failures only when they are already audible, which is usually too late. We spoke to a local equipment supplier who quoted us a full SCADA-linked sensor network at a price that was not realistic for us this year. What we want to understand is whether a smaller, lower-cost approach — even just sensors on the highest-risk bearing points — would give us enough warning to schedule replacements during planned stops. We have basic electrical infrastructure in place. Our maintenance foreman, Zoltan Fekete, keeps a paper log of every failure with date, mill number, and bearing location, so we have nine years of incident history. A good outcome is fewer than three unplanned stops per year and a simple alert system the team can actually use.

challenges.text: Dust concentrations in our B-mill building regularly hit 28–35 mg/m³ during peak shifts, which is above the legal occupational exposure limit and has triggered two labour-inspection warnings this year — we have tried adding extraction hoods but it does not seem to help enough.
challenges.detail: Our B-mill building is the oldest part of the site, built in 1978, and it handles the primary break rolls. During peak shifts — typically the six hours around midday — dust concentration measurements taken by our safety officer, Dragana Molnar, have repeatedly come in between 28 and 35 mg per cubic metre. The legal occupational exposure limit for flour dust in Serbia is 10 mg per cubic metre. We received two formal warnings from the labour inspectorate this year, and if we receive a third we face a possible production suspension. We installed two additional extraction hoods above the main break roll section in March, which cost us around 400,000 dinars, but the follow-up measurements showed only marginal improvement. The ceiling in B-mill is low — about 4.2 metres — and the layout is constrained by fixed machinery positions. We believe the airflow pattern is wrong but we do not have the tools to model it. Our extraction fan is a single unit rated at 8,500 cubic metres per hour. A good outcome is a documented, verified solution that brings dust levels below 8 mg per cubic metre on a consistent basis and satisfies the inspectorate before the next scheduled inspection in the first quarter of next year.

challenges.text: We want to add a whole-grain spelt and emmer flour line to capture the premium health-food segment in Germany and Austria, but we have no idea how to certify and label these products under EU Regulation 1169/2011 or whether our existing organic certificate covers the new raw materials — we need a legal opinion before we invest in equipment.
challenges.detail: We have identified a market opportunity in Germany and Austria for whole-grain spelt and emmer flours sold through health-food distributors. Demand signals come from two distributors we met at a trade fair in Nürnberg in October 2023. Before we spend anything on dedicated milling equipment — rough estimate is 1.2 million dinars for a small stone mill and separating line — we need clarity on two regulatory questions. First, what labelling is required under EU Regulation 1169/2011 for whole-grain flour, and specifically how do we handle allergen declarations for emmer, which is a wheat subspecies and may need specific wording. Second, our current organic certificate is issued by a domestic certification body and covers incoming wheat from three contracted farms. If we source spelt and emmer from different farms, possibly in Vojvodina or across the border in Hungary, does the certificate extend, and what additional audit steps are required for EU market access under the EU organic regulation. We do not have a lawyer with food-law expertise on staff. We need a written legal opinion we can show to our board and to the distributors. Timeline is before the end of this year, since the equipment procurement decision needs to happen in Q1 2025.

challenges.text: We are getting sink marks and voids in thick-walled ABS housings for a home-appliance client — roughly 9% of shots are scrapped. We have tried adjusting packing pressure and cooling time by trial and error for three weeks and the reject rate is barely moving. Each mould-modification attempt costs us around €3,000 and two days of downtime.
challenges.detail: We are producing thick-walled ABS enclosures for a home-appliance client — wall sections range from 4.5 to 7 mm in the problematic areas. Since January we have been seeing sink marks on the visible outer face and voids revealed when we section rejected parts. About 9% of shots are going straight to scrap, which on a run of 2,000 parts per week adds up quickly. We have a basic Moldflow licence but nobody on the floor is trained to use it properly, so our process adjustments have been manual — we have tried raising packing pressure in steps of 5 bar, extending cooling time by two and four seconds, and shifting gate position on one cavity, none of which moved the reject rate below 8%. Each mould modification requires us to take the tool off the press, go into the toolmaking cell, and come back — roughly €3,000 in machining and lost press time per attempt. We have a deadline from the client of end of Q2 to hit below 2% defect rate or they review the contract. A good outcome would be a structured, simulation-backed set of process parameters and possibly a gate or cooling-channel change recommendation that we can implement in one or two controlled trials rather than guessing.

challenges.text: One automotive Tier-1 customer now requires us to measure and report the carbon footprint of each part we ship. We have no idea how to calculate it — we do not even have a full inventory of how much energy each press consumes per kilogram of output.
challenges.detail: One of our automotive Tier-1 customers, Kovač Automotive Components from Subotica, has sent us a supplier questionnaire requiring a per-part carbon footprint figure, expressed in kg CO2-equivalent, starting with the next annual contract renewal in October. We have never done this before. We do not have sub-metering on individual presses, so we cannot say with confidence how many kilowatt-hours go into one kilogram of moulded ABS versus PA66. We have monthly electricity invoices and a bulk gas meter for heating, but nothing broken down by machine or product family. We also buy resin from three different distributors and have no data on their upstream emissions. We are not looking to become a sustainability consultancy — we just need a defensible, auditable calculation method that satisfies the customer's questionnaire and can be updated each year without hiring a specialist full-time. Budget for this project is modest; we are thinking in the range of €8,000–€15,000 including any metering equipment we might need to install.

challenges.text: We recycle about 4 tonnes of sprues and runners per month by reground mixing, but our recycled-content parts are failing impact tests at a rate 30% higher than virgin-material parts, and we cannot explain why — contamination, degradation, something else.
challenges.detail: We generate around four tonnes of sprues, runners and occasional short shots per month. We regrind them in-house, blend at up to 20% by weight with virgin material, and use that blend on non-appearance parts for white-goods internals and secondary automotive brackets. Since November we have been seeing impact-test failures on these parts at a rate roughly 30% higher than on equivalent virgin-material runs. We test according to the client's spec using Charpy notched specimens at room temperature. We have ruled out obvious contamination at the hopper by colour-coding bins by resin type, but we have not done any analytical work — no melt-flow index measurements, no thermal analysis, nothing systematic. We suspect either thermal degradation from multiple heat cycles or possible cross-contamination between PA and ABS regrind streams, but we cannot confirm either. We do not have a DSC or MFI tester on site. A useful outcome would be a root-cause diagnosis and a set of practical controls — whether that means tighter sorting, limiting regrind heat cycles, or changing the blend ratio — that brings our recycled-content reject rate within 5% of the virgin baseline.

challenges.text: Our toolmaking team of four people is swamped — lead time for a new mould is 14 weeks and clients are asking for 8. We need two more experienced mould designers but have advertised three times and cannot find candidates willing to work in Zrenjanin at the salaries we can offer.
challenges.detail: Our toolmaking cell has four people: one senior mould designer with 22 years of experience, two CNC machinists, and one apprentice. The senior designer, Branko Ilić, is the only person who can take a customer's part drawing from concept through full tool design. That bottleneck means our new-mould lead time is sitting at 14 weeks end-to-end, and several customers are telling us they need 8. We have advertised for an additional mould designer three times — once in a local paper, once on a Serbian job portal, and once through a technical school in Novi Sad — with no hire resulting. The candidates who apply either lack the CAD experience for complex two-shot or side-action tools, or they decline the role because the salary we can offer in Zrenjanin is below what similar roles pay in Novi Sad or Belgrade. We are not looking to outsource all toolmaking; the in-house cell is a genuine competitive advantage. What we need is either a way to restructure the design workflow so less-experienced people can handle more of it with appropriate checking, or a realistic plan for where to find and develop the right candidates in our region.

challenges.text: Our platform runs A/B tests but clients with fewer than 2 000 monthly transactions can never reach statistical significance before the promotion period ends; they churn after three months saying the tool 'doesn't work for small shops', and that segment is 40 % of our leads.
challenges.detail: About 40 percent of the merchants who book a demo run fewer than 2 000 transactions per month. That volume is too low for a standard frequentist A/B test to reach significance in the three or four weeks a typical seasonal promotion runs. We have tried shortening test duration and relaxing the significance threshold, but that just means we call winners on noise, which is worse. We looked at Bayesian testing and have a basic Bayesian model in our Python library already, but it was built by one analyst who has since left and the rest of the team does not trust the output enough to show it to clients. We have also considered "cuped" variance reduction but nobody on the team has implemented it in production before. The problem is real: our churn data shows that merchants under the 2 000-transaction threshold cancel at twice the rate of larger clients, and their cancellation notes consistently say the tool did not produce results. We need a way to extract a reliable signal from small samples within a defined test window, and ideally a method we can explain plainly to a shop owner, not just to a statistician.

challenges.text: We collect on-page heatmap and scroll data but have no way to automatically identify which UI patterns correlate with drop-off; our analysts spend 15 hours per client report doing this by hand.
challenges.detail: We record heatmaps, scroll depth and click events for every client. The data sits in ClickHouse and we export it to CSV for analysis. Right now each analyst goes through that export manually, compares heatmap screenshots side by side and writes a narrative about where users seem to lose interest. That takes roughly 15 hours per client per monthly report cycle. We have 90 clients and two full-time analysts, which means reporting is the bottleneck and we have started capping new clients to avoid falling behind. We tried a rules-based script that flagged pages where scroll depth dropped below 40 percent, but it generated too many false positives and analysts stopped using it after two weeks. What we actually need is something that looks at the combination of signals — where people click, how far they scroll, where they exit — and surfaces the two or three UI patterns that are most likely causing a drop-off on that specific page type. It does not have to be fully automatic; even a tool that narrows the search from 200 events to 20 candidates would cut reporting time significantly. We have the raw data and we own the ClickHouse instance.

challenges.text: DACH clients are increasingly asking for a data-processing addendum that complies with GDPR Article 28, and our legal template drafted two years ago has gaps that three clients' procurement teams have flagged; we need a proper review but our local lawyer doesn't know EU data law well enough.
challenges.detail: GDPR Article 28 requires a written data-processing addendum between a controller and any processor handling personal data on their behalf. We have a template we drafted in 2022 with help from a local lawyer who handles mostly contract and employment law. Three procurement teams at DACH clients — two German retailers and one Swiss logistics company — have come back with specific objections: our template does not name sub-processors with enough detail, the data-deletion timescales are vague, and the security measures section references an internal policy document we have never actually published. Two of the three clients are holding contract renewals until this is resolved, and those renewals together represent roughly €68 000 in annual recurring revenue. We need someone who understands EU data-protection law in practice, not just in theory, and who can review the template, identify the gaps and help us rewrite the relevant sections. We are not looking to replace our lawyer for everything, just to fix this document and put in place a process for keeping it current as regulations or our sub-processor list changes.

challenges.text: Our platform collects heart rate, skin temperature and galvanic skin response from wristbands during spa sessions, but the algorithm that recommends treatment duration keeps flagging healthy guests as 'fatigued' — false positive rate is around 22%, and three resort partners have threatened to switch off the feature entirely.
challenges.detail: Our fatigue-detection algorithm looks at rolling averages of heart rate, skin temperature and GSR over the course of a spa session and fires a recommendation when any two of the three signals cross a threshold we set during our 2021 internal study with about 180 participants. The problem is that in real resort conditions the false positive rate sits around 22%. Guests who are perfectly comfortable get flagged as fatigued, staff see the alert, and it erodes trust in the whole platform. Three resort partners have told us they will disable the feature before the summer season unless we fix it. We have tried adjusting the thresholds manually twice and the false positive rate barely moved. We have roughly 14 months of session logs covering around 340,000 sessions, including staff override records when a recommendation was dismissed. We also have a smaller labelled dataset of about 1,200 sessions where guests filled in a short comfort survey. Our data team has the logs and the baseline code, but nobody here has a strong background in physiological signal modelling. A good result for us is getting the false positive rate below 8% without making the model so conservative that it misses genuine fatigue cases.

challenges.text: We have 14 resorts live, but our mobile app reviews average 3.1 stars mostly because guests say the recommendation texts feel robotic and generic — we need the in-app wellness coaching content to feel personal and motivating, not like a medical pamphlet.
challenges.detail: Every recommendation in Termalis Go is currently generated from a fixed library of about 60 text templates written by our product team in 2022. The templates were translated into Serbian, Hungarian and English and they cover things like 'your session is going well, consider extending by ten minutes' or 'your heart rate suggests a rest period would be beneficial.' Guests read them once and then describe the app as robotic, which shows up consistently in store reviews. Our average rating is 3.1 stars across roughly 2,800 reviews. We have tried rewriting some templates to sound friendlier and adding a guest name placeholder, but the improvement in ratings was marginal. What we want is content that adapts to where someone is in their session, what they have done before, and something about their stated goals when they signed up. We have session history, onboarding preference data and the current template library to work from. We do not have a content writer or anyone with a language technology background on the team. Our constraint is that the output must be short — two to four sentences — and must not make any clinical or medical claims. We want to reach a 3.8-star average within two seasons.

challenges.text: We want to expand into Germany and Austria but our data processing agreement with resort partners does not clearly comply with GDPR Article 28 requirements, and two prospective clients in Bavaria already asked for a legal opinion we cannot currently provide.
challenges.detail: We process biometric data from guests on behalf of resort operators, which makes us a data processor under GDPR. Our current data processing agreements were drafted by a general commercial lawyer in 2019 and updated once in 2021. When two prospective resort clients in Bavaria reviewed our contracts, their legal teams came back with specific questions about Article 28 obligations: sub-processor lists, audit rights, deletion timelines and the technical and organisational measures annex. We could not give clear answers and both deals stalled. We are also not confident our current AWS configuration with Frankfurt-region hosting fully satisfies what those clients expect in terms of documented data residency. We have no in-house legal counsel. We used a Novi Sad law firm for the original contracts but they do not specialise in EU data protection. We need a clear, updated DPA template that we can actually hand to a German or Austrian resort operator, along with a short written summary of our technical safeguards that their legal team can review. We want this completed before we attend the thermae trade fair in Vienna in October 2025, which is our main target for closing two new Central European clients.

challenges.text: Our clause-risk scoring engine flags roughly 40% of standard boilerplate as high-risk, which means lawyers stop trusting the tool after the first week; we need a way to distinguish genuinely dangerous deviations from harmless standard language.
challenges.detail: Our ClauseGuard engine scores every clause against a set of rules we wrote by hand in 2021, plus a classifier we trained on roughly 4,000 annotated contract clauses. The problem is the classifier does not reliably separate a clause that is genuinely risky — say, an uncapped liability provision — from a clause that looks unusual only because a lawyer wrote it in a slightly non-standard way. Right now about 40% of the flags in a typical NDA or supply agreement are false positives. We know this because three of our clients told us their legal teams just turned off the risk alerts after the first week. We have the annotated dataset and we have two in-house ML engineers, but they have been going back and forth between tweaking thresholds and adding more rules without a systematic improvement. We want to get the false-positive rate below 10% without reducing recall on genuinely dangerous clauses. A good outcome would be a method or a model architecture we can retrain on our existing data within our current infrastructure, with no new annotation budget above €5,000.

challenges.text: We want to expand into the Hungarian and Romanian markets in 2025 but our entire NLP pipeline was trained on Serbian-language contracts only; retraining from scratch for two more languages would cost us at least €80,000 we don't have.
challenges.detail: We want to sign our first Hungarian and Romanian clients before the end of 2025. The sales pipeline is already open — we are in early talks with a Hungarian logistics company and a Romanian HR software firm that both need contract tooling in their local languages. The blocker is that every part of our NLP pipeline — tokenisation, entity recognition, clause classification — was trained exclusively on Serbian-language contracts. We collected that training data over four years and it took significant effort. We do not have equivalent corpora for Hungarian or Romanian, and we cannot afford to repeat that data collection and training process twice. We have looked at multilingual pre-trained models but we are not sure how much domain-specific fine-tuning they would need to be reliable enough for legal text. We have two ML engineers and a product manager who can allocate perhaps three months of work to this. The constraint is a budget of around €15,000 for external data, compute or consultancy, and we need a working prototype before Q3 2025.

challenges.text: Our biggest prospect, a leasing company in Zrenjanin, walked away because we couldn't show them a SOC 2-equivalent audit report; we have no in-house compliance officer and can't afford an external audit firm right now.
challenges.detail: We lost a significant deal — a leasing company called Pannonia Lizing d.o.o. in Zrenjanin — because their IT security team asked for a SOC 2 Type II report or an equivalent third-party audit and we could not produce one. We operate under an internal ISO 27001-aligned policy that our CTO wrote, but it has never been audited by anyone outside the company. We have no compliance officer on staff. We got one quote from an external audit firm in Belgrade and it came to €28,000, which is more than we can spend right now. We are also not sure SOC 2 is even the right framework for a Serbian company selling to regional clients — it might be that a lighter certification would satisfy most prospects. What we need is clarity on which framework actually matters to our target customer profile, and a realistic path to getting some form of verified security assurance within roughly €10,000 and twelve months. A good outcome is a credential or report we can hand to a procurement team that makes the security objection go away.

challenges.text: Contract search inside the platform returns poor results when users type a term in Latin script but the stored document uses Cyrillic, or vice versa; about 1 in 5 searches returns zero hits even though the document exists.
challenges.detail: Serbia uses both Cyrillic and Latin scripts for the same language, and our clients upload contracts in both. When a user types a search term in Latin script and the stored document uses Cyrillic — or the other way around — our search returns no results even though the document is there. We estimated this affects roughly one in five searches based on a sample we pulled from server logs in January 2024. The root cause is that our full-text search index in PostgreSQL treats the two scripts as completely different character sets. We know transliteration is a solved problem in principle, but we have not implemented it because it is not clear where the right place in the pipeline is — at indexing time, at query time, or both — and there are edge cases where the same Latin sequence maps to different Cyrillic letters depending on dialect conventions. We have one backend engineer who can work on this for up to six weeks. We want a solution that is robust enough to handle mixed-script documents, not just fully-Cyrillic or fully-Latin ones, and that does not slow down search response times noticeably.

challenges.text: Our gripper can handle maybe 80% of the part geometries our customers actually present; for shiny or transparent parts — like clear plastic caps or polished shaft ends — the 3D point-cloud from our depth camera is too sparse and the robot misses the pick about 1 in 6 attempts.
challenges.detail: Our depth camera gives us a reliable point cloud for most machined metal parts, painted surfaces, and matte plastics. The problem is transparent or highly reflective parts. Clear polypropylene caps, glass vials, and polished steel shaft ends either scatter the structured light or let it pass straight through, so we end up with a cloud that has maybe a few hundred points where we need several thousand to localize the pick pose confidently. We have tried adjusting the camera exposure settings and adding a polarizing filter, which helped a little on polished metal but did nothing for clear plastics. We have also experimented with painting sample parts with developer spray to get ground-truth scans, but we cannot do that on a production line. One of our customers, a plastics packaging company in Zrenjanin, has told us that roughly 30 percent of what flows through their bin-picking cell is clear or translucent, and they are seeing a miss rate close to 17 percent on those parts. Our target is to get misses below 3 percent across all part types. We have the camera hardware, a modest GPU workstation for training, and a small library of about 800 labeled scans of the problematic parts. We need either a better sensing approach or a model that can work reliably with sparse, incomplete point clouds.

challenges.text: We want to sell into German automotive-tier suppliers but they require IEC 62443 cybersecurity certification for any device on their shop-floor network, and getting that certification will take us at least 14 months and €80,000 we don't currently have.
challenges.detail: Several German automotive-tier suppliers have asked us about installing FlexCell systems in their plants, and two of them have already sent us requests for quotation. The sticking point is IEC 62443, specifically the certification of our device as a component that can sit on a secured industrial control network. We understand why they require it — a robot on the shop-floor network is a real attack surface — but our current product was not designed with that certification in mind. We have done an internal gap assessment and we know we have weaknesses in secure boot, credential management, and software update authentication. We brought in an outside consultant for two days last autumn to help us map the gaps; his report is sitting with our CTO. The problem is the cost and the timeline. Accredited certification bodies are quoting us between €70,000 and €90,000 in fees, plus we estimate roughly six months of internal engineering work before we are even ready to go to audit. That is a lot for an eighteen-person company. We have looked at EU grant schemes but have not found one that fits our situation cleanly. A good outcome would be a credible certification roadmap, ideally with some cost-sharing or a phased approach that lets us sell to at least one German customer on a letter of intent while the full certification is in progress.

challenges.text: Our task-planning software assigns pick sequences correctly when the bin is full, but as parts become sparse the remaining objects can be in any orientation and the planner falls back to a brute-force search that can take over 40 seconds — too slow for our customers' cycle-time targets.
challenges.detail: When a bin is full or nearly full, picking the next part is straightforward: the objects are densely packed, orientations are fairly consistent, and our planner finds a good sequence quickly, usually under two seconds. As the bin empties, the remaining parts shift into random orientations, and the number of candidate pick poses the planner has to evaluate grows quickly. Right now the planner falls back to an exhaustive search over those candidates combined with collision checking against the bin walls and the robot arm configuration. On our test rig with a representative sparse-bin scenario, we have measured planning times between 35 and 55 seconds. Our customers' cycle-time targets allow at most five seconds for planning. We have tried pruning the candidate set using a simple confidence score from the pose estimator, which brought average times down somewhat but did not fix the worst cases. We have also looked at pre-computing reach maps offline, but the variety of bin sizes and part mixes our customers use makes that hard to generalize. We have logged data from about 2,400 real sparse-bin episodes across two customer sites, including the pose candidates generated, the scores assigned, and the outcome of each pick attempt. A good outcome is a planner that handles the sparse-bin case in under five seconds at least 95 percent of the time without making the collision-safety guarantees worse.

challenges.text: Cities want to retrofit 40 schools but don't know which to do first for the biggest energy savings per dinar.
challenges.detail: One of our longest-standing municipal clients manages a portfolio of 40 school buildings across three municipalities. They have secured a multi-year retrofit budget from a regional development fund, but the fund requires them to submit a ranked list of buildings before the first contract is signed, showing which interventions will deliver the largest reduction in energy costs relative to the money spent. Right now we have basic floor plans and some utility billing data for about 28 of the 40 schools, but the quality is uneven: a few buildings have full as-built drawings, others have nothing more than a hand-sketched plan from the 1980s. Milena has been running individual EnergyPlus simulations building by building, which takes roughly two weeks per site when the input data needs cleaning. At that pace we cannot finish all 40 before the fund's submission deadline, which is roughly eight months away. We need a faster way to estimate expected energy savings across the whole portfolio, even for buildings where the input data is thin, so we can produce a defensible ranking. A good result would be a method that gives the municipality a prioritised list they can justify to auditors, with clear confidence levels attached to each estimate.

challenges.text: Our scheduling engine works fine for up to about 80 staff, but two Austrian care-home chains that want to pilot us have 300–500 employees across multiple sites; when we run the optimizer for that scale it times out after 90 seconds without a solution, and we lose the deal.
challenges.detail: Our scheduling optimizer is built on Google OR-Tools with a set of constraints — shift coverage requirements, staff availability windows, maximum consecutive hours, and role qualifications. For clients with up to about eighty staff it finds a good solution in under ten seconds. When we tested it against anonymised data from a 340-person Austrian chain, the solver hit our ninety-second timeout every time without returning anything usable. We tried loosening some of the soft constraints and reducing the planning horizon from four weeks to two, which helped a little but still not enough. We also looked at splitting the problem by site and solving each site separately, but staff at that chain rotate across sites, so that approach breaks the solution quality badly. The two Austrian operators we are talking to both need a confirmed pilot by the end of Q3 2024 or they move on to another vendor. We do not have the internal expertise to redesign the solver architecture — we need someone who understands large-scale combinatorial optimisation and can either fix our current approach or tell us clearly that we need to replace it with something else. A good outcome is a solver that handles 500 staff across eight sites and returns an acceptable schedule in under sixty seconds.

challenges.text: Care-home managers in Austria tell us that staff call in sick at the last minute and the current system just shows a gap — it doesn't suggest who to call in; we want a model that predicts which shifts are likely to have absences 48 hours ahead so managers can line up cover, but we only have 14 months of absence data from our three paying clients.
challenges.detail: Care-home managers lose a lot of time every morning reacting to sick calls. They told us they would pay noticeably more for a product that flagged risky shifts the day before so they could arrange cover in advance rather than scrambling at seven in the morning. We think a simple absence-likelihood model per shift slot could do this, but we only have data from three clients covering fourteen months. The dataset has roughly 22,000 individual shift records with a binary absent or present label, plus some attributes like day of week, shift type, staff role, and whether the previous shift was a night shift. We ran a basic logistic regression and a random forest on it and got reasonable precision on the majority class but the model barely does better than the base rate on actual absences, which is the thing that matters. We suspect we do not have enough data to separate the signal from the noise, but we are not sure whether the answer is to collect more data, engineer better features, or try a different modelling approach altogether. Budget for this work is limited — we could fund a short collaboration or internship but not a full research contract. A useful outcome is an honest assessment of what is achievable with the data we have and, if something is achievable, a working prototype we can show to clients.

challenges.text: We are trying to raise a €400,000 seed round to hire two senior engineers and cover twelve months of runway, but every VC we speak to in Vienna says our ARR of €68,000 is too small and we don't know how to reach angel investors or apply for EU innovation grants — our founding team has no finance background.
challenges.detail: We have been running on founder savings and a small loan since 2019. Our three clients pay us a combined €68,000 ARR and we are growing, but slowly. We want to raise €400,000 to hire two senior engineers and give ourselves twelve months of runway to close the larger Austrian pilots and convert them to paying contracts. We have spoken to four early-stage funds in Vienna and two in Budapest. The consistent feedback is that our ARR is too low and our growth rate is not steep enough yet. We do not know how to find angel investors in the region who fund B2B SaaS at this stage, and we have no experience writing grant applications. We have heard that Horizon Europe and some Austrian national programmes fund software with a care-sector angle but the application processes look complicated and none of us has a finance or grant-writing background. We are not looking for someone to raise the money for us — we are looking for practical guidance on which programmes are realistic for a company at our stage, what the application requirements actually look like in plain terms, and how to find individual investors who back enterprise SaaS in Central Europe.

challenges.text: Our 868 MHz LoRaWAN nodes drop 12–18% of packets in reinforced-concrete factory buildings, and clients are starting to complain that dashboards show gaps of 10–20 minutes; we need to understand what is killing the signal and fix it without switching frequency bands.
challenges.detail: We deploy our LoRaWAN nodes at 868 MHz inside reinforced-concrete industrial buildings — production halls, water-treatment plants, that sort of environment. On open ground our packet delivery rate sits above 97%, but once the nodes go inside thick-walled structures we see packet loss of 12 to 18 percent. Customers monitor sensor dashboards and they are noticing gaps of 10 to 20 minutes where readings simply disappear. We have tried increasing transmit power to the regulatory limit, adjusting the spreading factor upward, and repositioning gateways closer to problematic zones. Some of that helped a little but not enough. We have Wireshark captures from the gateway side, RSSI and SNR logs from several sites, and floor-plan drawings of two of the worst-affected buildings. We cannot move to a different frequency band because our certification and our customers' infrastructure are both built around 868 MHz. We need someone who can look at the RF propagation picture in these specific building types and tell us what is actually happening, then help us make practical changes — antenna choice, gateway placement strategy, MAC-layer retransmit tuning — that will bring loss below 3 percent. A clear written recommendation we can implement ourselves would be a good outcome.

challenges.text: We are porting our sensor firmware to a new RISC-V microcontroller to cut BOM cost by roughly 22%, but our team has no experience with the toolchain and we have lost six weeks already; we need someone who can either help port the RTOS or train our three firmware engineers fast.
challenges.detail: We chose a RISC-V microcontroller from a Taiwanese supplier to replace the ARM Cortex-M4 we currently use, mainly because it cuts our bill-of-materials cost by about 22 percent on a 400-unit annual contract. The decision made sense on paper. In practice, our three firmware engineers all have ARM backgrounds and none of them have used a RISC-V toolchain before. We have been trying to port our FreeRTOS-based firmware for six weeks and we are still not past the startup code and interrupt controller. The RTOS vendor does not have an official port for this specific chip, so we are partly working from community sources of uncertain quality. We have the full chip reference manual, the vendor evaluation board, and a logic analyser. Our deadline is firm: we need working firmware on the new hardware within ten weeks from now, or we miss the production window for the contract renewal. We are open to two kinds of help: someone who can sit with our engineers and do the port together, or an intensive training that gets the team moving independently within two to three weeks. Either way, we need practical help, not slides about what RISC-V is.

challenges.text: Our biggest German customer now requires IEC 62443-4-2 device-level security certification before renewing a 400-unit annual framework contract; we have never gone through an IEC certification and do not know where to start with the paperwork, audit body selection or cost.
challenges.detail: Our largest German customer, a factory automation integrator, has told us that from the next contract cycle they will require IEC 62443-4-2 device-level security certification on any connected hardware they purchase. The contract covers roughly 400 units per year and is the single largest line item in our revenue. We have never gone through an IEC 62443 certification process. We do not know which audit bodies operate in the EU and are accredited for this standard, what the typical cost and timeline look like, or how much internal documentation and engineering work we will need to produce before an audit body even agrees to start. We have read the standard text but it is written for people who already know the ecosystem. We have about twelve months before the contract renewal discussion, which sounds like plenty of time but probably is not if we start from zero. What we need first is a practical map of the process: what has to be built or documented, in what order, who audits it, and a realistic cost estimate so we can decide whether to budget for it internally or look for co-funding. A trusted referral to an audit body would also be useful.

challenges.text: We connect 10–15 machines per plant and each machine speaks a different protocol — Profibus, Modbus RTU, MQTT, proprietary RS-485 — and building the translation layer by hand for each project accounts for about 60% of our billable hours on every engagement.
challenges.detail: Every plant we walk into has machines from different decades and different countries. One client's filling line alone has a 2003 Profibus segment, a Modbus RTU weighing terminal, two sensors that output a proprietary RS-485 frame the original vendor no longer supports, and a newer conveyor that only speaks MQTT. To get all of that onto one SCADA view we write custom translation code by hand each time. We have built maybe 40 of these bridges over the years and we keep copies, but every machine has slightly different register maps and timing quirks, so reusing old code still means two or three days of rework per device. That translation work eats roughly 60 percent of the hours we bill on a typical integration project. We have looked at a few off-the-shelf gateway products but either the licensing cost per node is too high for the size of plant we serve, or the gateway does not handle the specific proprietary framing we encounter. What we want is a faster, more systematic way to describe a device's protocol once and generate a working driver from that description, so our programmer is not rewriting the same logic from scratch every six months.

challenges.text: We've had three incidents where a sensor we retrofitted caused a pressure spike because nobody mapped the interaction with the existing pneumatic control loop; we need a systematic way to check for hazardous interactions before we go live, but we don't have an engineer with that background on staff.
challenges.detail: We had three separate incidents over the past four years where adding a new pressure or flow sensor to an existing pneumatic circuit caused a dangerous spike. In each case the sensor's sampling or the control loop's new set-point interacted with a part of the pneumatic system that nobody had fully documented. Nobody was hurt, but we had one burst hose and two emergency shutdowns that cost clients production time and cost us a repair bill and a difficult conversation. After the second incident we started asking clients for their original P&ID drawings before we touch anything pneumatic, and we added a manual checklist we put together ourselves. That helped with obvious cases but it is not enough — the third incident still slipped through because the interaction was two loops removed from where we were working. We do not have a process engineer or a safety specialist on staff, and we cannot afford to hire one full-time. What we need is a structured method, ideally something a technician can run through on-site before commissioning, that flags which parts of the existing control system might be affected by a change we are making. We are open to software tools, checklists backed by real engineering logic, or a part-time consulting arrangement.

challenges.text: I need to hire a second qualified automation engineer but the three candidates I interviewed in the past six months all took offers from larger companies in Novi Sad or relocated to Vienna — I simply can't match the salaries.
challenges.detail: The company needs a second engineer who can take over a full project from wiring diagram to client handover without Tibor supervising every step. Over the past six months three candidates came in for interviews — all had the right background, two with PLC experience, one with a process-instrumentation degree — and all three took jobs elsewhere before we could make a second offer. The salaries larger automation firms in Novi Sad are paying are simply out of reach for a six-person company whose clients are medium-sized food plants with tight margins. We are not looking for someone with a research profile; we need someone practical who is comfortable driving to a grain-dryer facility in January and spending two days debugging a Profibus segment. We would consider part-time arrangements, a structured apprenticeship with a junior technician we already trust, or a project-based collaboration that could grow into something permanent. The constraint is budget: we cannot offer more than what a mid-level technician earns at a large manufacturer in the region.

challenges.text: Our die-cutting machine is producing burrs and uneven creases on micro-corrugated E-flute when humidity in the hall goes above 65% — box compression strength drops by up to 18% and a pharma client has flagged two shipments for non-conformance this quarter. We control temperature but not moisture.
challenges.detail: U letnjem periodu i posle kiše, vlažnost u hali redovno prelazi 65%. Tada naša Rotermat DC-420 počinje da pravi srh na rezovima i neravnomerne linije savijanja na E-flute materijalu debljine 1,2–1,4 mm. Merili smo BCT na uzorcima — pad je između 14 i 18 posto u poređenju sa suvim danima. Dva puta ove godine farmaceutski kupac MedLogis Panonija vratio je dokumentaciju o neusklađenosti jer kutije nisu zadovoljile zahtev od 3,2 kN BCT. Pokušali smo da prilagodimo pritisak alata i brzinu mašine, ali efekt je manji od očekivanog. Klimatizaciju imamo, ali ona reguliše samo temperaturu. Nemamo sistem za kontrolu vlažnosti niti senzore raspoređene po hali koji bi nam dali podatke u realnom vremenu. Budžet za eventualno tehničko rešenje je ograničen — vlasnik je spreman da razmotri investiciju do oko 15.000 evra ako postoji jasna veza između merenja i kvaliteta proizvoda. Idealan ishod bi bio da znamo tačno pri kojoj vlažnosti i u kojim zonama hale nastaje problem, i da imamo praktičan, jeftin način da ga kontrolišemo ili bar predvidimo.

challenges.text: We print two-colour flexo on about 30% of our boxes and ink adhesion on recycled kraftliner is inconsistent — we see delamination on boxes that go into cold storage. We have changed ink suppliers twice and the problem persists, so it must be a surface or corona treatment issue.
challenges.detail: Oko 30 posto naše produkcije prolazi kroz dvobojni flekso štampač Lindograf F2-900. Koristimo waterbase boje na reciklovanom kraftlineru. Problem je sledeći: kutije koje idu u hladna skladišta — uglavnom za prehrambenog kupca Vojvodinapek-Komerc — pokazuju delaminaciju boje posle dva do tri dana na temperaturi ispod četiri stepena Celzijusa. Promenili smo dobavljača boja dva puta u poslednje dve godine i problem ostaje isti, pa zaključujemo da uzrok nije u boji nego u površini materijala ili u tome što ne radimo corona tretman pre štampe. Nemamo corona uređaj u pogonu. Takođe nemamo opremu za merenje površinske energije, pa ne možemo ni da potvrdimo tu pretpostavku. Pokušali smo da povećamo vreme sušenja i temperaturu sušare, bez trajnog efekta. Kupac nam je jasno rekao da ako problem ne rešimo do sledećeg kvartala, razmatraju drugog dobavljača. Dobar ishod bi bio razumevanje koji parametar površine treba da se menja i šta je najjeftinije rešenje za naše uslove — kupovina uređaja, izmena procesa ili nešto treće.

challenges.text: A Hungarian retail chain wants us to put a QR code on each box that links to product traceability data, but they also want the print to be machine-readable under poor warehouse lighting. We have no idea what print resolution and contrast specifications will reliably work, and our current flexo process may not be capable of it.
