challenges.detail: Mađarski maloprodajni lanac Nordbolt Retail zatražio je da od januara sledeće godine svaka kutija nosi QR kod koji vodi do podataka o poreklu i seriji proizvoda. Pored toga, QR kod mora da bude čitljiv skenerom u lošim svetlosnim uslovima tipičnim za raskladišta — difuzno osvetljenje, uglovi skeniranja do 30 stepeni, ponekad i oštećena površina kutije. Mi nemamo iskustvo sa specifikacijama za mašinski čitljivi štampani kod na flekso procesu. Ne znamo koji je minimalni DPI, koji odnos kontrasta tinte i podloge i koje dimenzije modula su dovoljne da skeneri pouzdano čitaju kod. Naš Lindograf F2-900 može tehnički da odštampa sitne detalje, ali do sad to nismo merili sistematski. Rok koji smo dobili je tri meseca. Nemamo softver za generisanje i testiranje QR kodova u serijskoj proizvodnji niti kontakt sa nekim ko je to rešavao za flekso štampu. Dobar ishod bi bio dokument sa konkretnim tehničkim parametrima i mogućnost da testiramo par serija pre zvaničnog početka isporuke Nordboltu.

challenges.text: Our tablet coating line produces roughly 4% of batches with uneven film thickness, leading to weight-variation failures at final QC and costing us about 60,000 EUR per year in rejected output and rework labour. We have process logs but can't identify which combination of parameters — inlet air temperature, spray rate, pan speed — is driving the drift.
challenges.detail:
Our pan coater runs about 110 coating batches per month. Roughly four or five of those fail final weight-variation checks because the film builds up unevenly across the tablet bed. When a batch fails we either rework it — which takes eight to ten hours of operator time plus extra coating suspension — or we scrap it outright. Last year we added it up: about 60,000 EUR in lost material and rework hours.

We have two years of process log data sitting in our batch records: inlet air temperature, outlet temperature, spray rate, atomisation pressure, pan speed, and batch weight. We have looked at each parameter individually and we cannot see a clear pattern. The failures seem to cluster in certain months, which makes us think humidity or seasonal air quality plays a role, but we have not been able to confirm that.

We tried adjusting the spray rate range based on supplier guidance last spring. It helped for about six weeks and then the failure rate came back. We do not have an in-house statistician or anyone with a design-of-experiments background. If someone could take our existing log data and help us find the real driver — and ideally tell us what process window to lock in — we could reduce failures to under 1% and save most of that 60,000 EUR annually. We are willing to share the full dataset and give site access for anyone who needs to observe a live run.

challenges.text: We want to add a sustained-release ibuprofen capsule to our portfolio by Q3 next year, but our formulation team lacks experience with polymer matrix excipients and in-vitro dissolution modelling — we'd need at least 18 months to figure it out ourselves and we don't have that runway.
challenges.detail:
One of our main clients, Medicor Pharma Distribution, has asked us to develop a sustained-release ibuprofen 400 mg capsule for their private-label portfolio. They want it on shelves by Q3 next year, which gives us roughly fourteen months from today. The problem is that our formulation team — three experienced pharmacists and two technicians — has mainly worked with immediate-release solid-dose forms. We have never designed a polymer matrix for controlled release, and we do not have solid experience choosing the right grades of HPMC or ethylcellulose, setting up a predictive dissolution model, or running the iterative prototype cycles that this kind of development requires.

If we try to build that knowledge from scratch internally, our own estimate is eighteen months minimum — and that assumes no dead ends. We do not have eighteen months. We are looking for a partner who already knows polymer matrix formulation and in-vitro dissolution modelling well enough to compress that timeline. We can provide our dissolution equipment, our analytical lab, and our production-scale capsule filling line for prototype work. The budget for external development support is limited, so we would prefer a collaborative arrangement to a full-service contract with a commercial CRO.

challenges.text: The new EU falsified-medicines serialisation rules require us to integrate a Track & Trace system with our SAP instance before the end of the year, and the integration vendor is quoting 140,000 EUR which is way above our budget. We're stuck between compliance risk and cash-flow constraints.
challenges.detail:
EU Falsified Medicines Directive serialisation requirements apply to us as a contract manufacturer supplying markets in the EU, and we have a hard deadline at the end of this calendar year. What we need is a verified integration between our serialisation hardware — Zebra printers and a camera-based verification unit already installed on Line 2 — and our SAP ECC 6.0 system so that every saleable unit gets a unique identifier and the data flows correctly to the EU Hub repository.

The integration vendor we approached quoted 140,000 EUR for the full project. That is simply not available to us right now without taking on debt that would create real cash-flow problems in a year where we already have capital commitments on the coater maintenance and cleanroom HVAC upgrade.

We are not looking for someone to replace the vendor entirely. What we need is technical help scoping a leaner solution — possibly middleware that sits between our existing SAP modules and the serialisation unit — that we could implement ourselves or with lighter vendor involvement. We have one IT staff member on site and the SAP system is standard with no unusual customisations. A working, compliant integration before December is the only acceptable outcome; a partial or delayed one carries regulatory risk we cannot accept.

challenges.text: Our parametric crop insurance pays out when rainfall drops below a threshold, but we have had three disputes this year where our weather-station reading differed from what the farmer experienced on the ground; we need a more spatially accurate precipitation estimate at field level rather than relying on a single station 15 km away.
challenges.detail: Our crop insurance pays out automatically when cumulative rainfall over a defined window drops below a contracted threshold. The data source is the Serbian Hydrometeorological Service station network, and in Vojvodina some stations are up to 15 or 20 km from the insured field. This year we had three formal disputes where farmers showed us their own rain-gauge records that were meaningfully different from what the nearest station recorded. In two cases we paid out anyway to preserve the relationship, but that is not a sustainable approach. We have tried blending ERA5 reanalysis data with station readings but the spatial resolution is still not fine enough for individual parcels. We have access to the cadastral parcel boundaries for all insured fields, historical station data going back 30 years, and a small set of on-farm sensors we placed with pilot customers last season. We do not have the internal expertise to build a proper spatial interpolation or downscaling model. We need something that can produce a defensible, auditable precipitation estimate at the field-parcel level for any day in our policy period. A good outcome is a method we can integrate into our existing trigger calculation engine before the 2025 spring planting season.

challenges.text: Our telematics-based motor insurance scores drivers on braking and cornering, but we cannot yet detect distracted driving — phones, fatigue, eye gaze — which our actuaries say accounts for roughly 40% of the high-severity claims we are seeing in the 22–35 age band.
challenges.detail: Our telematics motor product scores drivers on events we can detect reliably from accelerometer and GPS data — hard braking, sharp cornering, speeding. Actuaries reviewed three years of claims and found that in the 22–35 age group, around 40% of high-cost collisions show no abnormal kinematic signature in the seconds before impact, which points strongly to distraction rather than aggressive driving style. We want to detect phone handling, fatigue, and forward inattention using the smartphone camera and sensors already present on the customer's phone, since we already ask customers to mount their phone on the dashboard and run our app during trips. We have tried a third-party SDK from a German vendor but it was expensive, opaque, and performed poorly in Serbian lighting and road conditions. We have roughly 4,200 active telematics policyholders and can offer labelled near-miss video clips from customers who have consented to extended data sharing — about 600 of them. We need a model that runs on-device, does not stream raw video to our servers for privacy and cost reasons, and integrates with our existing trip-scoring API. We want a working proof of concept within six months.

challenges.text: We want to automate the first-notice-of-loss process for minor vehicle damage claims — customers upload three photos and we want a repair cost estimate within two minutes — but our current computer vision model was trained on Western European car models and performs poorly on the older domestic vehicle fleet we insure.
challenges.detail: When a customer reports minor vehicle damage — a dented door, a cracked bumper — we ask them to upload three photos through our app and we want to return a repair cost estimate in under two minutes so the customer feels heard and we can reserve the claim correctly without sending an assessor. We built an image classification and damage-area estimation pipeline using a model fine-tuned on a public Western European dataset. In internal testing it worked reasonably well on newer vehicles, but roughly 55% of our insured fleet is made up of vehicles that are more than 12 years old, including many Zastava, TAM, and locally assembled variants that look nothing like the training data. The model either fails to find the damage region or produces cost estimates that are off by a factor of two or more on these older models. We have about 1,800 annotated claims photos from our own portfolio covering the older fleet, which is not enough to retrain from scratch. We need either a transfer-learning approach that makes use of what we have, or a data augmentation or synthetic data strategy that lets us expand coverage without waiting years to accumulate more real claims. The business constraint is that estimates must meet a ±15% accuracy threshold against assessor valuations before we can use them in production.

challenges.text: We have been trying to raise a €3 million Series A for eight months; two VC funds walked away saying our cap table from the 2009 family founding round is messy and needs restructuring before they will invest, so the real blocker is a corporate restructuring and investor-readiness issue, not a technical one.
challenges.detail: We have been in fundraising conversations for about eight months trying to close a €3 million Series A to fund product development and expand into the Croatian and Romanian markets. Two funds that expressed serious interest both pulled back at due diligence, not because of our business fundamentals but because our ownership and share structure from the original 2009 family founding has never been formally cleaned up. There are informal agreements, undocumented transfers between family members, and a preference share class that was set up for an early silent investor and never properly resolved. The funds told us directly that they cannot invest until the cap table is clear, the articles of association are updated to modern investor terms, and there is a proper shareholders agreement in place. We are working with a Belgrade law firm on this but progress is slow and we are not sure we are asking the right questions. This is a legal and corporate governance problem, not a technology problem, and we mention it here only because it is the main constraint on everything else we want to do in the next 18 months.

challenges.text: Our anodising line produces about 8,000 m² of surface per month and the wastewater treatment plant generates 12–14 tonnes of aluminium-hydroxide sludge annually — disposal costs us around €28,000 per year and are rising. We have heard the sludge has secondary uses but we do not know what or whether any buyer would pay for it.
challenges.detail: Naša anodizaciona linija obrađuje oko 8.000 m² površine mesečno i za to koristimo kupku zasnovanu na sumpornoj kiselini. Posle neutralizacije i taloženja otpadnih voda, godišnje nam ostaje 12 do 14 tona mulja bogatog aluminijum-hidroksidom. Taj mulj trenutno odlazi registrovanom komunalnom prevozniku, što nas košta oko 28.000 evra godišnje, a cena je porasla dva puta u tri godine. Čuli smo da se ovaj mulj može koristiti kao sirovina — možda u građevinarstvu, keramici ili hemijskoj industriji — ali nemamo nikakvu konkretnu informaciju: ko bi to kupovao, u kom obliku materijal treba da bude, da li je potrebna neka dodatna obrada, koje sertifikate tražiti. Pokušali smo da pitamo našeg dobavljača hemikalija, ali oni nemaju odgovor. Idealno bi nam bilo da neko analizira šta tačno imamo u mulju, pronađe potencijalne kupce ili prerađivače i kaže nam da li je to realno ili ne. Čak i ako prihod nije veliki, samo smanjenje troškova zbrinjavanja bi nam pomoglo.

challenges.text: We die-cast our own extrusion dies in-house and die life is averaging only 35,000 metres before surface cracking forces replacement. Competitors apparently get 80,000+ metres from similar alloy dies. We suspect heat-treatment or surface nitriding is wrong, but our metallurgist retired last year and we have no one to diagnose it.
challenges.detail: Alate za ekstruziju pravimo sami u sopstvenoj livnici i to nam je dugo bila prednost jer ne čekamo dobavljače i možemo brzo da reagujemo na promenu preseka. Problem je što nam alati traju prosečno 35.000 metara pre nego što počne površinsko pucanje i moraju na popravku ili otpis. Razgovarali smo s kolegama iz jedne mađarske firme i oni kažu da od sličnih čelika dobijaju i 80.000 metara. Sumnjamo da negde grešimo u termičkoj obradi ili nitridiranju, ali naš jedini metallurg, Zoran Petreković, otišao je u penziju prošle godine i nije ostavio dokumentovane procedure. Imamo u fabrici podatke o tome koji kalupi su najbrže otkazivali, za koje legure i koji preseci — to bi se moglo izvući iz naše interné evidencije. Nismo u poziciji da kupimo nov sistem za termičku obradu odmah, ali možemo da razmatramo optimizaciju postojećeg procesa ili uslužno nitridiranje ako neko može da potvrdi da bi pomoglo. Dobar ishod bi bio pisani protokol koji naš operater može da primeni.

challenges.text: Power costs for the anodising bath rectifiers and extrusion press have risen 40% since 2021 and now represent 31% of our total cost base. We run a single shift but our electricity contract peaks are penalising us at certain hours and we do not have a clear picture of where the biggest consumption is.
challenges.detail: Struja je 2021. činila oko 22% našeg ukupnog troška. Danas je to 31% i još raste. Najveći potrošači su ekstruziona presa i ispravljači u anodizacionom pogonu, ali nemamo merenje po mašini — imamo samo ukupni mesečni račun i grubi raspored smena. Radimo jednu smenu, od 6 do 14 časova, ali naš ugovor s distributerom uključuje kazne za prekoračenje vršnog opterećenja u određenim intervalima i čini nam se da se to dešava kada presa i anodizacija rade istovremeno. Nismo nikada radili energetski audit ni ugradili podmerače. Imali smo razgovor s jednim konsultantom koji nam je odmah predložio kupovinu fotonaponskog sistema, ali to je investicija od koje nam se vrti u glavi i nismo sigurni da je to prvi korak. Hteli bismo najpre da razumemo gde tačno odlazi struja, zašto plaćamo penale i šta se može promeniti bez velikih ulaganja. Ako ima smisla premeštanje redosleda operacija ili neka automatizacija isključivanja, to nam je prihvatljivo. Budget za analizu je ograničen, ali ako se štednja dokaže, razgovaramo o implementaciji.

challenges.text: We applied last year for an EU COSME grant to expand into solar-mounting profiles for the German market, but the application was rejected and we do not understand why — the feedback was three lines saying 'insufficient innovation content'. We want to reapply but do not know how to reframe what we do.
challenges.detail: Prošle godine smo aplicirali na COSME program za proširenje na tržište Nemačke sa profilima za solarne konstrukcije. Odbijeni smo, a povratna informacija su bila tri rečenice — u suštini: 'nedovoljno inovativnog sadržaja'. Mi smo u prijavi opisali šta radimo: novi preseci profila, optimizovani za brzu montažu, s manjom težinom od standardnih rešenja. Mislili smo da je to inovacija. Izgleda da nismo dobro prikazali šta zapravo razvijamo. Nemamo iskustva s pisanjem EU projekata i niko u firmi se time nije bavio ozbiljno pre ovoga. Naš direktor razvoja, Branimir Stojaković, prikupio je tehničku dokumentaciju, ali ne zna kako da je uklopi u formular na način koji evaluatori prihvataju. Hteli bismo da apliciramo ponovo u sledećem roku — što znači da nam treba pomoć u roku od tri do četiri meseca. Ne tražimo nekoga ko će napisati projekat umesto nas, nego nekoga ko može da pogleda šta imamo, objasni nam šta ocenjivači traže i pomogne nam da to što radimo formulišemo na pravi način.

challenges.text: Our adaptive learning engine makes the same content recommendations for learners who perform very differently on assessments — we can't personalise the learning path beyond four static difficulty tiers, and our user-retention rate drops to 31% by week three.
challenges.detail: Our adaptive engine is basically a rule-based system that slots each learner into one of four difficulty tiers — beginner, elementary, intermediate, advanced — based on their score on an entry quiz. Once you are in a tier, you stay there unless you manually request a change or a trainer overrides it. We tried adding a mid-course checkpoint last year that was supposed to trigger a tier change, but it only fired correctly about 60% of the time and clients complained that learners were being moved backwards unexpectedly, so we rolled it back. The result is that a learner who scores 55% and one who scores 78% on the same entry quiz get identical content. Our week-three retention sits at 31%, and exit survey comments consistently mention that the course felt either too easy or too slow. We have the clickstream data and the quiz scores to work with, and our lead backend engineer has started reading about collaborative filtering, but we do not have the in-house expertise to validate an approach before committing to a rebuild. We need something we can ship inside nine months without rewriting the entire platform.

challenges.text: We have 18 months of clickstream data from about 12,000 learners but no validated methodology to turn it into insight about which course modules actually drive competency gains versus which ones learners just click through.
challenges.detail: Since mid-2022 we have been logging xAPI statements for every learner interaction — video plays, quiz attempts, module completions, time-on-task, navigation patterns. That gives us roughly 18 months of data covering about 12,000 learners across 200-plus course versions. The problem is we do not know what to do with it. We ran some basic completion-rate reports and presented them to two clients last spring, and both asked the obvious question: does finishing a module actually mean the person learned something? We could not answer that. We have tried correlating module completion with post-course assessment scores, and the correlation is weak, which suggests a lot of learners click through without engaging. But we do not have a defensible framework for separating signal from noise, and we do not know which engagement signals actually predict competency gain versus which ones just reflect learner habits. We want to be able to tell clients, with some evidence behind it, which parts of their courses are working. Our data is in PostgreSQL and we can export to CSV or Parquet. Budget for this work is modest — we are looking for a research collaboration rather than a consultancy contract.

challenges.text: We want to expand into the German B2B market but have no VAT registration there, no local legal entity and no idea how to handle the EU data-residency requirements under GDPR for employee training records — our lawyer says it will take six months minimum.
challenges.detail: We have two German manufacturing clients — both came to us through an Austrian partner — who want to roll out Orbita to their German employees in Q1 2025. The deal is worth roughly €180,000 in the first year. The obstacle is legal and operational, not technical. We do not have a German VAT number or a registered legal entity in Germany, which our clients' procurement teams say is a hard requirement. On top of that, their HR departments are asking for written confirmation that employee training records will be stored on infrastructure inside the EU and handled under a proper data processing agreement. Our platform already runs on AWS eu-central-1, so the data residency part should be manageable, but we have never written a DPA for a German B2B client and our current lawyer — who is excellent for Serbian law — has told us plainly that setting up a German GmbH or equivalent will take at minimum six months. We are weighing whether a fiscal representative arrangement or a local partner reseller model could get us to market faster, but we have no experience with either. If we miss Q1 2025 we risk losing both clients to a German-domiciled competitor.

challenges.text: Our transaction fraud model flags about 4.2% of legitimate payments as suspicious, which is three times the industry benchmark; merchants are threatening to drop us because their customers get blocked at checkout for no reason.
challenges.detail: Naš model za detekciju prevara trenutno označava oko 4,2% legitimnih plaćanja kao sumnjiva. Industrijský prosek je negde oko 1,4%, tako da mi blokiramo tri puta više ispravnih transakcija nego što bi trebalo. Posledica je direktna: dva trgovca su nam u poslednjih mesec dana pretila raskidom ugovora jer su im kupci bili blokirani u trenutku plaćanja. Koristimo XGBoost model treniran na istorijskim podacima iz 2021–2023. godine. Problem je delimično u tome što skup podataka nije dovoljno reprezentativan za nove tipove transakcija koje vidimo od kako smo ušli u rumunsko i slovačko tržište. Pokušali smo da ručno podešavamo prag odluke, ali to samo pomera problem — ili blokiramo više, ili propuštamo više sumnjivih. Imamo oznake za potvrđene prevare i potvrđena legitimna plaćanja, ali su prevare retke (manje od 0,3% svih transakcija), što otežava treniranje. Rok koji smo si zadali je kraj trećeg kvartala 2025. Dobar ishod bi bio da stopa lažno pozitivnih padne ispod 1,5% bez povećanja propuštenih prevara.

challenges.text: We process roughly 180,000 transactions a day and our PostgreSQL cluster is starting to miss our 200 ms SLA during evening peaks; we need to either rearchitect the data layer or find a smarter query routing strategy before we scale to 500,000 transactions.
challenges.detail: Dnevno procesuiramo oko 180.000 transakcija, a naš sporazum o nivou usluge definiše maksimalno vreme odgovora od 200 milisekundi po zahtevu. U večernjim satima između 18:00 i 21:00, PostgreSQL klaster počinje da kasni — beleži latenciju od 320 do 450 ms u koničnim trenucima. Imamo tri čvora u klasteru, jedan primarni i dva replike. Praćenje kroz Grafanu pokazuje da su najskuplje operacije složeni JOIN upiti koji spajaju tabele transakcija, korisničkih profila i konfiguracija partnera. Pokušali smo sa indeksiranjem i particionisanjem tabela po datumu, što je pomoglo, ali nije dovoljno. Procenjujemo da ćemo do kraja 2025. godine dostići 500.000 transakcija dnevno, a do tada moramo da rešimo ovaj problem jer ne možemo da kršimo SLA pred klijentima koji su upravo potpisali ugovore. Razmišljamo o uvođenju sloja za keširanje ili o preraspodeli čitanja na replike, ali nismo sigurni koji pristup donosi najveći dobitak bez potpunog rearchitekturisanja. Budžet za infrastrukturu je ograničen, pa radije tražimo pametnije korišćenje onoga što imamo.

challenges.text: PSD2 compliance documentation for our new German partner bank requires a qualified legal opinion on liability allocation under EU electronic money regulations and BaFin licensing rules — this is a pure regulatory and cross-border commercial law question that no engineering team can answer.
challenges.detail: Sklopili smo poslovni ugovor sa nemačkom partnerskom bankom Nordelbank AG i sad ulazimo u fazu usklađivanja dokumentacije sa zahtevima BaFin-a. Nemački regulator traži pravno mišljenje o tome kako je odgovornost podeljena između nas kao tehničkog pružaoca usluga i banke kao nosioca licence za elektronski novac, sve u skladu sa EU direktivom o elektronskom novcu (EMD2) i PSD2. Naš interni pravnik pokriva srpsko i regionalno pravo, ali nema dovoljno iskustva sa nemačkim finansijskim regulatornim okvirom ni sa BaFin procedurama. Pokušali smo da kontaktiramo jednu beogradsku advokatsku kancelariju koja ima EU praksu, ali oni nisu hteli da daju formalno mišljenje za nemačku jurisdikciju. Rok koji je Nordelbank postavio je 15. septembar 2025. Ako ne dostavimo dokumentaciju na vreme, ugovor se automatski odlaže za sledeći kvartal, što znači gubitak prihoda i šteta po reputaciju. Tražimo nekoga ko može da nas poveže sa odgovarajućim pravnim stručnjakom ili ko razume ovaj regulatorni okvir dovoljno da nam pomogne da definišemo pitanja koja treba da postavljamo.

challenges.text: We want to show business customers a 12-month cash-flow forecast inside our dashboard, but our current time-series model has a mean absolute percentage error of 18% on accounts with irregular income, which is too high for anyone to trust it.
challenges.detail: Unutar našeg analitičkog dashboarda nudimo poslovnim korisnicima pregled finansijskog stanja i planirali smo da dodamo prognozu tokova gotovine za narednih 12 meseci. Izgradili smo model zasnovan na vremenskim serijama koristeći Prophet biblioteku. Na računima sa redovnim mesečnim prihodima model radi relativno dobro — greška je oko 7–9%. Problem su računi sa nepravilnim prihodima: freelanceri, sezonski biznisi, firme sa projektnim fakturisanjem. Na toj grupi, koja čini oko 35% naše baze poslovnih korisnika, srednja apsolutna procentualna greška iznosi 18%. To je previše da bismo mogli da prezentujemo prognozu kao nešto korisno — korisnici bi videli broj ali mu ne bi verovali, što je gore nego da ga nema. Imamo istorijske podatke o transakcijama za poslednjih 36 meseci za sve korisnike koji su pristali na analitiku. Nismo probali hibridne pristupe koji kombinuju statističke modele sa modelima zasnovanim na obrascima ponašanja. Rok za lansiranje ove funkcionalnosti je kraj prve polovine 2026, ali bismo voleli da imamo funkcionalan prototip ranije kako bismo ga testirali sa odabranim korisnicima.

challenges.text: Our protease yield from the main Bacillus fermentation has dropped about 18% over the past 18 months and we can't pin down the cause — we've changed nothing intentionally in the process, but we suspect strain drift since we've been sub-culturing the working bank for years without refreshing it.
challenges.detail: Over the past 18 months our main protease fermentation has lost roughly 18% of the activity we used to see at harvest, measured by our standard Anson assay on every batch. Nothing in the written process has changed — same media recipe, same aeration rates, same temperature profile. We kept detailed batch records going back to 2019 and the drop is gradual, not sudden. Our best guess is that the working cell bank has drifted because we have been pulling from the same set of vials and sub-culturing repeatedly without going back to a verified master bank. We do not currently have a master bank for this strain; we set one up years ago but the freezer failed in 2018 and we lost it. We have tried adjusting dissolved-oxygen setpoints and tweaking the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio in the feed, and neither moved the numbers. We have basic microbiology capability — microscopy, plate counts, standard biochemical ID — but we do not have 16S sequencing or any genomic tools in-house. A good outcome would be confirming whether strain drift is the cause and, if so, getting a stable, high-yielding isolate back into production within one production season.

challenges.text: Downstream purification — specifically the ultrafiltration step — runs at only 55% of nominal throughput because the membranes foul with residual biomass within 36 hours; we're doing two cleaning cycles per batch instead of one, and that alone adds 11% to our production cost.
challenges.detail: Our ultrafiltration step is supposed to run for about 72 hours per batch at rated flux. In practice the membranes foul within 36 hours and we have to stop, do a full CIP cycle, and restart — twice per batch instead of once. That extra cleaning cycle adds chemical cost, water, time, and roughly 11% to total production cost per batch of protease concentrate. We have tried varying the transmembrane pressure and the crossflow velocity, and we have switched membrane suppliers once, without improvement. We suspect the problem is residual whole cells and cell debris passing the pre-filtration stage, but our depth-filter setup before the UF skid is not catching enough of it. We have pressure and flow data logged for every batch going back two years. The membranes we use are 10 kDa cut-off polyethersulfone in spiral-wound configuration. We have no membrane characterisation tools beyond visual inspection and water-flux recovery testing. Budget for process modifications is limited — we can consider equipment changes under roughly 40,000 EUR without board approval. A good result would be reliably reaching the full 72-hour run at close to nominal flux on every batch.

challenges.text: A large German detergent customer is asking us to provide a full environmental footprint figure — scope 1, 2 and 3 — for our amylase product within six months, or they will move to an Austrian supplier; we have never done a life cycle assessment and don't know where to start.
challenges.detail: One of our German customers, a detergent manufacturer we have supplied for nine years, has told us in writing that they need a full environmental footprint figure for our amylase product — covering their scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions requirements — within six months. If we cannot provide it, they will switch to an Austrian supplier who already has this documentation. We have never done a life cycle assessment of any product. We do have utility metering for electricity and steam, we track raw material purchases, and we have rough data on our transport distances, but it is not organised in any format suited to an LCA. We do not own LCA software and nobody on staff has done this before. Our quality manager Nemanja Filipov has been reading about it but describes the methodology as unfamiliar. The six-month deadline is fixed — the customer has a corporate sustainability reporting cycle that drives it. Losing this account would cost us approximately 14% of annual revenue. A good outcome is a credible, documented footprint figure we can hand to the customer and, ideally, a process we can repeat for other products without outside help every time.

challenges.text: We need to raise 800,000 EUR to install a second 10,000-litre fermenter but local banks are quoting us 9.5% interest and require collateral we don't have; we've heard about EU Horizon and EBRD instruments but don't have the staff to write the applications.
challenges.detail: We need a second 10,000-litre fermenter to meet demand that our current 5,000-litre vessels cannot handle, and we have a quotation from a local engineering firm putting the total installed cost at 800,000 EUR. Local bank financing has come back at 9.5% interest with collateral requirements we cannot meet because our main asset — the production building — is already pledged against an earlier loan. We have heard that instruments through EU Horizon programmes and the EBRD might offer better terms for companies like ours, but every time we look into it the application documentation is extensive and written in a way that assumes a dedicated grants team. We have nobody to write that kind of application. Our production manager and financial director are the same person — Dragan Kovačević junior — and his time is fully occupied running the business. We are not opposed to bringing in a partner or taking on a minority investor if that is how the financing works, but we would want to stay operationally independent. A good outcome is securing the financing within 18 months on terms that do not put the family's existing equity at serious risk.

challenges.text: Our adtech platform inserts pre-roll ads into podcast episodes, but the targeting is purely demographic; click-through rates are stuck at 0.9 % and advertisers want 2.5 % before they renew; we think smarter content-context matching would help but do not know how to build it.
challenges.detail: SoundSlot currently targets listeners using three variables: age bracket, city and device type, all pulled from registration data and IP lookup. Our average pre-roll click-through sits at 0.9 percent across the network. Advertisers — especially the packaged-goods and finance clients who make up the bulk of our revenue — are telling us they will not renew above a certain spend level until we can demonstrate 2.5 percent CTR. We have tried splitting inventory by show genre, which moved the needle by about 0.1 percentage points, but that is not enough. What we believe is missing is matching the content of a specific episode to the intent signals an ad is trying to reach. For example, a personal-finance ad placed in an episode where the host is discussing savings accounts should outperform the same ad placed in a true-crime episode. We have episode transcripts going back four years and we have the campaign performance logs, but we do not have anyone internally who knows how to build a content-embedding or topic-classification layer and connect it to our ad-decision logic. Budget for a working prototype: roughly €18,000, deliverable within six months.

challenges.text: We have eight years of listener panel surveys, episode ratings and social engagement numbers, but our commercial team still sets ad prices by gut feel; we'd like a model that tells us what a 30-second slot in a given show is actually worth before we send the rate card.
challenges.detail: Every quarter our commercial director Tomislav Ferić sits down with a printed spreadsheet and sets rate cards for the next 90 days based on last year's figures adjusted by feel. We have data that should make this much more rigorous: eight years of listener panel surveys covering 1,200 recurring panellists, weekly episode ratings, social share counts, download trends and historical CPM data from sold campaigns. The problem is that nobody has connected these datasets into a model that can say, for a given show, episode slot and month, what a 30-second spot is actually worth to an advertiser relative to alternatives in our network. We have tried a simple regression that Tomislav built in Excel, but it explains only about 22 percent of variance in actual sold price. We want something that accounts for seasonal patterns, show momentum and audience overlap between programmes. Output we want is a suggested floor price and a suggested ceiling per slot, updated monthly. The data is all ours and already cleaned to a reasonable standard. A good outcome is a model our commercial team trusts enough to use in client meetings without Tomislav having to override it more than 20 percent of the time.

challenges.text: Background noise in field-recorded podcast episodes recorded on mobile phones varies wildly; our editors spend 40 minutes per episode on manual cleanup, and that cost is eating our margin on lower-budget shows.
challenges.detail: About a third of our podcast episodes — primarily interview shows recorded in guests' homes or in cafés — arrive from the field with background noise problems: HVAC hum, street traffic, overlapping voices, handling noise. Our editors currently use iZotope RX on every such file, working through it manually, and the average remediation time is 40 minutes per episode. At our current volume of around 18 field-recorded episodes per week, that is 12 editor-hours per week spent purely on noise cleanup rather than on editorial decisions. We have tried setting recording guidelines and sending hosts a checklist, which reduced the worst cases but did not materially change the average. We have also tested the automatic repair functions inside iZotope RX, but without a human guiding the parameters the results are sometimes worse than the raw file. What we want is an automated or semi-automated pipeline that can ingest a raw audio file, classify the noise type and apply appropriate processing with minimal manual intervention, so that editors review the output rather than drive the process. We have roughly 6,000 archived field-recorded episodes we could use as training or evaluation material. Target is to cut manual time to under 10 minutes per episode. We have around €10,000 set aside for tooling or a custom solution.

challenges.text: We incorporated a Croatian subsidiary last year to chase Zagreb ad budgets and the dual-entity VAT and transfer-pricing paperwork is consuming almost one full-time equivalent of our finance person's time every month.
challenges.detail: We opened Mediavox d.o.o. in Zagreb in February 2023 to invoice Croatian clients locally and to compete for Zagreb municipal and corporate ad budgets. The subsidiary is real and already billing, but the compliance workload has grown faster than we expected. Our finance manager Vesna Blagojević estimates she spends close to one full working week every month reconciling inter-company invoices, preparing transfer-pricing documentation that satisfies both Serbian and Croatian tax authorities, and handling the dual VAT registration calendars. We are using Microsoft Dynamics 365 on the Serbian side and a Croatian accounting bureau for the subsidiary, and the two systems do not talk to each other. We are not looking for legal advice — we have an accountancy firm in Zagreb for that — but we need either a process redesign, a middleware integration between the two accounting environments, or some combination that brings Vesna's monthly cross-border compliance time below eight hours. We would also like the solution to scale to a potential third entity if we expand to Bosnia. Budget is modest, around €6,000 for implementation, but the monthly time saving justifies it clearly.

challenges.text: Our lateral-flow strip for Salmonella gives false positives when the food matrix has high fat content — roughly 1 in 8 results is wrong on meat samples above 15% fat, and two retail clients have already threatened to switch suppliers.
challenges.detail: Our Salmonella strip works well on low-fat matrices — broths, surface swabs, vegetable samples — but on meat samples with fat content above roughly 15%, we see false positives at a rate of about one in eight. We first noticed this pattern about eighteen months ago when two retail food manufacturers, both processing pork and mixed-meat products, started reporting inconsistencies. We have tried adding a higher-concentration blocking buffer to the sample pad and adjusting the surfactant blend in the running buffer, but neither change moved the false-positive rate significantly. We have fat content data and strip result records for around 340 individual samples tested internally, and we can share those with anyone working on the problem. The main constraint is that we cannot change the capture antibody pair without repeating a full validation, which takes three to four months and costs us in the region of 12,000 to 15,000 EUR. We need a fix that sits in the sample preparation or buffer chemistry side. Retaining those two clients is the immediate driver — one has given us until the end of Q3 this year to show measurable improvement.

challenges.text: We produce nitrocellulose membranes in-house on a single coating line, and our batch rejection rate has crept up to 22% this year — we lose about 18,000 EUR worth of membrane per quarter and we still don't know which process variable is driving it.
challenges.detail: We coat nitrocellulose membranes on a single slot-die line that we have operated since 2016. Until 2022 our batch rejection rate was around 8 to 10 percent, which we considered acceptable. Since early 2023 it has climbed to 22 percent, and we have not been able to pin down the cause. Rejected batches fail either on flow-rate uniformity testing or on line-width consistency when we deposit the antibody stripes. We log coating speed, temperature, humidity, nitrocellulose lot number, and backing material lot for every run, and we have that data for the past two years. We have changed backing material supplier once and swapped nitrocellulose lots multiple times without a clear effect. Our quality lead has run basic correlation checks but we do not have strong statistical process control expertise in-house. The financial impact is about 18,000 EUR per quarter in scrapped material alone, not counting the lost production time. We are not in a position to replace the coating line in the near term — capital budget for equipment is limited. A good outcome would be identifying which one or two variables are the likely drivers so we can run targeted experiments to confirm and then control them.

challenges.text: We want to register our Salmonella strip under EU IVDR but the regulatory consultant we hired left the project halfway through and we can't find a replacement who knows IVDR for Class B devices — we've been stuck for four months.
challenges.detail: We started our EU IVDR registration process for the Salmonella strip in mid-2023. The strip falls under Class B under IVDR Annex VIII, which means we need a notified body review. We brought in a regulatory consultant, Dragana Filić, who had worked with us on earlier CE marking for a simpler product. She left the project in November 2023 due to personal reasons and took all the draft technical documentation with her — we have since recovered most files but some sections of the performance evaluation report are incomplete. Since then we have approached four other consultants; none had hands-on IVDR Class B experience, only general medical device background. We have a notified body slot provisionally reserved with a body in Austria for Q4 2024, and if we miss it we will lose the slot and likely face a wait of at least another year. Our internal team can handle the quality system documentation, but the performance evaluation and analytical performance sections require someone who knows the specific IVDR expectations for pathogen detection IVDs. Budget for the consultancy is up to 20,000 EUR. A good outcome is submitting a complete technical file by September 2024.

challenges.text: Farmeri žele upozorenje na mastitis pre nego što se vide simptomi.
challenges.detail: Farmeri koji koriste naš sistem dolaze nam sa jednim glavnim zahtevom: žele da znaju da će krava dobiti mastitis dva do tri dana pre nego što se pojave vidljivi znaci – oticanje vimena, bol pri muži, promena izgleda mleka. Trenutno naša ogrlica meri aktivnost i preživanje, i oba parametra padaju kada krava nije dobro, ali to je nedovoljno specifično – isti pad se dešava i kod hromosti, estrusnog ciklusa i metaboličkih problema. Imamo podatke za oko hiljadu i po krava tokom poslednje dve godine, sa labelong koje su nam davali farmeri i veterinari kada bi dijagnostikovali mastitis. Problem je što je mastitis dosta redak događaj u skupu podataka, pa imamo nebalansiran dataset. Pokušali smo da primenimo jednostavan prag na osnovu pada preživanja, ali dobijamo previše lažnih uzbuna i farmeri počinju da ignorišu obaveštenja. Treba nam bolji model koji uzima u obzir kombinaciju parametara tokom vremena. Nemamo dovoljno internog kapaciteta za ovo – jedan data inženjer ne može sam da radi i na infrastrukturi i na modeliranju. Budžet za saradnju je ograničen, ali smo otvoreni za model deljenja podataka kao deo dogovora. Cilj je smanjiti broj lažnih uzbuna ispod deset posto, a pravi slučajevi da budu uhvaćeni bar u sedamdeset pet posto slučajeva.

challenges.text: We have twelve years of anonymised discharge records from three hospitals — roughly 480,000 patient episodes — but we can't build reliable readmission-risk scores because our data scientists say the ICD-10 codes were entered inconsistently before 2018 and half the comorbidity fields are blank.
challenges.detail: We have discharge records covering twelve years from three hospitals — roughly 480,000 patient episodes in total. The data sits in our MediCore HIS PostgreSQL database and has been anonymised in line with Serbian data protection rules. The idea is to build a readmission-risk scoring tool so ward staff get a flag before they discharge a patient who is likely to return within thirty days. The problem is that ICD-10 codes were entered by whoever was available before 2018, not always a trained coder, and we see the same condition coded four or five different ways across hospitals. On top of that, roughly half the comorbidity fields — things like diabetes status or heart failure stage — are simply blank. We tried a basic logistic regression last year using only the post-2018 records, which gave us about 55,000 cleaner episodes, but the model did not perform well enough for clinical use. We do not have machine-learning expertise in-house; our two data scientists come from a statistics background. We need either a way to recover usable signal from the messy older data or a smarter modelling approach that handles the missingness without inventing data. A good outcome would be a validated scoring tool we can embed in the discharge workflow by the end of next year.

challenges.text: Our telemedicine module sends video consultations over standard internet connections at rural health centres, and call quality collapses whenever bandwidth drops below 2 Mbps — we lose about 30% of scheduled teleconsultations in Bačka Topola and Kanjiža because of this.
challenges.detail: Our TeleKonsult module uses a standard WebRTC implementation for video calls between rural health centres and specialists. In towns with decent fibre or 4G coverage it works acceptably. The issue is in Bačka Topola and Kanjiža, where several health centres are on DSL or shared municipal wireless links that rarely deliver more than 1.5 Mbps reliably. When bandwidth drops below 2 Mbps the call breaks up badly enough that the specialist cannot examine the patient properly, and around 30 percent of scheduled sessions are abandoned or rescheduled. We have tried reducing video resolution and frame rate on our side, but the WebRTC stack we use does not adapt fast enough when the connection degrades mid-call. We have also looked at commercial adaptive-bitrate video SDKs but the licensing costs are not compatible with what our health centre customers can pay. We need an approach — whether that is a different streaming protocol, a smarter codec configuration, or a lightweight relay architecture — that keeps consultations usable down to about 0.8 Mbps. We do not want to rebuild the entire module, just the transport and encoding layer.

challenges.text: The Ministry of Health is requiring us to migrate all patient data to a national FHIR R4 repository by Q3 next year, but our legacy database schema is relational and over 200 custom fields have no direct FHIR equivalent — we estimate 14 months of migration work with our current team of five developers.
challenges.detail: The Ministry of Health has set a Q3 next-year deadline for all patient data to be accessible through a national FHIR R4 repository. Our MediCore HIS stores data in a relational PostgreSQL schema we have been extending since 2006. We have mapped about 60 percent of our fields to standard FHIR resources — Patient, Encounter, Condition, Observation — without much difficulty. The remaining 40 percent, roughly 200 custom fields covering things like Serbian-specific administrative codes, regional health fund billing categories, and some legacy diagnostic fields that have no FHIR equivalent, are the problem. We cannot simply drop those fields because some are legally required for Ministry reporting under separate regulations. We have five developers who can work on this, but they also have to maintain live production systems for six hospitals and cannot go fully dark on everything else. Our internal estimate is 14 months of work, which overshoots the deadline. We have started building a MediMig toolkit to handle the mapping logic, but we need either a faster approach to modelling the non-standard fields as FHIR extensions or an architecture that lets us expose a compliant FHIR endpoint without a full database restructure — essentially a translation layer. Missing the deadline risks our contracts with public institutions.

challenges.text: We sell 18,000 tonnes of bran a year as cheap animal feed; we'd like a higher-value use.
challenges.detail: Every tonne of wheat we mill leaves behind roughly 220 kg of bran, and across a year that adds up to about 18,000 tonnes. Right now we bag it loose and sell it to livestock farms and feed compounders at around 12–14 euros per tonne — barely above the cost of handling and transport. The margins are thin enough that in a bad year this stream is nearly breakeven. We know bran has dietary fibre content that food manufacturers talk about, and we have heard that some mills abroad sell it as a food ingredient at several times our current price. What we do not know is which fractions matter, what processing steps are needed, what food-safety or compositional standards apply, and whether any buyers in our accessible markets would actually pay a premium. We have the raw material sitting here every day; we have a basic quality lab and a NIR analyser. We do not have the knowledge to reformulate it or the contacts in food-ingredient markets. Our budget for this is modest — we can fund a feasibility study and some lab trials, but not a full capital project yet. A useful outcome for us would be a clear picture of one or two realistic uses, the processing steps required, and an honest estimate of whether the numbers work.

challenges.text: Electricity is our second-largest cost and peaks at bad times.
challenges.detail: Electricity is the second-largest line item on our cost sheet, after raw wheat. Our total annual consumption is around 4.2 GWh, and the problem is not just the volume — it is the timing. The roller-mill line, pneumatic conveying, aspiration fans and the bagging equipment all run together, and during morning start-up, typically between 05:30 and 07:30, our demand peak regularly hits 820–850 kW. That peak is what drives our network tariff band upward for the whole billing period. We run continuously six days a week during the main milling season. We have looked at simply staggering start-up sequences, and our production manager Jelena Horvatović has already shaved about 40 kW off the worst spikes manually over the past year, but there is a limit to what scheduling by hand can achieve without disrupting the milling sequence or product quality. We have twelve months of sub-hourly SCADA consumption logs that we can share. We do not have in-house expertise in energy modelling or load optimisation. We are not looking to install solar panels or batteries at this stage — the roof structure and capital budget do not allow it. A practical outcome would be a data-backed recommendation on how to reschedule or shed load during peak windows, quantified savings, and something we could actually implement with our existing SCADA setup.

challenges.text: Our dispenser's acoustic sensor is supposed to detect the click of a pill being taken, but in real home environments — TV on, background noise — it produces a false-positive rate of about 22%, which destroys patient trust and generates useless alerts for caregivers.
challenges.detail: The dispenser is supposed to know when a patient has actually taken a pill by listening for the small mechanical click when a compartment is opened and the rattle of a tablet leaving the tray. In a quiet room it works reasonably well. In a real home with a television running, a radio on in the kitchen, or a grandchild visiting, our current threshold-based acoustic classifier flags false positives about 22% of the time. That means roughly one in five alerts sent to the family app is wrong. Caregivers quickly learn to ignore all alerts, which defeats the whole purpose. We have tried raising and lowering the detection threshold and adding a short time-window filter, but every adjustment that reduces false positives increases false negatives instead. We have logged about 4,200 compartment-open events across our pilot devices, and we have manually labelled about 1,800 of those with ground-truth outcome data. We have the raw audio clips stored. What we need is a way to build a more robust classifier — something that can handle variable background noise without requiring expensive microphone hardware we cannot afford to put in a 90-euro device. We have a budget of roughly 3,000 euros for this work and need a working prototype by the end of Q3 2025.

challenges.text: We interviewed 60 elderly users and found that 40% stop using the app within three weeks because the font sizes and navigation flow do not match the cognitive and motor patterns of people over 70; we need a systematic redesign but our two-person team has no UX research background.
challenges.detail: We interviewed 60 people over the age of 70 during our Subotica and Sombor pilots. Forty percent of them stopped opening the companion app within three weeks of starting. When we asked why, the answers were consistent: text was hard to read even when they zoomed in, the main navigation required remembering which icon meant what, and confirmation dialogs appeared in sequences that confused people who had minor tremor or slower reaction times. We know the problem exists and we have the interview notes and a set of recorded screen-capture sessions showing where users get stuck. What we do not have is anyone on the team with a background in designing for older adults. Our two developers are good at building features quickly but have no training in accessibility research or age-appropriate interaction patterns. We have tried applying standard WCAG guidelines but that alone does not address the cognitive flow issues. We need someone who can look at what we have, run structured usability sessions with real users in the 70-plus age range, and give us a prioritised list of specific changes to make. We have a small budget for this — around 2,500 euros — and the redesign needs to ship before we approach a second distribution partner who has asked to see the app.

challenges.text: A potential distribution partner in Hungary wants exclusivity for two years and our lawyer says the contract draft they sent has clauses that would prevent us from selling through pharmacies in Slovakia and Austria; we need specialised cross-border commercial contract review but cannot afford a full international law firm.
challenges.detail: A distribution company based in Debrecen reached out to us after seeing a short piece about our device in a regional medtech newsletter. They want to be the exclusive channel for PillaBox in Hungary for a two-year period. That is attractive to us because we have no sales presence there. However, the contract draft they sent contains language that our local lawyer interprets as preventing us from entering any arrangement with pharmacy chains or distributors in Slovakia and Austria during the same period. Both of those markets are on our twelve-month roadmap and we have already had preliminary conversations with a pharmacy network in Bratislava. Our lawyer handles general commercial work and is honest that cross-border EU distribution contracts in the medical device space are outside her experience. A full international law firm has quoted us fees we cannot pay at this stage. We need someone who can review the specific clauses, explain clearly what we would and would not be agreeing to, suggest concrete alternative wording that protects our ability to operate in third markets, and ideally help us understand whether there are standard frameworks for this kind of regional exclusivity arrangement in the EU medtech distribution space. We have a deadline: the Debrecen company wants a response within six weeks.

challenges.text: Our fraud detection model flags about 8% of applications as suspicious, but manual review shows that roughly 60% of those flags are false positives — we're turning away good customers and the review team is overwhelmed.
challenges.detail:
Our fraud model was trained on roughly 18 months of data when we first deployed it in 2021. It catches clear-cut fraud well, but it generates a large volume of uncertain flags. Right now about 8% of all incoming applications get flagged — that is around 200–250 applications a month at our current volumes. When our operations team reviews those manually, they approve about 60% of them, meaning the model was wrong more than half the time. Those false positives cost us real customers and they are burying our two-person review team.

We retrained the model once in 2023 with a larger feature set and the false-positive rate dropped slightly but not enough. We suspect the main issue is that our feature engineering does not distinguish well between genuinely suspicious behavioural patterns and the irregular-but-legitimate patterns that are normal for gig workers — which is almost our entire customer base. We have full application data going back to 2019, including the outcome labels from manual review, so the training data is there. We need someone who can help us redesign the feature set and the decision threshold logic. Our constraint is that we cannot reduce true-positive detection — catching actual fraud is non-negotiable for our banking partner. A good outcome would be cutting the false-positive rate to under 20% within six months.

challenges.text: We want to use open banking transaction data to enrich our scoring, but the PSD2 consent flows we've built convert at only 23% — most applicants abandon before granting access.
challenges.detail:
Open banking data would genuinely improve our scoring — we have run internal tests on a small opted-in cohort and the predictive lift is meaningful. The problem is that only about 23% of applicants complete the PSD2 consent flow we built. The rest abandon partway through, usually at the bank-redirect step or when they see the permissions screen.

We have looked at our funnel data in Segment. Drop-off is highest on mobile, among applicants over 45, and among people connecting to smaller regional banks where the redirect UX is poor. We have tried shortening the copy, adding a short explainer video, and making the consent step optional until later in the flow — none of those moved the number by more than two percentage points.

We do not think the product is broken; we think people do not understand what they are consenting to or what they get in return. We need help figuring out whether this is a UX problem, a trust problem, a literacy problem, or some combination. We have session-recording data for around 4,000 abandonment events and we would be willing to do structured interviews with real applicants. Budget for this work is modest — we are not looking for a full agency engagement, more a focused research and redesign sprint. A good outcome is getting conversion above 45% within Q3 2025.

challenges.text: We have three years of repayment data now — roughly 41,000 closed loans — but we still can't quantify how much of the default risk is explained by macroeconomic conditions versus individual borrower behaviour, and the regulator is asking us to separate the two.
challenges.detail:
We now have 41,000 closed loans with full repayment histories, originated between early 2019 and late 2024. That period includes some turbulent macro conditions — inflation spikes, currency moves, changes in gig-platform activity during and after the pandemic period. Our observed default rate has moved around quite a bit year to year, and internally we argue about how much of that is our scoring getting better or worse versus the economy just being harder or easier for our borrowers.

The National Bank of Serbia has asked us to demonstrate, in our next supervisory submission, that our risk models account for macroeconomic sensitivity and that we can separate systematic risk from idiosyncratic borrower risk. We do not currently have a formal way to do that. Our risk team has basic econometrics skills but no one has built a two-component model of this kind before.

We have the full loan-level dataset, monthly macro series (inflation, unemployment, RSD exchange rates, a gig-employment proxy index we built ourselves), and borrower-level panel data across repeat customers. We need a methodology that is explainable to a non-specialist regulator — complex black-box approaches will not work here. Deadline is tied to our supervisory review, which is scheduled for autumn 2025. A good outcome is a documented, defensible decomposition of default variance that we can present in a written report.

challenges.text: Our whey-pea protein blend clumps in humid warehouse conditions above 60% RH, causing roughly 8% of sachets to fail the dissolution test that our German client requires, and we are getting chargebacks on about 2,000 units per month.
challenges.detail: Our protein blend is roughly 60% whey concentrate and 40% pea protein isolate, and the pea fraction is hygroscopic. When the warehouse sits above 60% relative humidity — which happens from May to September in our building — the powder picks up enough moisture to form soft agglomerates before filling. Those agglomerates end up inside sealed sachets and then fail the 30-second cold-water dissolution test that our German client, SupraNutrition GmbH, runs on every incoming pallet. We are seeing about 8% of units fail, which works out to roughly 2,000 rejected sachets per month and a chargeback that costs us around 1,400 euros monthly. We have tried reducing the fill-to-seal time window, adding a small amount of silicon dioxide as a flow agent up to 0.5% by weight, and running a portable dehumidifier in the blending room, but none of those steps brought rejection below 4%. We have aw meter readings and humidity logs going back eighteen months. We need the rejection rate below 1.5% before the next summer season without adding equipment that costs more than 8,000 euros.

challenges.text: We need to design a sachet packaging that keeps oxygen transmission below 0.5 cc/m²/day but every laminate supplier we talk to quotes a 12-month MOQ that we can't fund at our current volume of 60,000 sachets per month.
challenges.detail: Our current sachet laminate is a three-layer PET/ALU/PE structure that gives acceptable oxygen barrier performance at around 0.8 cc per square metre per day, which is above the 0.5 cc threshold written into our contract with Alpenfit Handels GmbH starting with their autumn 2025 order. To get below 0.5 cc we need either a thicker aluminium layer or a high-barrier metallised film alternative. Every laminate converter we have approached — four in Serbia, two in Hungary, one in Austria — requires a minimum order quantity that covers twelve months of supply, which at our current 60,000-sachet monthly volume means committing to stock we cannot finance. We have no long-term credit line and our working capital covers about six weeks of material at a time. Ideally we would find either a laminate structure we can source in smaller rolls with the right barrier spec, or a way to demonstrate to our bank that a co-development arrangement with a research partner reduces the technical risk enough to support a short facility. The deadline is an Alpenfit audit scheduled for October 2025.

challenges.text: We claim 27 g of protein per 32 g sachet on the label, but our NIR inline measurement drifts by ±2 g over a production run because the instrument was calibrated only on pure whey and our blend ratio changes per client recipe.
challenges.detail: We label each sachet as containing 27 g of protein in a 32 g total fill weight. Our NIR instrument was calibrated by the previous owner using a standard curve built on pure whey concentrate. Because different clients require different whey-to-pea ratios — ranging from 50:50 to 80:20 — the same NIR reading can correspond to protein values that differ by up to 2 g depending on which blend is running. Across a single 10,000-unit production run we have measured drift of ±2 g from start to finish even on a fixed recipe, probably because the NIR surface reading is sensitive to particle size changes as the batch compacts. We catch this with end-of-run Kjeldahl checks but those results come back the next day, so mislabelled stock sometimes gets sealed and palletised before we know there is a problem. We have all the raw spectra from the last fourteen months stored on a laptop, plus Kjeldahl reference values for about 120 batches. We need either a better calibration model built on our actual blend range or a different measurement approach that can give a reliable number in real time, so we can adjust fill weight during the run rather than after.

challenges.text: Our drying chambers run for 21 days per batch and energy costs for those chambers rose 38% last year; we have no real-time monitoring inside the chamber, just one thermostat and one humidity sensor per room, so we can't tell where we are wasting energy.
challenges.detail: Each of our drying chambers runs a 21-day cycle before a batch is ready to move to packaging. We have eight chambers in total. Last year our electricity bill for those rooms alone went up 38% compared to the year before, which is a serious number when you are talking about a process that runs continuously around the clock. The problem is that we cannot see what is actually happening inside the chamber in real time. Every room has one thermostat fixed to the wall and one humidity sensor, both feeding a single analogue display outside the door. If the temperature or humidity is uneven — warmer near the ceiling, drier near the fans — we do not know. Operators check the display twice per shift and write it in a logbook. That is all the data we have. We suspect the fans are cycling more than they need to, or running at full speed when partial speed would hold the same conditions, but we cannot prove it. We want to install some kind of sensor network inside the chambers that gives us spatial data and could eventually feed into smarter fan or heating control. We have a rough budget of around 25,000 euros for a pilot on two chambers. A good result would be documented energy savings and a map of where the inefficiencies actually are.

challenges.text: We found Listeria monocytogenes in environmental swabs in two of our slicing rooms three times in the last 18 months; we have intensified cleaning but can't identify the persistent harborage point and this is threatening our BRCGS Grade A certificate.
challenges.detail: We have had three positive environmental swab results for Listeria monocytogenes in our slicing rooms over the last 18 months. Each time we responded with a deep clean, retrained the staff on hygiene protocol and re-swabbed until we got negatives. But the positives keep coming back in the same general area — the slicing room on the east side of the packaging hall. We have not had a positive in product itself, but that is not something we can rely on continuing. Our BRCGS Grade A certificate is under review because of the pattern of environmental positives, and we know the next audit will ask hard questions. We have looked at the floor drains, the conveyor belt joints, the blade storage racks and the condensation pattern on the ceiling, but we do not have a method for tracing which specific surface or void is the persistent source. We would like help designing a systematic sampling plan that uses enough swab points and a logical sequence to triangulate the harborage. We also want to understand whether there are surface materials or drain designs we should be replacing. The certificate renewal deadline is in ten months.

challenges.text: The collagen casings we import from Austria jumped 60% in price since 2022; we want to know if locally sourced natural casings from Serbian slaughterhouses can meet our standardised calibre tolerances at scale.
challenges.detail: Until about two years ago we sourced all our collagen casings from a supplier in Graz. The price per metre has gone up roughly 60% since 2022, partly due to raw material costs and partly exchange rate movement. For kulen in particular, casing quality directly affects how the product looks on the shelf and how evenly it dries — calibre consistency matters a lot. We have heard from other producers that natural casings from pig and sheep intestines processed at Serbian slaughterhouses can be competitive on price, but we do not know whether local processors can deliver the calibre tolerances we need at the volumes we use, which run to around 40,000 metres per year. We have made one informal visit to a slaughterhouse near Sombor but did not get usable technical data from it. What we need is a structured comparison: collect samples from two or three local casing suppliers, test them against our current collagen casing on calibre uniformity, burst pressure and surface consistency, and give us a clear yes or no on whether local natural casings are viable for standardised production. We are open to adjusting our stuffing equipment if the modification cost is reasonable.
